Source and destination IP: unchanged end to end (barring NAT).
Source and destination MAC: rewritten at every hop. Each router strips the old Ethernet header and builds a new one for the next link.
detail:
Layer 2 addressing is local to a single link and Layer 3 addressing is end to end. This one fact explains most of what routers actually do.
How it works
  • The router de-encapsulates and re-encapsulates: It strips the incoming Ethernet frame, examines the IP destination, consults its routing table, then builds a brand new frame with its own MAC as source and the next hop's MAC as destination.
  • ARP is per-link: Each router must ARP for the next hop on its own segment. A host never learns the MAC of a remote server — it learns the MAC of its default gateway and sends everything off-subnet there.
  • This is why MACs are not routable: MAC addresses are flat, with no hierarchy to summarize. They cannot be aggregated, so they cannot scale beyond a broadcast domain.
  • Only the TTL and checksum change in the IP header: The router decrements TTL by one and recomputes the header checksum. The addresses inside stay put unless a NAT device deliberately rewrites them.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why arp -a on a client shows the gateway, not the remote web server
  • Reading a traceroute and understanding each hop is a separate Layer 2 delivery
  • Understanding why changing a switch does not change IP reachability, but changing a router does
exam: CompTIA tests this as a scenario: 'a packet travels from a workstation to a server across two routers — which addresses change?' The correct answer is MAC addresses change at every hop, IP addresses do not. The distractor reverses it, or claims both change. If NAT is explicitly mentioned in the stem, then the source IP does change at the NAT boundary.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::02 OSI Model & Encapsulation
front: Map the four-layer TCP/IP (DoD) model onto the seven OSI layers.
answer:
Application = OSI 7 + 6 + 5
Transport (Host-to-Host) = OSI 4
Internet = OSI 3
Network Access (Link) = OSI 2 + 1
detail:
The model the internet was actually built on. It collapses OSI's top three layers into one and its bottom two into one, because real implementations never separated them.
How it works
  • Application absorbs 7, 6 and 5: HTTP does its own formatting and session handling, so there was never a reason to split them. This is why OSI Layers 5 and 6 feel thin — TCP/IP simply does not have them.
  • Transport and Internet map one to one: TCP/IP's Transport layer is OSI Layer 4 exactly, and its Internet layer is OSI Layer 3 exactly. These two are the unambiguous part of the mapping.
  • Network Access absorbs 2 and 1: Ethernet defines both the framing and the electrical signalling in one standard, so TCP/IP treats them as a single layer.
  • OSI survives because it is better for troubleshooting: TCP/IP describes what runs; OSI describes where a fault sits. That is why both are taught and why the exam expects the mapping between them.
Where you see it
  • Reading RFCs and vendor docs, which use TCP/IP terminology
  • Translating a colleague's 'internet layer problem' into 'Layer 3 problem'
  • Understanding why some sources say there are four layers and others say seven
exam: The exam asks for the mapping directly. The two facts to lock in: the OSI Application, Presentation and Session layers all collapse into the TCP/IP Application layer, and OSI Data Link and Physical collapse into Network Access. Watch for a five-layer variant in answer choices that splits Network Access back into Data Link and Physical — that is the 'TCP/IP updated' model, not the classic four-layer DoD model.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::02 OSI Model & Encapsulation
front: Which OSI layer does each of these operate at: hub, switch, router, multilayer switch, wireless AP, stateful firewall, NGFW, load balancer, NIC?
answer:
L1: hub, repeater, media converter, cable
L2: switch, bridge, NIC, wireless access point
L3: router; multilayer/Layer 3 switch does L2 and L3
L3–L4: traditional stateful firewall, Layer 4 load balancer
L7: NGFW, proxy, WAF, Layer 7 load balancer
detail:
Devices are classified by the deepest header they read to make a forwarding decision. Nothing else about the box matters for this question.
How it works
  • The rule is 'what does it read to decide?': A hub reads nothing and copies bits, so Layer 1. A switch reads the destination MAC, so Layer 2. A router reads the destination IP, so Layer 3. Apply this test and you never have to memorize a list.
  • An access point is a Layer 2 device: It bridges wireless clients onto the wired LAN using MAC addresses. It does have a radio, which is Layer 1, but its forwarding decision is Layer 2.
  • Multilayer switches straddle two layers: A Layer 3 switch switches within a VLAN using MACs and routes between VLANs using SVIs (switched virtual interfaces). Both statements are true simultaneously.
  • Load balancers exist at two tiers: A Layer 4 load balancer distributes TCP connections by IP and port and cannot see the URL. A Layer 7 load balancer terminates the connection and routes on hostname, path or cookie.
Where you see it
  • Specifying hardware: a plain switch cannot do inter-VLAN routing, a Layer 3 switch can
  • Choosing a firewall when the requirement is 'block a named application regardless of port'
  • Explaining to a colleague why a hub is a security problem — it copies every frame everywhere
exam: This is one of the most heavily tested items in Domain 1. The two reliable traps: a wireless access point is Layer 2, not Layer 1, and a hub is Layer 1, not Layer 2. Expect a scenario asking which device to deploy where the requirement wording hides the layer: 'must inspect application content' → Layer 7, 'must separate broadcast domains' → Layer 3.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::02 OSI Model & Encapsulation
front: Match each troubleshooting symptom to its OSI layer.
answer:
No link light / CRC errors → L1
Port up but no MAC learned, VLAN mismatch, STP loop → L2
Can ping locally but not off-subnet, wrong gateway, bad route → L3
Ping works but the service is unreachable, port blocked by a firewall → L4
Certificate error, cipher mismatch → L6
Site loads but returns an application error, DNS name fails → L7
detail:
A structured way to convert a user complaint into a place to look. The point of the model in daily work is exactly this triage step.
How it works
  • 'Ping works but the app does not' is the key discriminator: ICMP proves Layers 1 through 3 are healthy end to end. If the application still fails, the fault is at Layer 4 or above — usually a blocked port or a stopped service.
  • 'Can ping by IP but not by name' is always DNS: Name resolution is a Layer 7 service. Connectivity is fine; the lookup is not.
  • Local works, remote does not, points at Layer 3: That pattern means framing and the local segment are healthy, so suspect the default gateway, the subnet mask, or a missing route.
  • Bottom-up unless you have a reason: Start at Layer 1 because it is fastest to check and most often wrong. Use top-down only when the symptom is clearly application specific, such as one website failing while everything else works.
Where you see it
  • Triaging a helpdesk ticket before touching anything
  • Deciding whether to send a technician to the desk or check a firewall rule
  • Justifying the escalation path in an incident write-up
exam: CompTIA writes many Domain 5 questions as 'which layer is the problem most likely at?' Learn the two flagship pairs: ping succeeds but the application fails → Layer 4 or above (never Layer 1), and ping by IP succeeds but by name fails → DNS, Layer 7. The common trap answer is Layer 1 for a symptom where the link is demonstrably up.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::02 OSI Model & Encapsulation
front: Describe the TCP three-way handshake and what each message accomplishes.
answer:
SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK
1. Client sends SYN with its initial sequence number.
2. Server replies SYN-ACK: acknowledges the client's ISN and sends its own.
3. Client sends ACK acknowledging the server's ISN. The connection is now established.
detail:
The setup exchange that makes TCP connection-oriented. It exists so both ends agree on starting sequence numbers and confirm the other side is actually there and willing before any data is sent.
How it works
  • It synchronizes sequence numbers in both directions: TCP is full duplex, so each direction needs its own sequence numbering. Three messages is the minimum to establish and acknowledge both — the server's ACK and SYN are combined into one packet.
  • It proves bidirectional reachability: After the handshake, both ends know traffic flows in both directions. A one-way path failure shows up as a connection that never completes rather than as silent data loss.
  • A half-open connection is a SYN with no completing ACK: A SYN flood attack exploits this by sending many SYNs and never replying, exhausting the server's table of pending connections.
  • Teardown is a separate four-way exchange: Closing uses FIN → ACK → FIN → ACK, because each direction must be closed independently. An abrupt RST tears the connection down immediately instead.
Where you see it
  • Reading a Wireshark capture where the handshake never completes — a firewall is dropping SYN
  • Recognizing a SYN flood in connection-state counters
  • Explaining why UDP-based services respond faster on first contact
exam: Sequence order is the direct recall item, and CompTIA does test the exact flag names. The trap answers are a two-way handshake, a four-way handshake, or listing the flags as SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK. Know also that close is four-way (FIN/ACK, FIN/ACK) — that contrast appears as a distractor. A scenario describing 'many half-open connections' is a SYN flood.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::02 OSI Model & Encapsulation
front: TCP vs UDP — what does TCP add, and when is UDP the correct choice?
answer:
TCP adds: connection setup (handshake), acknowledgements and retransmission, sequencing and reordering, flow control via windowing. Header 20 bytes minimum.
UDP adds: ports and a checksum. Header 8 bytes. No setup, no ACKs, no ordering.
Choose UDP when late data is worthless — real-time voice and video, or when one small query and one reply is the whole transaction.
detail:
The two transport protocols represent one design tradeoff: reliability bought with latency and overhead, versus speed bought by accepting loss.
How it works
  • Retransmission is useless for real time: In a VoIP call, a resent audio packet arrives after the moment it was needed. Dropping it and moving on produces a small glitch; waiting for it produces a stall. That is why voice is UDP.
  • Handshake cost dominates tiny transactions: A DNS lookup is one small request and one small answer. A three-way handshake would triple the packets for no gain, so DNS queries use UDP and fall back to TCP only for large responses and zone transfers.
  • UDP is the only sensible choice for broadcast and multicast: TCP requires a point-to-point connection with a single peer. One-to-many delivery cannot acknowledge from every receiver, so DHCP discovery and streaming multicast use UDP.
  • Reliability can be rebuilt above UDP: TFTP runs over UDP but implements its own lock-step block acknowledgement. QUIC does the same at much greater sophistication. 'UDP' does not have to mean 'unreliable application'.
Where you see it
  • VoIP, video conferencing and live streaming media
  • DNS queries, DHCP, TFTP, SNMP, syslog and NTP
  • File transfers, email and web pages, which all need TCP's guarantees
exam: The exam almost never asks 'what is TCP' — it asks you to pick one for a scenario. The reliable rule: if the stem says 'real time', 'low latency', 'voice', 'video' or 'streaming', answer UDP; if it says 'guaranteed delivery', 'reliable' or 'file integrity', answer TCP. The standard distractor is calling UDP 'connectionless and unreliable' as if that disqualifies it — for voice, connectionless is the feature.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::02 OSI Model & Encapsulation
front: What is MTU, what is the Ethernet default, and what is a jumbo frame?
answer:
MTU = the largest Layer 3 payload a single frame can carry. Ethernet default is 1500 bytes.
A jumbo frame carries an MTU of up to about 9000 bytes. It must be enabled consistently on every device in the path.
detail:
MTU is the ceiling on how much data fits in one frame. It exists because framing, error checking and fair media sharing all get worse as frames get arbitrarily large.
How it works
  • MTU measures the payload, not the whole frame: A 1500-byte MTU plus a 14-byte Ethernet header and 4-byte FCS gives a 1518-byte frame on the wire, or 1522 with an 802.1Q VLAN tag. Vendors sometimes quote frame size instead of MTU, which is a common source of confusion.
  • Bigger frames mean less overhead per byte: One 9000-byte frame carries the same headers as one 1500-byte frame. For sustained bulk transfer that is a measurable efficiency and CPU-interrupt gain, which is why storage networks use it.
  • Every device in the path must agree: If one switch in the middle is still at 1500, oversized frames are simply dropped. Jumbo frames are an all-or-nothing setting for a given path.
  • Tunnels reduce the usable MTU: A VPN or GRE tunnel adds its own header inside the 1500 bytes, so the inner payload must shrink. This is why VPN users see MTU problems that non-VPN users on the same network do not.
Where you see it
  • iSCSI and NFS storage networks, where jumbo frames are standard practice
  • Data centre east-west traffic between hypervisors
  • Setting the tunnel MTU on a site-to-site VPN so large packets survive
exam: Memorize 1500 default, ~9000 jumbo. The exam's favourite framing is a performance scenario: 'a storage network is underperforming, what setting improves throughput?' → enable jumbo frames. The trap is enabling it on only one device — the correct answer always mentions consistency end to end.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::02 OSI Model & Encapsulation
front: What symptoms does an MTU mismatch produce, and why does blocking ICMP make it worse?
answer:
Symptom: small pings and logins succeed, but large transfers hang or time out — traffic is black-holed, not obviously broken.
Cause: Path MTU Discovery relies on the router returning an ICMP Destination Unreachable / Fragmentation Needed message. If a firewall blocks ICMP, the sender never learns to send smaller packets and keeps retransmitting the same oversized ones.
detail:
The classic silent network fault. Everything appears reachable while any transfer of real size fails, because the failure signal itself is being filtered.
How it works
  • The Don't Fragment bit forces the failure: Modern TCP stacks set DF on. A router that cannot forward the packet must drop it and send back ICMP type 3 code 4. With DF clear, the packet would be fragmented instead — slower, but working.
  • Blocking all ICMP breaks PMTUD: Administrators block ICMP to 'harden' a firewall and inadvertently kill the only feedback channel. This is the standard argument against blanket ICMP denial.
  • Test it with a large, do-not-fragment ping: ping -f -l 1472 8.8.8.8 on Windows or ping -M do -s 1472 8.8.8.8 on Linux. 1472 bytes of payload plus 8 bytes of ICMP header plus 20 bytes of IP header equals 1500. If that fails but a small ping succeeds, the path MTU is below 1500.
  • The fix is either raise the MTU or lower it consistently: Correct the MTU on the offending link, permit the necessary ICMP types, or clamp TCP MSS at the tunnel endpoint so hosts negotiate a smaller segment size in the first place.
Where you see it
  • VPN users who can log in but cannot load large pages or download files
  • A new tunnel where SSH connects and then freezes as soon as output scrolls
  • Justifying why 'block all ICMP' is a bad firewall policy
exam: The scenario wording is the giveaway: 'small packets get through, large ones do not' or 'users can ping the server but file transfers fail'. The answer is MTU mismatch or a PMTUD failure. Distractors will offer a duplex mismatch or a bad cable, both of which would degrade small traffic too. If the stem mentions a VPN or a tunnel, MTU is almost always the intended answer.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: The four DHCP messages in order, and what each one is?
answer: DORA — Discover (client asks) → Offer (server proposes an address) → Request (client accepts one offer) → Acknowledge (server commits the lease). Server UDP 67, client UDP 68.
detail:
The exchange that gets a host an IP address, mask, gateway and DNS servers without anyone typing them. It has to work before the client has any address at all, which is why every step is built on broadcast.
How it works
  • Discover is a shout into the dark: The client has no address, so it sends from source 0.0.0.0:68 to destination 255.255.255.255:67. It cannot address a specific server because it does not yet know one exists. The message carries the client's MAC in the chaddr field, which is how the server knows who to answer.
  • Offer is a proposal, not an assignment: A server picks a free address from the scope, marks it tentatively reserved, and offers it along with the mask, gateway, DNS and lease length. If two servers hear the Discover, the client gets two Offers and normally takes the first one to arrive.
  • Request is also broadcast, deliberately: The client broadcasts its acceptance naming the chosen server in the server-identifier option. Every other server that made an offer sees that broadcast, learns it was not chosen, and releases the address it had held back.
  • Acknowledge is the binding: The ACK commits the lease in the server database and repeats the full option set. Only after the ACK does the client configure the interface. A well-behaved client then ARPs for its own new address to confirm nobody else is using it, and sends a DHCPDECLINE if someone answers.
  • The negative case is DHCPNAK: If the client asks to renew an address that is no longer valid — a laptop that moved to a different subnet — the server replies DHCPNAK and the client starts over at Discover.
Where you see it
  • Every laptop and phone joining a wired or wireless network
  • Reading a packet capture to prove whether the client asked and got no answer, or never asked at all
  • Explaining why a client that gets 169.254.x.x never received an Offer
exam: DORA is memorized as a unit and the exam tests order directly, so know that Request comes after Offer and not before. The most common trap is a scenario where the client sends Discover and gets nothing back — that points at a relay or VLAN problem, not at a broken client. Distractors reverse the ports: the server listens on 67 and the client on 68, not the other way around.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: Which parts of DHCP are broadcast and which can be unicast?
answer: Discover and Request are always broadcast. Offer and ACK are broadcast or unicast depending on the client's broadcast flag. Renewals are unicast straight to the leasing server.
detail:
Broadcast is required only while the client has no usable address. Once it has one, DHCP stops broadcasting, and that difference explains why renewals work across a relay while initial requests need help.
How it works
  • The client has no address, so it must broadcast: A device with source 0.0.0.0 cannot be replied to by unicast in the normal way, so the initial exchange floods the broadcast domain. This is the reason DHCP is a per-VLAN problem: a broadcast stops at the router.
  • The broadcast flag decides the reply: The DHCP header has a one-bit broadcast flag. If the client sets it, the server must send the Offer and ACK to 255.255.255.255. If not, the server may unicast to the offered address by writing an ARP entry for the client's MAC directly.
  • Renewal is unicast and needs no relay: At T1 the client already has a working address, so it sends a DHCPREQUEST directly to the server's IP. That packet is routed like any other traffic, which is why renewals succeed even if the helper-address configuration is broken.
  • Rebinding goes back to broadcast: If the unicast renewal is not answered by T2, the client broadcasts a request to any server that will listen. This is the fallback that lets a second DHCP server on the segment keep the client alive.
Where you see it
  • Deciding whether a DHCP fault is a relay problem or a server problem
  • Explaining a network where clients keep existing leases but no new client can get one
  • Filtering a capture on UDP 67 and 68 to see which direction is failing
exam: The exam uses this as the mechanism behind the relay question. If existing clients work but new clients fail, the broadcast half is broken — suspect the missing ip helper-address — because renewals are unicast and route normally. Do not answer that DHCP is 'all broadcast'; the renewal being unicast is the load-bearing detail.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: Define scope, pool, exclusion and reservation.
answer: Scope: the range of addresses configured for one subnet. Pool: the addresses in the scope actually free to hand out. Exclusion: addresses inside the scope the server must never assign. Reservation: a specific address always given to one specific MAC.
detail:
These four terms describe the same address range from four angles. The exam separates them precisely, and each solves a different real problem.
How it works
  • The scope defines one subnet: A scope carries the range, the mask, the lease length and the options for one broadcast domain. A DHCP server serving five VLANs has five scopes, and it chooses between them using the relay agent's address.
  • Exclusions protect statically addressed devices: Routers, switches, printers and servers are often given static addresses at the low end of the subnet. You exclude that range so the server never leases an address that is already hard-coded on a device, which would cause a duplicate-address conflict.
  • A reservation is DHCP, not static: The device still runs DORA and still receives the full option set, but the server always answers with the same address for that MAC. Change the DNS server in the scope and every reserved device picks it up on renewal, which a static configuration will not do.
  • Reservation versus static assignment: A static address is typed into the device and known only to the device. A reservation lives in the server database, is centrally visible, and follows the machine when policy changes. If the DHCP server dies, statically addressed devices survive and reserved devices only survive until their lease expires.
Where you see it
  • Reserving addresses for printers so their queues never break
  • Excluding 10.1.1.1–10.1.1.20 where the gateway and switches live
  • Auditing an IPAM system for addresses assigned twice
exam: CompTIA tests these as vocabulary matching, so the definitions must be crisp. The classic scenario is a printer whose address keeps changing — the correct fix is a reservation, and the distractor is 'assign it statically', which works but loses central management and is not the DHCP answer. Another common one: a device with a static address stops responding after a new client joins, which means the static address was never excluded from the scope.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What does lease time control, and how do you choose it?
answer: How long a client may keep an address before it must renew. Short leases (hours) for high-turnover guest and wireless networks; long leases (days) for stable wired offices.
detail:
The lease is a timer on the server's promise. It exists so that addresses handed to devices that never come back eventually return to the pool.
How it works
  • The address is not freed when the device leaves: A laptop that is shut down or carried out of the building does not tell the server anything. The address stays bound until the lease expires. On a network where hundreds of devices come and go daily, long leases mean the pool fills with ghosts.
  • Short leases cost traffic and server load: Halving the lease doubles the renewal rate. On a very large network that is real load on the DHCP server, and a client that cannot reach the server has a much shorter window before it loses its address entirely.
  • Long leases make changes slow to land: Option changes — a new DNS server, a new gateway — reach a client only at renewal. With an eight-day lease the first renewal attempt is at four days, so a change can take days to propagate to every device.
  • Infinite leases are almost always a mistake: An unlimited lease turns DHCP into permanent assignment with no reclamation and no visibility into what is still alive. Use reservations instead when a device must keep one address.
Where you see it
  • Conference-centre and guest Wi-Fi where a two- or four-hour lease is normal
  • Corporate wired desktops on an eight-day lease
  • Shortening the lease as an emergency response to scope exhaustion
exam: The exam almost always frames this as a guest or public-Wi-Fi capacity scenario: many transient devices, pool running dry, what do you change? The answer is shorten the lease time. Expanding the scope is a valid distractor and is right when the subnet genuinely has more simultaneous devices than addresses, so read for whether the devices are transient or concurrent.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: At what points in a lease does a client try to renew?
answer: T1 = 50% of the lease — unicast renewal to the server that issued it. T2 = 87.5% (7/8) — broadcast rebinding to any DHCP server. At 100% the client gives up the address.
detail:
Renewal is staged so that a client gets several chances to keep its address before losing it. Each stage widens who the client is willing to talk to.
How it works
  • T1 at half the lease — RENEWING: The client unicasts a DHCPREQUEST to its own server. Nothing changes for the user; on a healthy network this succeeds and the lease clock resets. A four-day lease means the first renewal attempt is at two days.
  • T2 at seven-eighths — REBINDING: If the original server has not answered by 87.5 percent, the client stops trusting it and broadcasts a request that any server on the segment may answer. This is the mechanism that lets a redundant DHCP server take over a lease.
  • Expiry means release the interface: At 100 percent with no answer, the client must stop using the address, tear down the binding and start again at DHCPDISCOVER. If nothing answers that either, it self-assigns an APIPA address and loses off-link connectivity.
  • The client keeps working the whole time: Between T1 and expiry the address is still valid and traffic still flows. A DHCP server outage is therefore invisible for roughly half a lease period, which is why a dead DHCP server is often noticed hours or days later.
Where you see it
  • Judging how long you can leave a DHCP server down before users notice
  • Explaining why clients survived an overnight DHCP outage but failed the next morning
  • Sizing lease length against a planned maintenance window
exam: The two numbers 50% and 87.5% are directly tested, and 87.5 is the one people miss — distractors offer 75% or 90%. Know the names too: T1 is renewing (unicast to the original server) and T2 is rebinding (broadcast to any server). A scenario stating that clients kept working for two days after the server failed is testing whether you know renewal starts at half the lease, not at expiry.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is a DHCP relay agent and why is ip helper-address needed?
answer: DHCP Discover is a broadcast and routers do not forward broadcasts. The relay agent catches it, rewrites it as a unicast to the DHCP server, and stamps the interface's address into the giaddr field so the server knows which scope to use.
detail:
One central DHCP server can serve dozens of subnets it is not attached to. The relay agent on each router interface is what bridges the broadcast-only start of the conversation onto a routed network.
How it works
  • The router is the relay, configured per interface: On Cisco the command is ip helper-address 10.10.10.5 applied to the SVI or interface facing the clients — the interface where the broadcast arrives, not the one facing the server. Missing that placement is the most common configuration error.
  • giaddr picks the scope: The relay writes its own interface IP into the gateway-address field. The server compares giaddr to its scopes and answers from the one matching that subnet, then sends the reply back to giaddr for the relay to deliver locally. Without giaddr the server would have no way to know which of its ten scopes applied.
  • ip helper-address forwards more than DHCP: By default the Cisco command relays a set of UDP broadcasts, including BOOTP/DHCP 67 and 68, TFTP 69, DNS 53, time 37, TACACS 49 and NetBIOS 137/138. That can be narrowed with no ip forward-protocol udp for the services you do not want relayed.
  • Option 82 adds the client's location: Relay agent information option 82 records which switch port and VLAN the request came from. A server can use it to assign addresses by physical port, and DHCP snooping uses it for validation.
Where you see it
  • A single Windows or Infoblox DHCP server serving every VLAN in a building
  • Configuring a new VLAN and finding clients get no address until the helper is added
  • Layer 3 switches with an SVI per VLAN and a helper-address on each
exam: This is one of the most reliably tested DHCP items. The scenario is always: a new VLAN was created, clients on it get APIPA, clients on other VLANs are fine. The answer is a missing ip helper-address / DHCP relay on that VLAN's gateway interface. Distractors offer 'add a second DHCP server' or 'the scope is exhausted' — both are wrong when only the new subnet is affected.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: Which DHCP option numbers should you recognize?
answer: 3 default gateway · 6 DNS servers · 15 domain name · 42 NTP servers · 51 lease time · 66 TFTP server name · 67 boot filename
detail:
The address and mask come from the scope itself. Everything else a client needs arrives as numbered options in the Offer and ACK, and a handful of those numbers are worth knowing by sight.
How it works
  • 3, 6 and 15 build a usable host: Option 3 is the default gateway, so the client can leave its subnet. Option 6 is the list of DNS resolvers, in order. Option 15 is the DNS domain suffix appended to unqualified names, so that ping server1 becomes server1.corp.local.
  • 42 keeps clocks correct: Option 42 hands out NTP server addresses. Without it, clients rely on hard-coded public time sources or drift, which breaks Kerberos authentication and certificate validation.
  • 66 and 67 are the boot pair: Option 66 gives the TFTP server's name or address and option 67 gives the filename to fetch. Together they drive PXE network boot and VoIP phone provisioning: the phone gets an address, learns where its configuration lives, and downloads it. Some Cisco phone deployments use option 150 instead, which carries a list of TFTP server IPs.
  • Options ride in every Offer and ACK: They are not a separate exchange. Change option 6 in the scope and clients pick up the new DNS servers on their next renewal, which is why option changes are slow to propagate on long leases.
Where you see it
  • Provisioning IP phones and thin clients that boot from the network
  • Pushing a new internal DNS server to a whole site by editing one scope
  • Setting the search suffix so short hostnames resolve
exam: Expect a straight number-to-function match, most often option 3 = gateway and option 6 = DNS, which are easily swapped in distractors. The scenario version is a PXE or VoIP boot failure where devices get an address but never load their image — that points at options 66 and 67. If clients can ping by IP but not by short name, suspect option 15.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is scope exhaustion, and what address does a client take when DHCP fails?
answer: Exhaustion means every address in the pool is leased, so new clients get no Offer. A Windows or macOS client that gets no reply self-assigns APIPA: 169.254.x.x /16, which reaches only the local link.
detail:
APIPA is the visible symptom of a failed DHCP exchange. It is not a fix, it is the client telling you nobody answered.
How it works
  • What APIPA actually gives you: The client picks a random address in 169.254.1.0 through 169.254.254.255, ARPs to check nothing else has it, and configures the interface with a /16 mask, no default gateway and no DNS. Two APIPA hosts on the same switch can ping each other; nothing can leave the subnet.
  • Exhaustion is one cause, not the only one: The same 169.254 symptom appears when the DHCP server is down, when the relay is missing, when the client is in the wrong VLAN, or when a switch port is not forwarding. Confirm exhaustion by looking at the server's lease list, not by looking at the client.
  • Diagnosing it on the server: Free-address counters at zero, and a lease table full of entries for devices that are not on site, are the signature. Common causes are transient devices with long leases, an undersized subnet, and rogue or duplicated MACs.
  • The three fixes, in order of speed: Shorten the lease time to reclaim ghosts quickly, expand the scope or add a second subnet if concurrent devices genuinely exceed the pool, and hunt for a client or attacker consuming addresses in bulk.
Where you see it
  • Guest Wi-Fi at an event where the /24 runs out mid-morning
  • Reading ipconfig /all and seeing 169.254 with 'Autoconfiguration Enabled'
  • Deciding between a shorter lease and a bigger subnet
exam: The 169.254 address is one of the highest-frequency exam signals: whenever you see it, the answer involves DHCP not being reachable. Do not pick 'the DNS server is misconfigured' — the client never got that far. Know that APIPA is link-local only with no gateway, and that 169.254 is IPv4's equivalent of IPv6's fe80::/10 link-local range.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is a rogue DHCP server and how do you stop it?
answer: An unauthorized DHCP server — usually a consumer router plugged in backwards — that answers Discover messages with wrong addresses or a wrong gateway. Stop it with DHCP snooping, which permits server replies only on trusted ports.
detail:
DHCP has no authentication. The client takes the first Offer it receives, so whoever answers fastest wins, whether or not they are supposed to be there.
How it works
  • The usual accident: Somebody plugs a home wireless router into a wall jack with the LAN port instead of the WAN port. It hands out 192.168.1.x addresses with itself as the gateway. Clients that get an offer from it lose access to everything, and which clients are affected looks random because it depends on timing.
  • The malicious version is a man in the middle: An attacker who controls DHCP controls the default gateway and the DNS servers. Traffic is routed through the attacker's box before reaching the real gateway, so it can be read or modified. This is the setup step for on-path attacks.
  • DHCP snooping is the switch-level fix: The switch classifies ports as trusted or untrusted. On an untrusted port it drops server-sourced messages — Offer, ACK and NAK — so only uplinks toward the real server can carry them. It also builds a binding table of MAC, IP, VLAN and port.
  • The binding table feeds other protections: Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard both read the snooping table, so enabling snooping is the prerequisite for defending against ARP poisoning and spoofed source addresses.
Where you see it
  • A branch office where a few users get 192.168.0.x while everyone else is correct
  • Enabling DHCP snooping on all access VLANs with only uplinks trusted
  • Tracing a rogue by matching the offered gateway address back to a switch port
exam: The exam signature is 'some users receive incorrect IP addressing while others are fine' — that is a rogue DHCP server, and the mitigation is DHCP snooping. Do not choose port security, which filters MAC addresses and does nothing about DHCP payloads, and do not choose DAI, which depends on snooping and defends ARP rather than DHCP.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: Walk a DNS lookup from a client typing a name to getting an address.
answer: Stub resolver → local cache/hosts → recursive resolver → root (referral to .com) → TLD (referral to the domain's NS) → authoritative server (the answer) → cached and returned. UDP 53.
detail:
DNS is a distributed tree walked from the top down. No single server knows every name; each level only knows who to ask next.
How it works
  • The client barely participates: The stub resolver on the host sends one recursive query to the configured resolver and waits for a final answer. It checks its own cache and the hosts file first. Everything else happens on the resolver's behalf.
  • The root knows only the TLDs: There are 13 root server identities, each anycast to hundreds of physical machines worldwide. A root server does not know www.example.com. It replies with a referral naming the servers for .com.
  • The TLD knows only the delegation: The .com servers reply with another referral: the NS records for example.com and their glue A records. Still no answer, just a smaller haystack.
  • The authoritative server holds the actual record: The name server for the zone returns the A record with an authoritative-answer flag set. The resolver caches it for the record's TTL and hands it to the client, so the next user asking is answered from cache in a millisecond.
  • Ports and sizes: Queries and answers use UDP 53. TCP 53 is used for zone transfers and for any response too large for a single UDP datagram, historically 512 bytes before EDNS0 raised the limit.
Where you see it
  • Reading dig +trace example.com, which prints exactly this walk
  • Explaining why the first lookup of a name is slow and the rest are instant
  • Diagnosing whether a resolution failure is local cache, resolver, or authoritative
exam: The exam tests the order of the hierarchy — root, then TLD, then authoritative — and the fact that the root does not hold the answer. A common distractor claims the root server returns the IP address. Also expect TCP 53 for zone transfers versus UDP 53 for queries; a firewall blocking TCP 53 breaks replication while ordinary lookups still work.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: Recursive versus iterative DNS queries?
answer: Recursive: 'get me the answer' — the resolver does all the work and returns a final result. Iterative: 'tell me what you know' — each server returns a referral to the next server down.
detail:
The same lookup contains both kinds. Which one is in play depends on who is asking whom.
How it works
  • The client always asks recursively: A workstation sends one query with the recursion-desired bit set and expects either an answer or an error. It has no code to follow referrals and does not want to make ten round trips.
  • The resolver always queries iteratively: Root, TLD and authoritative servers refuse recursion. They answer with what they hold: a referral or a final record. The recursive resolver is the component that walks that chain, which is why it is also called a recursive server.
  • Recursion costs the resolver, not the client: One recursive query can trigger several iterative round trips. That is also why an open resolver — one that accepts recursive queries from the internet — is dangerous: it can be used to amplify reflection attacks.
  • Authoritative and recursive are different roles: An authoritative server publishes zones it owns. A recursive resolver answers for anything by asking around and caching. Running both on one box is possible but is generally considered bad practice.
Where you see it
  • A workstation pointed at 10.1.1.10, which recurses out to the internet on its behalf
  • Disabling recursion on a public-facing authoritative name server
  • Interpreting the RD and RA flags in a DNS packet capture
exam: This is a definition-contrast question. The trap is assuming the client does the walking — it does not. If a question describes a server that 'returns a referral to another name server', that is iterative. If it describes one that 'queries other servers on the client's behalf and returns the final answer', that is recursive.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is a DNS record's TTL, and why lower it before a migration?
answer: TTL is how many seconds a resolver may cache a record before asking again. Lower it well before a planned IP change so caches expire quickly, then raise it once the change has settled.
detail:
Caching is what makes DNS fast, and TTL is the only lever you have over it. The cost of caching is that a change is not visible until every cache expires.
How it works
  • You cannot flush the internet's caches: Once a resolver has cached a record it will use it for the full TTL no matter what you do to your authoritative server. If the TTL is 86400 seconds, some users will keep hitting the old address for a full day after the cutover.
  • Lower the TTL at least one old TTL in advance: Drop it to 300 seconds a day before a migration with a 24-hour TTL. Caches holding the old long TTL must expire on their own schedule first, then they re-fetch and learn the short one. Lowering it an hour before cutover accomplishes nothing.
  • Raise it again afterwards: Short TTLs multiply query volume against your authoritative servers and make you more exposed to a resolution outage. Once the new address is proven, put the TTL back to something like an hour or a day.
  • Negative answers are cached too: An NXDOMAIN is cached according to the minimum field in the zone's SOA record. Creating a record that somebody just failed to resolve does not fix them instantly.
Where you see it
  • Moving a public website to a new hosting provider or a new IP
  • Failing a service over to a DR site by changing DNS
  • Explaining why half the users see the new server and half still see the old one
exam: The exam scenario is always a migration where 'some users still reach the old server'. The correct action is that the TTL should have been lowered in advance; the correct immediate action is to wait for the TTL to expire. Flushing the local client cache with ipconfig /flushdns fixes one machine and is a common partial-credit distractor.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: Forwarders versus root hints?
answer: Forwarder: send anything you cannot answer to a specific upstream resolver. Root hints: walk the DNS tree yourself starting from the root servers.
detail:
Both are answers to the same question — what does an internal DNS server do with a name it does not own? They differ in who does the work and where the traffic goes.
How it works
  • A forwarder centralizes and simplifies: Branch servers forward to a hub server or to a provider such as an ISP resolver or a filtering service. Only the forwarder needs outbound DNS access, the shared cache gets warmer, and content filtering or logging can be applied in one place.
  • Root hints make the server independent: A named.ca or cache.dns file lists the 13 root servers. The server then performs the full iterative walk itself for every uncached name. It needs unrestricted outbound UDP/TCP 53 and it builds its own cache from scratch.
  • Conditional forwarding is the middle ground: You can forward only a specific domain to a specific server — typical after a merger, or for an internal domain hosted by a partner — while everything else goes to the normal path.
  • Failure behaviour differs: If the forwarder is down, a server configured to fall back to root hints keeps resolving. A server configured to forward only will fail all external resolution. That fallback setting is often the difference between a partial and a total outage.
Where you see it
  • Branch DNS servers forwarding to a central filtered resolver
  • Conditional forwarding of a partner's internal zone across a site-to-site VPN
  • Recovering resolution after an upstream resolver outage
exam: Expect a definition contrast. The trap is thinking a forwarder is a type of DNS record — it is a server setting. If a scenario wants DNS filtering, logging or a single egress point, the answer is a forwarder; if it says the server must resolve without depending on any external resolver, the answer is root hints.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: A, AAAA and CNAME — what does each map?
answer: A: hostname → IPv4 address. AAAA: hostname → IPv6 address. CNAME: hostname → another hostname (an alias).
detail:
These are the records that actually get a client to a host. A and AAAA end the lookup; a CNAME sends the resolver around again.
How it works
  • A and AAAA can coexist for one name: A dual-stack host publishes both. The client asks for whichever families it supports and typically prefers IPv6 when a AAAA exists. Publishing a AAAA for a host whose IPv6 path is broken causes slow or failing connections for dual-stack clients.
  • A CNAME costs an extra lookup: The resolver receives 'www is really webhost.cdn.example.net' and must then resolve that name. Chains of CNAMEs are legal but each hop adds latency.
  • CNAME restrictions are real and tested: A name with a CNAME cannot have any other record of the same name, so a CNAME cannot exist at the zone apex — example.com itself must be an A or AAAA record, or a provider-specific alias record. MX and NS records must not point at a CNAME.
  • Where the alias earns its place: One CNAME to a provider's hostname means the provider can change addresses freely and you never touch your zone. That is exactly how CDN and SaaS onboarding works.
Where you see it
  • Pointing www at a CDN hostname rather than at an IP you must maintain
  • Adding a AAAA record when enabling IPv6 on a public service
  • Giving one server several service names — intranet, wiki, helpdesk — with CNAMEs
exam: CompTIA tests these as straight matching, and AAAA = IPv6 is the one people fumble under time pressure. The scenario version: a hostname must follow a cloud provider's changing addresses, so the answer is CNAME. Watch for the apex trap — a question asking why example.com cannot be a CNAME is testing that a CNAME cannot coexist with the zone's SOA and NS records.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: MX and TXT records — what is each for?
answer: MX: names the mail servers for a domain, with a preference value where lower is preferred. TXT: arbitrary text, used in practice for SPF, DKIM and DMARC and for domain-ownership proof.
detail:
Both are about mail, in different ways. MX says where mail goes; TXT says which senders are legitimate.
How it works
  • MX points at a name, never an IP: The record holds a preference number and a hostname, and that hostname must resolve via A or AAAA — it must not be a CNAME. A sending server sorts by preference, tries 10 before 20, and uses higher values as backup relays.
  • SPF lives in a TXT record: An SPF record lists the IP addresses and hostnames allowed to send mail for the domain, ending in a policy such as -all. A receiving server checks the sending IP against it. There is no dedicated SPF record type in current use; it is a TXT record.
  • DKIM and DMARC are also TXT: DKIM publishes the public key used to verify signatures on outgoing mail, at a selector name. DMARC publishes what a receiver should do when SPF or DKIM fails — none, quarantine or reject — plus where to send reports.
  • TXT is also the ownership handshake: Cloud providers routinely ask you to publish a random string as a TXT record to prove you control the domain before they will issue a certificate or host a service for it.
Where you see it
  • Cutting mail over to a hosted provider by changing MX records
  • Fixing outbound mail landing in spam by publishing correct SPF and DKIM
  • Proving domain ownership to a certificate authority or cloud tenant
exam: MX and TXT show up together because the exam likes mail scenarios. If legitimate outbound mail is being rejected or marked as spam, the answer is a missing or incorrect TXT record holding SPF/DKIM/DMARC — not a missing MX, which would stop inbound mail entirely. Remember that on MX preference, the lower number wins.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: NS and SOA records — what does each define?
answer: NS: which name servers are authoritative for a zone — this is what delegation is made of. SOA: the zone's start-of-authority record, holding the primary server, admin contact, serial number and the refresh, retry, expire and minimum timers.
detail:
These two records describe the zone itself rather than any host in it. Every zone has exactly one SOA and at least one NS.
How it works
  • NS records perform delegation: The .com servers hold NS records for example.com pointing at its name servers, and the zone itself repeats them. That parent-side NS set is what makes the referral chain work. Registrar changes to name servers are edits to the parent's NS records.
  • The SOA serial drives replication: Secondary servers periodically ask the primary for the SOA and compare serial numbers. A higher serial means the zone changed and triggers a transfer. Forgetting to increment the serial after editing a zone file is the classic reason a change never reaches the secondaries.
  • The SOA timers control secondary behaviour: Refresh is how often a secondary checks, retry is how soon it tries again after a failed check, and expire is how long it keeps serving stale data before it stops answering at all. Minimum is the negative-caching TTL for NXDOMAIN answers.
  • Zone transfers move the records: A full transfer is AXFR and an incremental one is IXFR, both over TCP 53. Transfers should be restricted to known secondaries, since an open transfer hands an attacker a complete inventory of your hosts.
Where you see it
  • Delegating a subdomain to a different team's name servers
  • Troubleshooting a secondary DNS server still serving yesterday's records
  • Restricting AXFR so the zone cannot be enumerated from the internet
exam: Expect the serial-number scenario: a record was edited on the primary but the secondary still returns the old value, and the answer is that the SOA serial was not incremented. Also know that NS is the record that delegates. A distractor sometimes claims the SOA lists all name servers — it names only the primary; NS records list them all.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is a PTR record and what is a reverse zone?
answer: A PTR maps an IP address back to a name. It lives in a reverse zone under in-addr.arpa for IPv4 or ip6.arpa for IPv6, not in the normal forward zone.
detail:
Forward DNS answers 'what address is this name?' Reverse DNS answers the opposite question, and it is a separate zone that must be maintained separately.
How it works
  • The address is reversed to build the name: 10.1.2.3 is queried as 3.2.1.10.in-addr.arpa. Reversing the octets puts the most general part first, which is what lets the hierarchy delegate reverse zones the same way it delegates forward ones.
  • Forward and reverse are not linked: Creating an A record does not create a PTR. Many DHCP and DDNS setups create both automatically, but on manually managed zones the reverse record is routinely forgotten, which is why reverse lookups fail while everything else works.
  • Mail servers care: Receiving mail servers commonly check that the sending IP has a PTR and that the PTR name forward-resolves back to that IP. A missing or generic PTR is a frequent reason outbound mail is rejected or scored as spam. Only the address block's owner — usually the ISP — can set it.
  • Logging and tooling care too: nslookup 10.1.2.3, traceroute output, firewall logs and monitoring dashboards all try reverse lookups so humans can read them. Missing PTRs make traces slow and logs unreadable.
Where you see it
  • Getting the ISP to set a PTR for an on-premises mail server's public IP
  • Reading a traceroute where hops resolve to router names
  • Building the reverse zone for an internal /16 so log entries show hostnames
exam: The exam asks 'which record type resolves an IP address to a hostname' — the answer is PTR, and the distractor is A or CNAME. The scenario version is outbound mail being rejected by a recipient's server despite valid SPF, which points to a missing reverse DNS/PTR record. Know the zone names in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa by sight.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is an SRV record for?
answer: It publishes which host and which port provide a named service, plus priority and weight. Format: _service._proto.domain → priority weight port target.
detail:
A and CNAME records tell you where a host is. SRV tells you where a service is, including the port, so clients can find infrastructure without it being hard-coded.
How it works
  • The name encodes the service: _ldap._tcp.corp.example.com or _sip._udp.example.com. A client that wants LDAP over TCP queries that exact name rather than guessing at a hostname convention.
  • Priority and weight give failover and load sharing: Clients use the lowest priority value first, exactly like MX. Among equal priorities, weight distributes traffic proportionally. This gives you client-side failover with no load balancer involved.
  • Active Directory depends on it entirely: Domain controllers register SRV records for LDAP, Kerberos and the global catalog. A workstation joins and locates a DC by SRV lookup. If those records are missing or the client points at a non-AD DNS server, domain login fails even though the network is fine.
  • SIP and XMPP use it the same way: A VoIP phone finds its registrar and proxy through SRV, which is why moving a SIP server can be a DNS change instead of a reconfiguration of every handset.
Where you see it
  • Domain-join and logon failures traced to missing AD SRV records
  • VoIP handsets locating a SIP proxy after a server move
  • Publishing a service on a non-standard port without telling every client
exam: SRV is tested as 'which record identifies the host and port of a service'. Only SRV carries a port number, which is the discriminator against A, CNAME and TXT. The scenario is usually Active Directory: clients cannot find a domain controller, which means DNS — and specifically the SRV records — not connectivity.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is split-horizon (split-brain) DNS?
answer: Serving different answers for the same name depending on where the query came from — internal clients get the private address, external clients get the public one.
detail:
One name, two audiences. It exists so that a service can have a single memorable name whether you are on the LAN or on the internet.
How it works
  • Two zones for the same domain: The internal DNS server holds a zone for example.com answering intranet.example.com with 10.1.5.20. The public authoritative servers hold their own example.com answering the same name with 203.0.113.20. Neither knows about the other's contents.
  • It avoids hairpinning: Without it, an internal user resolving the public address sends traffic out to the firewall and back in, which many firewalls handle badly and which wastes the internet link. Resolving to the private address keeps the traffic on the LAN.
  • It hides the internal map: External queries never reveal internal hostnames or RFC 1918 addressing. Publishing internal records to the world is a genuine reconnaissance gift to an attacker.
  • The failure mode is drift between the two: A record added to one side and not the other produces the classic 'it works from home but not in the office' complaint, or vice versa. Both zones must be maintained together.
Where you see it
  • A VPN-less office where an intranet name must resolve to a private IP inside and a public IP outside
  • Preventing internal traffic to a public web service from hairpinning through the edge firewall
  • Diagnosing a name that works on the guest Wi-Fi but not on the corporate VLAN
exam: The exam presents it as a scenario: the same hostname resolves to different IPs for internal and external users, and it asks what that is called or why it is done. Answer split-horizon DNS, and the reason is keeping internal traffic internal and internal names private. Do not confuse it with round robin, which returns different addresses to everyone regardless of source.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: DNSSEC versus DoH versus DoT — what does each actually protect?
answer: DNSSEC: signs records so answers can be proven authentic and unmodified — integrity, not encryption. DoT: DNS over TLS on TCP 853. DoH: DNS over HTTPS on TCP 443. The last two give confidentiality of the query, not proof of the answer.
detail:
Two separate problems with plain DNS: anybody can forge an answer, and anybody can read the question. DNSSEC fixes the first. DoH and DoT fix the second. They are complementary, not alternatives.
How it works
  • DNSSEC signs, it does not hide: RRSIG holds the signature over a record set, DNSKEY publishes the zone's keys, and DS in the parent fingerprints the child's key, chaining trust up to the signed root. NSEC/NSEC3 proves a name genuinely does not exist, which stops forged NXDOMAIN. Queries and answers remain plaintext, so an observer still sees every name you looked up.
  • What DNSSEC defeats: Cache poisoning and spoofed responses: an attacker injecting a false address into a resolver's cache cannot produce a valid signature, so a validating resolver discards the answer. The operational cost is that signatures expire and keys must be rolled — a zone with expired RRSIGs becomes unresolvable for validating resolvers.
  • DoT is encrypted and manageable: A dedicated port means a firewall can see DNS-over-TLS, permit it only to approved resolvers, or block it and force clients back to the internal server. Administrators generally prefer it for that visibility.
  • DoH is encrypted and hard to control: It rides inside ordinary HTTPS on 443, indistinguishable from web browsing. A browser configured for DoH bypasses corporate DNS filtering, logging and split-horizon answers, which is why managed devices normally have browser DoH disabled by policy.
  • Neither encrypted transport validates the record: They protect the channel to the resolver. A DoH or DoT resolver can still return a wrong answer; it just does so privately. Only DNSSEC proves the record came from the zone owner.
Where you see it
  • Signing a public zone so answers cannot be forged
  • Blocking or allowing TCP 853 at the perimeter as a deliberate policy
  • Disabling browser-level DoH by GPO so DNS filtering still works
exam: The single most tested fact is that DNSSEC gives integrity and authentication but not confidentiality; the distractor is 'DNSSEC encrypts DNS queries'. Know the ports cold: DoT = 853, DoH = 443. If the question is about preventing cache poisoning or spoofed responses, answer DNSSEC; if it is about hiding lookups from an observer or about DNS traffic that cannot easily be blocked, answer DoH/DoT.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is the hosts file and where does it sit in the lookup order?
answer: A local static name-to-IP text file, consulted before any DNS server is queried. Windows: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts. Linux/macOS: /etc/hosts.
detail:
The hosts file predates DNS and still overrides it. That makes it both a useful test tool and a favourite hiding place for malware.
How it works
  • The resolution order on a typical host: The stub resolver checks its own in-memory cache, then the hosts file, then the configured DNS servers in order. A hosts entry therefore wins over anything DNS says, and no TTL applies to it — it is permanent until edited.
  • It is a legitimate testing tool: Before cutting a name over to a new server you can point one workstation at the new IP with a hosts entry and validate the application end to end without touching public DNS.
  • It is a classic malware and persistence trick: Adding an entry that maps a bank or antivirus update domain to an attacker's address redirects the user with no DNS involvement at all. If one machine resolves a name differently from every other machine, check the hosts file first.
  • Stale entries cause maddening faults: A hosts entry left behind after a test keeps working until the real server moves, then that one machine breaks and DNS looks innocent because nslookup queries the server directly and returns the correct answer.
Where you see it
  • Testing a migration on one workstation before changing DNS
  • Investigating a single PC that resolves a name differently from everyone else
  • Explaining why ping and nslookup disagree about an address
exam: The tested subtlety is that nslookup and dig bypass the hosts file because they talk to the DNS server directly, while ping and browsers use the resolver and honour it. A scenario where nslookup returns the correct address but the application still connects to the wrong host is pointing at the hosts file. It is also the answer to 'one user is redirected to a malicious site but DNS is clean'.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is NTP and how does it work?
answer: Network Time Protocol, UDP 123. Clients exchange timestamps with servers, measure round-trip delay, and slew the local clock gradually toward UTC — typically to within a few milliseconds.
detail:
Every device's clock drifts. NTP is the service that keeps a whole network agreeing on what time it is, which turns out to be a prerequisite for security and for troubleshooting.
How it works
  • It corrects for network delay: Each exchange records four timestamps: when the client sent, when the server received, when the server replied, and when the client received. From those it computes the offset and the round-trip delay, so the answer is not just skewed by however long the packet took.
  • It steers rather than jumps: Small errors are corrected by slewing — speeding up or slowing down the clock until it converges — because a clock that jumps backwards breaks databases, log ordering and file timestamps. A very large offset causes a step, and many clients refuse to step at all beyond a threshold such as 1000 seconds.
  • Everything is UTC internally: NTP distributes UTC. Time zones and daylight saving are applied locally by the operating system. A device showing the wrong local time with correct UTC is a time-zone configuration problem, not an NTP problem.
  • Clients get servers from DHCP or configuration: DHCP option 42 can hand out NTP servers. In an Active Directory domain the PDC emulator is normally the internal time source and members sync up the domain hierarchy.
Where you see it
  • Pointing every switch, router and server at two or three internal NTP servers
  • Fixing certificate validation errors caused by a clock that is days out
  • Making logs from a firewall and a server line up during an incident
exam: Know UDP 123 and know that NTP distributes UTC, not local time. The commonest exam framing is indirect: a scenario where authentication fails or logs cannot be correlated, and the root cause is time. Do not pick 'the certificate expired' when the scenario says the device clock is wrong.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What does NTP stratum mean?
answer: Distance in hops from the reference clock. Stratum 0 is the reference source itself (atomic clock, GPS receiver). Stratum 1 is a server directly attached to one. Each layer down adds one. 16 means unsynchronized.
detail:
Stratum is a measure of how far removed a time source is from a real physical clock. Lower is generally better, but it is a distance metric, not a guarantee of accuracy.
How it works
  • Stratum 0 is hardware, not a server you query: It is the caesium clock, the GPS-disciplined oscillator or the radio receiver. It has no network interface in the NTP sense. Only stratum 1 servers, physically wired to it, are reachable.
  • Each hop adds a stratum and some error: A stratum 2 server syncs from a stratum 1, a stratum 3 from a stratum 2, and so on to a maximum of 15. Error accumulates slowly, so a stratum 3 or 4 internal server is entirely adequate for a business network.
  • 16 is the 'do not trust me' value: A server that has not achieved synchronization advertises stratum 16, and clients ignore it. A freshly booted NTP server sits at 16 for a few minutes while it converges — that is normal and not a fault.
  • Design implication: A typical enterprise has two or three internal servers at stratum 2 or 3 syncing to external stratum 1 or 2 sources, and every other device syncing from those. That keeps outbound NTP traffic small and keeps internal time consistent even if the internet link drops.
Where you see it
  • A core router with a GPS antenna acting as the site's stratum 1 source
  • Reading show ntp status and seeing stratum 16 on a device that never synchronized
  • Designing a two-tier internal time hierarchy for a multi-site network
exam: The exam wants stratum 0 = the reference clock itself and stratum 1 = the server attached to it. The frequent error is calling the first NTP server stratum 0. Also remember that a higher stratum number is further from the source, so if a question asks which server is most accurate, pick the lowest number that is not 16.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What breaks when clocks are out of sync?
answer: Kerberos authentication (default tolerance is about 5 minutes), certificate validation (not-before / not-after windows), log correlation, scheduled jobs, MFA token codes and backup consistency.
detail:
Time is a silent dependency. Nothing announces itself as a time failure; it shows up as authentication errors, TLS errors and logs that make no sense.
How it works
  • Kerberos rejects stale tickets by design: Timestamps inside Kerberos tickets are what prevent replay attacks. If the client and the KDC disagree by more than the allowed skew — five minutes by default in Active Directory — the ticket is refused and the user sees a logon failure, not a clock warning.
  • Certificates are valid only inside a time window: A device whose clock is a year fast will reject a perfectly good certificate as expired. A device whose clock is wildly slow rejects it as not yet valid. Browser and VPN certificate errors on one machine while everyone else is fine almost always mean that machine's clock.
  • Correlation across devices becomes impossible: An incident investigation lines up firewall, proxy, server and endpoint logs on timestamp. If one device is eleven minutes off, its events appear in the wrong order and the causal chain is invisible. This is why every device points at the same NTP source.
  • Time-based one-time passwords fail: TOTP codes are derived from the current 30-second window. A phone or server whose clock has drifted produces codes the other side will not accept.
Where you see it
  • A user who cannot log in to the domain after their laptop's CMOS battery died
  • A VPN client failing certificate validation with the right certificate installed
  • An incident timeline that cannot be reconstructed because two devices disagree
exam: This is CompTIA's favourite indirect question. The scenario gives you an authentication or certificate failure plus a hint that a device was recently reimaged, had its battery replaced, or lost NTP — and the answer is clock skew / time synchronization. Memorize the Kerberos five-minute default; it appears verbatim in distractors.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What are PTP and NTS, and when would you use each?
answer: PTP (Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588) gives sub-microsecond accuracy using hardware timestamping — used where NTP's milliseconds are not good enough. NTS (Network Time Security) adds authentication and integrity to NTP using TLS.
detail:
NTP is accurate enough for logs and Kerberos and is trivially spoofable. These two protocols fix, respectively, its precision limit and its lack of security.
How it works
  • PTP timestamps in the hardware: Switches and NICs that support 1588 stamp packets at the physical layer, so the variable delay of the operating system's software stack is removed from the measurement. A grandmaster clock distributes time, and boundary or transparent clocks in between correct for their own transit delay.
  • PTP needs network support to hit its numbers: Running PTP across switches that do not participate reduces it to something not much better than NTP, because the queuing delay it was designed to eliminate creeps back in. It is normally deployed on a purpose-built LAN segment.
  • PTP's markets are specific: Financial trading with regulatory timestamp requirements, broadcast video where frames must align, industrial control and power-grid protection, and mobile base stations that need phase alignment.
  • NTS secures NTP without changing its accuracy: It uses a TLS-based key exchange, NTS-KE on TCP 4460, to establish keys, then adds authentication to ordinary NTP packets on UDP 123. It stops an attacker from feeding a client a false time, which would otherwise be an easy path to forcing acceptance of expired certificates.
Where you see it
  • A trading floor or broadcast facility that must timestamp to sub-microsecond
  • Cellular and industrial networks requiring phase-aligned clocks
  • Hardening public time sources so a client cannot be fed a forged time
exam: The comparison to have ready is accuracy: NTP is milliseconds, PTP is sub-microsecond, and PTP requires hardware support in the network. If a scenario names financial, broadcast or industrial timing requirements, the answer is PTP. NTS is the answer when the question is about securing or authenticating time, and DNSSEC-style reasoning applies — it authenticates, it does not make time more accurate.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: Site-to-site versus client-to-site VPN?
answer: Site-to-site: an always-on tunnel between two gateways that joins two networks; users run no software and do not know it exists. Client-to-site (remote access): software on one device builds a tunnel to a concentrator to put that one device on the network.
detail:
Both carry private traffic over an untrusted network. They differ in what is being connected — networks or individual devices — and therefore in where the tunnel terminates.
How it works
  • Site-to-site terminates on the routers or firewalls: The tunnel endpoints are the two edge devices. Routes on each side point the other site's subnets at the tunnel. Any host on either side reaches the other transparently, and the tunnel stays up whether or not anyone is using it.
  • Client-to-site terminates on the endpoint: The laptop runs a client, authenticates as a user — often with MFA — and is given an address from a VPN pool. Only that device is on the network, and only while the client is connected.
  • They scale differently: Site-to-site is a small number of long-lived tunnels, sized by aggregate bandwidth between offices. Remote access is sized by the number of concurrent users and their traffic, and the concentrator becomes a capacity and availability chokepoint.
  • Authentication differs accordingly: Site-to-site normally authenticates with a pre-shared key or a device certificate configured once. Remote access authenticates a human, which means directory integration, MFA and posture checks.
  • A hub-and-spoke choice appears at scale: Many branches meshed directly is n-squared tunnels; hub-and-spoke through the datacentre is simpler but backhauls branch-to-branch traffic. Dynamic multipoint designs exist to get both.
Where you see it
  • A branch office permanently joined to headquarters over the internet
  • A home worker connecting a laptop to the corporate network
  • Connecting an on-premises datacentre to a cloud VPC
exam: This is a straight contrast question and the discriminator is who runs software. If the scenario says users at a branch need transparent access with nothing installed, it is site-to-site. If it says individual remote employees, it is client-to-site. A distractor sometimes describes a site-to-site tunnel but asks about per-user MFA, which belongs to remote access.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What are a clientless VPN and an always-on VPN?
answer: Clientless: remote access through a browser over TLS with no software installed — usually limited to web applications and a few published tools. Always-on: the tunnel establishes automatically at boot or logon and stays up, so the device is never off-policy.
detail:
Both are variations on remote access that trade convenience against control in opposite directions.
How it works
  • Clientless is a portal, not a network connection: The user authenticates to an SSL/TLS portal on TCP 443 and is presented with links to internal web apps, and sometimes RDP or SSH proxied through the browser. The device does not get an IP on the corporate network, so arbitrary applications will not work.
  • Clientless suits unmanaged devices: Contractors, partners and personal machines can be given access to a specific set of applications without installing anything or trusting the endpoint with full network reachability. The reduced access is the feature, not a limitation.
  • Always-on removes the user's choice: The connection is established by the machine, often before logon, so patching, group policy, endpoint management and DNS filtering apply continuously. Users cannot forget to connect, and cannot deliberately disconnect to avoid inspection.
  • Always-on needs a captive-portal exception: Hotel and airport Wi-Fi require a browser sign-in before any traffic passes. An always-on client has to detect that and allow limited access until the portal is satisfied, or the machine simply has no connectivity.
Where you see it
  • Giving an auditor access to one internal web application from their own laptop
  • A corporate laptop fleet that is under management the moment it powers on
  • Enforcing web filtering on remote workers who cannot turn the tunnel off
exam: Clientless is tested as the answer to 'access without installing software', with the key qualifier that it is browser-based and application-limited. Always-on is the answer to 'ensure remote devices are always subject to corporate security policy'. The distractor for always-on is split tunnelling, which is about what traffic goes down the tunnel, not about whether the tunnel exists.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: Split tunnel versus full tunnel VPN?
answer: Full tunnel: all client traffic goes through the VPN, including internet traffic. Split tunnel: only traffic for corporate subnets goes down the tunnel; everything else goes direct to the internet.
detail:
The choice is where the remote user's internet traffic exits. It is a direct trade of security inspection against bandwidth and user experience.
How it works
  • Full tunnel gives you inspection and enforcement: Every packet passes the corporate proxy, firewall and DLP. Web filtering, logging and threat detection apply exactly as they do in the office, and the user's public IP is the company's.
  • Full tunnel costs concentrator bandwidth: Video calls, streaming, large cloud downloads and software updates all traverse the VPN head-end twice. On a large remote workforce this is the constraint that forces the decision, and it is why so many organizations split-tunnel Teams and Zoom traffic explicitly.
  • Split tunnel is fast and less controlled: Internet-bound traffic goes straight out of the home connection. Latency to SaaS is lower and the concentrator carries only corporate traffic, but that traffic is unfiltered and unlogged unless a cloud-delivered security service picks it up.
  • The classic split-tunnel risk: A device is simultaneously on the corporate network and on an untrusted local network. A compromise arriving from the local side has a live path into the corporate side, which is why regulated environments often mandate full tunnel.
  • DNS behaviour is the practical detail: Split-tunnel clients must be told which DNS queries go to the internal resolver and which go out locally, or internal names fail to resolve while everything else works.
Where you see it
  • Excluding a video-conferencing service from the tunnel to save head-end bandwidth
  • Mandating full tunnel for a regulated environment where all traffic must be logged
  • Troubleshooting a remote user who can reach file servers but not the intranet website
exam: The exam frames this as a bandwidth-versus-security tradeoff. If the scenario complains that the VPN concentrator is saturated or that video calls are poor for remote users, the answer is split tunnelling. If it says all user web traffic must be inspected and logged, the answer is full tunnel. Watch for the security-risk phrasing — split tunnel is the one that bypasses corporate inspection.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: IPsec transport mode versus tunnel mode?
answer: Transport: protects only the payload; the original IP header is kept. Host-to-host. Tunnel: encrypts the entire original packet and wraps it in a new IP header. Gateway-to-gateway, and what site-to-site VPNs use.
detail:
The difference is whether IPsec protects a packet in place or puts the whole packet inside a new one. That determines what an observer can see and what endpoints can be used.
How it works
  • Transport mode leaves the addressing visible: The original source and destination IP addresses stay in the clear because the header is reused. Anyone watching sees who is talking to whom and only the payload is protected. It is used between two hosts that both run IPsec themselves.
  • Tunnel mode hides the inner addresses: The complete original packet, header included, becomes the payload of a new packet addressed from gateway to gateway. Internal RFC 1918 addressing never appears on the internet, which is exactly what a site-to-site VPN needs.
  • Tunnel mode costs overhead and MTU: The new IP header plus the ESP header and trailer add roughly 50 to 60 bytes. That pushes packets over the path MTU, which is why VPN links so often need MSS clamping or a lowered tunnel MTU to stop large transfers from stalling.
  • Choosing between them: Two gateways joining two networks require tunnel mode. Two servers securing traffic directly between themselves, with no networks behind them, can use transport mode and save the overhead.
Where you see it
