  • A site-to-site VPN between two firewalls, which is always tunnel mode
  • L2TP over IPsec, where IPsec transport mode protects the L2TP tunnel
  • Diagnosing a VPN where small pings succeed and large file transfers hang — an MTU problem
exam: The tested discriminator is the new IP header: tunnel mode has one, transport mode does not. Site-to-site VPN always maps to tunnel mode on the exam. The MTU angle also appears: if a scenario says the tunnel comes up and ping works but applications fail on large transfers, the answer is fragmentation/MTU, not a broken tunnel.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: IPsec AH versus ESP — what does each provide?
answer: AH (protocol 51): authentication and integrity of the whole packet, no encryption. ESP (protocol 50): encryption plus authentication and integrity of the payload. Real deployments use ESP.
detail:
IPsec has two protection headers. One proves the packet was not altered, the other also makes it unreadable. Only one of them survives NAT.
How it works
  • AH signs the immutable parts of the IP header too: That is its distinguishing feature and also its fatal flaw. Because the source and destination addresses are covered by the integrity check, any NAT device that rewrites them invalidates the packet. AH cannot traverse NAT, which rules it out on almost every internet path.
  • ESP protects the payload and can be NAT-traversed: ESP's integrity check covers the ESP header and payload, not the outer IP header, so address translation does not break it. NAT-Traversal encapsulates ESP in UDP 4500 when a NAT device is detected between the peers.
  • Confidentiality only comes from ESP: AH provides no encryption at all. If a question asks which IPsec component encrypts, there is exactly one right answer. ESP can technically be used with null encryption for integrity only, but that is a niche configuration.
  • The ports and protocol numbers are tested: IKE negotiates on UDP 500, NAT-T uses UDP 4500, ESP is IP protocol 50 and AH is IP protocol 51. ESP and AH are not TCP or UDP; they are protocols in their own right, which is why some firewalls need an explicit rule for them.
Where you see it
  • Configuring a site-to-site VPN's phase 2 proposal with ESP and AES
  • Opening UDP 500 and 4500 plus IP protocol 50 on an edge firewall
  • Explaining why a tunnel works from the datacentre but not from behind a NAT router
exam: The single most reliable fact here is AH does not encrypt. Expect a question asking which provides confidentiality — the answer is ESP. The second favourite is NAT: AH breaks through NAT, ESP with NAT-T (UDP 4500) does not. Distractors reverse the protocol numbers, so remember ESP is 50 and AH is 51.

front: What does IKE do in an IPsec VPN?
answer: Internet Key Exchange, UDP 500, negotiates the tunnel: it authenticates the peers, agrees the ciphers, and derives the keys. Phase 1 builds a secure management channel; Phase 2 builds the actual data SAs.
detail:
IPsec's ESP header carries protected data but says nothing about how the two ends agreed on keys. IKE is the negotiation that has to happen first.
How it works
  • Phase 1 authenticates the peers: Using a pre-shared key or certificates, the two gateways prove identity and perform a Diffie-Hellman exchange to create a shared secret over an untrusted path. The result is an ISAKMP/IKE security association — an encrypted channel used only for further negotiation. IKEv1 does this in main mode (six messages) or aggressive mode (three, faster but exposes identities); IKEv2 replaces both with a shorter, more robust exchange.
  • Phase 2 creates the tunnels that carry traffic: Inside the phase 1 channel, the peers negotiate the IPsec SAs: which traffic is protected (the interesting traffic or proxy IDs), which encryption and hash, and the lifetime. SAs are unidirectional, so a working tunnel has one in each direction.
  • Mismatched proposals are the standard failure: Both ends must agree on encryption, hash, DH group, authentication method and lifetime. A mismatch in phase 1 means the tunnel never forms; a mismatch in phase 2 means phase 1 comes up and no traffic passes — which is the fastest way to tell which phase is failing.
  • Rekeying is normal and periodic: SAs expire by time or by volume of data and are renegotiated. Perfect forward secrecy forces a fresh DH exchange at rekey so a compromised key does not expose past traffic.
Where you see it
  • Matching phase 1 and phase 2 proposals between a Cisco ASA and a Fortigate
  • Reading a log that says 'IKE phase 1 complete, no phase 2 SA'
  • Choosing certificates over a pre-shared key for a many-site deployment
exam: Know that IKE runs on UDP 500 and that phase 1 secures the negotiation while phase 2 secures the data. The exam's diagnostic angle is the split: if the tunnel establishes but no traffic passes, the problem is in phase 2 or in the interesting-traffic definition, not in authentication. If the tunnel never comes up at all, suspect the pre-shared key or a phase 1 mismatch.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What does a VPN not protect you from?
answer: Anything at the endpoints. Malware on the connecting device, a compromised or unpatched laptop, a malicious insider, and any weakness in the applications themselves. It secures the transport, not the trust of what is at either end.
detail:
A VPN's guarantee is narrow and precise: data in transit between two points is confidential and unmodified. Everything outside that sentence is somebody else's job.
How it works
  • The tunnel carries malware faithfully: Ransomware on a home laptop reaches the file server just as reliably over an encrypted tunnel as over the LAN. This is the argument for posture assessment, endpoint protection and network access control before a client is admitted.
  • Full-tunnel does not mean fully inspected: Traffic is decrypted at the concentrator and then it is ordinary traffic that still has to pass a firewall, proxy and segmentation policy. A VPN that dumps clients onto a flat internal network gives every remote device the reach of a domain administrator's desktop.
  • It does not hide you from the far end: The service you connect to still sees your traffic. A commercial VPN moves the point of trust from the local ISP to the VPN provider; it does not create anonymity, and the destination server still logs the session.
  • Zero trust is the direction of travel: Because the tunnel proves only that the packets are encrypted, modern designs authenticate the user and the device per application rather than granting network-level access on the strength of a successful VPN login.
Where you see it
  • Requiring endpoint posture checks before a VPN client is allowed on
  • Segmenting the VPN pool so remote users reach only what they need
  • Explaining to a user that a VPN does not make a phishing link safe
exam: The exam likes 'what does a VPN not provide'. The answer is endpoint security — it does not protect against malware on the client or an already-compromised device. Distractors claim it prevents malware, provides anonymity, or authenticates the destination application. It provides confidentiality and integrity in transit, plus authentication of the tunnel peers, and nothing more.

front: What does a load balancer do, and what is a VIP?
answer: It spreads client requests across a pool of backend servers and removes failed members from rotation. Clients connect to a single virtual IP (VIP) on the balancer, not to any real server address.
detail:
The VIP is the abstraction that makes the server pool look like one machine. Everything else the load balancer does depends on clients never addressing a server directly.
How it works
  • One name, one address, many servers: DNS publishes the VIP. The balancer accepts the connection, picks a pool member by whichever algorithm is configured, and proxies or forwards the request. Servers can be added, patched or removed without touching DNS or the client.
  • Health checks are what turn it into availability: The balancer probes each member — a TCP connect, an HTTP GET of a status page, or a scripted transaction — and marks failures down. A server that has crashed stops receiving requests within one or two check intervals. A shallow check (ping only) will keep sending traffic to a server whose application has hung, which is a common real-world failure.
  • Layer 4 versus Layer 7: A Layer 4 balancer decides on IP and port only and is fast. A Layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request, so it can route by URL or hostname, terminate TLS, insert headers and rewrite content — at higher cost per connection.
  • The balancer itself must not be the single point of failure: Production pairs run active-passive or active-active with a shared VIP, usually failed over with VRRP or a vendor equivalent.
Where you see it
  • A pair of web servers behind one published address
  • Draining a server for patching by disabling it in the pool instead of powering it off
  • Terminating TLS at the balancer so certificates live in one place
exam: The tested term is VIP — the address clients connect to, which does not belong to any single server. A frequent scenario: one backend server fails and some users get errors, which means the health check is missing or too shallow to detect the failure. Do not answer 'add another server' when the pool already has capacity.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: Name the common load-balancing algorithms.
answer: Round robin · weighted round robin · least connections · least response time · source IP hash
detail:
The algorithm decides which pool member receives the next request. Each one is a different assumption about what makes servers unequal.
How it works
  • Round robin assumes all servers and all requests are equal: Requests go to each member in turn. It is simple and stateless, and it is wrong whenever some requests are far more expensive than others or some servers are bigger.
  • Weighted round robin handles unequal hardware: Each member gets a weight, so a server with twice the CPU receives twice the requests. This is the standard answer when a pool contains a mix of old and new hardware.
  • Least connections tracks actual load: The next request goes to whichever member currently holds the fewest active connections. It adapts automatically when some sessions are long-lived, which round robin cannot do. Least response time extends this by also measuring how fast each member is answering.
  • Source IP hash gives persistence for free: Hashing the client address always maps a given client to the same server. It provides session stickiness without cookies, but it distributes badly when many clients arrive from behind one NAT address.
  • DNS round robin is not the same thing: Publishing several A records for one name spreads clients across addresses, but there is no health checking and cached answers keep sending users to a dead server. It is a poor substitute for a real balancer.
Where you see it
  • Weighting a new server higher than the two it is replacing
  • Switching a pool with long-lived connections from round robin to least connections
  • Explaining uneven load on a pool whose clients all come from one corporate NAT
exam: Expect algorithm-to-scenario matching. Servers of unequal capacity means weighted round robin. Sessions of unequal duration or uneven load despite equal request counts means least connections. If the requirement is that a client keeps reaching the same server, that is persistence — source IP hash or a cookie — and not an algorithm choice at all.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What are sticky sessions (session persistence/affinity) and why are they needed?
answer: A load balancer setting that keeps one client on the same backend server for the duration of a session, usually by inserting a cookie or by hashing the source IP.
detail:
Load balancing assumes any server can handle any request. That assumption breaks the moment a server keeps session state locally, and persistence is the workaround.
How it works
  • The failure it prevents: A user logs in on server A, which stores the session in local memory. Their next request lands on server B, which has never heard of them, so they are logged out or the shopping cart is empty. The symptom is intermittent and looks random because it depends on which server the request hit.
  • Cookie-based persistence is the precise method: The Layer 7 balancer inserts its own cookie identifying the chosen server and reads it on subsequent requests. It survives NAT and changing client addresses, and it works per browser session rather than per IP.
  • Source IP persistence is the blunt method: Simple, works at Layer 4 and for non-HTTP protocols, but every client behind one corporate NAT hashes to the same server, and a mobile client that changes networks loses its affinity.
  • Persistence limits the load balancer: A sticky pool cannot rebalance in real time, and taking a server out of service drops the sessions pinned to it unless connections are drained first. The better fix is to externalize session state to a shared cache or database so any server can serve any request.
Where you see it
  • An e-commerce site where the cart is held in server memory
  • Draining connections before patching a member of a sticky pool
  • Diagnosing users being logged out at random after a second web server was added
exam: The exam scenario is almost always 'users are randomly logged out or lose their shopping cart after a second server was added'. The answer is enable session persistence / sticky sessions. Distractors offer round robin, adding capacity, or increasing the session timeout, none of which address a request landing on a server that lacks the state.

front: Forward proxy versus reverse proxy?
answer: Forward proxy: sits in front of clients, making outbound requests on their behalf — filtering, caching, logging, anonymity. Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers, accepting inbound requests on their behalf — TLS offload, caching, load distribution, WAF.
detail:
Both are intermediaries that terminate one connection and open another. The only structural difference is which side they are protecting, and that determines everything else.
How it works
  • The forward proxy knows the user: Clients are configured, by browser setting, PAC file or transparent interception, to send requests to it. It can enforce acceptable-use policy by category, block downloads, cache popular content and produce per-user browsing logs. It is a control point on the way out.
  • The reverse proxy knows the service: The internet resolves the published name to the reverse proxy. It terminates TLS so certificates and cipher policy live in one place, may cache static content, forwards to whichever backend is appropriate, and hides the real server addresses and count.
  • Both break end-to-end TLS by design: To inspect or cache HTTPS, a proxy has to terminate the session. A forward proxy doing this must install its own CA on every client, which is exactly how corporate TLS inspection works and why certificate warnings appear when a device is missing that CA.
  • The reverse proxy is where a WAF lives: Because it parses the HTTP request before the application does, it is the natural place to inspect for injection and other application attacks, and to rate-limit abusive clients.
Where you see it
  • A corporate web proxy enforcing category-based filtering on outbound browsing
  • An NGINX or F5 device fronting a farm of application servers
  • Certificate errors on a device missing the inspection CA
exam: The discriminator on the exam is whose side it is on: forward protects and controls clients, reverse protects and fronts servers. If a scenario mentions content filtering or employee browsing logs, it is a forward proxy. If it mentions SSL/TLS offload, hiding backend servers, or serving a public website, it is a reverse proxy. A reverse proxy is also a valid answer to 'how do I add caching and TLS termination without changing the application'.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::10 Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, VPN)
front: What is a CDN and what problem does it solve?
answer: A Content Delivery Network — geographically distributed cache servers that serve content from a point of presence near the user, cutting latency and offloading the origin.
detail:
Distance costs milliseconds that no amount of bandwidth can buy back. A CDN attacks the problem by moving copies of the content closer to the people asking for it.
How it works
  • Latency is a function of distance, not bandwidth: A round trip from Sydney to Virginia is roughly 200 ms no matter how fast the link. A web page needing many round trips is therefore slow regardless of the origin's capacity. Serving it from a local PoP removes most of that distance.
  • Clients are steered by DNS or anycast: Either the CDN's DNS returns the address of the nearest edge node for the requesting resolver, or the same anycast address is announced from every PoP and routing delivers the user to the closest one. This is why a CNAME to the provider is the normal onboarding step.
  • Static content caches, dynamic content does not: Images, video, scripts and stylesheets are cached at the edge and served without touching the origin. Personalized and transactional responses are proxied back to the origin, though the CDN's optimized network path often still helps.
  • It is also a DDoS and availability layer: A distributed edge with enormous aggregate capacity absorbs volumetric attacks that would flatten a single origin, and it keeps serving cached content when the origin is down. Purging or versioning cached objects is the operational cost — a stale edge copy outlives an origin change.
Where you see it
  • Streaming video and large downloads served from regional edge nodes
  • A global website whose origin is in one region but whose users are worldwide
  • Absorbing a volumetric DDoS in front of a small origin
exam: The exam frames CDN as the fix for high latency for geographically distant users. The distractors are 'add bandwidth at the origin' and 'add a load balancer', neither of which reduces propagation delay. Also know the secondary benefits: origin offload and DDoS absorption. A CDN is a distributed reverse-proxy cache, which is a useful way to keep the two concepts linked.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: FTP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 20 (data) / 21 (control)  ·  TCP
detail:
The original file transfer protocol. It is unusual in using two separate connections at once: a control channel for commands and a data channel for the file itself.
How it works
  • Two channels: Port 21 carries commands (LIST, GET, PUT) and stays open for the whole session. Port 20 carries the actual file bytes in active mode.
  • Active vs passive mode: In active mode the server opens the data connection back to the client from port 20 — which firewalls and NAT routinely block. In passive mode the client opens both connections, which is why passive is the default nearly everywhere.
  • No encryption: Usernames, passwords and file contents all travel in cleartext. Anyone capturing packets reads them.
Where you see it
  • Legacy file servers and web hosting uploads
  • Anonymous public file archives
  • Bulk transfers where the network is already trusted
exam: The exam wants two things: that FTP uses two ports, and that it is insecure. Expect a scenario where 'files must be transferred securely' — the answer is SFTP (22) or FTPS (989/990), never FTP. Also watch for a firewall question where active-mode FTP fails and passive mode is the fix.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: Telnet — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 23  ·  TCP
detail:
The legacy remote terminal protocol. Functionally similar to SSH but with no encryption whatsoever.
How it works
  • Everything is cleartext: A packet capture shows the username, the password and every command typed, character by character.
  • Still present on old gear: Many older switches and routers ship with Telnet enabled by default, which is why 'disable Telnet' appears on every device-hardening checklist.
  • Occasionally useful as a test tool: telnet host 25 is still a quick way to check whether a TCP port is open and a service is answering — that use is fine, remote administration is not.
Where you see it
  • Legacy device administration (should be disabled)
  • Quick manual port-reachability testing
  • Some industrial and embedded systems that never got SSH
exam: Telnet appears on the exam almost entirely as the wrong answer and as a hardening target. If a question describes an auditor finding cleartext credentials on the wire during device management, Telnet is the cause and SSH is the fix.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: SMTP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 25  ·  TCP
detail:
The protocol that pushes mail outward — from a client to its mail server, and between mail servers on the way to the destination.
How it works
  • Send only: SMTP moves mail out. Retrieving mail into a mailbox client is POP3 or IMAP. This send/receive split is the single most tested idea about mail ports.
  • Server to server: When you email another company, their mail server accepts the message over SMTP from yours.
  • Port 25 is widely blocked: Consumer ISPs block outbound 25 to limit spam relays, which is why mail clients submit on 587 instead.
  • Uses MX records: The sending server does a DNS lookup for the recipient domain's MX record to find where to deliver.
Where you see it
  • Outbound mail from an application or scanner
  • Mail relay between organizations
  • Alerting systems that email on an event
exam: Learn the mail ports as a set, because the exam tests them together: 25 SMTP (send), 110 POP3 (retrieve, downloads), 143 IMAP (retrieve, syncs), 587 submission, 993 IMAPS, 995 POP3S. A scenario where a user can receive but not send mail points at 25/587; can send but not receive points at 110/143.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: TACACS+ — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 49  ·  TCP
detail:
Cisco's AAA protocol for controlling who may log into network devices and what commands they may run.
How it works
  • Encrypts the entire packet: Not just the password — the whole payload, including which commands are being authorized. RADIUS encrypts only the password field.
  • Separates the three A's: Authentication, authorization and accounting are independent operations, so you can authenticate against one system and authorize commands granularly per user.
  • Uses TCP: Connection-oriented, so the device knows whether the AAA server actually received the request.
  • Built for device administration: Its per-command authorization is why it dominates router and switch admin rather than end-user network access.
Where you see it
  • Controlling admin login to routers, switches and firewalls
  • Restricting which IOS commands each engineer may run
  • Auditing exactly what an administrator typed
exam: This is nearly always tested as a comparison with RADIUS. The three discriminators: TACACS+ is TCP 49 / RADIUS is UDP 1812-1813; TACACS+ encrypts the whole packet / RADIUS encrypts only the password; TACACS+ separates AAA / RADIUS combines authentication and authorization. If the scenario is device administration, expect TACACS+. If it is Wi-Fi or 802.1X user access, expect RADIUS.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: DNS — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 53  ·  TCP and UDP
detail:
The system that translates human-readable names into IP addresses, and the single most common cause of 'the internet is down' complaints that are not actually the internet.
How it works
  • UDP for queries: A normal lookup is one small request and one small reply. UDP has no handshake, so it is far faster at scale.
  • TCP for zone transfers: Replicating a whole zone between name servers, or returning a response too large for a single datagram, uses TCP 53 for reliability.
  • Hierarchical and cached: Resolvers walk from root to TLD to authoritative server, then cache the answer for the record's TTL.
  • Record types matter: A and AAAA map names to addresses, CNAME aliases one name to another, MX finds mail servers, PTR does reverse lookups, TXT holds SPF and DKIM.
Where you see it
  • Every name-based connection a user makes
  • Mail routing via MX records
  • Service discovery in Active Directory via SRV records
  • Domain ownership verification via TXT records
exam: Two guaranteed exam patterns. First, the port: DNS is the classic 'uses both TCP and UDP' answer, and knowing why (queries vs zone transfers) is often the actual question. Second, the symptom: 'can ping by IP but not by name' is always DNS. Expect to identify record types from a description too.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: DHCP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 67 (server) / 68 (client)  ·  UDP
detail:
The service that hands out IP addresses, masks, gateways and DNS servers automatically, so nobody configures a laptop by hand.
How it works
  • DORA: Discover (client broadcasts looking for a server) → Offer (server proposes an address) → Request (client asks for it) → Acknowledge (server confirms and records the lease).
  • Two ports, and the direction matters: The server listens on 67, the client on 68. Discover and Request go to 67; Offer and Acknowledge come back to 68.
  • It starts as a broadcast: The client has no address yet, so Discover is a broadcast — and routers do not forward broadcasts. Crossing a subnet requires a relay agent / IP helper-address.
  • Leases, reservations, exclusions: A lease expires and must be renewed at 50% elapsed. A reservation ties an address to a MAC. An exclusion keeps addresses out of the pool for static devices.
Where you see it
  • Assigning addresses to every laptop, phone and printer on a network
  • Delivering DNS servers, domain name and NTP servers via DHCP options
  • PXE boot, using options 66 and 67 to point at a TFTP server
exam: The two highest-frequency exam items: DORA in order, and the 169.254.x.x symptom — an APIPA address means DHCP failed, so check the server, the scope for exhaustion, and the IP helper on the router. Rogue DHCP servers and DHCP snooping show up on the security side.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: TFTP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 69  ·  UDP
detail:
A deliberately stripped-down file transfer protocol. It exists to be small and simple enough to fit inside firmware, not to be secure or full-featured.
How it works
  • Runs over UDP: No connection setup, no sequencing from the transport. TFTP does its own minimal lock-step acknowledgement of each block.
  • No authentication at all: There are no usernames, no passwords and no encryption. Anyone who can reach the server can read or write files.
  • No directory browsing: You cannot list files. You must already know the exact filename you want, which is why it only works in automated, preconfigured workflows.
  • Tiny footprint: The whole implementation is small enough to burn into ROM, which is exactly why network hardware and diskless clients use it at boot time.
Where you see it
  • PXE network boot of diskless workstations and thin clients
  • Pushing firmware and IOS images to routers and switches
  • Backing up and restoring device configuration files
  • Provisioning VoIP phones with their config at power-on
exam: The exam tests TFTP through contrast and through boot scenarios. Contrast: TFTP is UDP 69 and unauthenticated, FTP is TCP 20/21 and authenticated but cleartext, SFTP is TCP 22 and encrypted. Boot: any question about PXE, network booting, or pushing firmware to a switch points at TFTP, usually alongside DHCP options 66 and 67. If a question asks why TFTP is unsuitable for transferring sensitive data, the answer is no authentication and no encryption — not speed.

front: HTTP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 80  ·  TCP
detail:
The request-response protocol behind the unencrypted web.
How it works
  • Cleartext: Page content, form submissions and cookies are all readable by anyone on the path.

  • Device management interfaces on older hardware
  • Redirecting visitors to the HTTPS version of a site

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: Kerberos — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 88  ·  TCP and UDP
detail:
The ticket-based authentication protocol that Active Directory uses to prove identity without sending passwords across the network.
How it works
  • Tickets, not passwords: The client authenticates once to a Key Distribution Center, receives a ticket-granting ticket, and presents tickets to services afterward.
  • Time-sensitive: Tickets carry timestamps and are rejected if clocks are skewed more than a few minutes — typically five. This is why Kerberos depends on NTP.
  • Mutual authentication: Both the client and the service prove identity, which resists impersonation.
Where you see it
  • Windows domain logon
  • Single sign-on to file shares, SQL and internal web apps
  • Any Active Directory-integrated service
exam: Two traps. First, port 88 is Kerberos, but IP protocol 88 is EIGRP — the exam exploits that collision. Second, the classic scenario: domain logons fail after a time change, and the answer is NTP/clock skew breaking Kerberos.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: POP3 — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 110  ·  TCP
detail:
A mail retrieval protocol that downloads messages to one device.
How it works
  • Download and (traditionally) delete: Classic POP3 pulls mail off the server, so it lives on that one machine. Most clients can be told to leave a copy, but the model is still single-device.
  • No server-side folder sync: Read/unread status and folders are local. Read something on your laptop and your phone will not know.
  • Secure version is POP3S on 995: Same protocol wrapped in TLS.
Where you see it
  • Single-device mail access
  • Low-bandwidth or offline-first mail clients
  • Legacy mail setups
exam: Tested as the counterpart to IMAP. The discriminator the exam uses: if a user needs mail synchronized across multiple devices, the answer is IMAP (143/993), not POP3 (110/995).

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: NTP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 123  ·  UDP
detail:
The protocol that keeps every clock on the network agreeing with every other clock.
How it works
  • Stratum hierarchy: Stratum 0 is a reference source such as GPS or an atomic clock. Stratum 1 is a server directly attached to it. Each hop away increments the number and loses a little accuracy.
  • Millisecond accuracy: Good enough for logs, certificates and authentication. Where sub-microsecond accuracy is needed — finance, industrial, broadcast — PTP is used instead.
  • Nearly everything depends on it: Kerberos rejects tickets with skewed clocks, TLS certificates validate against time, and correlating logs across devices is impossible if their timestamps disagree.
  • NTS is the secure version: Network Time Security adds authentication so an attacker cannot feed you a false time.
Where you see it
  • Synchronizing switches, routers, servers and workstations
  • Making log correlation across devices meaningful
  • Supporting Kerberos and certificate validation
exam: The exam's favorite NTP scenario is indirect: something else breaks and the root cause is time. Domain authentication failing, certificates showing as invalid, or logs that cannot be correlated all point to NTP. Know that it is UDP 123 and that stratum counts distance from the reference clock, not quality of the server.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: NetBIOS (name / datagram / session) — port number and transport protocol?
detail:
The legacy Windows networking suite for name registration, connectionless messaging and file-sharing sessions, largely replaced by SMB over TCP 445.
How it works
  • Three services, three ports: 137 name service (registration and resolution), 138 datagram service (connectionless), 139 session service (file and printer sharing).
  • Superseded by 445: Modern Windows runs SMB directly over TCP 445 without the NetBIOS layer.
  • A hardening target: Open 137-139 on an internet-facing host is a finding — it leaks host and domain names and enables old attacks.
Where you see it
  • Legacy Windows file and printer sharing
  • Old applications hardcoded to NetBIOS names
exam: Usually appears as a group of three numbers you must recognize, and as something to disable. If a question mentions modern Windows file sharing, the answer is SMB on 445, not 139.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: IMAP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 143  ·  TCP
detail:
A mail retrieval protocol that keeps the mailbox on the server and synchronizes state to every client.
How it works
  • Server-side mailbox: Messages stay on the server. The client shows a view of it rather than owning the only copy.
  • Full synchronization: Folders, read/unread status and deletions propagate to every device. Read an email on your phone and your laptop shows it read.
  • Secure version is IMAPS on 993: Same protocol inside TLS.
Where you see it
  • Mail on a phone, laptop and desktop simultaneously
  • Webmail backends
  • Any modern corporate mail deployment
exam: The exam's IMAP question is almost always the multi-device scenario: a user reads mail on several devices and wants consistent state, so the answer is IMAP over POP3. Pair 143 with 993 the way you pair 110 with 995.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: SNMP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 161 (poll) / 162 (trap)  ·  UDP
detail:
The protocol network monitoring systems use to collect health and performance data from devices, and the way devices raise alarms on their own.
How it works
  • Manager and agent: The monitoring system (manager) polls agents running on switches, routers, servers and printers.
  • Two directions, two ports: The manager polls the agent on 161. The agent sends an unsolicited trap to the manager on 162 when something breaks.
  • MIB and OID: The MIB is the catalog of what can be queried on a device. An OID is the numeric address of one specific value inside it, such as an interface's input error count.
  • Version matters for security: v1 and v2c authenticate with a cleartext community string, commonly left as 'public'. v3 adds authentication, encryption and message integrity.
Where you see it
  • Graphing interface utilization and errors over time
  • Alerting when a link goes down or a device reboots
  • Building a capacity baseline
  • Inventory and uptime reporting
exam: Three reliable items. The 161 vs 162 direction (poll out, trap in). The v3 answer to any question about securing SNMP or a finding about cleartext community strings. And the vocabulary — expect to be asked which term describes the database of manageable objects (MIB) versus a single identifier (OID).

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: LDAP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 389  ·  TCP and UDP
detail:
The protocol applications use to query a directory service for users, groups and their attributes.
How it works
  • Directory queries, not authentication by itself: LDAP looks up objects. It can also 'bind' with credentials, which many applications use as a crude authentication check.
  • Cleartext on 389: Including the bind credentials, unless StartTLS is negotiated.
  • LDAPS on 636 is the encrypted version: The straightforward fix for a cleartext-directory finding.
  • Active Directory speaks it: AD is an LDAP directory with Kerberos authentication layered on.
Where you see it
  • Applications looking up user accounts and group membership
  • Address book lookups in mail clients
  • Centralized authentication for VPNs, wikis and internal tools
exam: Tested as the 389 → 636 secure-swap pair, alongside HTTP→HTTPS and SMTP→SMTPS. Also expect LDAP in a list of identity technologies (RADIUS, LDAP, SAML, TACACS+, Kerberos) where you must pick the one that fits the scenario — LDAP is the directory lookup one.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: HTTPS — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 443  ·  TCP
detail:
HTTP inside a TLS tunnel. The default for essentially all web traffic, and increasingly for traffic that is not web at all.
How it works
  • TLS provides three things: Confidentiality (encryption), integrity (tampering is detected), and authentication of the server via its certificate.
  • Certificate trust is the common failure: Expired certificates, name mismatches and self-signed certificates all produce browser warnings — a frequent troubleshooting scenario.
  • Also UDP 443: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP 443. A firewall rule that only permits TCP 443 can cause odd, slow-but-working behavior.
  • Hard to inspect: Because it is encrypted, content filtering requires TLS interception at the proxy or firewall.
Where you see it
  • All modern web traffic
  • Device and cloud management interfaces
  • Clientless VPN portals
  • APIs and application traffic tunneled to look like web traffic
exam: Beyond the number itself, 443 shows up in certificate troubleshooting (the fix for 'not trusted' is a CA-signed certificate, correct name, and correct time) and in firewall/proxy questions about why encrypted traffic cannot be content-filtered without interception.

answer: 445  ·  TCP
detail:
The Windows file and printer sharing protocol.
How it works
  • Runs directly over TCP now: Modern SMB does not need the old NetBIOS ports 137-139.

  • Windows file shares and mapped drives
  • Network printer sharing
  • Deployment and management tooling inside a domain

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: Syslog — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 514  ·  UDP
detail:
The standard for shipping log messages from devices to a central collector.
How it works
  • Severity levels 0-7: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debug. Lower number is more severe.
  • UDP by default: Fire and forget, so log messages can be lost under load. TCP and TLS variants exist for reliability and encryption.
  • Centralization is the point: Logs on a device that just failed are logs you cannot read. A collector also makes correlation across devices possible, and is the input to a SIEM.
Where you see it
  • Collecting switch, router and firewall logs centrally
  • Feeding a SIEM
  • Meeting log retention requirements
  • Post-incident investigation
exam: The severity level table is directly testable — know that 0 is most severe and 7 (Debug) is most verbose, and that setting a device to level 7 in production floods the collector. Also expect syslog in comparison questions against SNMP: syslog carries event messages, SNMP carries polled metrics and traps.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: SMTPS / mail submission — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 587  ·  TCP
detail:
The modern port a mail client uses to hand outbound mail to its own server, secured with STARTTLS.
How it works
  • Submission, not relay: 587 is for authenticated clients submitting mail. Port 25 is for server-to-server relay.
  • Requires authentication: Which is precisely why it is not a spam relay, and why ISPs permit it while blocking 25.
  • 465 is the older implicit-TLS port: Still seen in the wild; CompTIA's objectives list 587.
Where you see it
  • Outlook, Thunderbird or a phone sending mail through a provider
  • Applications sending authenticated mail
exam: Tested inside the mail-port cluster. The distinguishing sentence is 'client submitting mail to its own server' = 587, versus 'server relaying to another server' = 25.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: RDP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 3389  ·  TCP
detail:
Microsoft's protocol for full graphical remote control of a Windows desktop or server.
How it works
  • Graphical, not command line: This is the discriminator against SSH, which is text-only.
  • Encrypted, but heavily targeted: Internet-exposed RDP is one of the most common ransomware entry points — brute-forced or hit with stolen credentials.
  • Should be behind something: Best practice is RDP over a VPN or through a jump box, with MFA and network-level authentication, never open to the internet.
Where you see it
  • Remote support of Windows workstations
  • Administering Windows servers
  • Virtual desktop infrastructure
exam: Two angles. Recall: 3389 = RDP = graphical Windows remote access. Security: any scenario describing RDP open to the internet expects you to recognize the risk and answer with a VPN, a jump box, MFA, or restricting the source addresses.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: SIP — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 5060 (cleartext) / 5061 (TLS)  ·  5060 TCP and UDP, 5061 TCP
detail:
The signaling protocol that sets up, modifies and tears down VoIP and video calls.
How it works
  • Signaling only: SIP negotiates the call. The audio itself flows separately over RTP on a dynamic UDP port range.
  • 5061 is the encrypted variant: SIP over TLS. The media is separately encrypted with SRTP.
  • Sensitive to NAT and firewalls: Because SIP embeds addresses in its messages and the media uses separate dynamic ports, NAT traversal is a frequent source of one-way-audio problems.
Where you see it
  • IP phone registration and call setup
  • SIP trunks between a phone system and a carrier
  • Video conferencing session establishment
exam: The most valuable exam idea here is the signaling versus media split — it explains the classic 'call connects but there is no audio' scenario, which is a firewall or NAT problem with RTP, not with SIP. Also know 5060 cleartext versus 5061 TLS.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: RADIUS — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 1812 (authentication) / 1813 (accounting)  ·  UDP
detail:
The AAA protocol that authenticates end users onto networks, most visibly Wi-Fi and 802.1X wired ports.
How it works
  • Encrypts only the password: The rest of the packet, including the username, is in the clear. TACACS+ encrypts everything.
  • Combines authentication and authorization: They arrive together in one exchange, which makes granular per-command control impossible.
  • Two ports: 1812 for authentication, 1813 for accounting records. Older implementations used 1645 and 1646.
  • The server in 802.1X: In the supplicant → authenticator → authentication server model, RADIUS is the authentication server.
Where you see it
  • WPA2/WPA3 Enterprise Wi-Fi
  • 802.1X port-based access control on wired switches
  • VPN user authentication
  • Session accounting for billing or audit
exam: Expect the RADIUS vs TACACS+ comparison and the 802.1X role question. Anchor it this way: RADIUS authenticates users onto the network; TACACS+ authorizes administrators on devices. If the scenario is enterprise Wi-Fi with individual credentials, RADIUS is the answer.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: IKE / IPsec NAT-T — port number and transport protocol?
answer: 500 (IKE) / 4500 (NAT-T)  ·  UDP
detail:
The negotiation ports that let an IPsec VPN tunnel establish itself.
How it works
  • IKE builds the tunnel: UDP 500 negotiates the security association — the agreed encryption, hashing and keys — before any protected data flows.
  • NAT-T rescues IPsec through NAT: IPsec ESP is IP protocol 50, which has no port numbers for a NAT device to translate. NAT-T encapsulates ESP in UDP 4500 so it survives NAT.
  • The data itself is not on a port: Once established, traffic flows as ESP, IP protocol 50 — a protocol number, not a port.
Where you see it
  • Site-to-site VPN between offices
  • Remote-access IPsec VPN clients
  • Securing traffic across an untrusted carrier link
exam: The high-value exam idea is that IPsec uses protocol numbers, not just ports: ESP is 50, AH is 51, IKE is UDP 500. A firewall that permits only TCP/UDP will silently break IPsec, and the fix is permitting protocol 50 or enabling NAT-T on 4500.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: ICMP — IP protocol number? (a protocol number, not a port)
detail:
The diagnostic and error-reporting protocol of the IP suite. It carries no application data — its whole job is to report on the delivery of other traffic.
How it works
  • No ports at all: ICMP sits directly on IP with a type and code instead of port numbers. That is why a firewall rule for ICMP looks different from a TCP or UDP rule.
  • Types you should know: Echo request/reply (ping), Destination Unreachable, Time Exceeded (how traceroute discovers each hop), and Fragmentation Needed (which Path MTU Discovery depends on).
  • Often filtered: Many organizations block ICMP inbound to reduce reconnaissance — which is why a failed ping does not prove a host is down.
Where you see it
  • ping for reachability and latency
  • traceroute for path discovery
  • Path MTU Discovery
  • Reporting unreachable networks back to a sender
exam: Two traps. First, ICMP is protocol 1, not a port — a question offering 'port 1' is wrong by construction. Second, blocking ICMP breaks Path MTU Discovery, producing the classic scenario where small pings succeed but large file transfers hang.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: TCP — IP protocol number? (a protocol number, not a port)
detail:
The connection-oriented transport protocol: reliable, ordered, and willing to trade speed for correctness.
How it works
  • Three-way handshake: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK establishes the connection and synchronizes sequence numbers before data flows.
  • Reliability through acknowledgement: Unacknowledged segments are retransmitted. Sequence numbers let the receiver reorder anything that arrives out of order.
  • Flow and congestion control: Windowing lets the receiver throttle the sender; congestion control backs off when loss is detected — which is why even 1-2% packet loss collapses TCP throughput.
  • Higher overhead: Larger header, connection state on both ends, and delay while retransmitting.
Where you see it
  • Web, email and file transfer
  • Database connections
  • Anything where a missing byte would corrupt the result
exam: Expect the handshake in order, and the TCP vs UDP choice presented as a scenario. Also know that TCP's congestion response is why a lossy link feels far slower than the loss percentage suggests.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: UDP — IP protocol number? (a protocol number, not a port)
detail:
The connectionless transport protocol: no handshake, no acknowledgement, no reordering — just send it.
How it works
  • No connection setup: The first packet is the data. This removes a full round trip of latency before anything useful happens.
  • No retransmission: A lost datagram is simply gone. For voice and video that is preferable to a late one arriving out of order.
  • Minimal header: Eight bytes versus TCP's twenty, which matters at high packet rates.
  • Reliability moves up a layer: If an application needs it, the application implements it — as TFTP does with its own per-block acknowledgements.
Where you see it
  • VoIP and video streaming
  • DNS queries
  • DHCP, TFTP, SNMP, syslog, NTP
  • Online gaming
exam: The exam tests UDP as a design choice: given a real-time or low-overhead requirement, pick UDP. Memorize which common services use it — DHCP, DNS queries, TFTP, NTP, SNMP, syslog and SIP are the ones that recur.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: GRE — IP protocol number? (a protocol number, not a port)
detail:
A tunneling protocol that wraps one protocol's packets inside IP so they can cross a network that would not otherwise carry them.
How it works
  • Encapsulation, not encryption: GRE hides nothing. It is frequently paired with IPsec, which supplies the encryption GRE lacks.
  • Carries what IPsec alone cannot: GRE can tunnel multicast and non-IP traffic, which is why routing protocols like OSPF run over GRE-over-IPsec rather than plain IPsec.
  • Adds overhead: The extra header reduces effective MTU, which is a common cause of fragmentation problems on tunnels.
Where you see it
  • Site-to-site tunnels carrying routing protocol traffic
  • Connecting networks with incompatible addressing
  • GRE over IPsec for encrypted multi-protocol tunnels
exam: The single most tested fact: GRE does not encrypt. If a question describes a tunnel that must be confidential, GRE alone is wrong and IPsec (or GRE over IPsec) is right.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: ESP — IP protocol number? (a protocol number, not a port)
detail:
The IPsec component that actually protects the data — it encrypts and authenticates the payload.
How it works
  • Encryption and integrity: ESP provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the payload. This is what real VPNs use.
  • Protocol number, no ports: Which is why NAT devices cannot translate it and NAT-T (UDP 4500) exists.
  • Transport vs tunnel mode: Transport mode encrypts only the payload and keeps the original IP header. Tunnel mode encrypts the entire original packet and adds a new header — the mode used for gateway-to-gateway VPNs.
Where you see it
  • Site-to-site and remote-access IPsec VPNs
  • Encrypting traffic across an untrusted carrier

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: AH — IP protocol number? (a protocol number, not a port)
detail:
The IPsec component that authenticates and integrity-protects a packet without encrypting it.
How it works
  • No confidentiality: AH proves the packet came from the claimed source and was not altered. It does not hide the contents.
  • Covers the IP header too: AH authenticates parts of the outer header, which is exactly why it breaks through NAT — NAT rewrites those fields and invalidates the check.
  • Rarely used alone: Most deployments use ESP, which provides integrity as well as encryption.
Where you see it
  • Integrity-only scenarios where contents need not be hidden
  • Legacy IPsec configurations
exam: Two exam facts: AH provides no encryption, and AH is incompatible with NAT. A question describing an IPsec tunnel that fails only when a NAT device is in the path is pointing at AH, with ESP plus NAT-T as the fix.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: EIGRP — IP protocol number? (a protocol number, not a port)
detail:
Cisco's advanced distance-vector interior gateway protocol.
How it works
  • Hybrid characteristics: Distance-vector at heart, but with link-state-like fast convergence through the DUAL algorithm.
  • Successors and feasible successors: DUAL precomputes a loop-free backup path, so failover is near-instant rather than requiring recalculation.
  • Composite metric: Bandwidth and delay by default, optionally load and reliability.
  • Administrative distance 90 internal: Lower than OSPF's 110, so EIGRP wins when both offer the same prefix.
Where you see it
  • Cisco-only enterprise networks
  • Environments needing fast convergence with simple configuration
exam: The high-value trap: EIGRP is IP protocol 88, while port 88 is Kerberos. Also memorize the administrative distance table — EIGRP internal 90 versus OSPF 110 is a common route-selection question.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::01 Ports and Protocols
front: OSPF — IP protocol number? (a protocol number, not a port)
detail:
The open-standard link-state interior gateway protocol.
How it works
  • Every router builds the same map: Routers flood link-state advertisements until all share an identical topology database, then each runs Dijkstra to compute its own shortest paths.
  • Cost is the metric: Derived from interface bandwidth. Costs add along a path, and lowest total cost wins.
  • Areas control scale: Flooding is confined within an area. Area 0 is the backbone and every other area must attach to it.
  • Administrative distance 110: Higher than EIGRP's 90, lower than RIP's 120.
Where you see it
  • Multi-vendor enterprise routing
  • Large campus networks
  • The interior protocol underneath a BGP edge
exam: Expect OSPF in route selection questions (longest prefix match first, then administrative distance, then metric) and in area design questions where the answer hinges on area 0 being the backbone.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what?
answer:
IaaS: provider gives compute, storage and network; you manage the OS, patching, runtime and application.
PaaS: provider manages the OS and runtime; you manage only your application and data.
SaaS: provider manages everything; you manage configuration, users and your data.
detail:
The three models differ in one dimension: how far up the stack the provider's responsibility reaches. Everything above that line remains yours.
How it works
  • IaaS is a rented data centre: Virtual machines, block storage, virtual networks and load balancers. You still install the operating system, patch it, configure the firewall and back it up. Maximum control, maximum work.
  • PaaS is a rented runtime: You push code or a container and the platform runs it. You never see or patch the OS. The trade is less control: you take the platform's language versions, scaling model and limits.
  • SaaS is finished software: Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Workday. You configure the product and control who can use it. You cannot change how it works, and your responsibility narrows to identity, access and the data you put in.
  • Your data is always yours: At every level, the customer owns and is accountable for the data and for who can reach it. No service model transfers that.
Where you see it
  • Choosing between a lift-and-shift VM migration (IaaS) and re-platforming (PaaS)
  • Assigning patching responsibility during an audit
  • Explaining why a SaaS breach caused by a public sharing link is the customer's fault
exam: Identification from a description is the test. Key discriminators: if you patch the OS it is IaaS; if you deploy only code it is PaaS; if you just log in it is SaaS. The classic distractor is calling a hosted email service PaaS — Microsoft 365 is SaaS. Anything that names a virtual machine is IaaS.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: Public, private, hybrid and community cloud.
answer:
Public: provider-owned infrastructure shared by many customers.
Private: infrastructure dedicated to one organization, on-premises or hosted.
Hybrid: both, connected, with workloads spanning them.
Community: shared by several organizations with common requirements.
detail:
These describe who the infrastructure is shared with, which drives cost, control and compliance. They are independent of IaaS/PaaS/SaaS.
How it works
  • Public cloud trades control for economics: Multitenant, pay-as-you-go, effectively unlimited capacity. You accept the provider's controls and the fact that your workload runs on shared hardware.
  • Private cloud is dedicated capacity: Cloud-like self-service and automation, but on hardware only your organization uses. Chosen for regulatory requirements, data residency or predictable heavy workloads. You keep the capital cost and the operational burden.
  • Hybrid is the normal end state: Sensitive systems stay private, elastic or seasonal workloads run public, and the two are joined by VPN or a direct connection. Cloud bursting — overflowing to public capacity at peak — is the textbook case.
  • Community cloud is shared by peers: Several organizations with the same compliance regime — healthcare providers, government agencies, universities — share an environment built to those requirements, splitting the cost of controls none could justify alone.
Where you see it
  • Regulated data kept private while public-facing web tiers run in public cloud
  • Seasonal retail capacity bursting into public cloud
  • Government or healthcare consortium platforms
exam: The exam gives a scenario and expects the model. 'Several hospitals share a compliant platform' → community. 'Sensitive records on-premises, web front end in AWS, connected' → hybrid. 'Dedicated hardware for one company due to regulation' → private. Do not mix these with the service models; a question may test both in one sentence.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is the shared responsibility model?
answer: The provider is responsible for security of the cloud — physical facilities, hardware, hypervisor, the underlying network. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud — data, identity and access, configuration, and the guest OS in IaaS.
detail:
Moving to cloud moves some responsibilities and leaves others exactly where they were. Breaches overwhelmingly come from assuming more moved than actually did.
How it works
  • The line moves with the service model: In IaaS the customer patches the guest OS. In PaaS the provider does. In SaaS the customer is left with identity, access and data configuration. Same model, different boundary.
  • Identity and access is always the customer's: No provider decides who in your organization may read a bucket or an inbox. Misconfigured permissions are the single most common cause of cloud data exposure.
  • Configuration is the customer's too: A publicly readable storage bucket, a security group open to 0.0.0.0/0, or an unencrypted database are customer misconfigurations, not provider failures.
  • Availability is shared but not guaranteed: The provider offers zones and regions; using them is the customer's design choice. A single-zone deployment that fails is not the provider's fault.
  • Compliance is joint: The provider certifies its infrastructure and publishes attestations; the customer must still demonstrate the controls in their own configuration.
Where you see it
  • Audit and compliance conversations about who patches what
  • Post-incident review of an exposed storage bucket
  • Designing across availability zones rather than assuming the provider handles it
exam: The phrasing to recognize is security 'of' the cloud versus security 'in' the cloud. The scenario is usually a data leak from an open bucket or an over-permissive security group, and the answer is that this is the customer's responsibility. A distractor will suggest the provider is liable because the data was on their hardware.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: Region vs availability zone.
answer: A region is a geographic location containing multiple isolated data centres. An availability zone is one of those isolated facilities. Spreading across zones survives a data centre failure; spreading across regions survives a regional disaster and addresses data residency.
detail:
Cloud resilience is a design decision, not a default. The provider supplies the failure domains; the customer must actually use more than one.
How it works
  • Zones are isolated failure domains within a region: Separate buildings with independent power, cooling and network. They are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication between them, which is what makes multi-zone databases practical.
  • Regions are separated by geography: Hundreds or thousands of kilometres apart. Latency between regions is high enough that replication is usually asynchronous, and cross-region data transfer costs money.
  • Multi-zone handles the common failure: Fire, flood, power or cooling loss in one building. Running instances in two or three zones behind a load balancer is the standard high-availability pattern.
  • Multi-region handles the rare one, and the legal one: Regional outages, natural disasters, and data sovereignty requirements that say records must remain in a particular country. It is significantly more complex and more expensive.
  • Single-zone deployments still happen by accident: Launching everything in the default zone is easy and is the root cause of many outages that customers wrongly attribute to the provider.
Where you see it
  • Designing a highly available web tier across three zones
  • Meeting a requirement that customer data must stay within a country
  • Disaster recovery planning where the recovery site is another region
exam: Match to the requirement wording. 'Survive a data centre failure' → multiple availability zones. 'Survive a regional disaster' or 'data must remain in-country' → multiple regions. The distractor is answering 'multiple regions' for the data centre failure case; it works, but it is more complex and costly than the requirement calls for.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: Scalability vs elasticity (and vertical vs horizontal).
answer:
Scalability: the ability to grow to handle more load.
Elasticity: growing and shrinking automatically as demand changes.
Vertical (scale up): a bigger instance. Horizontal (scale out): more instances.
detail:
Two words that are used interchangeably in marketing and distinguished carefully on the exam. The difference is whether the change is automatic and reversible.
How it works
  • Scalability is capability: A system is scalable if adding resources increases what it can handle. That may be a manual change, planned in advance, and it may never be undone.
  • Elasticity is automatic and bidirectional: Resources are added when a metric crosses a threshold and removed when demand falls. Shrinking is the half people forget, and it is what makes consumption billing economical.
  • Vertical scaling has a ceiling and downtime: You can only buy so large an instance, and resizing usually requires a restart. It is simple and works for databases that cannot be sharded.
  • Horizontal scaling is what elasticity uses: Adding identical instances behind a load balancer has no practical ceiling and no downtime, but the application must be stateless or externalize its session state.
Where you see it
  • Auto-scaling groups adding web servers during a traffic spike and removing them overnight
  • Resizing a database instance during a maintenance window
  • Justifying cloud cost models to finance
exam: CompTIA tests the distinction directly. If the scenario says capacity adjusts automatically up and down with demand, that is elasticity. If it just says the system can be made bigger, that is scalability. Also know scale up = vertical = bigger box; scale out = horizontal = more boxes.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is multitenancy, and what is the risk?
answer: Multiple customers (tenants) sharing the same physical infrastructure, kept apart by logical isolation — hypervisor boundaries, separate virtual networks, and access control. The risk is that isolation failing, plus reduced visibility into who and what shares your hardware.
detail:
Multitenancy is the reason public cloud is cheap. Idle capacity from one customer is sold to another, and the isolation is software rather than physical separation.
How it works
  • Isolation is logical, not physical: Your VM may share a host with an unrelated company's VM. Separation comes from the hypervisor, virtual networking and storage encryption, all of which are software with potential flaws.
  • The noisy neighbour problem: Another tenant's workload can consume shared CPU, storage or network capacity and degrade your performance. Providers mitigate with quotas and dedicated instance options.
  • Escape is the severe risk: A hypervisor or side-channel vulnerability that lets one tenant read another's memory breaks the entire model. Rare, high impact, and the reason regulated workloads sometimes require dedicated hosts.
  • Single tenancy is the alternative: Dedicated hosts or a private cloud remove the shared-hardware risk at higher cost. This is a common regulatory requirement rather than a technical preference.
Where you see it
  • Assessing whether a regulated workload can run on shared public cloud
  • Explaining inconsistent performance caused by shared infrastructure
  • Choosing dedicated instances or a private cloud for compliance
exam: This is usually a definition item, sometimes framed as a risk question. Multitenancy = many customers, shared infrastructure, logical isolation. If a question asks the main security concern of public cloud, the expected answer is around shared infrastructure and loss of direct control, with dedicated/private hosting as the mitigation.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is a VPC?
answer: A Virtual Private Cloud — your own logically isolated network inside a provider's cloud, with an address range you choose, your own subnets, route tables, gateways and firewall rules. It is the cloud equivalent of your on-premises LAN.
detail:
Cloud resources need a network to live in. The VPC is that network: it exists in software, but it is configured with the same concepts as a physical one.
How it works
  • You choose the address space: A private CIDR block, typically from RFC 1918. Choosing it carelessly causes overlap with on-premises ranges, which breaks VPN routing later and cannot be changed easily afterwards.
  • Subnets are per availability zone: A subnet lives in exactly one zone. Building a highly available service therefore means creating a subnet in each zone you want to use.
  • Route tables decide what is public: A subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway is a public subnet. One without that route is private. There is no other flag — routing is the definition.
  • It is isolated by default: Nothing reaches a new VPC from outside until you attach a gateway and permit traffic. This default-deny posture is why misconfiguration, rather than the default, causes exposure.
Where you see it
  • Hosting an application tier in cloud with the same segmentation as on-premises
  • Connecting a cloud environment back to the corporate network over VPN
  • Planning non-overlapping IP address space across on-premises and cloud
exam: Know that a VPC is a logically isolated virtual network you control inside a provider's shared infrastructure. Expect subnet and routing detail as a follow-up: public versus private subnet is determined by the route table, not by the IP addresses. Overlapping CIDR ranges breaking a site-to-site VPN is a recurring scenario.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: Internet gateway vs NAT gateway in a cloud VPC.
answer:
Internet gateway: attaches to the VPC and allows bidirectional internet traffic for resources with public IP addresses — this is what makes a subnet public.
NAT gateway: lets instances in a private subnet initiate outbound connections while blocking all inbound.
detail:
Two different requirements: being reachable from the internet, and being able to reach the internet. Cloud designs separate them deliberately.
How it works
  • The internet gateway makes a subnet public: It is attached to the VPC, and a subnet becomes public when its route table points the default route at it. Instances also need a public or elastic IP to be reachable.
  • The NAT gateway is one-way: It sits in a public subnet. Private instances route their default route to it, so they can download patches and call APIs. Connections cannot be initiated inward, because the translation has no mapping until the instance starts one.
  • This is the standard tiering pattern: Load balancers and bastion hosts sit in public subnets behind an internet gateway. Application and database servers sit in private subnets and reach out through the NAT gateway.
  • It is the same NAT concept as on-premises: Many private sources sharing outbound public addresses, with inbound blocked as a side effect of stateful translation.
Where you see it
  • Keeping database and application servers off the public internet while still patching them
  • Placing a public load balancer in front of private application instances
  • Explaining why an instance can reach the internet but cannot be reached
exam: Match direction to gateway: inbound needed → internet gateway; outbound only → NAT gateway. The scenario is usually 'private instances must download updates but must not be reachable from the internet', and the answer is a NAT gateway. A distractor offering an internet gateway would satisfy outbound but wrongly permit inbound as well.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is a security group in cloud networking?
answer: A stateful virtual firewall attached to an instance or network interface. Rules are allow-only; anything not permitted is implicitly denied, and return traffic for an allowed connection is automatically permitted.
detail:
The cloud replacement for a host firewall, and often the only thing standing between an instance and the internet. It is also the control most often misconfigured.
How it works
  • Stateful means return traffic is automatic: Allow inbound TCP 443 and the response is permitted without an outbound rule. You do not write matching rule pairs the way you would on a stateless ACL.
  • Allow rules only: There is no deny rule. Everything is denied unless a rule permits it, so you cannot express 'permit everyone except this address' — that requires a stateless network ACL.
  • Attachment is to the workload, not the subnet: A security group follows the instance or interface. Two instances in the same subnet can have entirely different rules, which is the basis of micro-segmentation in cloud.
  • Rules can reference other security groups: Instead of an IP range, a rule can permit traffic from members of another group — 'allow 3306 from the app-tier group'. Instances can then be added or replaced without editing addresses.
  • 0.0.0.0/0 is the classic mistake: Opening SSH or RDP to the entire internet on a management port is the most common finding in every cloud security audit.
Where you see it
  • Restricting database instances to accept traffic only from the application tier
  • Locking administrative access to a corporate address range or a bastion host
  • Remediating an audit finding about an internet-exposed management port
exam: Two facts get tested: security groups are stateful, and they are allow-only. If a scenario needs an explicit deny for a specific address, the answer is a network ACL, not a security group. Expect the misconfiguration scenario as well, where an exposed instance traces back to an over-permissive inbound rule.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: Network ACL vs security group.
answer:
Security group: stateful, attached to the instance/interface, allow rules only, evaluated as a whole.
Network ACL: stateless, attached to the subnet, supports allow and deny, evaluated in numbered order, and needs explicit rules in both directions.
detail:
Two layers of cloud filtering that answer different questions: which workload may talk, and what may enter or leave a subnet at all.
How it works
  • Scope differs: A network ACL applies to every packet crossing the subnet boundary regardless of instance. A security group applies only to the interface it is attached to, including traffic between two instances in the same subnet.
  • State is the practical difference: Because a NACL is stateless, allowing inbound 443 does not allow the reply. You must also permit the outbound ephemeral port range. Forgetting this is a classic half-working configuration.
  • Only NACLs can deny: Blocking one specific malicious address while permitting everyone else requires a deny rule, which only a network ACL provides.
  • Order matters for NACLs: Rules are numbered and evaluated in order, first match wins. Security group rules have no order; if any rule permits the traffic, it is permitted.
Where you see it
  • Blocking a specific attacking IP range at the subnet edge
  • Defence in depth: a broad NACL at the subnet plus tight security groups per workload
  • Debugging traffic that is allowed inbound but never receives a reply
exam: The contrast is directly examinable: SG = stateful, instance level, allow only; NACL = stateless, subnet level, allow and deny, ordered. The scenario that separates them is 'block one specific IP address' — only a NACL can do it. The second scenario is a one-way connection failure, which points to a missing outbound ephemeral-port rule on a stateless NACL.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is a VPC endpoint (private endpoint / private link)?
answer: A private entrance to a cloud provider service from inside your VPC, so traffic to that service never traverses the public internet and the instances need no public IP, internet gateway or NAT gateway.
detail:
By default, calling a provider's storage or database API means going out to a public endpoint. An endpoint brings that service inside your private network instead.
How it works
  • Traffic stays on the provider's network: The service is reachable through a private address in your VPC. Packets do not leave the provider backbone, which removes exposure and usually removes data transfer charges through a NAT gateway.
  • No internet path is required at all: A fully private subnet with no NAT gateway can still reach object storage or a managed database through an endpoint. That is often the point: eliminating the internet route entirely.
  • Access can be restricted to the endpoint: The service resource can be configured to accept requests only through your endpoint, so even a leaked credential cannot be used from the open internet.
  • Two common forms: A gateway-style endpoint adds a route to a specific service; an interface-style endpoint places a private network interface in your subnet for the service. Both achieve private reachability.
Where you see it
  • Private subnets reaching object storage without a NAT gateway
  • Meeting a requirement that internal data never traverses the public internet
  • Reducing NAT data-processing charges for heavy storage traffic
exam: The exam asks this as a requirement match: 'access a cloud service without traffic crossing the public internet' → VPC endpoint / private link. Distractors are a NAT gateway (still uses the internet path) and a site-to-site VPN (connects your on-premises network, not your VPC to a provider service).

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: Cloud connectivity: site-to-site VPN vs direct connect.
answer:
VPN: an encrypted IPsec tunnel over the public internet — deployable in hours, cheap, but throughput and latency depend on the internet.
Direct connect: a dedicated private circuit from your premises into the provider — consistent bandwidth and latency, higher cost and weeks of lead time.
detail:
Two ways to join your network to your cloud VPC. The choice is between speed of deployment and predictability of performance.
How it works
  • VPN rides the internet you already have: IPsec between your edge firewall and a cloud VPN gateway. No new circuit, no carrier order, and encryption is built in because the path is untrusted.
  • Its performance is whatever the internet gives you: Bandwidth is capped by your internet circuit, latency varies, and encryption adds overhead. Acceptable for management traffic and modest workloads; not for latency-sensitive replication.
  • Direct connect is a private circuit: A cross-connect at a provider colocation facility, delivered by a carrier. Bandwidth is committed, latency is stable, and large transfers cost less per gigabyte.
  • Direct connect is not encrypted by default: It is private, not confidential. Regulated data usually runs an IPsec or MACsec layer over the top, which surprises people who assume private equals secure.
  • Many designs use both: The direct circuit carries production traffic and a VPN stands by as backup, because a single circuit is a single point of failure.
Where you see it
  • Extending a corporate network into a cloud VPC for internal applications
  • Large ongoing data transfer, backups or database replication into cloud
  • A VPN configured as failover for a direct connection
exam: Requirement wording drives the answer. 'Consistent, predictable bandwidth and low latency' → direct connect. 'Quick to set up, low cost, internet acceptable' → site-to-site VPN. The nuance CompTIA likes is that direct connect is private but not encrypted, so a requirement for encryption still means adding a VPN over it.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is NFV?
answer: Network Functions Virtualization — running network functions such as firewalls, routers, load balancers and WAN optimizers as software on general-purpose servers instead of as dedicated hardware appliances.
detail:
A network function is software that historically shipped welded to a specific box. NFV separates the two, so the function can run wherever there is compute.
How it works
  • The function is decoupled from the appliance: A virtual firewall is the same code that ran on the vendor's chassis, running instead on a hypervisor or in cloud. Capability is unchanged; the packaging is not.
  • Deployment becomes an instant operation: Standing up a firewall for a new branch or a new VPC is a software deployment rather than a hardware purchase, shipment and installation. Scaling and tearing down are equally quick.
  • Service chaining becomes possible: Traffic can be steered through an ordered sequence of virtual functions — firewall, then IDS, then load balancer — defined in configuration rather than by cabling.
  • Purpose-built hardware still wins on throughput: ASIC-based appliances handle very high packet rates more efficiently. NFV trades some performance density for flexibility.
  • NFV is not SDN: NFV virtualizes the functions. SDN centralizes the control of forwarding. They are complementary and frequently deployed together, but they are separate ideas.
Where you see it
  • Virtual firewalls and load balancers inside a cloud VPC
  • Branch offices running virtual routing and security functions on one x86 box
  • Service provider environments spinning up per-customer virtual network functions
exam: The likely confusion pair is NFV versus SDN, and the exam does test it. NFV = network functions as software; SDN = separating the control plane from the data plane with a central controller. If the scenario is 'replace physical firewall appliances with software instances', the answer is NFV.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is SDN, and what are its planes?
answer:
Software-Defined Networking separates the decision-making from the forwarding hardware.
Data (forwarding/infrastructure) plane: moves packets.
Control plane: decides where packets should go.
Application/management plane: where policy, orchestration and APIs live.
detail:
In a traditional network every switch runs its own control plane and reaches its own conclusions. SDN pulls that logic into one place so the network can be programmed as a whole.
How it works
  • The data plane is what forwards: It consults a table and moves the frame or packet out an interface. In hardware this is ASIC work, and it stays on the device under SDN — only the decision-making is centralized.
