  • The control plane is the routing and switching logic: Traditionally this is OSPF, BGP and spanning tree running independently on every device, each learning the topology on its own and converging by protocol.
  • SDN centralizes control in a controller: One controller holds a complete view of the topology and programs forwarding tables into the devices. Because it sees everything, it can compute paths no individual device could.
  • The application plane expresses intent: Business or operational policy — 'this application must not traverse this link', 'isolate these workloads' — is applied through the controller rather than translated by hand into per-device configuration.
  • Configuration becomes an API call: Change is made once, centrally, and pushed. That removes per-device drift and makes the network programmable by automation.
Where you see it
  • Data centre fabrics programmed centrally rather than switch by switch
  • Applying a policy change consistently across hundreds of devices
  • Automated provisioning of network paths from an orchestration system
exam: Plane identification is the exam item: 'which plane forwards traffic' → data plane; 'which plane decides the path' → control plane. The defining phrase to recognize is separation of the control plane from the data plane. A distractor may describe NFV, which virtualizes functions rather than separating planes.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: In SDN, what are the northbound and southbound interfaces?
answer:
Northbound: from the controller up to applications and orchestration — usually a REST API, where intent and policy come in.
Southbound: from the controller down to the network devices — protocols like OpenFlow, NETCONF or vendor APIs, where forwarding instructions go out.
detail:
The controller sits in the middle. It receives requirements from software above and programs hardware below, and the two directions use different interfaces.
How it works
  • Northbound carries intent: An orchestration platform or monitoring system calls the controller's API: create this segment, apply this policy, report this state. It describes what is wanted, not per-device commands.
  • Southbound carries instructions: The controller translates intent into forwarding entries and pushes them to switches. OpenFlow is the classic example; NETCONF/YANG and vendor-specific APIs are common in practice.
  • The direction naming is from the controller's viewpoint: Draw the controller in the middle: applications above, devices below. North is up toward software, south is down toward hardware. That picture is all the exam requires.
  • The controller is a single point of failure: Centralizing control means the controller must be highly available. Most implementations run a cluster, and devices typically keep forwarding on last-known state if the controller is unreachable.
Where you see it
  • Automating network provisioning from a cloud orchestration platform
  • Integrating monitoring or security tooling with a network controller via REST
  • Programming data centre switch forwarding tables centrally
exam: Remember the picture rather than the words: northbound = toward applications, southbound = toward devices. If a question names OpenFlow, it is describing a southbound interface. If it names a REST API used by an orchestration tool, that is northbound.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is SD-WAN and what problem does it solve?
answer: Software-defined control over WAN links. It runs multiple transports — MPLS, broadband, LTE/5G — as one logical WAN and steers each application over the best path by policy and live link quality. It solves the cost and rigidity of backhauling all branch traffic through headquarters.
detail:
Branch WAN design assumed applications lived in the corporate data centre. When they moved to SaaS, sending every packet to headquarters first became expensive and slow.
How it works
  • The old model was hairpinning: A branch sent all traffic over MPLS to the data centre, where it was inspected and then sent out to the internet. For a SaaS application that meant a long detour in both directions, and MPLS bandwidth is expensive.
  • SD-WAN allows local internet breakout: Trusted SaaS traffic exits directly at the branch while internal traffic still goes over the private path. That removes the detour and offloads the expensive circuit.
  • Path selection is per application and dynamic: The edge device measures latency, jitter and loss on each transport continuously and moves sessions in real time. Voice can be pinned to the best link while bulk backup uses the cheapest.
  • Cheap links become usable: Broadband and LTE are unreliable individually but acceptable when the device can fail over instantly and encrypt everything, which reduces or removes the MPLS requirement.
  • Central management is the operational win: Policy is defined once in a controller and pushed to every branch, and new sites can be brought up with minimal on-site configuration.
Where you see it
  • Retail and branch networks with dozens or hundreds of small sites
  • Migrating away from expensive MPLS toward broadband with policy-based failover
  • Improving SaaS performance by breaking out to the internet locally
exam: The scenario is nearly always branch offices, SaaS performance, and MPLS cost. The answer is SD-WAN, and the reason is application-aware path selection with local breakout. The distractor is a plain site-to-site VPN, which connects sites but does not choose paths per application or measure link quality.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is VXLAN and what does it solve?
answer: Virtual Extensible LAN — encapsulates Layer 2 frames inside UDP so a Layer 2 segment can stretch across a Layer 3 network. Its 24-bit VNI allows about 16 million segments versus VLAN's 4094, and it is the standard mechanism for data centre interconnect.
detail:
Two limits drove it: VLAN IDs run out in large multitenant data centres, and virtual machines need to keep their addresses when they move between racks or sites separated by routers.
How it works
  • The 12-bit VLAN ID is the first limit: 802.1Q gives 4096 IDs, of which 4094 are usable. A cloud provider with thousands of tenants exhausts that quickly. VXLAN's 24-bit VNI removes the constraint.
  • Encapsulation in UDP is the second answer: The original Ethernet frame is wrapped in UDP/IP and routed normally across the underlay. Any Layer 3 network in between can carry it without understanding it.
  • VTEPs do the work: A VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint — a switch or a hypervisor vSwitch — adds the header on the way in and strips it on the way out. Everything between the VTEPs sees ordinary routed IP traffic.
  • Overlay and underlay: The physical routed network is the underlay; the stretched Layer 2 segments are the overlay. The underlay can use ECMP across all links instead of blocking them with spanning tree.
  • The cost is overhead and MTU: The added headers are roughly 50 bytes, so the underlay needs a larger MTU — jumbo frames — or traffic fragments and performance suffers.
Where you see it
  • Multitenant data centres needing far more than 4094 segments
  • Stretching a subnet between two data centres so VMs can migrate live
  • Spine-and-leaf fabrics using a routed underlay with an overlay for tenants
exam: Memorize the numbers: 24-bit VNI, about 16 million segments, encapsulated in UDP. The comparison card is VLAN's 12-bit, 4094 limit. The scenario is either 'we have run out of VLANs' or 'we need the same Layer 2 segment in two data centres' — both answer VXLAN. Note the MTU consequence, which appears as a troubleshooting twist.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is Zero Trust Architecture?
answer: A model with no implicit trust based on network location. Every request is authenticated, authorized and encrypted regardless of whether it comes from inside or outside, and access is granted at least privilege, per session.
detail:
The old model trusted anything inside the perimeter. Once attackers get inside — and they do — that trust becomes free movement across the whole network.
How it works
  • Location stops being a credential: Sitting on the corporate LAN, or arriving through a VPN, grants nothing on its own. The device and the identity must be verified for every resource request.
  • Verify explicitly, every time: Identity, device posture, and context such as location and time are evaluated at each access decision, not once at login. A session that was valid an hour ago is re-evaluated.
  • Least privilege, narrowly scoped: Access is granted to a specific application or resource for a specific need, not to a network range. This is the difference from a traditional VPN, which typically drops a user onto a subnet.
  • Assume breach: Design as though an attacker is already inside. That drives micro-segmentation, extensive logging and encryption of internal traffic — controls that would look excessive under a perimeter model.
  • A policy engine makes the decision: A policy decision point evaluates the request and a policy enforcement point in the traffic path allows or blocks it. Naming varies, but the split between deciding and enforcing is consistent.
Where you see it
  • Replacing full-tunnel remote-access VPN with per-application access
  • Limiting lateral movement after a workstation compromise
  • Compliance programmes requiring continuous verification rather than perimeter controls
exam: The phrase to recognize is never trust, always verify and the idea that trust is not granted by network location. If a scenario says an attacker moved freely after compromising one internal host, the expected answer is zero trust with micro-segmentation. The distractor is a stronger firewall, which is still a perimeter control.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is micro-segmentation, and how is it different from VLAN segmentation?
answer: Applying security policy per workload rather than per network segment. Traffic between two servers in the same subnet is inspected and permitted or denied individually — something a VLAN boundary, which only filters at the edge, cannot do.
detail:
Traditional segmentation controls traffic between subnets. Once inside a subnet, servers can talk freely, and that is exactly the path lateral movement uses.
How it works
  • VLANs filter only at the boundary: Two servers in VLAN 20 talk directly through the switch. No router or firewall is in the path, so no policy is applied. East-west traffic inside a segment is effectively unrestricted.
  • Micro-segmentation moves the enforcement point to the workload: Policy is attached to the VM, container or interface — through hypervisor-level firewalling, host agents or cloud security groups — so it applies to every flow regardless of subnet.
  • Policy follows the workload: Because the rule is bound to the workload's identity or tags rather than to an IP address, moving or rebuilding the machine does not lose its policy or require renumbering.
  • It is the practical implementation of zero trust inside the data centre: Zero trust says do not trust the internal network; micro-segmentation is how that is enforced between servers rather than only at the user's edge.
  • The hard part is knowing what should be allowed: You must map real application flows first. Deploying deny-by-default without that mapping breaks production, which is why rollouts start in monitor mode.
Where you see it
  • Preventing lateral movement between servers in the same data centre subnet
  • Cloud security groups restricting the app tier to only the database port
  • Isolating payment or medical systems from general workloads for compliance
exam: The exam tests it as the answer to lateral movement. Anchor the contrast: VLANs segment networks; micro-segmentation segments workloads, including inside the same subnet. If the scenario says one compromised server reached every other server on its subnet, VLANs would not have helped and micro-segmentation is the fix.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What are SASE and SSE?
answer:
SASE (Secure Access Service Edge): networking (SD-WAN) and security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) delivered together as a cloud service at the edge, close to the user.
SSE (Security Service Edge): the security half of SASE, without the SD-WAN networking component.
detail:
When both users and applications left the building, backhauling traffic to a data centre firewall stopped making sense. SASE moves inspection to a cloud edge near the user instead.
How it works
  • Users and applications are both outside now: Remote workers reaching SaaS have no reason to route through headquarters. The perimeter model has no natural place to inspect that traffic.
  • SASE inspects at a cloud point of presence: The user connects to the nearest provider edge, where policy is applied, and then goes on to the destination. One policy set covers office, home and mobile users identically.
  • The component list is worth knowing: Secure Web Gateway for internet traffic, Cloud Access Security Broker for SaaS visibility and control, Zero Trust Network Access for per-application access, Firewall as a Service, plus SD-WAN for the branch.
  • SSE is SASE minus SD-WAN: Organizations that already have a WAN solution, or that are mostly remote workers with no branches, adopt the security services alone.
  • It is a convergence, not a new protocol: SASE describes packaging existing functions into one cloud-delivered service with a single policy engine. Recognizing that is enough for the exam.
Where you see it
  • Remote-first organizations replacing VPN concentrators and on-premises web filtering
  • Branch offices needing consistent security with local internet breakout
  • Applying one policy to users regardless of where they connect from
exam: The exam tests the definition and the difference. SASE = SD-WAN + cloud-delivered security; SSE = the security part only. If a question describes converging networking and security into a single cloud service at the edge, it is SASE. If it lists only SWG, CASB and ZTNA with no WAN component, it is SSE.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: How does ZTNA differ from a traditional remote-access VPN?
answer: A VPN authenticates once and places the user on the network, where they can reach whatever routing allows. ZTNA grants access to specific applications only, per session, after verifying identity and device posture — the rest of the network stays invisible.
detail:
The distinction is network access versus application access. A VPN's implicit trust after login is exactly what zero trust removes.
How it works
  • VPN access is broad by default: Once the tunnel is up, the user is an IP address on an internal subnet. Anything not blocked by a firewall rule is reachable, including systems the user has no business touching.
  • ZTNA brokers each application individually: A trust broker authenticates the user and device and then proxies the connection to one authorized application. Other applications are not routed to and are not discoverable.
  • The network is not exposed: Applications typically sit behind an outbound-only connector, so there is no inbound listener for an attacker to scan or exploit. That removes the VPN concentrator as an internet-facing target.
  • Device posture is part of the decision: Patch level, disk encryption and endpoint protection status can gate access, and can be re-evaluated during the session rather than only at connect time.
  • It limits blast radius: A compromised laptop with a VPN can scan the internal network. The same laptop with ZTNA reaches only the applications that identity is authorized for.
Where you see it
  • Contractor and third-party access to a single internal application
  • Replacing an aging VPN concentrator for a mostly remote workforce
  • Reducing lateral movement risk from compromised remote endpoints
exam: Expect ZTNA as the answer when a scenario requires giving an outside party access to one application without exposing the internal network. The distractor is a site-to-site or remote-access VPN, which works but grants network-level reach. ZTNA is also the access component listed inside SASE.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is Infrastructure as Code?
answer: Defining infrastructure and network configuration in version-controlled files that a tool applies, rather than configuring devices by hand. Terraform, Ansible, and cloud templates are typical. It gives repeatability, peer review, rollback and drift detection.
detail:
Manual configuration produces environments nobody can reproduce and changes nobody can explain. IaC makes the desired state a file, which can be reviewed and re-applied.
How it works
  • The file is the source of truth: The intended state lives in a repository. Rebuilding an environment means applying the file, not following a runbook and hoping the result matches.
  • Version control brings software practice to infrastructure: Every change is a commit with an author, a reason and a diff. Peer review happens before the change lands, and rolling back means reverting a commit.
  • Idempotency makes re-running safe: Applying the same definition twice produces the same result. The tool compares actual state to desired state and changes only the difference, so re-application is a repair rather than a duplication.
  • Drift detection catches manual edits: When someone changes a device by hand, the next run reports the difference between reality and the definition. That is how configuration drift is found rather than discovered during an outage.
  • Declarative versus procedural: Declarative tools describe the end state and work out the steps. Procedural tools list the steps. Most network and cloud IaC is declarative.
Where you see it
  • Building identical dev, test and production environments in cloud
  • Standardizing switch and firewall configuration across branch sites
  • Recovering an environment after a failure by re-applying the definitions
exam: Recognition plus benefits is what is tested: version-controlled, repeatable, automated configuration. The scenario is usually inconsistent environments or undocumented manual changes, and the expected answer is IaC with configuration drift as the named problem. Distractors offer better documentation or change tickets, which describe the process rather than solving reproducibility.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisor.
answer:
Type 1 (bare metal): runs directly on the hardware — ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, Xen. Used in production.
Type 2 (hosted): runs as an application on top of an existing OS — VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels. Used for labs and desktops.
detail:
The distinction is whether there is a general-purpose operating system between the hypervisor and the hardware.
How it works
  • Type 1 owns the hardware: The hypervisor is the operating system. There is no host OS competing for resources or adding a failure and attack surface, so performance and isolation are better.
  • Type 2 is a program on your desktop: It requests resources from the host OS like any other application. If the host OS crashes, patches or reboots, every VM goes with it.
  • Overhead follows the layering: Type 2 adds a translation layer, so it is slower. That is acceptable for testing and irrelevant for a lab, and unacceptable for a production database.
  • Attack surface differs: A Type 1 hypervisor is small and purpose-built. A Type 2 sits on Windows or macOS with browsers and everything else, any of which can be compromised and used to reach the VMs.
Where you see it
  • Data centre and cloud virtualization hosts running Type 1
  • Running a lab topology or a test VM on an engineer's laptop with Type 2
  • Explaining why a production workload should not run on a hosted hypervisor
exam: This is a straightforward recall item, usually asked by naming a product. Anchor on: ESXi and Hyper-V are Type 1; VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are Type 2. The trap is the phrase 'bare metal', which always means Type 1. Expect a scenario asking which is appropriate for production — Type 1.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: What is a virtual switch (vSwitch)?
answer: A software Layer 2 switch inside a hypervisor that connects virtual machine NICs to each other and to the host's physical uplinks. It supports VLAN tagging, port groups, and policies such as security and traffic shaping.
detail:
Virtual machines need a switch just as physical servers do. When the servers became software, so did the switch they plug into.
How it works
  • VM-to-VM traffic may never leave the host: Two VMs on the same host and same port group are switched in memory. No packet reaches the physical network, which means physical monitoring and firewalls never see that traffic. This is a real blind spot.
  • Port groups carry policy and VLAN: A port group defines a VLAN ID and a set of policies. Attaching a VM to a port group is the virtual equivalent of patching it into a configured access port.
  • Uplinks connect to the physical network: The host's physical NICs are the vSwitch's uplinks, usually configured as 802.1Q trunks so multiple VLANs reach the VMs, with teaming for redundancy and load distribution.
  • It is not a full managed switch: A standard vSwitch does not participate in spanning tree and does not learn MAC addresses from the uplink the way a physical switch does — it knows its VMs' addresses directly. Distributed virtual switches add central management across many hosts.
Where you see it
  • Connecting VMs to specific VLANs through port groups
  • Explaining why an IDS on the physical network misses VM-to-VM traffic
  • Troubleshooting a VM with no connectivity due to a wrong port group or untrunked uplink
exam: Two testable points: a vSwitch is a Layer 2 software switch inside the hypervisor, and traffic between VMs on the same host may never traverse the physical network, which is why virtual-layer monitoring or micro-segmentation is required. A common troubleshooting scenario is a VM with no network access because the physical uplink is not trunked for its VLAN.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::09 Cloud, Virtualization & SDN
front: Containers vs virtual machines.
answer:
VMs each run a full guest OS on a hypervisor — heavier, slower to start, stronger isolation.
Containers share the host's kernel and package only the application and its dependencies — seconds to start, far denser, a weaker isolation boundary.
detail:
Both isolate workloads, but at different layers. A VM virtualizes hardware; a container isolates processes within one operating system.
How it works
  • The kernel is the dividing line: Every VM has its own kernel, drivers and system services, costing gigabytes and a boot cycle. Containers use the host kernel, so an image can be tens of megabytes and start in under a second.
  • Density and start time drive adoption: A host runs far more containers than VMs, and containers can be created and destroyed constantly. That is what makes them suitable for elastic, short-lived workloads.
  • Isolation is weaker: A hypervisor boundary is a much stronger separation than kernel namespaces and cgroups. A kernel vulnerability can affect every container on the host, which is why untrusted multitenant workloads often still get VMs.
  • Containers must share the kernel's OS family: Linux containers need a Linux kernel. You cannot run a Windows container on a Linux kernel without a VM underneath it — which is exactly what desktop container tooling does.
  • Networking is virtualized per container: Each container gets a virtual interface on a host bridge or overlay network, with port mapping or a service mesh handling reachability. Orchestration platforms manage that at scale.
Where you see it
  • Microservices deployed and scaled independently
  • CI/CD pipelines building and testing in disposable environments
  • Running many instances of a lightweight service on a single host
exam: The exam asks for the core difference: containers share the host OS kernel; VMs each include a full guest OS. Consequences follow from that — faster start, smaller footprint, higher density, weaker isolation. The distractor usually claims containers include their own OS, which is wrong; they include the application and its dependencies only.

front: The CIA triad — name each element and one concrete control that delivers it.
answer:
Confidentiality — encryption (TLS, IPsec, full-disk).
Integrity — hashing and digital signatures (SHA-256, code signing).
Availability — redundancy (HA pairs, backups, UPS, load balancing).
detail:
The three properties every security control is trying to protect. Naming which one a control serves is how you decide whether a proposed fix actually addresses the problem described.
How it works
  • Confidentiality is about who can read it: Encryption makes the data unreadable without the key; access control decides who gets the key or the file in the first place. A stolen encrypted laptop is a confidentiality control working correctly.
  • Integrity is about whether it changed: A hash computed before and after transmission proves the bits are identical. A digital signature adds proof of who produced them. Integrity does not hide the data, and encryption alone does not prove the data is unaltered.
  • Availability is about being there when needed: Redundant links, redundant power, clustering, backups and DDoS mitigation all serve availability. A DoS attack is purely an availability attack — nothing is read and nothing is altered.
  • Controls usually serve one leg strongly: TLS gives confidentiality and integrity but nothing for availability. RAID gives availability but zero confidentiality. Matching the control to the leg is the whole exercise.
Where you see it
  • Classifying a proposed control during a security design review
  • Deciding what a given incident actually damaged
  • Justifying why encrypted backups are needed and not just backups
exam: The exam asks which element of the triad an event or control maps to. A DDoS attack, a failed hard drive and a severed fibre are all availability. Someone altering a database record without permission is integrity, not confidentiality — the classic trap is picking confidentiality because the data was 'compromised'. Watch for a fourth distractor such as authentication or non-repudiation, which are not part of the triad.

front: Vulnerability vs threat vs exploit vs risk — define each and their relationship.
answer:
Vulnerability: the weakness itself.
Threat: the actor or event that could act on it.
Exploit: the actual technique or code that uses it.
Risk: likelihood x impact — the chance a threat successfully exploits the vulnerability.
detail:
Four words that mean different things and are used interchangeably in casual speech. CompTIA tests exactly this distinction, so learn them as a chain rather than as four separate definitions.
How it works
  • Vulnerability is a property of your system: An unpatched SMB service, a default admin password, an open switch port in a lobby. It exists whether or not anyone ever attacks it, and you can enumerate it with a vulnerability scanner.
  • Threat is external to the system: A ransomware crew, a careless employee, a flood. Threats exist whether or not you are vulnerable. You cannot remove a threat, only reduce what it can reach.
  • Exploit is the mechanism connecting them: The specific packet, script or social manipulation that turns a weakness into an outcome. A vulnerability with no known exploit is still real, just harder to use.
  • Risk is the calculated exposure: Risk needs both sides: a serious vulnerability that no threat can reach is low risk, and a determined threat against a patched system is also low risk. Risk is what you manage; you accept it, avoid it, transfer it via insurance, or mitigate it with controls.
Where you see it
  • Reading a vulnerability scan report and prioritizing what to fix first
  • Writing a risk register entry after an audit finding
  • Explaining to management why a critical CVE on an isolated lab host is not the top priority
exam: The exam gives a scenario sentence and asks which term it describes. 'An unpatched web server' is a vulnerability. 'A hacking group targeting the industry' is a threat. 'The proof-of-concept code published for that CVE' is an exploit. 'The likelihood that group uses that code against your server and what it would cost' is risk. The trap is that all four answers appear in every one of these questions.

front: What is defense in depth and what assumption is it built on?
answer: Layering multiple independent controls so no single failure is fatal. It assumes every layer will eventually fail.
detail:
A design philosophy, not a product. You stack controls of different kinds so that defeating one does not hand over the network.
How it works
  • Layers must be independent: Two firewalls from the same vendor running the same rules are one layer, not two, because the same bug or the same misconfiguration defeats both. Genuine depth mixes control types: perimeter filtering, internal segmentation, host protection, encryption and monitoring.
  • Each layer buys time and visibility: A control that only slows an attacker still has value, because detection and response happen in that window. Depth is as much about increasing the number of chances to notice as about blocking.
  • It covers administrative and physical layers too: Policies, background checks, user training, locked wiring closets and badge access are layers. The exam counts a security awareness program as a genuine control, not as filler.
  • It is the opposite of a hard shell: The failure mode it fixes is the crunchy-outside, soft-inside network where one phishing click gives an attacker free lateral movement across a flat LAN.
Where you see it
  • Justifying internal segmentation on a network that already has a perimeter firewall
  • Designing controls around a public-facing web application
  • Post-incident review asking why one compromised workstation reached the domain controller
exam: Scenario questions describe an organization with a strong firewall and nothing else, then ask what principle is missing — the answer is defense in depth. Do not confuse it with redundancy: redundancy is duplicate identical components for availability, defense in depth is different control types for security. Micro-segmentation and zero trust are how depth is applied inside the perimeter.

front: What is the principle of least privilege, and what does it look like when done properly?
answer: Grant every user, service and device the minimum access needed to do the job, and nothing more — including for how long.
detail:
The single control that most limits the blast radius of a compromised account. It is a policy, enforced through access control mechanisms.
How it works
  • It applies to accounts you never think about: Service accounts, backup agents, monitoring pollers and vendor support logins accumulate rights and are rarely reviewed. A monitoring account with domain admin is the classic finding.
  • Administrators need two accounts: A standard account for email and browsing, and a separate privileged account used only for administration. That way a phishing click executes as a non-privileged user.
  • Privilege must expire: Access granted for a project, an audit or an on-call rotation needs an end date. Privilege creep is what happens when a user transfers departments and keeps both sets of rights.
  • Enforcement usually means RBAC: Least privilege is the goal; role-based access control is the practical mechanism that makes it repeatable and auditable at scale.
Where you see it
  • Setting up a helpdesk role that can reset passwords but not create accounts
  • Restricting a vendor's remote access to one host on one port for one week
  • Reviewing accounts after a user changes departments
exam: The exam pairs least privilege with a scenario about excessive rights — a user who can reach a payroll share they do not need, or an admin browsing the web as domain admin. The distractor is separation of duties, which is different: that splits a sensitive task across two people so no one person can complete it alone. Least privilege limits scope; separation of duties limits completion.

front: What does zero trust mean in security terms, and what does it replace?
answer: No implicit trust from network location. Every request is authenticated, authorized and encrypted regardless of whether it comes from inside or outside the perimeter.
detail:
A response to the failure of perimeter-based security. Being on the corporate LAN, or on the VPN, stops being evidence that a device or user is legitimate.
How it works
  • It kills the trusted-inside assumption: Traditional design treats internal subnets as trusted and everything else as untrusted. Zero trust says an internal host is exactly as suspect as an internet host, because attackers and infected laptops live inside too.
  • Verification is per request, not per session: Identity, device posture, location and time are evaluated on each access attempt. A laptop that fails a posture check mid-session loses access rather than keeping it until logout.
  • It is built from controls you already know: MFA for identity, NAC and posture assessment for the device, micro-segmentation to enforce host-to-host policy, encryption everywhere, and continuous logging. Zero trust is the architecture that ties them together, not a box you buy.
  • Least privilege is the enforcement rule: Once a request is verified, access is granted to that one resource, not to the whole subnet. This is why zero trust and micro-segmentation appear together.
Where you see it
  • Replacing a flat VPN that dumps remote users onto the internal LAN
  • Securing SaaS access for a workforce with no fixed office
  • Limiting east-west movement inside a data centre
exam: Expect the phrase 'never trust, always verify' in the stem or the answer. The tested contrast is against the perimeter or castle-and-moat model. If a scenario says an attacker who got onto the internal network moved freely between servers, the design fix is zero trust with micro-segmentation, not a bigger perimeter firewall.

front: Authentication vs authorization vs accounting — what does each answer?
answer:
Authentication: who are you?
Authorization: what are you allowed to do?
Accounting: what did you actually do, and for how long?
detail:
The three phases of every access control system, in order. AAA protocols such as RADIUS and TACACS+ exist to carry all three.
How it works
  • Authentication proves identity: Username plus password, certificate, token code or biometric. It happens first and it produces nothing but a yes or no on identity — it says nothing about permissions.
  • Authorization applies policy to that identity: Once the system knows you are a helpdesk technician, it decides you may reset passwords but may not touch the firewall. The same identity can be authorized differently by different systems.
  • Accounting is the audit record: Login time, logout time, commands entered, bytes transferred, resources touched. It supports billing, capacity reporting, forensics and non-repudiation. RADIUS uses a separate port and separate messages for it.
  • The three can live in different places: TACACS+ deliberately separates them so you can authenticate against a central server while authorizing per device. RADIUS bundles authentication and authorization into one exchange.
Where you see it
  • Configuring a switch so admins log in with domain credentials and every command is logged
  • Explaining an audit finding that logins are tracked but commands are not
  • Reading a RADIUS accounting record to see how long a user was on the wireless network
exam: The exam tests this by describing an activity and asking which A it is. Logging the commands a network administrator typed is accounting. Deciding that a user may read but not write a share is authorization. The most common trap is answering authentication for a scenario that is clearly about permissions — read whether the identity was already established.

front: Name the authentication factor types with an example of each.
answer:
Something you know — password, PIN.
Something you have — smart card, token, phone.
Something you are — fingerprint, iris, face.
Attributes often listed alongside: somewhere you are (location), something you do (behaviour).
detail:
The category system behind multifactor authentication. The categories matter more than the examples because MFA is defined by using different categories.
How it works
  • Something you know is the weakest: Knowledge can be guessed, phished, reused across sites, shoulder-surfed or cracked offline from a stolen hash. Every other factor exists because this one keeps failing.
  • Something you have needs physical possession: A hardware token, a smart card, or a phone running an authenticator app. Theft is the failure mode, and SMS codes are the weak version because SIM swapping steals possession remotely.
  • Something you are cannot be changed after a breach: Biometrics are convenient and hard to share, but you cannot reissue a fingerprint. They also fail open or closed at rates measured as false acceptance and false rejection.
  • Location and behaviour are attributes, not classic factors: Somewhere you are underpins geofencing and conditional access. Something you do covers signature dynamics and typing rhythm. CompTIA lists them, but the three classic categories are what MFA is built from.
Where you see it
  • Choosing a second factor for VPN access
  • Explaining why a smart card plus PIN is stronger than two passwords
  • Deciding whether a proposed login flow meets an MFA requirement
exam: The exam gives a pair of credentials and asks whether it qualifies as MFA, so classify each item by category first. A smart card (have) plus a PIN (know) is MFA. A fingerprint (are) plus a password (know) is MFA. A password plus a security question is not MFA — both are something you know.

front: Why is a password plus a security question not multifactor authentication?
answer: Both are something you know. MFA requires two or more credentials from different factor categories, not just two credentials.
detail:
The most commonly misunderstood definition in the security domain. Adding a second secret adds friction, not a second factor.
How it works
  • Multiple means multiple categories: Two knowledge items fail to the same attack. A phishing page that captures a password can capture the security answer on the next screen, and a breach dump exposes both.
  • 2FA is exactly two, MFA is two or more: The terms are used interchangeably on the exam, and both require the categories to differ. Three factors is still MFA.
  • This is why push and TOTP work: A time-based one-time code from an authenticator app is something you have, because possession of the enrolled device is what generates it. That is a genuinely different category from the password.
  • MFA is the mitigation for credential theft: Stolen, sprayed, stuffed or phished passwords all stop being sufficient. It is the standard answer to any scenario about compromised credentials being reused.
Where you see it
  • Auditing whether an application's 'two-step' login really meets an MFA policy
  • Selecting a control after a credential stuffing incident
  • Rolling out authenticator apps to replace SMS codes
exam: This is a guaranteed question in some form. The two classic non-MFA distractors are password plus security question and password plus PIN — both knowledge. If a question asks for the best defence against stolen or reused credentials, the answer is MFA, ahead of longer passwords or more frequent rotation.

front: What is SSO, and what is its main security trade-off?
answer: Authenticate once and gain access to many applications without logging in again. The trade-off: one compromised credential opens everything, so SSO must be paired with MFA.
detail:
A usability and administration control with security side effects in both directions. Fewer passwords means fewer weak reused passwords, but also one very valuable password.
How it works
  • It removes the password sprawl problem: Users with fifteen application passwords write them down, reuse them and never rotate them. Centralizing authentication removes that behaviour and gives one place to disable an account on termination.
  • The applications never see the password: The user authenticates to the identity provider. Applications receive a signed assertion or token that vouches for the identity. That is why SAML and OAuth-style flows exist.
  • The identity provider becomes critical infrastructure: If it is down, nobody logs in anywhere. It needs redundancy, and it needs the strongest authentication you have in front of it.
  • SSO is not the same as using the same password everywhere: Same-password reuse across systems is credential sharing, not SSO. In real SSO there is one authentication event and a trust relationship carrying the result.
Where you see it
  • Logging into a workstation and getting mail, file shares and intranet without re-authenticating
  • Federating with a cloud provider so staff use corporate credentials for SaaS
  • Disabling one account on termination and immediately cutting off every application
exam: The exam pairs SSO with SAML and with MFA. If a scenario complains that users have too many passwords, the answer is SSO. If it asks what mitigates the risk that SSO creates, the answer is MFA in front of the identity provider. Do not confuse SSO with the identical-credentials-everywhere setup, which is the distractor.

front: What is SAML and what are its two roles?
answer: Security Assertion Markup Language — an XML standard for exchanging authentication and authorization assertions between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). It is the basis of browser-based federated SSO.
detail:
The protocol that lets one organization vouch for a user to another organization. It is what makes SSO work across company or cloud boundaries.
How it works
  • The assertion is a signed XML document: The IdP builds an assertion saying this user authenticated at this time with these attributes, signs it with its private key, and the SP validates the signature against the IdP's certificate. The SP never sees the password.
  • Trust is established in advance: Administrators exchange metadata and certificates between IdP and SP before any user logs in. That pre-established trust is what the assertion relies on.
  • It is browser-centric: The classic flow redirects the browser from the SP to the IdP and back, carrying the assertion. This is why SAML dominates web application SSO and is not used for logging into a switch.
  • Certificate expiry is the usual failure: When federated logins break for everyone at once on a specific date, the signing certificate on either side has expired. It is a scheduled-renewal task, not a user problem.
Where you see it
  • Signing into a cloud HR or CRM platform with corporate credentials
  • Federating a university identity system with an external research portal
  • Providing customer SSO into a hosted application
exam: N10-009 lists SAML under identity and access management, so know it as the XML-based federated SSO standard. The contrast set is SAML for web SSO, RADIUS for network access, TACACS+ for device administration, LDAP for directory lookups and Kerberos for Windows domain authentication. Picking RADIUS for a SaaS web-login scenario is the common error.

front: What is LDAP, what ports does it use, and what is it actually for?
answer: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol — TCP/UDP 389, secure as LDAPS on TCP 636. It queries and modifies a directory of users, groups, computers and their attributes.
detail:
A directory access protocol, not an authentication protocol in the AAA sense. Applications use it to look up who someone is and what groups they are in, and can also use it to verify a password by binding.
How it works
  • The directory is a hierarchical tree: Entries are addressed by distinguished name, built from components such as CN for common name, OU for organizational unit and DC for domain component. Active Directory is an LDAP-compatible directory with Kerberos and other services layered on.
  • Authentication happens through a bind: A simple bind sends the distinguished name and password to the server. Over plain LDAP that password crosses the network readable, which is exactly why LDAPS or LDAP with StartTLS exists.
  • It answers group membership questions: Most applications use LDAP after authentication to decide authorization: is this user in the VPN-Users group. That makes it the lookup half of many identity designs.
  • 389 versus 636 is the tested pair: 389 is cleartext LDAP, 636 is LDAP over SSL/TLS. Global Catalog in Active Directory adds 3268 and 3269, which is a step beyond core Network+ but appears in port lists.
Where you see it
  • An application checking a user's group membership before granting admin rights
  • A network appliance validating logins against Active Directory
  • Directory-integrated address books in mail clients
exam: The exam tests the port pair and the difference between a directory and an authentication protocol. If the scenario is 'credentials are visible in a packet capture during directory authentication', the fix is LDAPS on 636. Do not answer LDAP for device administration logging — that is TACACS+ — or for Wi-Fi authentication, which is RADIUS.

front: RADIUS — transport, ports, what it encrypts, and where it is used?
answer: UDP 1812 authentication and 1813 accounting (legacy 1645/1646). Encrypts only the password field. Combines authentication and authorization in one exchange. Open standard.
detail:
The default AAA protocol for network access: wireless, wired 802.1X, VPN and dial-up. It is an IETF standard, so every vendor implements it.
How it works
  • Only the password is protected: The shared secret between the client and server is used to obscure the User-Password attribute. Usernames, authorization attributes and accounting data travel readable in the packet, which is a real weakness on an untrusted management path.
  • Authentication and authorization arrive together: The Access-Accept message carries the authorization attributes with it — the VLAN to assign, session timeout, filter ID. You cannot authenticate a user without also receiving their authorization in the same response.
  • Accounting is separate messages on a separate port: Accounting-Start and Accounting-Stop on 1813 record session duration and volume. This is what generates wireless session reports.
  • The RADIUS client is the network device: The switch, AP, VPN concentrator or firewall is the RADIUS client. The end user's laptop never talks RADIUS — in 802.1X it speaks EAPoL to the switch, which relays to RADIUS.
Where you see it
  • 802.1X authentication on wired switch ports and WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise wireless
  • VPN concentrators validating remote users against a central identity store
  • Producing per-user session accounting for guest or student networks
exam: The port numbers and the 'encrypts only the password' fact are both directly tested. The exam's favourite comparison is RADIUS versus TACACS+: if the scenario is about network access for users, choose RADIUS; if it is about administering network devices with per-command control, choose TACACS+. Watch for answers offering the legacy 1645/1646 pair as a distractor.

front: TACACS+ — transport, port, what it encrypts, and where it is used?
answer: TCP 49. Encrypts the entire payload. Separates authentication, authorization and accounting into independent functions. Cisco-developed.
detail:
The AAA protocol built for administering network devices. Its separation of the three A's is what allows per-command authorization.
How it works
  • Full payload encryption: Everything after the header is encrypted with the shared secret, including usernames and the commands being authorized. RADIUS protects only the password field, which is the tested contrast.
  • Separation enables per-command authorization: Because authorization is its own exchange, the device can ask the server about every single command the administrator types, in real time, and the server can approve show commands while denying configure terminal.
  • TCP gives reliable delivery: TCP 49 means retransmission and connection state are handled by the transport. RADIUS uses UDP and has to handle retries itself.
  • It is Cisco-originated but widely supported: TACACS+ is not compatible with earlier TACACS or XTACACS. Non-Cisco vendors and open-source servers implement it, but it remains associated with device administration in Cisco environments.
Where you see it
  • Central login for switch and router administrators with command-level control
  • Meeting an audit requirement to log every configuration command by username
  • Granting junior staff read-only CLI access on all devices from one policy
exam: The three tested facts are TCP 49, full-payload encryption, and separation of AAA. The exam scenario that points here is 'administrators must authenticate centrally and every command must be authorized and logged individually'. RADIUS is the distractor and cannot do per-command authorization because it bundles authorization into the authentication response.

front: What is Kerberos, what port does it use, and why is time so important to it?
answer: Ticket-based network authentication using symmetric keys — port 88. The KDC issues a TGT after login, which is exchanged for service tickets. Tickets are timestamped, so clocks must be within about 5 minutes.
detail:
The default authentication protocol for Windows Active Directory domains. It provides mutual authentication and avoids sending the password across the network at all.
How it works
  • The KDC has two parts: The Authentication Service verifies the user at logon and issues a Ticket Granting Ticket. The Ticket Granting Service later exchanges that TGT for service tickets to individual resources. In Active Directory both run on every domain controller.
  • The password never crosses the wire: The client proves knowledge of the password by decrypting material encrypted with a key derived from it. That is why passive sniffing of a Kerberos logon yields no reusable password.
  • Tickets expire and clocks must agree: Timestamps are what stop an attacker replaying a captured ticket. If a client's clock drifts beyond the allowed skew, commonly five minutes, authentication fails outright. This is why domain members must sync to the same NTP source.
  • It provides mutual authentication: The service also proves its identity to the client, which defeats an attacker who simply stands up an impostor server with the right name.
Where you see it
  • Windows domain logon and access to domain file shares and SQL servers
  • Diagnosing a workstation that cannot log in after its CMOS battery died
  • Single sign-on inside an Active Directory forest
exam: Two things are tested: port 88, and the time dependency. A scenario where domain logons fail on one machine whose clock is wrong by ten minutes is a Kerberos clock-skew question, and the fix is NTP synchronization. Do not confuse the Kerberos ticket model with RADIUS or with SAML assertions; Kerberos is symmetric-key and LAN-oriented, SAML is XML and web-oriented.

front: Compare RADIUS, TACACS+, LDAP, Kerberos and SAML — one line of use case each.
answer:
RADIUS: UDP 1812/1813, network access (Wi-Fi, 802.1X, VPN).
TACACS+: TCP 49, device administration with per-command control.
LDAP: TCP 389 / 636, directory lookup of users and groups.
Kerberos: port 88, Windows domain ticket authentication.
SAML: XML assertions, federated web SSO to cloud apps.
detail:
These five appear together in the objectives and are constantly swapped as distractors. The fastest way to answer is to identify what is being logged into, not what is being proven.
How it works
  • Match on the target of the login: Wireless or a switch port for a user means RADIUS. A router's CLI means TACACS+. A cloud web application means SAML. A domain file share means Kerberos. A group membership lookup means LDAP.
  • Encryption scope separates the two AAA protocols: RADIUS protects only the password field; TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload. That fact alone resolves most RADIUS-versus-TACACS+ questions about sensitive command data.
  • Only TACACS+ splits the three A's: Per-command authorization is impossible in RADIUS because authorization rides along with the Access-Accept. If a question mentions authorizing individual commands, it is TACACS+.
  • LDAP is not really an AAA protocol: It is the directory the others often consult. Active Directory combines an LDAP directory with Kerberos authentication, which is why both appear in the same environment.
Where you see it
  • Selecting an authentication back end during a network design
  • Reading an exam scenario and eliminating three of four answers immediately
  • Explaining why the wireless controller and the switch CLI use different servers
exam: Expect at least one question that hinges purely on this table. The most frequently missed pairing is TACACS+ for device administration versus RADIUS for end-user network access. The second most missed is picking RADIUS or LDAP when the scenario clearly describes browser-based sign-on to an external cloud service, which is SAML.

front: 802.1X — what does it do, and name its three roles.
answer: Port-based network access control. Supplicant (client software) → Authenticator (switch or AP) → Authentication server (RADIUS). The port passes nothing but EAPoL until authentication succeeds.
detail:
The standard that turns a physical switch port or a wireless association into an authenticated event. It is the enforcement point behind most NAC deployments.
How it works
  • The port has two states: Before authentication the port is unauthorized and drops all traffic except EAP over LAN frames. After a successful Access-Accept the port is authorized and forwards normally. Plugging a laptop into a wall jack no longer gets you on the network by itself.
  • EAPoL runs on the local link only: The supplicant speaks EAP over LAN to the authenticator. The authenticator repackages those EAP messages inside RADIUS and forwards them to the authentication server. The client and the RADIUS server never talk directly.
  • The authenticator is a relay, not a decision maker: The switch does not know any passwords or certificates. It enforces whatever the RADIUS server returns, including dynamic VLAN assignment or a downloadable ACL delivered in the Access-Accept.
  • Devices with no supplicant need a fallback: Printers, cameras and badge readers cannot run 802.1X. MAC Authentication Bypass or a guest/restricted VLAN handles them, which is a deliberate weakening because MAC addresses are spoofable.
Where you see it
  • Requiring authentication on every wired port in a public-facing building
  • WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise wireless where each user has their own credentials
  • Assigning a user to a VLAN dynamically based on their identity
exam: Memorize the three role names and that the client-to-switch protocol is EAPoL. A scenario about someone plugging an unauthorized laptop into a conference room jack is answered by 802.1X. The distractor is port security, which limits MAC addresses but authenticates nobody. Also expect 'which device is the authenticator' — it is the switch or access point, never the RADIUS server and never the laptop.

front: EAP-TLS vs PEAP — what is the difference in credentials?
answer:
EAP-TLS: certificates on both sides — mutual certificate authentication, no passwords. Strongest, needs a PKI.
PEAP: a server-side certificate only, which builds a TLS tunnel, and the user's password is sent inside it.
detail:
EAP is a framework, not one protocol, and 802.1X carries whichever method you choose. The choice decides what credential the user needs and what an attacker can steal.
How it works
  • EAP-TLS removes the password entirely: Every client holds a certificate issued by your CA and the server holds one too. Nothing phishable is transmitted. The cost is running a PKI and enrolling every device, including reissuing on expiry.
  • PEAP protects a password with a tunnel: The client validates the server's certificate, builds an encrypted tunnel, then runs an inner method such as MSCHAPv2 with the username and password. It is far easier to deploy because only the server needs a certificate.
  • Server certificate validation is the load-bearing step: If the client is configured to skip validation or the user clicks through a warning, an evil twin can present its own certificate and capture the inner credentials. Configuring clients to trust only your CA and your server name is what actually stops that.
  • EAP-TTLS and EAP-FAST fill the same slot: EAP-TTLS also tunnels an inner method with a server certificate. EAP-FAST is Cisco's certificate-less tunnel using a Protected Access Credential.
Where you see it
  • Choosing an enterprise wireless authentication method during a WPA3-Enterprise rollout
  • Hardening laptops against evil twin credential capture
  • Explaining why the Wi-Fi broke for everyone the day the RADIUS certificate expired
exam: Network+ tests this lightly but consistently through the WPA-Enterprise angle. If a question asks for the most secure wireless authentication, the answer is EAP-TLS with client certificates. If it asks how a client avoids handing credentials to an evil twin, the answer is validating the server certificate, not a stronger password.

front: What is role-based access control, and why is it used instead of per-user permissions?
answer: Permissions are attached to roles, and users are assigned to roles. Access follows the job function, so it is consistent, repeatable and auditable.
detail:
The practical mechanism most organizations use to implement least privilege. It changes the question from 'what should this person have' to 'what should this job have'.
How it works
  • Two mappings instead of one: Permissions map to roles once, and users map to roles as they join, move or leave. Adding a tenth helpdesk technician is one role assignment rather than a fresh set of hand-built permissions.
  • It makes reviews possible: An auditor can inspect a dozen role definitions instead of thousands of individual ACL entries. Drift is visible because a user either is or is not in a role.
  • It fixes privilege creep on transfer: When a user changes departments you remove the old role and add the new one. With per-user permissions the old rights are invisible and simply stay.
  • Contrast with the other models: Mandatory access control uses labels and clearances set by the system. Discretionary access control lets the data owner decide. Attribute-based control evaluates properties such as department, device and time at request time.
Where you see it
  • Building helpdesk, network admin and read-only auditor roles on network devices
  • Group-based file share permissions in Active Directory
  • Onboarding and offboarding staff without hand-editing permissions
exam: The exam pairs RBAC directly with least privilege: least privilege is the principle, RBAC is the implementation. A scenario about users accumulating rights as they move between departments, or about permissions being inconsistent between people doing the same job, is answered by RBAC. The distractors are MAC and DAC, which are about who decides, not about grouping by job.

front: What is time-based authentication?
answer: Tying access to time. Two forms: restricting logins to permitted hours or days, and one-time codes valid only for a short window (TOTP, typically 30 seconds).
detail:
A control that shrinks the window in which a stolen credential is useful, and that flags activity at times a legitimate user would never work.
How it works
  • Time-of-day restrictions limit the attack window: An account allowed to log in only 07:00 to 19:00 on weekdays is unusable during the hours attackers most like. It also generates a clean alert when someone tries at 03:00.
  • TOTP codes expire almost immediately: The authenticator app and the server share a seed and both compute a code from the current time. A code captured by a keylogger or shoulder surfer is worthless within seconds, which is what makes it a good second factor.
  • Both depend on synchronized clocks: TOTP fails if the phone's clock drifts far from the server's. Time restrictions and log timestamps are meaningless if devices disagree, which is why NTP is a security dependency.
  • It is often combined with other conditions: Conditional access policies commonly evaluate time together with location and device posture, so an unusual hour plus an unusual country blocks or challenges the login.
Where you see it
  • Restricting contractor and vendor accounts to business hours only
  • Rolling out authenticator apps as the second MFA factor
  • Investigating a login recorded outside a user's permitted schedule
exam: N10-009 lists time-based authentication explicitly under IAM, so recognize both meanings. If the scenario says a contractor should not be able to log in at night, the control is a time-based restriction. If it describes a six-digit code that changes every thirty seconds, that is TOTP, and it counts as something you have, not something you know.

front: What is geofencing, and what factor category does it map to?
answer: Allowing or denying access based on physical location, using GPS or IP geolocation. It maps to somewhere you are.
detail:
A location-aware boundary drawn around where access is legitimate. It blocks whole categories of remote attack without touching credentials.
How it works
  • Two very different location sources: Mobile devices report GPS coordinates, which are precise but spoofable on a rooted device. Server-side controls usually use IP geolocation, which is coarser and defeated by a VPN or proxy but requires no client cooperation.
  • It is usually deny-by-default on countries: The common deployment blocks authentication attempts originating outside the countries where the organization operates. That alone removes an enormous volume of credential stuffing traffic.
  • It can enable as well as restrict: A warehouse app that only functions inside the facility, or a mobile device that unlocks a corporate profile only on site, uses the same mechanism in the positive direction.
  • Treat it as one signal, not a boundary: Because VPNs, travel and mobile carrier routing all move a user's apparent location, geofencing is a risk-reduction layer that belongs alongside MFA rather than replacing it.
Where you see it
  • Blocking VPN or webmail logins from countries where the company has no staff
  • A mobile device management policy that wipes or locks a device outside a campus
  • Triggering a step-up MFA prompt when a login arrives from an unusual country
exam: The exam usually tests geofencing as the answer to 'restrict access based on physical location'. It also appears as the factor category question, where the answer is somewhere you are. Do not confuse it with geotagging, which is attaching location metadata to a file or photo rather than enforcing anything.

front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption — how do they differ and where is each used?
answer:
Symmetric (AES): one shared key encrypts and decrypts. Fast — used for bulk data.
Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): a public/private key pair. Slow — used to exchange keys, to sign, and to authenticate.
TLS uses both.
detail:
Two families with opposite strengths. Real protocols use asymmetric cryptography to solve the key distribution problem, then switch to symmetric for the actual data.
How it works
  • Symmetric is fast but cannot bootstrap itself: AES encrypts gigabytes efficiently, often with hardware acceleration. The problem is getting the same key to both ends without an attacker seeing it, and the number of keys explodes as the number of participants grows.
  • Asymmetric solves distribution, not throughput: Anything encrypted with a public key can only be decrypted by the matching private key, so the public key can be published freely. The mathematics is far slower, so nobody encrypts bulk traffic with it.
  • Signing is the reverse direction: The holder encrypts a hash with the private key; anyone can verify it with the public key. That gives authentication and non-repudiation, which symmetric keys cannot provide because both parties hold the same key.
  • Hybrid is the normal design: TLS, IPsec, SSH and PGP all negotiate or exchange a symmetric session key using asymmetric cryptography, then encrypt the session symmetrically.
Where you see it
  • TLS protecting a web session after the handshake
  • SSH key-based login where the private key stays on the client
  • Full-disk encryption, which is purely symmetric
exam: The exam tests which family is used where. Bulk or at-rest data means symmetric; key exchange, digital signatures and certificates mean asymmetric. A frequent distractor claims asymmetric encryption protects the whole TLS session — it does not; it protects the negotiation of the symmetric key. Speed comparisons also appear: symmetric is the fast one.

front: Hashing vs encryption — what does each provide?
answer: Hashing is one-way and provides integrity. Encryption is reversible with a key and provides confidentiality. A hash is not encryption and cannot be decrypted.
detail:
Two operations constantly confused because both turn readable data into unreadable output. Only one of them is meant to be undone.
How it works
  • A hash is fixed length and irreversible: SHA-256 produces 256 bits whether the input is one byte or a terabyte. There is no key and no decrypt operation. Recovering the input means guessing candidates and comparing hashes, which is what password cracking is.
  • Any change alters the hash completely: Flipping a single bit produces a completely different digest. That property is what makes hashes usable for verifying downloads, detecting file tampering and confirming a config backup is intact.
  • Passwords are stored hashed, and salted: A salt is random data added per user before hashing, so identical passwords produce different digests and a precomputed rainbow table is useless. Slow algorithms such as bcrypt make offline cracking expensive.
  • Use current algorithms: MD5 and SHA-1 both have practical collision attacks and are unacceptable for integrity or signatures. SHA-256 or better is the expected answer. HMAC adds a secret key to a hash so an attacker cannot recompute it after altering the data.
Where you see it
  • Verifying a downloaded ISO or firmware image against a published checksum
  • Storing user passwords so a database breach does not reveal them
  • File integrity monitoring that alerts when a system binary changes
exam: The tested statement is that hashing gives integrity, not confidentiality. If a question asks how to prove a file was not modified in transit, the answer is a hash or a digital signature, not encryption. If it asks how to prevent it being read, the answer is encryption. MD5 and SHA-1 appear as deprecated distractors when the correct answer is SHA-256.

front: Conceptually, what happens in a TLS handshake?
answer: Client offers cipher suites → server replies with its choice and its certificate → client validates the certificate → both derive a shared symmetric session key via asymmetric key exchange → encrypted session begins.
detail:
The negotiation that turns an open TCP connection into an authenticated, encrypted one. It solves identity and key agreement before any application data moves.
How it works
  • The certificate authenticates the server: The server proves it holds the private key matching the public key in its certificate, and the client checks that certificate chains to a trusted CA, matches the hostname, and has not expired or been revoked. Encryption without this check would happily protect a conversation with an attacker.
  • Key exchange produces a key neither side sent: Modern handshakes use ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE), where both sides contribute to a shared secret that never crosses the wire. Because the key is ephemeral, capturing the server's private key later does not decrypt yesterday's traffic — that property is forward secrecy.
  • Cipher suite negotiation picks the algorithms: The client lists what it supports and the server chooses. A misconfigured server that still accepts obsolete suites is how downgrade attacks succeed, which is why old SSL and TLS 1.0/1.1 versions are disabled.
  • Everything after the handshake is symmetric: Application data is encrypted with AES or a similar cipher using the session key, with an integrity check on every record. TLS 1.3 trims the handshake to one round trip and removes the legacy options entirely.
Where you see it
  • Every HTTPS page load, and the certificate padlock in the browser
  • Troubleshooting a failed handshake caused by protocol version mismatch
  • Explaining why a captured HTTPS session cannot be read from the server key alone
exam: Network+ tests the concept, not the byte format. Know that the server presents a certificate, that the outcome is a symmetric session key, and that asymmetric cryptography is used only to get there. A common distractor claims the client sends the session key encrypted with its own private key — a private key is never used to encrypt something only the holder should read.

front: What is a digital certificate and what does it actually bind?
answer: A signed file binding a public key to an identity (hostname or organization). It carries the subject name, SANs, the issuer, a validity period, and the CA's signature.
detail:
The document that makes public key cryptography usable, because it answers whose key this is. Without it you have a key with no trustworthy owner.
How it works
  • The signature is the whole value: A certificate authority checks the requester's control of the name, then signs the certificate with its private key. Anyone holding the CA's public key can verify that signature and therefore trust the binding.
  • Names live in the Subject Alternative Name field: Modern clients ignore the legacy Common Name and match the hostname against the SAN list. A certificate issued for www.example.com with no SAN for example.com produces a name-mismatch error on the bare domain.
  • Validity dates are hard limits: Public certificates are issued for at most about a year, and clients reject one that is expired or not yet valid. Automated renewal exists because manual renewal is forgotten.
  • PKI is the surrounding machinery: The CA that issues, the registration authority that verifies requests, the CRL and OCSP services that publish revocation, and the trust store on every client that lists trusted roots.
Where you see it
  • HTTPS on a web server or a management interface
  • Client certificates for EAP-TLS wireless authentication
  • Code signing and signed firmware images
exam: Know that a certificate binds a public key to an identity and is validated by checking the issuer's signature. The exam trap is thinking the certificate contains or transmits the private key — it never does; the private key stays on the server. Expect certificate content questions to hinge on the SAN, the validity period and the issuer.

front: CA-signed vs self-signed certificate — what is the practical difference?
answer: A CA-signed certificate chains up to a root already in the client's trust store, so it is trusted silently. A self-signed certificate is signed by its own key, chains to nothing, and produces a trust warning on every client.
detail:
Both provide identical encryption. The difference is entirely about whether anything vouches for the identity.
How it works
  • Trust comes from the chain, not the crypto: Clients ship with a list of trusted root CAs. A server certificate signed by an intermediate, which is signed by one of those roots, validates automatically. A self-signed certificate has no path to any root, so the client has no reason to believe the name.
  • Self-signed is legitimate internally: For a lab, an internal appliance or a device management page, self-signed is normal and free. The proper internal solution is running a private CA and pushing its root certificate to every managed device, which gets silent trust without paying a public CA.
  • Warning fatigue is the real damage: If staff are trained to click through certificate warnings on internal systems, they will click through the one that matters. That habit is exactly what an on-path attacker relies on.
  • A missing intermediate looks like a broken chain: Servers must serve the intermediate certificates as well as their own. When a site works in one browser and fails in another, an incomplete chain is the usual cause, because some clients cache intermediates and some do not.
Where you see it
  • A public web server, which needs a CA-signed certificate
  • An internal switch or firewall management page using a private-CA certificate
  • Diagnosing a browser warning on a newly deployed appliance
exam: The classic exam scenario is users receiving 'certificate not trusted' warnings on an internal site, and the answer is that it uses a self-signed certificate. The correct fix in a managed environment is to issue from an internal CA and distribute that CA's root, not to tell users to accept the warning. Note that self-signed still encrypts — do not choose an answer saying the traffic is unencrypted.

front: CRL vs OCSP — how does a client learn a certificate was revoked?
answer:
CRL: a list of revoked serial numbers the client downloads periodically. Large and can be stale.
OCSP: a real-time query for one certificate's status. OCSP stapling lets the server present a recent signed status during the handshake.
detail:
Certificates can be issued for a year but need to be killable the day a private key leaks. Revocation checking is how that kill is communicated.
How it works
  • A CRL is a bulk download: The CA publishes a signed list of revoked serial numbers at an address included in the certificate. Clients fetch it on a schedule, so there is a window between revocation and the client noticing, and the list keeps growing.
  • OCSP asks about one certificate: The client sends the serial number to the CA's responder and gets good, revoked or unknown. It is current and small, but it costs a round trip on every connection and tells the CA which sites the client visits.
  • Stapling fixes both problems: The web server queries the responder itself, caches the signed timestamped response, and includes it in its own TLS handshake. The client gets fresh status with no extra connection and no privacy leak.
  • Revocation only matters if it is checked: Many clients soft-fail: if the CRL or responder is unreachable they proceed anyway rather than break the internet. That limitation is why short certificate lifetimes have become the practical mitigation.
Where you see it
  • A private key compromise forcing immediate certificate revocation
  • Revoking a departing employee's client certificate
  • Enabling OCSP stapling on a web server to reduce handshake latency
exam: The exam expects you to know that CRL is the list and OCSP is the real-time check, and that OCSP largely replaced CRL for speed. If a scenario mentions a compromised private key, the required action is to revoke the certificate and reissue — not merely to change the password or wait for expiry.

front: Name the common certificate errors and what causes each.
answer:
Expired — past validity date, or the client clock is wrong.
Name mismatch — hostname not in the SAN.
Untrusted issuer — self-signed, or a private CA root not installed.
Incomplete chain — server not sending intermediates.
Revoked — listed in the CRL or OCSP.
detail:
Certificate problems present as one generic browser warning, so the troubleshooting skill is mapping the specific message to the specific cause.
How it works
  • Expired versus wrong clock look identical: If one machine shows the error and every other machine is fine, suspect that machine's date and time, not the certificate. If everyone sees it at once on a specific date, the certificate genuinely expired.
  • Name mismatch is about what you typed: Reaching a server by IP address, by its short hostname, or by an alias that is not in the SAN list produces a mismatch even though the certificate is perfectly valid for its real name.
  • Untrusted issuer means a trust store gap: An internal CA works only on devices that have its root installed. Newly imaged machines, BYOD phones and guests will all fail until that root is distributed.
  • Incomplete chain is intermittent by client: Because some clients can fetch or have cached the missing intermediate, the same site can work on one browser and fail on another. Installing the full chain bundle on the server is the fix.
Where you see it
  • Users reporting a security warning on an internal application after a rebuild
  • A single laptop that fails HTTPS everywhere after its battery died
  • A mobile device failing to trust an internal portal that desktops accept
exam: This is a scenario-heavy topic. One host affected and everything else fine points to the client's clock. Everyone affected on the same day points to expiry. Access by IP address instead of hostname points to name mismatch. Managed desktops fine but BYOD failing points to a missing internal root CA in the trust store.

front: Data in transit vs data at rest — name the controls for each.
answer:
In transit: TLS/HTTPS, IPsec, SSH, WPA3, SFTP.
At rest: full-disk encryption, file or database encryption, encrypted backups, self-encrypting drives.
detail:
Two separate states needing two separate controls. Protecting one says nothing about the other, and audits routinely find one of them missing.
How it works
  • In transit protects against interception: Anything crossing a network can be captured by an on-path attacker, a rogue AP or a tap. Encrypting the session makes the capture useless. This is the control that answers sniffing and MITM scenarios.
  • At rest protects against physical loss: A stolen laptop, a decommissioned drive, a lost backup tape or a copied database file. Full-disk encryption is why a stolen powered-off laptop is a lost asset rather than a data breach.
  • They cover different moments and both are needed: TLS to a database server does nothing if the disk holding it is unencrypted, and disk encryption does nothing once the file is being sent over cleartext FTP.
  • Data in use is the third state: Data decrypted in memory while an application works on it is the hardest to protect and is where endpoint controls matter. CompTIA lists in transit and at rest, but knowing the third state prevents surprise.
Where you see it
  • Requiring HTTPS on an internal application that currently runs plain HTTP
  • BitLocker or FileVault on every laptop that leaves the building
  • Encrypting backup media before it is shipped to offsite storage
exam: The exam asks you to classify a control or pick one for a stated risk. A stolen laptop is at rest, answered by full-disk encryption. Traffic captured on a wireless network is in transit, answered by TLS or WPA3.
