The trap is offering a strong at-rest control for an in-transit problem, such as answering full-disk encryption for a packet capture scenario.

front: What does key management cover, and why is it the weak point of any cryptosystem?
answer: The full lifecycle: generation, secure distribution, storage, rotation, revocation and destruction. The algorithm is rarely broken; the key is stolen, shared, hardcoded or never changed.
detail:
Encryption is only as strong as the secrecy of the key. Key management is the operational discipline that keeps that true.
How it works
  • Generation must be genuinely random: Keys from a weak or predictable random source are guessable no matter how strong the cipher. Hardware random number generators and vetted libraries exist for this reason.
  • Storage should keep the key out of the file system: A private key sitting in a world-readable file or committed to a git repository is the most common real-world failure. Hardware security modules, TPMs and cloud key vaults hold keys in hardware and perform operations without exporting them.
  • Rotation limits exposure: Changing keys on a schedule limits how much data one compromised key exposes, and it forces you to prove you can rotate before an emergency requires it. Pre-shared keys shared with departing staff must be changed on departure.
  • Escrow and destruction are both required: Escrow keeps a recoverable copy so encrypted data is not lost when an employee leaves, which itself must be tightly controlled. Destruction at end of life makes remaining ciphertext permanently unreadable — the basis of crypto-erase on a decommissioned drive.
Where you see it
  • Rotating the pre-shared key on a site-to-site VPN after an engineer leaves
  • Storing a certificate authority's private key in an HSM
  • Crypto-shredding a self-encrypting drive by destroying its key instead of wiping it
exam: N10-009 lists key management as its own item under security solutions, so expect a direct question. The tested idea is that compromise of the key defeats the encryption entirely, so protection, rotation and revocation matter more than choosing a stronger cipher. Watch for scenarios about a shared VPN key known to former employees — the answer is to rotate the key.

front: DoS vs DDoS — what is the difference and how is each mitigated?
answer:
DoS: one source exhausts a resource — block the source.
DDoS: thousands of compromised hosts (a botnet) do it at once, so source blocking fails. Mitigate with upstream scrubbing, a CDN or anycast, and rate limiting.
detail:
An attack on availability alone. Nothing is stolen or altered; the service simply stops answering legitimate users.
How it works
  • The resource being exhausted varies: Bandwidth floods fill the pipe. Protocol attacks such as a SYN flood fill a connection table with half-open sessions. Application-layer attacks send expensive but valid requests that consume CPU and database time while looking legitimate.
  • Distribution is what defeats the obvious fix: One source IP is trivially dropped by an ACL. Ten thousand sources across the world, many of them also serving real users, cannot be filtered by address without blocking customers.
  • Amplification and reflection multiply traffic: The attacker sends small spoofed requests to open DNS or NTP servers, which send much larger responses to the victim. This is why open resolvers are dangerous and why source address validation at the edge matters.
  • A saturated link cannot be fixed at the far end: Once the internet circuit itself is full, the on-premises firewall is already too late. Mitigation must happen upstream at the provider or in a scrubbing service, which is why DDoS protection is bought, not installed.
Where you see it
  • A public website knocked offline during a volumetric flood
  • A SYN flood filling a load balancer's connection table
  • Contracting an ISP scrubbing service or fronting a site with a CDN
exam: The exam wants you to recognize this as an attack on availability. The distinguishing feature of DDoS in a scenario is many distinct source addresses or the word botnet. If a question asks why blocking the source IP will not work, that is the DDoS marker. A firewall rule is the wrong answer for a volumetric attack that has already saturated the WAN link.

front: What is ARP poisoning / spoofing, and why does it work?
answer: The attacker sends forged ARP replies so victims map the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC. Traffic is then delivered to the attacker, placing them on-path. It works because ARP has no authentication and hosts accept unsolicited replies.
detail:
The classic Layer 2 attack on a switched LAN. It does not break the switch; it corrupts what the hosts believe.
How it works
  • ARP was designed with no verification: A host that receives an ARP reply simply caches it. Many implementations accept gratuitous ARP announcements they never asked for, and the newest answer wins. Nothing in the protocol proves the sender owns the address it claims.
  • Poisoning is usually done in both directions: The attacker tells the victim it is the gateway and tells the gateway it is the victim, then forwards packets between them. Both sides continue to work normally, which is why the attack goes unnoticed.
  • What it enables is the real payload: Sitting on-path allows sniffing cleartext credentials, session hijacking, DNS answer tampering and selective packet dropping. It is a stepping stone, not an end in itself.
  • It is confined to one broadcast domain: ARP does not cross a router, so the attacker must already be on the same VLAN as the victim. That is what makes segmentation a partial control and rogue devices on the LAN so dangerous.
Where you see it
  • An attacker on a conference room jack intercepting internal traffic
  • A compromised workstation used to capture credentials from its own subnet
  • Explaining why a suspicious host shows the gateway's IP with the wrong MAC in arp -a
exam: The single tested mitigation is Dynamic ARP Inspection, backed by DHCP snooping. If a scenario shows two IP addresses resolving to the same MAC, or the gateway's MAC suddenly changing, that is ARP poisoning. The consequence to select is on-path attack. Encryption does not prevent the poisoning, it only limits what the attacker can read afterwards.

front: What is Dynamic ARP Inspection and what does it depend on?
answer: A switch feature that validates every ARP packet on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table and drops any whose IP-to-MAC pairing does not match. It requires DHCP snooping to be enabled first.
detail:
The direct, purpose-built mitigation for ARP poisoning. It gives the switch the authentication that ARP itself never had.
How it works
  • The binding table is the source of truth: DHCP snooping watches real DHCP transactions and records which MAC received which IP on which port and VLAN. DAI compares each ARP packet against that record and discards mismatches.
  • Trusted ports are exempt: Uplinks and ports toward other switches are configured as trusted and pass ARP without inspection. Access ports facing users are untrusted and inspected. Getting this backwards breaks the network or leaves the hole open.
  • Statically addressed hosts need ARP ACLs: A server with a fixed IP never appears in the snooping table, so its legitimate ARP would be dropped. Those hosts need static ARP access-list entries to be permitted.
  • Rate limiting comes with it: DAI typically rate-limits ARP on untrusted ports, so a host generating a flood of ARP traffic is err-disabled. That also blunts ARP-based scanning and denial of service.
Where you see it
  • Hardening access switches in an office with unattended network jacks
  • Responding to an incident where a workstation was intercepting subnet traffic
  • A campus or hotel network where untrusted devices connect freely
exam: Exam questions give the symptom of ARP poisoning and ask for the mitigation — the answer is Dynamic ARP Inspection. The follow-up detail worth knowing is the dependency: DAI uses the DHCP snooping binding table, so the two are configured together. Port security is the distractor and does not inspect ARP at all.

front: What is MAC flooding and what does it do to the switch?
answer: The attacker generates frames with thousands of fake source MAC addresses to overflow the switch's MAC address table (CAM table). The switch can no longer learn real entries and begins flooding unknown unicast out every port, turning it into a hub.
detail:
An attack that exploits a hard resource limit rather than a protocol flaw. Every switch has a finite table, and filling it changes the switch's default behaviour.
How it works
  • Switching depends on a finite table: A switch learns source MAC addresses and forwards frames only out the port where the destination was learned. That table has a fixed size, from a few thousand entries on access switches upward.
  • Full table means fail-open: When there is no room to learn and no entry for a destination, the switch does the only thing it can: flood the frame out every port in the VLAN. The attacker now receives copies of traffic meant for other hosts.
  • The goal is passive sniffing: Unlike ARP poisoning, no host is deceived and nothing is redirected. The attacker simply receives everything, which yields cleartext credentials and session data on any unencrypted protocol.
  • It is loud and degrades performance: Flooding every frame out every port wastes bandwidth across the whole VLAN, so users notice slowness. The MAC table filling with random addresses is visible in the switch's table.
Where you see it
  • A tool such as macof run from a laptop on an access port
  • Investigating unexplained switch slowness with a full MAC address table
  • Justifying port security on user-facing ports
exam: The mitigation to answer is port security, which limits how many MAC addresses a port may learn. The tested detail is what the switch does when the table fills: it floods unknown unicast frames out all ports, behaving like a hub. Do not confuse MAC flooding, which fills the CAM table, with MAC spoofing, which impersonates one specific address.

front: What does port security do, and what are its violation modes?
answer: Limits which and how many MAC addresses may be seen on a switch access port. On violation the port shuts down (err-disabled), restricts (drops and logs), or protects (drops silently). Sticky MAC learns the first address and keeps it.
detail:
The switch-level control that stops MAC flooding and casually plugged-in devices. It is enforcement at Layer 2 based on hardware address, nothing more.
How it works
  • A maximum MAC count stops flooding: Setting a limit of one or two addresses per access port means an attacker cannot present thousands. The port reacts on the very first excess address rather than after the table is full.
  • Sticky learning avoids manual entry: The port learns the connected device's MAC and writes it into the running configuration, so only that device works there afterwards. It saves typing but must be re-learned when equipment legitimately moves.
  • Violation mode changes the operational cost: Shutdown is the most secure and the most disruptive — the port stays down until an administrator clears it or an errdisable recovery timer fires. Restrict keeps the port up while dropping and counting offending frames.
  • An IP phone with a PC behind it needs two MACs: The phone and the attached computer both appear on the same port, in different VLANs. A maximum of one will break the desk on day one, which is the most common real deployment mistake.
Where you see it
  • Locking a lobby or conference room port to a single known device
  • Preventing a user from attaching an unmanaged switch under their desk
  • Diagnosing a port stuck in err-disabled after someone swapped a docking station
exam: Port security is the answer to MAC flooding and to unauthorized devices when 802.1X is not in play. Its weakness is directly tested: MAC addresses are easily spoofed, so port security authenticates nothing. If a question asks for real authentication of the device or user on the port, the answer is 802.1X, not port security.

front: VLAN hopping by switch spoofing — how does it work and how do you stop it?
answer: The attacker's host pretends to be a switch and negotiates a trunk with the real switch using DTP. A trunk carries all VLANs, so the attacker reaches every VLAN. Fix: hardcode access ports and disable DTP negotiation.
detail:
An attack that abuses automatic trunk negotiation, a convenience feature enabled by default on many switches.
How it works
  • DTP negotiates trunks automatically: Dynamic Trunking Protocol lets two switches agree to form a trunk with no configuration. A port left in dynamic auto or dynamic desirable will happily form a trunk with anything that asks — including a laptop running software that speaks DTP.
  • A trunk exposes every VLAN: Once trunked, the port carries tagged frames for all allowed VLANs. The attacker can now send and receive traffic in the server VLAN, the voice VLAN and the management VLAN from an ordinary desk jack.
  • The fix is two commands: Set user ports explicitly to access mode and turn off negotiation: switchport mode access plus switchport nonegotiate. A port that cannot become a trunk cannot be spoofed into one.
  • Prune what real trunks carry: On genuine inter-switch trunks, restrict the allowed VLAN list so a compromised link exposes only the VLANs that actually need to cross it.
Where you see it
  • Hardening every access port during a switch deployment standard
  • An audit finding that user ports are in dynamic auto mode
  • A penetration test that reached the management VLAN from a lobby jack
exam: This is one of two VLAN hopping methods and both are testable. The marker is the word trunk or DTP in the stem, and the answer is disable DTP and set ports to access mode. Do not answer 'change the native VLAN' here — that is the fix for the other method, double tagging.

front: VLAN hopping by double tagging — how does it work and how do you stop it?
answer: The attacker sends a frame with two 802.1Q tags: an outer tag matching the trunk's native VLAN and an inner tag for the target VLAN. The first switch strips the outer tag and forwards; the second switch reads the inner tag and delivers into the target VLAN. Fix: set the native VLAN to an unused VLAN, put no hosts on it, and do not use VLAN 1.
detail:
An attack that exploits one specific rule of 802.1Q: frames in the native VLAN cross a trunk untagged.
How it works
  • The native VLAN is sent untagged: By design, a trunk carries the native VLAN's frames with no tag so that legacy devices can participate. That is the hole: the first switch removes the outer tag because it matches the native VLAN, exposing the inner tag it never inspected.
  • Two switches are required: The first switch strips one tag; the second switch acts on the remaining tag. The attacker must be in the native VLAN on the first switch, which is why leaving user ports in the default native VLAN 1 is dangerous.
  • It is one-way only: Return traffic comes back through normal switching and never reaches the attacker, because nothing double-tags the reply. That makes it useful for injection or denial of service rather than for reading data.
  • Mitigation is native VLAN hygiene: Change the native VLAN on every trunk to a dedicated unused VLAN with no access ports, or force tagging of the native VLAN. Also move all user ports off VLAN 1 as a general practice.
Where you see it
  • Reviewing trunk configuration where the native VLAN is still VLAN 1
  • Explaining why a device on a user VLAN received frames from another VLAN
  • Writing a switch hardening standard for a new site
exam: The identifying phrase in the stem is two 802.1Q tags or 'double tagging'. The answer is to change the native VLAN to an unused VLAN and never carry user traffic on it. Disabling DTP is the distractor pulled from the switch spoofing variant — it does not stop double tagging. Also know that this attack sends traffic one way only.

front: What is DNS poisoning / spoofing, and what is the mitigation?
answer: Injecting false records so a name resolves to the attacker's address — into a resolver's cache, into a hosts file, or by forging a reply. Mitigate with DNSSEC, restricting recursion, using secured resolvers, and protecting the hosts file.
detail:
An attack on the naming layer. The victim's traffic goes to the wrong server while everything on the screen still shows the correct name.
How it works
  • The cache is the high-value target: Poison one recursive resolver and every client using it is redirected until the record's time-to-live expires. That leverage is what makes cache poisoning worse than attacking a single host.
  • Forged replies race the real ones: Classic DNS uses UDP with a 16-bit transaction ID. An attacker who can guess or observe the query can answer before the legitimate server does. Source port randomization made this much harder but did not fix the underlying lack of authentication.
  • The hosts file is the local version: Malware that writes an entry into the local hosts file redirects that machine only, and the entry is checked before DNS is even queried. Checking the hosts file is a standard step when one machine is affected and others are not.
  • Open recursion turns your server into a weapon: A resolver that answers recursive queries from the internet can be both poisoned and used for amplification attacks. Recursion should be limited to internal clients.
Where you see it
  • A user reaching a convincing fake login page while the URL bar looks correct
  • Checking ipconfig /displaydns or the hosts file during a redirect investigation
  • Restricting recursion on an internet-facing authoritative DNS server
exam: The mitigation CompTIA wants is DNSSEC. The scenario marker is a correct name resolving to an unexpected IP address, or one host being redirected while others are not, which points at the hosts file. Do not choose HTTPS as the fix for the poisoning itself, although certificate validation is what causes the browser to warn the user.

front: What does DNSSEC actually provide — and what does it not?
answer: It digitally signs DNS records so a resolver can verify origin authenticity and integrity, using a chain of trust up to the root. It does not encrypt DNS — queries and answers remain readable.
detail:
Authentication added to a protocol that had none. It proves an answer came from the zone's real owner and was not modified, nothing more.
How it works
  • Every record set is signed: The zone owner signs record sets with a private key and publishes the corresponding public key in the zone. A validating resolver checks the signature before accepting the answer.
  • Trust chains from the root down: Each zone's key is vouched for by its parent zone, up to the signed root. That chain is what stops an attacker publishing their own signed version of a name.
  • It proves nonexistence too: Signed denial-of-existence records stop an attacker from forging a 'no such name' answer, which would otherwise be an easy way to break a service.
  • Privacy needs a different protocol: Because DNSSEC leaves queries in the clear, DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS exist to encrypt the transport. They are complementary: DNSSEC authenticates the data, DoT and DoH hide the conversation.
Where you see it
  • Signing a public zone so resolvers can detect forged answers
  • Enabling validation on internal recursive resolvers
  • Explaining to an auditor why DNSSEC does not satisfy an encryption requirement
exam: The tested trap is exactly the confidentiality question: DNSSEC provides integrity and authentication, not encryption. Choosing 'it encrypts DNS traffic' is the most common wrong answer. When a scenario describes cache poisoning or forged DNS responses, DNSSEC is the correct control.

front: What is a rogue DHCP server and what damage does it do?
answer: An unauthorized DHCP server on the LAN. It answers clients with its own address as the default gateway and DNS server, putting the attacker on-path — or hands out wrong addresses and breaks connectivity outright.
detail:
An attack that exploits the fact that DHCP clients accept the first offer they receive and have no way to tell a legitimate server from an impostor.
How it works
  • First offer wins: A broadcasting client takes whichever DHCPOFFER arrives first. A rogue server on the same segment as the client often wins simply by being closer than the real one across a relay.
  • Gateway and DNS are the payload: Options 3 and 6 in the offer determine where the client sends everything and how it resolves names. Controlling those two values is enough to intercept or redirect all of the client's traffic.
  • Most incidents are accidental: A home router plugged into a wall jack by an employee, with its LAN port facing the office, is the usual cause. The symptom is a subset of users receiving addresses from an unfamiliar subnet.
  • It is confined to a broadcast domain: DHCP broadcasts do not cross a router, so a rogue server affects only its own VLAN unless a relay is misconfigured. That is why the affected users cluster in one area.
Where you see it
  • Users on one floor suddenly getting 192.168.0.x addresses and losing access
  • An employee plugging a consumer wireless router into a desk jack
  • A deliberate on-path attack staged from a laptop on the LAN
exam: The mitigation to answer is DHCP snooping. The scenario marker is some clients receiving addresses from the wrong subnet or an unexpected gateway shown in ipconfig /all. A DHCP scope exhaustion answer is a distractor: exhaustion means clients get no address at all, while a rogue server means they get the wrong one.

front: What is DHCP snooping, and what does a 'trusted port' mean?
answer: A switch feature that only allows DHCP server messages (OFFER, ACK) from ports you explicitly designate trusted — the ports toward the real server. Server messages arriving on any untrusted port are dropped.
detail:
The switch takes over the job of deciding which DHCP servers are real, because the client cannot. It also produces the binding table other features depend on.
How it works
  • Direction is what is filtered: Client messages such as DISCOVER and REQUEST are allowed from user ports. Server messages are not. A rogue server plugged into a user port is silenced the moment it tries to answer.
  • Trusted ports face the infrastructure: Uplinks toward the distribution switch, the router or the DHCP relay are trusted. Every access port is untrusted by default once the feature is on, which is what makes it safe to deploy widely.
  • The binding table is a valuable by-product: Snooping records MAC, IP, lease, VLAN and port for every successful DHCP transaction. Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard both consume this table, so DHCP snooping is a prerequisite for them.
  • Rate limiting stops starvation: The feature can also limit DHCP messages per second on untrusted ports, blunting a DHCP starvation attack in which an attacker requests every address in the scope to force clients toward a rogue server.
Where you see it
  • Standard access-layer hardening alongside DAI and port security
  • Stopping an employee's home router from handing out addresses
  • Building the binding table that Dynamic ARP Inspection needs
exam: The exam pairs the attack and the control directly: rogue DHCP is stopped by DHCP snooping. The extra fact worth carrying is the dependency chain — DHCP snooping builds the binding table that Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP against. Expect a question asking which ports should be trusted; the answer is the ones toward the legitimate DHCP server, not the user ports.

front: Rogue AP vs evil twin — what is the difference?
answer:
Rogue AP: any unauthorized access point attached to your network, often installed by an employee for convenience.
Evil twin: an attacker's AP that impersonates your SSID to lure clients into associating with it.
detail:
Both are unauthorized wireless, but one is an accidental hole in your perimeter and the other is a deliberate trap for your users.
How it works
  • A rogue AP bypasses your controls: It is usually a cheap AP plugged into a wall jack by a well-meaning employee, with weak or no encryption. It creates an unmonitored path into the wired network from the parking lot. The connection to the wired LAN is what defines it.
  • An evil twin need not touch your network at all: It broadcasts your SSID from a laptop or a portable AP, often with a stronger signal, and provides its own internet path. Clients that roam by signal strength associate with it, and the attacker sees all of their traffic.
  • The evil twin's goal is credentials and traffic: Combined with a cloned captive portal, it harvests logins. On an open network, it reads everything not protected by TLS. It is an on-path attack delivered wirelessly.
  • Detection differs: Rogue APs are found by wireless intrusion detection and by correlating unknown MAC addresses on switch ports. Evil twins are found by site surveys spotting a second AP broadcasting a known SSID from an unexpected BSSID or location.
Where you see it
  • An employee installing a personal AP to get better signal in their office
  • An attacker in a café or lobby cloning the corporate or public SSID
  • Running periodic wireless surveys to find unknown BSSIDs
exam: The distinguishing question is whether the AP is connected to your wired network (rogue) or impersonating your SSID (evil twin). Defences are also tested: 802.1X with server certificate validation stops clients handing credentials to an evil twin, while 802.1X on wired ports and port security stop the rogue AP being plugged in at all.

front: What is an on-path (man-in-the-middle) attack, and how is it normally achieved?
answer: The attacker positions between two parties and relays traffic, able to read or modify it while both sides believe they are talking directly. Achieved by ARP poisoning, a rogue AP or evil twin, DNS poisoning, or a rogue DHCP server. Mitigate with end-to-end encryption and certificate validation.
detail:
Not a single technique but a position. Several different attacks all exist to reach it, and once there the attacker can do far more than eavesdrop.
How it works
  • Relaying is what keeps it hidden: The attacker forwards packets so the session continues to function. Nothing breaks, no error appears, and the only clues are timing and Layer 2 or DNS anomalies.
  • Modification is worse than reading: An on-path attacker can inject content, strip an HTTPS upgrade, alter a bank account number in a form, or hijack an authenticated session cookie. Confidentiality and integrity are both lost.
  • Encryption alone is not enough without identity checks: TLS defeats an on-path attacker only because the client validates the server's certificate. A user who clicks through a certificate warning re-opens the entire attack, which is why warning fatigue is a security problem.
  • Layer 2 hygiene removes the easy routes: DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, disabling unused ports and 802.1X remove the common ways of achieving the position in the first place.
Where you see it
  • Credential capture on an open or cloned wireless network
  • An internal attacker ARP poisoning a subnet to read cleartext protocols
  • A downgrade attempt stripped by HSTS on a web application
exam: N10-009 uses the term on-path attack rather than man-in-the-middle, but both appear. Expect a question that names ARP poisoning or an evil twin and asks what it enables — the answer is on-path. The mitigation to choose is end-to-end encryption with certificate validation, and at Layer 2, DAI and DHCP snooping.

front: What is a deauthentication attack and what stops it?
answer: The attacker sends spoofed 802.11 deauthentication management frames to force clients off an AP. It works because legacy management frames are unauthenticated. Stopped by 802.11w Protected Management Frames, which are mandatory in WPA3.
detail:
A wireless denial-of-service that is also the setup step for other attacks, because a disconnected client will reconnect to whichever AP looks best.
How it works
  • Management frames were never protected: In the original 802.11 design, deauthentication and disassociation frames carry no integrity protection, so anyone can forge one claiming to be from the AP or the client. Data frames may be encrypted while these are not.
  • Repeating it is a denial of service: Continuously flooding deauth frames keeps clients from staying associated. The wireless network appears to be failing intermittently, with clients dropping and reconnecting.
  • It is a stepping stone to an evil twin: Knock a client off the legitimate AP and it will re-associate, possibly to the attacker's stronger impostor AP. It is also used to capture the WPA2 four-way handshake for offline cracking.
  • PMF adds integrity to those frames: 802.11w protects management frames so a forged deauthentication is ignored. WPA3 requires it, and WPA2 can enable it optionally where clients support it.
Where you see it
  • Users repeatedly dropping from Wi-Fi in a specific area of a building
  • A wireless survey showing a flood of deauthentication frames from an unknown source
  • Migrating to WPA3 to close a known wireless denial-of-service vector
exam: The scenario marker is clients repeatedly disconnecting and reconnecting with no wired or AP fault found. The mitigation to choose is 802.11w / Protected Management Frames or moving to WPA3. Do not answer 'change the pre-shared key' or 'change the channel' — the attack does not need the key and does not depend on the channel.

front: Distinguish phishing, spear phishing, whaling, vishing and smishing.
answer:
Phishing: mass fraudulent email.
Spear phishing: targeted at a specific person or team using researched detail.
Whaling: spear phishing aimed at executives.
Vishing: voice or phone call.
Smishing: SMS or text message.
detail:
One attack with five delivery labels. CompTIA separates them by target and channel, so classify on those two axes.
How it works
  • Targeting separates the first three: Phishing is sent to thousands with no personalization. Spear phishing names your manager and your project because the attacker researched you. Whaling is spear phishing where the target is a CFO or CEO, usually to authorize a payment.
  • Channel separates the last two: Vishing is voice, typically an urgent call claiming to be the helpdesk or the bank, often with a spoofed caller ID. Smishing is a text message with a link or a callback number.
  • They all exploit urgency and authority: The message manufactures a deadline and appears to come from someone who can give orders. That pressure is what stops the victim verifying through another channel.
  • Business email compromise is the expensive variant: A whaling or spoofed-executive email instructing finance to wire funds or change bank details causes the largest single losses, because no malware is involved and no technical control is triggered.
Where you see it
  • A fake password-expiry email harvesting credentials
  • An urgent text claiming to be from the CEO asking for gift cards
  • A phone call from 'IT support' asking a user to read out an MFA code
exam: Every one of these appears in the objectives, and the exam separates them purely by who is targeted and which channel is used. Executives means whaling; a phone call means vishing; a text means smishing. The mitigation answer for the whole family is user security awareness training, with MFA as the technical backstop against the stolen credentials.

front: Define tailgating, piggybacking, shoulder surfing, dumpster diving and pretexting.
answer:
Tailgating: following someone through a secure door without their knowledge.
Piggybacking: the same entry but with consent — they held the door.
Shoulder surfing: reading a screen or keypad over someone's shoulder.
Dumpster diving: retrieving information from discarded material.
Pretexting: inventing a believable scenario to justify the request.
detail:
The in-person half of social engineering. These attacks need no malware and defeat network controls entirely by walking past them.
How it works
  • Consent is the tailgating versus piggybacking line: Both are unauthorized entry behind an authorized person. CompTIA distinguishes them by whether the authorized person knowingly allowed it. An access control vestibule (mantrap) physically prevents both by admitting one person at a time.
  • Shoulder surfing is defeated by physical measures: Privacy screens, positioning monitors away from walkways, and covering keypads. It is the reason PIN pads have shields and why entering an MFA code in a crowded lobby is risky.
  • Dumpster diving harvests what was thrown away: Old network diagrams, employee directories, invoices, decommissioned drives and sticky notes. The control is cross-cut shredding and a documented media destruction policy, not a fence.
  • Pretexting is the story behind the other attacks: The fake auditor, the delivery driver, the new hire on their first day. It is what makes vishing and tailgating work, and it is defeated by a verification procedure that staff are permitted to follow without fear.
Where you see it
  • An unbadged visitor entering a data centre behind a staff member
  • Sensitive documents recovered from an unsecured bin
  • A caller posing as a vendor engineer to obtain a device password
exam: Tailgating and piggybacking are the most commonly confused pair, split on consent. Tailgating, dumpster diving and shoulder surfing are named directly in N10-009's social engineering list. For a physical entry scenario the control to choose is an access control vestibule or badge-enforced single entry, not a camera — a camera records the breach but does not prevent it.

front: Name the main malware types and the key distinction among them.
answer:
Virus: attaches to a file, needs user action.
Worm: self-replicating, spreads over the network with no user action.
Trojan: disguised as legitimate software.
Ransomware: encrypts data and demands payment.
Rootkit: hides itself with system-level privilege.
Spyware/keylogger: harvests activity and credentials.
Botnet: compromised hosts under remote command and control.
detail:
Malicious code categorized by how it spreads and what it does. The spreading mechanism is what CompTIA tests hardest.
How it works
  • Worm versus virus is the load-bearing pair: A virus needs a host file and a user to run it. A worm carries its own propagation code and moves host to host over the network by itself, which is why worms cause sudden network-wide outbreaks and generate abnormal traffic volume.
  • Trojans depend on the user installing them: The malicious payload rides inside something the user wants. There is no self-replication; the deception is the delivery mechanism, which is why they arrive through downloads and phishing attachments.
  • Ransomware's real control is backup: Antivirus may miss it and paying does not guarantee recovery. Tested, offline or immutable backups plus segmentation to limit spread are what actually restore service.
  • Rootkits break trust in the operating system: Because the rootkit runs at or below the OS level, tools running on that machine may report clean. Detection often requires booting from external media, and the safe remediation is to rebuild the host.
Where you see it
  • A network flooded with scanning traffic from a worm outbreak
  • A ransomware incident where segmentation limited the encrypted file shares
  • A workstation reporting clean while still exhibiting compromised behaviour
exam: The most frequent question is worm versus virus, decided by whether user interaction is required — worms need none. For ransomware the best answer is almost always restore from backup rather than paying or relying on antivirus. Malware is listed by name in objective 4.2, so also expect it as the cause in scenario questions about strange outbound traffic.

front: Brute force vs dictionary vs credential stuffing vs password spraying.
answer:
Brute force: try every combination.
Dictionary: try likely words and known passwords.
Credential stuffing: replay username/password pairs stolen from another breach.
Password spraying: try one common password against many accounts to avoid lockout.
detail:
Four different ways of guessing, each shaped by a different constraint. What separates them is where the candidate passwords come from.
How it works
  • Online guessing is slow and noisy: Attempting logins against a live service is limited by rate limiting, lockout and logging. This is why attackers prefer stealing the hash database and cracking offline, where they can attempt billions per second.
  • Dictionary attacks exploit human choice: Real password lists from previous breaches, plus rule-based mutations such as adding a year or capitalizing the first letter, crack most human-chosen passwords far faster than brute force ever would.
  • Credential stuffing is a reuse attack: The attacker already has valid pairs from another site. Nothing is guessed. It succeeds only because the user reused the password, and it is why MFA rather than complexity rules is the correct defence.
  • Spraying is designed to dodge lockout: Lockout policies trigger on many failures for one account. Trying one password against ten thousand accounts stays under every per-account threshold while still finding the handful using it.
Where you see it
  • A surge of failed logins spread thinly across many accounts
  • Account takeovers on a service whose users reused passwords from a breached site
  • Selecting MFA and lockout thresholds after a credential attack
exam: The exam separates these by mechanism. Reused credentials from another site is credential stuffing. One password against many accounts is password spraying. Word lists means dictionary. The universal mitigation to pick is MFA; account lockout is the correct answer specifically for online brute force, and salting plus a slow hash is the answer for protecting stored passwords.

front: What belongs on a device hardening checklist for a switch, router or firewall?
answer: Change default credentials; disable unused ports and services; disable insecure protocols (Telnet, HTTP, SNMPv1/v2c); patch firmware; manage over SSH/HTTPS only; restrict management with ACLs to a management VLAN; enable logging and NTP; use individual named admin accounts.
detail:
Reducing the attack surface of a device to the minimum it needs to do its job. Two items — default passwords and unused ports and services — are named directly in the objectives.
How it works
  • Default credentials are the first thing tried: Vendor default usernames and passwords are published and are the first thing any scanner or attacker attempts. Changing them, on every device including the ones nobody logs into, is the highest-value single action.
  • Unused ports and services are free attack surface: An administratively shut-down switch port cannot be used by someone plugging into a wall jack. A disabled HTTP server or unused discovery protocol cannot be exploited or fingerprinted.
  • Replace cleartext management protocols: Telnet, HTTP and SNMPv1/v2c send credentials and community strings in the clear. SSH, HTTPS and SNMPv3 are the direct replacements and the expected answers.
  • Restrict who may even reach management: An ACL or management VLAN that only permits administrative access from a jump host means a stolen credential is useless from a user subnet. Combine with individual accounts so accounting identifies the person.
Where you see it
  • Commissioning a new switch against a hardening standard
  • Remediating an audit finding of default SNMP community strings
  • Responding to a vulnerability scan flagging Telnet and HTTP on infrastructure
exam: Objective 4.3 lists device hardening with two explicit sub-items: disable unused ports and services and change default passwords. Those two are the highest-probability answers. If a scan finds Telnet or SNMPv1, the fix is to disable them and use SSH and SNMPv3, not to firewall them off.

front: What is NAC, and what is a posture assessment?
answer: Network access control decides whether a device may join the network, based on identity and device health. The posture assessment is the health check — OS patch level, antivirus present and current, firewall on, disk encryption — before access is granted.
detail:
The control that asks not just who you are but whether your device is safe to admit. It is what turns 802.1X into a health gate.
How it works
  • Failing devices are quarantined, not just rejected: A non-compliant device is typically placed in a remediation VLAN with access only to patch and antivirus servers. It updates itself, is reassessed, and is then admitted, which keeps the control usable in practice.
  • Agents can be persistent or dissolvable: A persistent agent is installed on managed corporate devices and reports continuously. A dissolvable agent is downloaded for one assessment and removed, which suits contractors and guests. Agentless checks infer posture from scans and are weaker.
  • 802.1X is the usual enforcement point: The RADIUS server makes the decision and returns a VLAN assignment or a downloadable ACL in the Access-Accept. Without an enforcement mechanism, NAC is only a report.
  • Reassessment matters as much as admission: A laptop that passes at 09:00 and disables its antivirus at 11:00 should lose access. Continuous or periodic posture checking is what makes NAC part of a zero trust design rather than a one-time gate.
Where you see it
  • Requiring contractor laptops to prove patch level before joining the LAN
  • Quarantining a device with out-of-date antivirus into a remediation VLAN
  • BYOD onboarding where personal phones get internet only
exam: NAC is the answer when a scenario mentions checking a device's health, patch level or antivirus status before granting access — not merely its identity. The distractors are port security and MAC filtering, which check a hardware address and nothing else. Expect quarantine or remediation VLAN as the correct handling of a failed check.

front: Port security vs MAC filtering vs NAC — how do they differ in what they verify?
answer:
Port security: limits how many and which MACs a switch port accepts.
MAC filtering: an allow/deny list of hardware addresses, commonly on wireless — trivially defeated by spoofing.
NAC: verifies identity and device posture, and can quarantine.
detail:
Three controls that all sound like access control but operate at different levels of assurance. Sorting them by what they actually verify makes exam questions easy.
How it works
  • The first two verify only a hardware address: A MAC address is transmitted in the clear in every frame and can be changed in software in seconds. Anyone who can sniff a permitted address can clone it, so both controls stop the casual and the accidental, not the deliberate.
  • Port security is per switch port; MAC filtering is per list: Port security is a Layer 2 feature that reacts to a violation with shutdown, restrict or protect. MAC filtering is a static allow or deny list, most often seen on an access point, and it is administratively painful at scale.
  • NAC verifies something the device must prove: Certificates or credentials establish identity, and an agent or scan establishes health. That cannot be faked by editing an interface property, which is why NAC is the only one of the three that provides real assurance.
  • They are complementary, not alternatives: A hardened network uses port security to bound MAC learning, 802.1X for authentication, and NAC for posture. Each removes a different class of unauthorized device.
Where you see it
  • Choosing a control after an unauthorized device is found on the LAN
  • Explaining to management why MAC filtering on the guest Wi-Fi is not sufficient
  • Designing access-layer security for a building with public areas
exam: The exam loves the weakness of MAC-based controls: the correct criticism is MAC addresses are easily spoofed. If a question asks for the strongest control, choose NAC or 802.1X. If it asks specifically about limiting addresses per switch port or stopping MAC flooding, choose port security.

front: How is an ACL processed, and what is at the end of every one?
answer: Top-down, first match wins — processing stops at the first matching rule. There is an implicit deny all at the end, so anything not explicitly permitted is dropped.
detail:
The rule evaluation model shared by router ACLs and firewall rule sets. Almost every ACL troubleshooting question comes down to these two facts.
How it works
  • Order changes behaviour: Because the first match wins, a broad permit placed above a specific deny makes the deny unreachable. Specific rules belong above general ones, and the classic misconfiguration is a permit-any near the top that shadows everything below it.
  • The implicit deny is invisible: It is not shown in the configuration but it is always there. An ACL containing only deny statements blocks everything, because the traffic you wanted to allow was never explicitly permitted.
  • Direction and placement matter: An ACL is applied to an interface inbound or outbound. Applying a rule set in the wrong direction filters return traffic instead of the intended flow, which presents as a one-way connectivity failure.
  • Match criteria are the five-tuple: Source address, destination address, protocol, source port and destination port. Standard ACLs match source only; extended ACLs match the full set, which is what allows permitting HTTPS to one server while denying everything else to it.
Where you see it
  • Traffic still blocked after adding a permit rule at the bottom of a list
  • Restricting management access to a switch from one subnet only
  • A firewall change that unexpectedly blocks return traffic
exam: Two facts are tested relentlessly: first match wins and implicit deny at the end. The signature scenario is a new permit rule added below an existing deny that has no effect — the fix is to reorder the rules, not to add another permit. Also expect questions where the answer is that the ACL was applied in the wrong direction or on the wrong interface.

front: URL filtering vs content filtering vs DLP — what does each control?
answer:
URL filtering: allow or block by web address or category.
Content filtering: inspects the payload itself for prohibited material.
DLP: detects and blocks sensitive data leaving the organization.
detail:
Three filters distinguished by what they examine and which direction they care about. Two are about what comes in; DLP is about what goes out.
How it works
  • URL filtering works on the destination: A category database classifies sites as gambling, malware, social media and so on, and the policy allows or blocks by category or specific address. It never looks inside the traffic, so it is fast and coarse.
  • Content filtering works on the payload: It inspects what is actually being transferred — file types, keywords, attachments, scripts — and can block an allowed site delivering a prohibited file. Encrypted traffic requires TLS inspection to see anything, which is the deployment cost.
  • DLP is outbound and data-aware: It matches patterns such as card numbers, national identity numbers, medical record formats or tagged source code in email, uploads and removable media, and blocks or quarantines the transfer. It is the control an auditor asks for.
  • They operate at different points: URL and content filtering usually sit in a proxy or next-generation firewall. DLP additionally needs endpoint and mail gateway coverage, because USB copies and outbound mail bypass the web path.
Where you see it
  • Blocking a category of websites as an acceptable-use policy control
  • Stopping an employee emailing a spreadsheet of customer card numbers
  • Preventing a known-malicious download from an otherwise permitted site
exam: URL filtering and content filtering are both named in objective 4.3. The tested split is destination versus payload, and DLP is separated by direction — data leaving. If the scenario mentions sensitive information being sent out, the answer is DLP even when web filtering appears as a plausible option.

front: What are firewall zones, and what do trusted and untrusted mean?
answer: A zone groups interfaces or networks with the same trust level, and rules are written between zones rather than between individual addresses. Trusted is the internal network; untrusted is the internet. Traffic from lower to higher trust is denied by default.
detail:
A way of expressing policy at the level of network role instead of address. It makes rule sets readable and it survives readdressing.
How it works
  • Default direction of trust: Sessions initiated from the trusted zone outward are generally permitted, and their return traffic is allowed by the state table. Sessions initiated from the untrusted zone inward are denied unless a rule explicitly permits them to a specific host and port.
  • Zones scale better than address rules: Adding a new subnet to the trusted zone inherits the policy automatically. Writing rules per subnet means every network change becomes a firewall change and rule sets grow until nobody dares remove anything.
  • Three zones is the classic minimum: Trusted inside, untrusted outside, and a screened subnet for public-facing servers. More mature designs add zones for guest, IoT, management and partner connections.
  • Statefulness is what makes it workable: A stateful firewall tracks established sessions, so a single outbound permit does not require a matching inbound rule for the replies. A stateless ACL would require both, which is why ACLs are longer and easier to get wrong.
Where you see it
  • Writing a firewall policy as inside-to-outside and outside-to-DMZ rules
  • Adding a new internal VLAN without touching the firewall rule base
  • Explaining why unsolicited inbound traffic is dropped without any rule saying so
exam: Objective 4.3 names trusted versus untrusted zones directly. The tested behaviour is that traffic from an untrusted zone to a trusted zone is denied by default while the reverse is permitted, and that return traffic is allowed by state, not by a rule. Expect a scenario where the missing element is a zone for public servers — that is the screened subnet.

front: What is a screened subnet (DMZ) and what specific scenario does it protect against?
answer: A separate zone between the internet and the internal LAN that hosts public-facing servers. It protects against the case where one of those servers is compromised: the attacker gains a web server, not a path into the LAN.
detail:
The design assumes the public server will eventually be breached and positions it so that the breach is contained.
How it works
  • Two rule sets, not one: The internet may reach the screened subnet on specific ports only. The screened subnet may reach the internal LAN on almost nothing — ideally only a defined database or authentication port to a defined host. That second rule set is what makes it a DMZ rather than just a subnet.
  • Internal clients still reach it normally: Staff access the servers from inside, but the reverse path is what is restricted. Traffic initiated from the DMZ toward the LAN is the direction that must be tightly constrained.
  • It contains, it does not prevent: The web server is exposed by design and can be exploited. The value is that the attacker lands in a zone with no domain controllers, no file shares and no route inward.
  • Modern equivalents keep the same shape: Cloud designs use public and private subnets with security groups, and reverse proxies front applications the same way. The concept — a controlled intermediate zone — is unchanged.
Where you see it
  • Hosting a public web server, mail relay or VPN concentrator
  • Providing a partner-facing extranet application without exposing the LAN
  • Explaining after an incident why the compromised web server did not lead to a domain breach
exam: N10-009 names the screened subnet and treats DMZ as the older synonym. Expect a question that describes a public web server placed directly on the internal LAN and asks what should change — the answer is to move it to a screened subnet. The key rule to identify is the restriction on traffic from the DMZ into the internal network.

front: IDS vs IPS — what is the operational difference and the trade-off?
answer:
IDS: out of band, receives a copy of traffic, detects and alerts only — it cannot stop the attack.
IPS: inline in the traffic path, detects and blocks — but a false positive drops legitimate traffic and a failure can break the link.
detail:
Same detection engine, different placement. Where the device sits determines everything about what it can do and what it can break.
How it works
  • Placement is the whole distinction: An IDS is fed by a SPAN port or a network tap, so traffic reaches its destination whether the IDS likes it or not. An IPS sits in the forwarding path, so every packet must pass through it to continue.
  • Blocking has a cost: A false positive on an IDS is a wasted alert. A false positive on an IPS is an outage for real users. This is why IPS rules are often deployed in alert-only mode first and tuned before enforcement is enabled.
  • An inline device is a failure point: IPS hardware needs a defined behaviour when it fails or is overloaded — fail-open passes traffic unfiltered, fail-closed blocks everything. Choosing between them is an availability-versus-security decision.
  • Signature and anomaly detection are the two methods: Signature-based matching catches known attacks and misses novel ones. Anomaly or behaviour-based detection catches unusual activity but produces more false positives and needs a baseline of normal traffic.
Where you see it
  • A SPAN port feeding a detection sensor for monitoring only
  • An inline appliance blocking known exploit traffic at the perimeter
  • Tuning a noisy rule that blocked a legitimate application
exam: The tested pair is out of band and alerts versus inline and blocks. If a scenario says the device must not risk dropping legitimate traffic, the answer is IDS. If it says the attack must be stopped automatically, the answer is IPS. A question mentioning a SPAN or mirror port is describing an IDS placement.

front: Honeypot vs honeynet — what are they for?
answer:
Honeypot: a single decoy system deliberately made attractive to attackers so their activity can be observed.
Honeynet: a whole decoy network of them. Both are deception technologies.
detail:
Systems with no legitimate purpose, which is exactly what makes them useful: any interaction with them is suspicious by definition.
How it works
  • Zero false positives by design: Nobody has a business reason to touch a honeypot, so every connection is either a scan, a misconfiguration or an attacker. That signal-to-noise ratio is far better than a production IDS produces.
  • They buy intelligence and time: You learn which techniques and tools are being used against you, and an attacker spending hours on a fake file server is not attacking a real one.
  • A honeynet is more convincing: One lone server can look artificial. A network with several hosts, plausible traffic and fake data holds a sophisticated attacker's attention long enough to study them, at the cost of much more effort to build and maintain.
  • Isolation is mandatory: A honeypot is intended to be compromised. If it is not strictly segmented and monitored, it becomes a genuine foothold on your network, which is the main operational risk of deploying one.
Where you see it
  • Placing a decoy server in a DMZ to profile internet scanning activity
  • Early warning of an intruder already inside performing lateral movement
  • Research environments collecting live malware samples
exam: Both terms are named in objective 4.1 under deception technologies. The exam separates them purely by one system versus a network of systems. The purpose to select is detecting, diverting and studying attackers — not blocking them and not luring them into a trap for prosecution, which is the entrapment distractor.

front: Why are IoT, IIoT, SCADA, ICS and OT systems segmented, and what do those acronyms mean?
answer: IoT Internet of Things; IIoT Industrial IoT; SCADA Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition; ICS Industrial Control System; OT Operational Technology. They are segmented because they are often unpatchable, long-lived and insecure by design — isolation is the only viable control.
detail:
A category of devices you cannot secure the normal way. You cannot install an agent on a PLC or patch a camera whose vendor no longer exists, so you control what can reach them instead.
How it works
  • They cannot be patched on a normal cycle: Industrial controllers run validated firmware that a vendor may certify only every few years, and taking a production line down to patch it is not an option. A building's cameras and badge readers often ship with credentials that cannot be changed.
  • They were designed for isolated networks: SCADA and ICS protocols predate internet connectivity and frequently have no authentication or encryption at all. They were safe because nothing else was on the wire, and connecting them to the corporate network removed that assumption.
  • Consequences are physical, not just data: A compromised ICS can stop a pump, open a valve or halt a production line. Availability and safety outrank confidentiality in these networks, which reverses the usual priority order.
  • Segmentation is enforced, not just documented: A separate VLAN with a firewall or data diode between OT and IT, no direct internet path, jump hosts for engineering access, and strict rules on which IT systems may query the OT side.
Where you see it
  • Putting building cameras, badge readers and HVAC on their own VLAN
  • Separating a plant floor control network from the corporate LAN
  • Providing vendor remote support to an ICS through a monitored jump host
exam: These acronyms are listed explicitly under network segmentation enforcement, so know the expansions. The tested reasoning is that these devices cannot be patched or hardened, therefore the control is segmentation and isolation. Answering 'install antivirus' or 'apply patches' for a PLC or an IP camera is the trap.

front: How should guest and BYOD networks be segmented, and what is the captive portal caveat?
answer: Both go on separate VLANs or SSIDs with internet access only and no route to internal resources. A captive portal authorizes a device, not a person, and traffic before login is unencrypted — so segmentation must hold regardless of who logs in.
detail:
Two populations of devices you do not manage, on your infrastructure. The policy assumption must be that each device is already compromised.
How it works
  • Guest access should be internet-only: Deny all traffic from the guest VLAN toward internal subnets, and apply client isolation so guests cannot even see each other. Rate limiting stops one guest consuming the circuit.
  • BYOD is harder because users want access to real resources: The usual answer is conditional: MDM enrolment or NAC posture checks for full access, and a restricted VLAN or published applications for everyone else. Containerization separates corporate data from personal data on the device.
  • The captive portal is weak authentication: It commonly grants access after accepting terms or entering a shared code. It identifies a session, not a person, and the association itself is often on an open SSID with no encryption before and sometimes after login.
  • Encryption cannot be assumed: An open guest SSID leaves users exposed to on-path attacks from other guests. WPA3 Enhanced Open (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption) encrypts each session on an open network without a shared password.
Where you see it
  • A hotel, campus or lobby wireless network with terms-of-use login
  • Allowing personal phones on Wi-Fi with no access to file servers
  • A conditional access policy that requires enrolment before granting corporate resources
exam: Guest and BYOD are both named under network segmentation enforcement. The expected answer for a guest network is a separate VLAN or SSID with internet-only access. The tested caveat is that a captive portal does not authenticate the person and does not encrypt traffic, so it is not a substitute for segmentation.

front: What is micro-segmentation and what problem does it solve that VLANs do not?
answer: Enforcing policy between individual workloads, not just between subnets, so two servers in the same VLAN cannot talk unless policy allows it. It stops lateral movement after an attacker is already inside.
detail:
Traditional segmentation controls traffic that crosses a boundary. Micro-segmentation controls traffic that never leaves the segment at all.
How it works
  • VLANs leave east-west traffic unfiltered: Two hosts in the same VLAN communicate directly through the switch and never pass the firewall. An attacker who compromises one of them reaches all the others without crossing a single control point.
  • Policy follows the workload: Rules are written in terms of identity, tags or roles — 'web tier may reach app tier on 8443' — and enforced at each host or hypervisor. When a virtual machine moves or is rebuilt, its policy moves with it instead of being tied to an IP address.
  • Enforcement is distributed: A distributed firewall in the hypervisor, host-based firewalls, or a cloud provider's security groups apply the rule at the workload itself. There is no traffic-hairpinning through a central appliance.
  • It is the practical expression of zero trust inside a data centre: Every flow is authorized explicitly, including between machines in the same subnet, which is exactly the zero trust rule applied east to west.
Where you see it
  • Preventing a compromised application server from scanning its own subnet
  • Cloud security groups restricting instance-to-instance traffic
  • Isolating a payment environment down to individual workloads for PCI scope reduction
exam: The keyword in the stem is lateral movement or east-west traffic. The answer is micro-segmentation, and it is closely tied to zero trust. The distractor is a VLAN or a perimeter firewall, both of which control north-south traffic and do nothing about two servers in the same broadcast domain.

front: Name the main physical security controls and what each is actually good at.
answer:
Cameras: detect and provide evidence — they do not prevent.
Locks: prevent entry (key, cipher, biometric, electronic).
Badge readers: authenticate and log entry per person.
Access control vestibule (mantrap): stops tailgating by admitting one person at a time.
Asset tags: track and deter equipment removal.
detail:
The layer that matters because physical access defeats almost every logical control. Someone at the console of a switch can reset its password.
How it works
  • Cameras are detective, not preventive: Video records what happened and deters some attempts, but it does not stop anyone walking through a door. Getting this classification right is the single most tested physical security point.
  • Locks are the baseline preventive control: Wiring closets, server rooms and racks all need them. Electronic locks add per-person logging and instant revocation; a lost physical key means rekeying the lock.
  • Badge readers provide accountability: They tie an entry to an identity and produce a timestamped record, which is the physical equivalent of accounting. Badges can be cloned or lent, which is why sensitive areas add a PIN or biometric as a second factor.
  • The vestibule solves the human problem: Two interlocking doors where the second will not open until the first has closed makes tailgating and piggybacking physically impossible, regardless of how polite the employee in front is.
Where you see it
  • Securing a wiring closet and an MDF room in a shared building
  • Investigating equipment theft using badge logs and camera footage
  • Preventing unauthorized entry to a data hall behind an authorized employee
exam: N10-009 lists cameras and locks by name under physical security. The classification question is the common one: a camera is a detective control, a lock is preventive. For a tailgating scenario the correct answer is an access control vestibule, because a camera would only record the incident.

front: What is a rogue device on a network, and what controls detect or prevent it?
answer: Any unauthorized hardware attached to the network — a personal access point, an unmanaged switch, a Raspberry Pi behind a desk, or a device swapped into an existing jack. Controls: 802.1X, port security, disabling unused ports, and periodic discovery scans compared against the inventory.
detail:
The physical-access equivalent of an unauthorized account. It bypasses every perimeter control because it starts inside.
How it works
  • Most rogue devices are not malicious: An employee adding a small switch to gain more ports, or an access point for better signal, creates the same exposure as an attacker would. Intent does not change the risk.
  • Prevention is at the port: A jack that is administratively shut down when unused, or that requires 802.1X authentication before forwarding, cannot be used by an unknown device. Port security limits how many MAC addresses appear on a live port.
  • Detection is by comparison to inventory: Regular discovery scans, switch MAC address table and ARP table reviews, and wireless surveys all produce lists of what is present. Comparing that to what should be present is where a rogue device shows up.
  • Rogue services count too: The objectives name rogue DHCP and rogue AP specifically. An unauthorized service on an authorized host — a DHCP server, a wireless hotspot enabled on a laptop — is the same class of problem.
Where you see it
  • A discovery scan finding an unrecognized MAC address on an access port
  • A wireless survey detecting an unknown AP broadcasting inside the building
  • Shutting down every unused wall jack as part of a hardening standard
exam: Objective 4.2 lists rogue devices and services with DHCP and AP as the examples. The prevention answer that scores highest is 802.1X, because it authenticates the device before the port forwards anything. Disabling unused ports is the low-cost partial control and is also a correct hardening answer.

front: Why put device management interfaces on a separate network, and what is out-of-band management?
answer: So that compromising a user workstation does not expose switch, router and firewall administration. A dedicated management VLAN reachable only from a jump host, or a physically separate out-of-band network, keeps admin access off the production path.
detail:
Management planes are the highest-value target on the network. Reaching one means reconfiguring everything, so access to it is restricted far more tightly than access to data.
How it works
  • In-band management shares the fate of the network: If the management interface is reachable from the user VLAN, any compromised PC can attempt to log into every switch. Worse, if the network is broken, in-band management is broken with it — exactly when you need it.
  • Out-of-band uses a separate path: A dedicated management port on each device, connected to its own switch, often with a console server and a cellular or separate WAN link. That path works when the production network is down or misconfigured, which is what makes remote recovery possible.
  • Access is funnelled through a jump host: Administrators connect to one hardened bastion, authenticate with MFA, and manage devices from there. Nothing else is permitted to reach management addresses, and all activity is logged in one place.
  • Combine with hardened protocols and ACLs: SSH and HTTPS only, SNMPv3 rather than v2c, and an ACL on the management interface permitting only the jump host's address.
Where you see it
  • Recovering a switch after a configuration change cut off its production path
  • An audit requirement that administrative access originate only from a bastion host
  • Separating an out-of-band console server network in a data centre
exam: Network+ tests this as the design answer for protecting the management plane and as the reason out-of-band access exists. If a scenario asks how to reach a device whose production interface is unreachable, the answer is out-of-band management such as a console server. If it asks how to limit exposure of admin interfaces, the answer is a separate management VLAN with restricted access.

front: What is PCI DSS, and how does segmentation relate to it?
answer: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — a contractual standard from the card brands governing how cardholder data is stored, processed and transmitted. Segmenting the cardholder data environment reduces audit scope to only the systems that touch card data.
detail:
Not a law, but enforced through the merchant agreement with fines and loss of the ability to accept cards. It is the most prescriptive of the compliance regimes on the exam.
How it works
  • It is contractual, not legislative: It comes from the card brands rather than a government, and enforcement is through acquiring banks. That distinction is what separates it from GDPR in exam questions.
  • Scope is everything in the assessment: Every system that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data, and any system connected to those, falls in scope. A flat network puts the entire company in scope.
  • Segmentation is the standard scope-reduction technique: Isolating point-of-sale terminals and payment servers behind a firewall in their own VLAN removes the rest of the network from assessment, which cuts both cost and risk. This is the direct networking link CompTIA cares about.
  • Common requirements are recognizable: Do not use vendor default passwords, encrypt cardholder data in transit across public networks, restrict access on a need-to-know basis, segment wireless from the payment environment, and log and monitor access.
Where you see it
  • Placing payment terminals on a dedicated VLAN separate from staff and guest networks
  • An assessor asking for network diagrams showing the cardholder data environment boundary
  • Replacing default credentials on payment infrastructure
exam: Objective 4.1 names PCI DSS under audits and regulatory compliance. The networking answer is segmentation of the cardholder data environment to reduce scope. The exam contrast is PCI DSS as an industry standard for payment card data versus GDPR as a government privacy regulation — do not swap them.

front: What is GDPR and who does it apply to?
answer: The EU General Data Protection Regulation — a law governing the personal data of people in the EU. It applies to any organization processing that data regardless of where the organization is located. Breaches must be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours.
detail:
A privacy regulation that made data protection a legal obligation with meaningful penalties, and whose reach extends beyond Europe.
How it works
  • It follows the data subject, not the company: A company anywhere in the world that handles data on people in the EU is in scope. That extraterritorial reach is why it appears on a global certification exam.
  • Rights belong to the individual: Access to a copy of their data, correction of errors, erasure, portability to another provider, and objection to certain processing. Those rights create technical requirements: you must be able to find all copies of a person's data.
  • Breach notification is time-bound: The supervisory authority must be notified within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach, and affected individuals must be told when the risk to them is high. That deadline drives incident response planning.
  • Penalties scale with revenue: Fines reach up to 4 percent of global annual turnover or 20 million euro, whichever is higher, which is what changed organizational behaviour.
Where you see it
  • Storing EU customer records in a system that must support deletion requests
  • Reporting a data breach to a supervisory authority within the deadline
  • Choosing an EU region for a cloud deployment to satisfy transfer requirements
exam: GDPR is named in objective 4.1. Know it as an EU privacy regulation covering personal data, with the 72-hour breach notification as the memorable number. The exam contrast is against PCI DSS, which is payment card data and contractual rather than legal. GDPR is also the usual driver behind a data locality question.

front: What is data locality (data residency and sovereignty)?
answer: The requirement that data physically remain within a specified jurisdiction, and that it is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored. It constrains which cloud regions and which data centres you may use.
detail:
A legal constraint expressed as a networking and hosting decision. Where the bits sit determines whose laws apply to them.
How it works
  • Residency is about location, sovereignty is about law: Residency says the data must be stored in a named country or region. Sovereignty says whichever country holds the data can compel access under its own law, which is why some organizations avoid particular providers entirely.
  • It drives cloud region selection: Choosing an EU region rather than a global default, disabling cross-region replication, and pinning backups to the same jurisdiction. Content delivery and disaster recovery both have to respect the same boundary.
  • Backups and logs are commonly missed: Production may sit correctly in-region while backups, monitoring telemetry or support tooling quietly replicate elsewhere. Audits find the violation in those secondary copies.
  • It interacts with breach and transfer rules: GDPR restricts transfers of personal data outside the EU without adequate safeguards, so locality requirements are usually a consequence of a privacy regulation rather than a standalone rule.
Where you see it
  • Selecting a specific cloud region so customer records never leave the country
  • Contracting a provider that guarantees data centres in-jurisdiction
  • An audit finding that offsite backups are replicated to a foreign region
exam: Data locality is listed alongside PCI DSS and GDPR in objective 4.1. Expect it as the answer when a scenario says data must not leave a country or must be stored in a specific region — the control is choosing a compliant hosting location and restricting replication, not encryption. Encryption is a distractor because it protects the data but does not change where it resides.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: How does a switch build its MAC address table?
answer: It reads the source MAC of every frame that arrives and records that MAC against the port it came in on. Entries age out after a few minutes of silence.
detail:
A switch starts knowing nothing. It learns purely by observing traffic, which is why the table is built from source addresses even though it is used to look up destination addresses.
How it works
  • Learning uses the source address: When a frame arrives on port 5 with source MAC aaaa.bbbb.cccc, the switch now knows that MAC is reachable through port 5. It does not matter what the frame was for.
  • Forwarding uses the destination address: The switch looks up the destination MAC. A hit means forward out that one port. This is what makes a switch different from a hub, which repeats every frame everywhere.
  • A miss means flood: An unknown destination is sent out every port in the VLAN except the one it arrived on. The reply teaches the switch where that device is, so the flooding stops after one exchange.
  • Entries age out: A MAC that has not been heard from within the aging time — commonly five minutes — is removed. This is why moving a laptop to a different port works without intervention, and why an idle device's traffic gets flooded once when it wakes up.
  • The table is per-VLAN: The same MAC can appear in two VLANs. Lookups are always scoped to the VLAN the frame belongs to.
Where you see it
  • Finding which switch port a device is plugged into via show mac address-table
  • Tracing a rogue device by MAC address
  • Understanding why the first packet to a quiet host is flooded
exam: The exam asks how a switch populates its table — the answer is the source MAC address of incoming frames, and candidates frequently answer 'destination'. It also asks what a switch does with an unknown destination: it floods out all ports in the VLAN, it does not drop the frame. Contrast with a router, which drops a packet with no matching route.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is unknown unicast flooding, and when is it a problem?
answer: Sending a frame with an unknown destination MAC out every port in the VLAN. It is normal briefly while a switch learns. Constant flooding means MAC entries are expiring, traffic is asymmetric, or the table is under attack.
detail:
Flooding is the switch's fallback when it cannot make a forwarding decision. It is correct behavior, but sustained flooding wastes bandwidth and lets any port sniff traffic meant for others.
How it works
  • It is not the same as a broadcast: The destination MAC is a real, specific address — the switch just does not know where it lives. Every port receives a copy, but only the intended NIC accepts it. A broadcast is addressed to ffff.ffff.ffff and every NIC accepts it.
  • Aging plus one-way traffic causes chronic flooding: If a server only ever replies and never initiates, its MAC entry can age out while traffic to it continues. Every frame to that server is then flooded until it speaks again.
  • Asymmetric routing causes it at scale: When request and reply take different paths, one switch never sees the source MAC of a device it constantly forwards to, so it floods every frame for that device permanently.
  • It is the payoff of a MAC flooding attack: An attacker fills the table so legitimate entries cannot be stored. The switch then floods nearly everything, and the attacker captures traffic from a normal access port.
Where you see it
  • Investigating unexplained bandwidth on access ports
  • Explaining why a packet capture on one port shows another host's traffic
  • Correlating flooding with an ARP or MAC aging timer mismatch
exam: The exam contrast is unknown unicast flooding vs broadcast: flooding is one destination the switch cannot locate, a broadcast is addressed to everyone by design. It also uses sustained flooding as the observable symptom of a MAC flooding attack in a security question — the fix is port security.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: Collision domain vs broadcast domain — what defines each boundary on a modern network?
answer: A collision domain is bounded by every switch port (each port is its own; full duplex means collisions effectively do not occur). A broadcast domain is bounded by a VLAN or a router interface.
detail:
Two different segmentation concepts that get confused because both describe 'how far traffic spreads'. One is about contention on the wire, the other about the reach of a broadcast frame.
How it works
  • A hub is one collision domain: Every device on a hub shares the wire and must contend using CSMA/CD. Two simultaneous transmissions collide. A switch replaced this by giving each port its own segment with buffers.
