  • Switch ports segment collisions, not broadcasts: Adding a switch multiplies collision domains — one per port — but does nothing to broadcasts. A 48-port switch is 48 collision domains and, by default, one broadcast domain.
  • VLANs segment broadcasts: Creating a second VLAN creates a second broadcast domain on the same physical switch. A broadcast in VLAN 10 is never sent to a VLAN 20 port.
  • Routers do not forward broadcasts: A router interface is the hard boundary. This is the original meaning of 'routers break up broadcast domains, switches break up collision domains'.
  • Full duplex retires the collision domain entirely: With separate transmit and receive paths, there is nothing to collide with. CSMA/CD is disabled. Collision domains still appear on the exam as a concept but are historical in practice.
Where you see it
  • Counting domains in an exam diagram of hubs, switches and routers
  • Justifying VLANs to control broadcast traffic on a large flat network
  • Explaining why replacing a hub with a switch fixed performance
exam: This appears as a diagram question: count the collision domains and broadcast domains. Rules to apply: each switch port = one collision domain, each hub = one collision domain regardless of port count, each router interface or VLAN = one broadcast domain. The most common error is thinking a switch splits broadcast domains — it does not unless VLANs are configured.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is a VLAN, and what is the VLAN database?
answer: A VLAN is a logically separate Layer 2 broadcast domain on shared physical switches. The VLAN database is the switch's list of which VLAN IDs exist and their names — a VLAN must exist there before a port can be assigned to it.
detail:
VLANs decouple network segmentation from physical wiring. Two devices in the same room can be on different networks, and devices in different buildings can be on the same one.
How it works
  • Ports are assigned to VLANs, and VLANs are broadcast boundaries: A frame originating in VLAN 10 is only ever sent to VLAN 10 ports and trunks carrying VLAN 10. Reaching VLAN 20 requires a router or an SVI.
  • VLAN IDs are 12 bits: The 802.1Q tag holds a 12-bit VLAN ID, giving 0-4095. IDs 0 and 4095 are reserved, so 1-4094 are usable. VLAN 1 is the default and carries all ports until you change them.
  • The VLAN must be created before it can be used: Assigning a port to a VLAN that does not exist in the database leaves the port inactive. This is a frequent cause of 'the port is up but the host gets nothing'.
  • VLANs are a Layer 2 construct: They do not assign IP addresses. Mapping one subnet to one VLAN is a convention that makes routing sane, not a requirement of the technology.
Where you see it
  • Separating guest, corporate, voice and management traffic on one switch
  • Placing users from several floors into one logical network
  • Reducing broadcast traffic on a large flat network
exam: The exam tests the definition — a VLAN is a logical broadcast domain — and the count: 4094 usable VLANs from a 12-bit ID. It also tests the consequence: devices in different VLANs cannot communicate without a Layer 3 device, even if plugged into the same switch. That last statement is a very common question stem.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What does 802.1Q do, and how large is the tag?
answer: It is the VLAN trunking standard. It inserts a 4-byte tag into the Ethernet frame, carrying a 12-bit VLAN ID (1-4094 usable) and a 3-bit priority field. Frames on the native VLAN are sent untagged.
detail:
A trunk carries many VLANs over one link, so each frame must state which VLAN it belongs to. 802.1Q is how that label is attached.
How it works
  • The tag is inserted, not prepended: It goes between the source MAC address and the EtherType field of the original frame. The frame checksum is recalculated because the frame has changed.
  • Four bytes: 2 for the identifier, 2 for control: Two bytes mark the frame as tagged. The other two carry the 12-bit VLAN ID plus a 3-bit priority field used by Layer 2 QoS (802.1p) and a 1-bit drop-eligible flag.
  • It grows the frame beyond standard Ethernet: A maximum 1518-byte Ethernet frame becomes 1522 bytes when tagged. Old equipment that does not understand the extra four bytes reports these as baby giant errors.
  • The tag is stripped at the access port: The receiving switch reads the VLAN ID, removes the tag, and delivers a normal untagged frame to the end device. Hosts never see 802.1Q tags — with the exception of an IP phone on a voice VLAN.
Where you see it
  • Carrying all VLANs between two switches over one uplink
  • Trunking a hypervisor host so VMs land in different VLANs
  • Feeding a router-on-a-stick or firewall subinterfaces
exam: The two numbers CompTIA asks for are the tag size, 4 bytes, and the usable VLAN count, 4094. It also tests the name pairing: 802.1Q = VLAN tagging, versus 802.1X (port-based authentication), 802.1D (STP) and 802.3ad (link aggregation). Those four look alike in a multiple-choice list and are chosen as distractors for each other.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: Access port vs trunk port — what does each carry?
answer: An access port belongs to one VLAN and sends and receives untagged frames — it faces an end device. A trunk port carries many VLANs and tags them with 802.1Q — it faces another switch, a router or a hypervisor.
detail:
The distinction is whether the device on the far end understands VLAN tags. End devices do not, so their frames must be untagged; infrastructure devices do, so they get tags.
How it works
  • Access ports hide VLANs from the host: A PC has no VLAN configuration. The switch places its untagged frames into the port's assigned VLAN on the way in and strips the tag on the way out.
  • Trunk ports preserve the VLAN across the link: Every frame arrives labeled with its VLAN, so the far switch can keep the traffic separated. Without the tag, all VLANs would merge into one.
  • Trunks have an allowed VLAN list: You should permit only the VLANs that actually need to cross the link. Pruning the list limits broadcast propagation and reduces the impact if the trunk is compromised.
  • Misconfiguration fails in a characteristic way: An access port where a trunk is needed passes only one VLAN and silently blackholes the rest. A trunk where an access port is needed can expose every VLAN to whatever is plugged in.
Where you see it
  • Connecting user PCs, printers and cameras (access)
  • Switch-to-switch uplinks and ESXi or Hyper-V host uplinks (trunk)
  • Feeding a firewall or router that routes between VLANs (trunk)
exam: Straight recall on the exam: which port type carries multiple VLANs — trunk. The scenario version is 'a new switch was installed and only one VLAN works across the uplink', where the cause is that the uplink is an access port instead of a trunk. Remember that access ports are untagged; that word is often the discriminator between two otherwise identical answers.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is the native VLAN on an 802.1Q trunk?
answer: The single VLAN whose frames cross the trunk untagged. It defaults to VLAN 1 and should be changed to an unused VLAN.
detail:
802.1Q was designed to interoperate with older equipment that could not read tags, so exactly one VLAN per trunk is allowed to travel without a tag.
How it works
  • Untagged frames are assigned to the native VLAN: When a frame with no 802.1Q tag arrives on a trunk, the receiving switch places it in the native VLAN. That is the only way it can classify an unlabeled frame.
  • Both ends must agree: The native VLAN is a local configuration on each trunk port. If the two switches disagree, traffic in one switch's native VLAN silently lands in a different VLAN on the other.
  • VLAN 1 is a poor default: Every port starts in VLAN 1, and control protocols historically used it. Leaving the native VLAN as 1 means user traffic can share a VLAN with switch management and control traffic.
  • Best practice is a dedicated unused VLAN: Set the native VLAN to something like 999 that no host is in, and do not carry it anywhere it is not needed. That removes the double-tagging attack surface and the accidental-merge risk.
Where you see it
  • Hardening switch-to-switch uplinks in a security baseline
  • Interoperating with a device that sends untagged management traffic
  • Reading a trunk configuration during an audit
exam: The exam wants two facts: the native VLAN is untagged, and its default is VLAN 1. It then builds security questions on top of it — the hardening recommendation is to change the native VLAN away from VLAN 1. Do not confuse the native VLAN with the default VLAN or the management VLAN; the exam sometimes lists all three as options.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What happens on a native VLAN mismatch between two trunk ports?
answer: Untagged traffic from one switch's native VLAN is delivered into a different VLAN on the other switch. The two VLANs are effectively bridged together, breaking segmentation and creating an unintended Layer 2 path.
detail:
A mismatch is not a link failure. The trunk stays up and most VLANs work fine, which is exactly what makes it hard to find.
How it works
  • The frames have no label to check: Switch A sends VLAN 99 traffic untagged because 99 is its native VLAN. Switch B, whose native VLAN is 1, receives an untagged frame and files it into VLAN 1. Nothing in the frame contradicts that.
  • Segmentation silently disappears: Two VLANs that were designed to be isolated now exchange broadcasts and traffic. A guest VLAN merged into a corporate VLAN is a real security incident, not a cosmetic error.
  • It can also merge spanning-tree domains: Bridging two VLANs together joins their Layer 2 topologies. That can create a physical loop that STP was not expecting to have to block.
  • Cisco switches log it via CDP: Neighbor discovery detects the disagreement and generates a native VLAN mismatch message, which is often the only visible clue since the link itself is up.
Where you see it
  • Auditing trunk configuration after a switch replacement
  • Investigating hosts in one VLAN receiving another VLAN's broadcasts
  • Explaining a security finding that two isolated networks can reach each other
exam: CompTIA tests this as a cause of unexpected inter-VLAN communication or a VLAN hopping precondition. The symptom phrasing is 'devices in separate VLANs can unexpectedly communicate' or 'a trunk is up but traffic appears in the wrong VLAN'. The answer is native VLAN mismatch; the fix is to configure the same native VLAN on both ends.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is a voice VLAN and how does one switch port serve both a phone and a PC?
answer: A dedicated VLAN for IP phone traffic. The access port carries the PC's data VLAN untagged and the voice VLAN tagged, so the phone and the PC daisy-chained behind it land in different VLANs on one cable.
detail:
IP phones are usually placed between the wall port and the PC. The voice VLAN lets that single cable carry two logically separate networks so voice can get its own subnet and QoS treatment.
How it works
  • The port is a hybrid, not a full trunk: It behaves as an access port for the PC's untagged frames and additionally accepts one tagged VLAN from the phone. It is not carrying every VLAN like a real trunk.
  • The phone learns its VLAN automatically: The switch advertises the voice VLAN ID through LLDP-MED (or CDP on Cisco), so the phone tags its own traffic correctly with no manual configuration.
  • The phone switches the PC's traffic through untouched: The PC's frames pass through the phone's internal switch untagged and are placed in the data VLAN by the switch. The PC never knows a phone is in the path.
  • Separation buys QoS and addressing: Voice gets its own subnet, its own DHCP scope with option 66 for the provisioning server, and priority marking so a large file transfer on the PC does not cause jitter on a call.
Where you see it
  • Deploying IP phones with PCs daisy-chained behind them
  • Applying QoS policy to voice traffic by VLAN
  • Giving phones a separate DHCP scope and TFTP/provisioning server
exam: The exam asks why a voice VLAN exists: separating voice from data for QoS and addressing. The mechanical detail it likes is that voice is tagged and data is untagged on the same access port. Distractors include 'it increases bandwidth' and 'it encrypts voice traffic' — a VLAN does neither.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is an SVI and what does it provide?
answer: A Switch Virtual Interface — a logical Layer 3 interface representing a VLAN on a multilayer switch. It holds the IP address that becomes that VLAN's default gateway, enabling inter-VLAN routing inside the switch.
detail:
An SVI turns a VLAN into a routed subnet without any external router. It is the standard way a Layer 3 switch performs inter-VLAN routing at wire speed.
How it works
  • One SVI per routed VLAN: Interface VLAN 10 holds 10.0.10.1/24, interface VLAN 20 holds 10.0.20.1/24. Hosts in each VLAN use those addresses as their default gateway.
  • Routing happens in switching hardware: A multilayer switch forwards between SVIs in ASICs rather than in a router's CPU, which is why it is far faster than router-on-a-stick and has no single-link bottleneck.
  • The SVI needs the VLAN to be alive: An SVI stays down unless the VLAN exists in the database and at least one port in that VLAN is up (or the VLAN is carried on an active trunk). A down SVI is a common cause of 'the gateway does not respond'.
  • A management SVI is a separate use: Even a pure Layer 2 switch usually has one SVI holding a management IP so you can SSH to it. That SVI does not route anything.
Where you see it
  • Inter-VLAN routing on a campus distribution or core switch
  • Assigning a management IP address to a Layer 2 access switch
  • Providing a redundant gateway when paired with VRRP or HSRP
exam: The exam's phrasing is 'a logical interface that provides Layer 3 connectivity for a VLAN' — the answer is SVI. It contrasts with router-on-a-stick: SVI when the question mentions a multilayer or Layer 3 switch, subinterfaces when it mentions a router with one physical interface. Do not confuse an SVI with a subinterface; the naming and location differ even though both terminate a VLAN at Layer 3.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: Compare the three ways to route between VLANs.
answer:
Separate router interfaces: one physical port per VLAN — simple, doesn't scale.
Router-on-a-stick: one trunk with subinterfaces — cheap, one link is the bottleneck.
Layer 3 switch with SVIs: routing in hardware — fastest, the modern default.
detail:
All three give VLANs a gateway. They differ in cost, port count and how much traffic they can move.
How it works
  • One interface per VLAN wastes ports fast: Ten VLANs means ten router interfaces and ten switch ports. Routers have few interfaces, so this stops working almost immediately.
  • Router-on-a-stick trades ports for bandwidth: One trunk carries every VLAN, so inter-VLAN traffic traverses that link twice — once inbound, once outbound. The link's capacity is shared by all inter-VLAN flows.
  • A Layer 3 switch removes the bottleneck: Routing between SVIs happens inside the switch fabric at line rate, with no external link involved at all. This is why every modern campus design uses it.
  • Routing through a firewall is a deliberate fourth option: Sometimes you want the bottleneck, because inter-VLAN traffic must be inspected. Then all VLANs trunk to a firewall that acts as every gateway.
Where you see it
  • Choosing a design for a new office with several VLANs
  • Explaining poor performance between two VLANs on a router-on-a-stick
  • Justifying the cost of a Layer 3 switch
exam: The exam gives you the constraint and expects the design. 'Only one available router interface' → router-on-a-stick with subinterfaces. 'High-performance inter-VLAN routing' or 'multilayer switch' → SVIs. 'All inter-VLAN traffic must be inspected' → route through the firewall. The trap answer is a Layer 2 switch, which cannot route between VLANs at all.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What does a Layer 2 loop actually do to a network, and why don't the frames stop?
answer: Broadcast and unknown-unicast frames are copied around the loop endlessly and multiplied at every switch, producing a broadcast storm. They never stop because the Ethernet header has no TTL — nothing counts hops and nothing expires.
detail:
This is the failure spanning tree exists to prevent, and understanding it mechanically is what makes every STP question easy.
How it works
  • A broadcast is flooded out every port including the redundant one: Switch A floods a broadcast to switch B on both links. B floods each copy back out its other ports, including back to A. A floods them again. The frames circulate.
  • Each pass multiplies the copies: Every switch duplicates every frame onto every other port. With two paths the count doubles each lap. Within seconds the links are saturated and switch CPUs hit 100 percent.
  • The MAC table destabilizes at the same time: The same source MAC arrives on two different ports repeatedly, so the switch rewrites its table entry back and forth. This is MAC flapping, and it means even unicast forwarding becomes unreliable.
  • Nothing self-heals: There is no expiry mechanism to fall back on. The storm continues until a human disconnects a cable, a switch is power-cycled, or STP blocks a port.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why a user patching two wall ports together takes down a floor
  • Diagnosing a total network outage with no configuration change
  • Justifying BPDU guard on every access port
exam: The exam's why-question is 'why is a Layer 2 loop worse than a Layer 3 loop' — the answer is that Ethernet frames have no TTL to discard them, while IP packets do. It also lists the three consequences as a set: broadcast storm, MAC table instability, and duplicate frames. Expect at least one question that names all three symptoms and asks for the cause.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What does spanning tree do to prevent loops, and what does it cost you?
answer: It elects a root bridge, calculates the best path from every switch to it, and puts every remaining redundant port into a blocking state. The redundant links stay physically connected but carry no user traffic until they are needed.
detail:
STP creates a loop-free logical tree over a physically looped topology. Redundancy is preserved for failover, but never used simultaneously.
How it works
  • Blocking is logical, not physical: A blocked port still receives BPDUs so the switch can monitor the topology. It simply does not forward or learn from data frames. The cable is live and ready.
  • Failure of an active link unblocks a backup: When the forwarding path dies, STP recalculates and transitions the previously blocked port to forwarding. That is the entire point of leaving the redundant link in place.
  • Redundant bandwidth is idle by default: Classic STP wastes half your uplink capacity. MSTP or per-VLAN spanning tree recover some of it by giving different VLANs different roots, and link aggregation avoids the problem by making two links look like one.
  • BPDUs are how switches agree: Bridge Protocol Data Units are exchanged continuously between switches. They carry the root bridge ID and path cost, and they are what makes a distributed loop-free calculation possible.
Where you see it
  • Any topology with redundant switch uplinks
  • Protecting against a user accidentally cabling two ports together
  • Explaining why a redundant uplink shows no traffic under normal conditions
exam: The exam asks what STP prevents (Layer 2 loops / broadcast storms) and what it does to achieve it (blocks redundant ports). A frequently missed detail: the blocked port still receives BPDUs. Also expect the design consequence — the redundant path carries no traffic until a failure, which is why link aggregation is sometimes preferred.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: How is the root bridge elected, and what is a bridge ID?
answer: The switch with the lowest bridge ID wins. Bridge ID = bridge priority (default 32768) + the switch's MAC address. Lowest priority wins; if priorities tie, the lowest MAC address wins.
detail:
The root is the reference point for the whole topology — every path cost is measured toward it. Which switch becomes root therefore determines the shape of the network.
How it works
  • Priority is compared first: Priority is configurable in increments of 4096 (0, 4096, 8192, ... 32768, ...). Set your core switch to a low priority and it wins the election deterministically.
  • MAC address is the tiebreaker, and it is a bad one: If every switch keeps the default 32768, the lowest MAC address wins. MAC addresses tend to be lower on older hardware, so the default outcome is often that your oldest, slowest access switch becomes root.
  • A bad root makes every path suboptimal: All traffic is drawn toward the root. If the root is an access switch in a closet, inter-switch traffic detours through it, and its uplinks become the bottleneck.
  • Always set priority manually: Configure the core switch as root and the second core as the backup root with the next-lowest priority. This is standard hardening, not tuning.
  • Election is continuous: Switches keep exchanging BPDUs. If a new switch with a lower bridge ID is connected, it takes over as root and the whole topology recalculates — which is what root guard prevents.
Where you see it
  • Designing which switch anchors the spanning tree in a campus
  • Diagnosing why traffic between two access switches traverses a third
  • Explaining why adding a switch caused a network-wide topology change
exam: The exam wants lowest bridge ID = priority + MAC, the default priority 32768, and the tiebreak on lowest MAC address. The scenario version is 'a newly added switch became the root bridge and performance degraded' — the fix is to lower the intended root's priority, and to enable root guard on ports facing downstream switches.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: List the 802.1D port states and the timers behind them.
answer: Blocking → Listening → Learning → Forwarding (plus Disabled). Hello 2 s, forward delay 15 s per transition, max age 20 s. Total convergence is roughly 30 seconds for a direct failure and up to 50 seconds when max age must expire first.
detail:
The delays are not inefficiency — they are deliberate. A port must be certain the topology has settled before it forwards, because forwarding too early creates the very loop STP exists to prevent.
How it works
  • Blocking: Receives BPDUs but discards data frames and does not learn MAC addresses. This is the steady state for a redundant port.
  • Listening (15 s): The port processes and sends BPDUs to participate in the election, but still forwards nothing and learns no MACs. This window lets the topology stabilize before anything commits.
  • Learning (15 s): The port now records source MAC addresses into the table but still does not forward frames. This pre-populates the table so the port is useful the instant it starts forwarding.
  • Forwarding: Normal operation: learning MACs and forwarding frames.
  • Max age 20 s explains the 50-second case: A blocked port that stops hearing BPDUs must wait max age (20 s) before assuming the path is gone, then run listening and learning (30 s). Direct link failure is detected instantly, so it costs only the 30 s.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why a PC gets no DHCP address for 30 seconds after plugging in
  • Justifying PortFast on access ports
  • Estimating outage length after a switch uplink failure
exam: Memorize the four active states in order and the two headline numbers: 30 seconds typical, 50 seconds worst case. The distinguishing detail between listening and learning is that learning populates the MAC table and listening does not — neither forwards. The classic scenario is a PC or server failing DHCP or PXE boot because of this delay, with PortFast as the fix.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: Name the STP port roles and what each does.
answer: Root port: the one port on a non-root switch with the best path to the root. Designated port: the forwarding port for a given segment. Alternate/blocking port: a redundant path held in discarding state. Backup port: a redundant port to a segment already served by this switch.
detail:
Roles describe a port's job in the topology; states describe what it is currently doing. Every port has exactly one role, and the role determines the state.
How it works
  • Every non-root switch has exactly one root port: It is chosen by lowest cumulative path cost to the root, tiebroken by the neighbor's bridge ID and then port ID. The root bridge itself has no root port.
  • Every segment has exactly one designated port: The switch with the better path to the root owns the designated port for that link. All the root bridge's ports are designated.
  • Alternate ports are the blocked ones: A port that is neither root nor designated has no job, so it is blocked. It offers an alternate path to the root and takes over if the root port fails — RSTP promotes it almost instantly.
  • Backup ports are rare: A backup port exists only when one switch has two ports on the same shared segment, which requires a hub. On modern point-to-point links they essentially do not occur.
Where you see it
  • Reading show spanning-tree output to see which uplink is active
  • Predicting which link takes over when the primary uplink fails
  • Explaining why one of two uplinks shows no traffic
exam: The exam asks for the definition of root port (best path to the root bridge from a non-root switch) most often. The confusion it exploits is role versus state — 'blocking' is a state, 'alternate' is a role. Remember the root bridge has no root port: all of its ports are designated and forwarding.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What does RSTP (802.1w) change, and what are its port states?
answer: It converges in a few seconds instead of 30-50. States collapse to Discarding, Learning, Forwarding. It adds explicit alternate and backup roles, edge ports that forward immediately, and a proposal/agreement handshake on point-to-point links.
detail:
RSTP is a redesign of 802.1D that removes the reliance on timers. Instead of waiting out forward delay, switches negotiate directly with each other.
How it works
  • Three states instead of five: Blocking, listening and disabled all become discarding — none of them forward or learn, so distinguishing them served no purpose. Learning and forwarding are unchanged.
  • Proposal and agreement replaces waiting: Two switches on a point-to-point link explicitly negotiate which port becomes designated. Once they agree, the port forwards immediately rather than sitting through 30 seconds of timers.
  • Alternate ports are pre-designated backups: RSTP already knows which port takes over if the root port fails, so failover is a promotion rather than a recalculation — comparable to EIGRP's feasible successor.
  • Edge ports forward instantly: A port declared as an edge port (the RSTP equivalent of PortFast) skips the sequence entirely. If it ever receives a BPDU it loses edge status and reverts to normal RSTP behavior.
  • Any switch can originate a topology change BPDU: In 802.1D only the root generated BPDUs that others relayed. In RSTP every switch sends its own hellos, so a failure is detected after three missed hellos, about six seconds.
Where you see it
  • Modern switch deployments, where RSTP or a variant is the default
  • Reducing outage time after an uplink failure from tens of seconds to a few
  • Interoperating with legacy 802.1D switches, which RSTP falls back to
exam: The exam tests the standard numbers and the state list: 802.1D = STP, 802.1w = RSTP, 802.1s = MSTP, and RSTP's states are discarding, learning, forwarding. The most-asked fact is simply that RSTP converges much faster. The distractor is claiming RSTP eliminates blocking — it does not; discarding is still a blocked state.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is PortFast, where do you use it, and where must you never use it?
answer: It moves an access port straight to forwarding, skipping listening and learning. Use it on ports facing end devices only. Never use it on a port connected to another switch.
detail:
The 30-second STP delay is pointless on a port that cannot create a loop. PortFast removes it, at the cost of removing the safety check.
How it works
  • It eliminates the 30-second dead time: A PC plugged into a normal port waits through listening and learning before any traffic passes. DHCP requests and PXE boots time out in that window, which is the usual reason PortFast gets deployed.
  • It does not disable STP on the port: The port still participates in spanning tree and still sends and receives BPDUs. It just skips the transitional states when it comes up.
  • On a switch-to-switch link it creates a real loop: The port begins forwarding before STP has determined whether it should be blocked. For the seconds until the topology converges, frames circulate.
  • It should always be paired with BPDU guard: PortFast tells the switch 'no switch will ever be here'. BPDU guard enforces that claim by shutting the port down if a BPDU appears. The two features are deployed together as a unit.
Where you see it
  • Access ports serving PCs, printers, phones and cameras
  • Fixing DHCP or PXE boot timeouts on newly connected devices
  • Server ports where the boot process cannot tolerate a 30-second wait
exam: The exam scenario is 'workstations fail to obtain a DHCP address when first connected, but work if the user waits' — the answer is PortFast. The paired question asks what protects a PortFast port from a rogue switch: BPDU guard. The trap is applying PortFast to a trunk or uplink, which the exam presents as a cause of intermittent loops.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What does BPDU guard do?
answer: It shuts a port down (err-disable) the moment that port receives any BPDU. It is applied to access ports to guarantee no switch is ever connected there.
detail:
An access port should never hear from another switch. BPDU guard turns that assumption into enforcement, and does it before a loop can form.
How it works
  • A BPDU on an access port means a switch appeared: End devices do not generate BPDUs. Receiving one means someone plugged in a switch, a wireless access point in bridge mode, or a device with a virtual switch.
  • Err-disable is immediate and total: The port goes down instantly. This is intentional: shutting one port is far less damaging than allowing an unauthorized switch to join the spanning tree and potentially become root.
  • Recovery is manual or timed: The port stays down until an administrator bounces it, or until an err-disable recovery timer re-enables it automatically. A port that keeps err-disabling points at a persistent rogue device.
  • It complements PortFast rather than replacing it: PortFast gives up the loop-prevention delay; BPDU guard restores the protection in a stricter, faster form.
Where you see it
  • Hardening every user-facing access port in a campus
  • Preventing an employee's personal switch from joining the network
  • Investigating a port that repeatedly enters err-disable state
exam: The exam contrasts BPDU guard with root guard and expects the distinction: BPDU guard disables the port on any BPDU, root guard blocks the port only on a superior BPDU. The scenario 'a user connects an unauthorized switch to a wall port' calls for BPDU guard. A port found in err-disabled state after a user plugged something in is the observable symptom.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What does root guard do, and how is it different from BPDU guard?
answer: Root guard blocks a port if a superior BPDU arrives there, preventing that neighbor from becoming the root bridge. BPDU guard shuts the port down on any BPDU at all.
detail:
Root guard is used where a switch is legitimately expected — you accept it as a neighbor but refuse to let it take over the root role and reshape your topology.
How it works
  • Superior BPDU means a lower bridge ID: A switch advertising a better bridge ID would win the root election. Root guard sees that BPDU and instead places the port into a root-inconsistent blocking state.
  • The block is automatic and self-clearing: Once the superior BPDUs stop, the port returns to normal forwarding on its own. No administrator action is needed, unlike err-disable from BPDU guard.
  • It protects the designed topology: Without it, a customer switch, a contractor's device or a misconfigured lab switch with priority 0 can become root and pull all traffic through a slow link.
  • Placement differs from BPDU guard: Root guard goes on ports facing downstream or partner switches that should never be root. BPDU guard goes on access ports where no switch belongs at all.
Where you see it
  • Distribution switch ports facing access switches
  • Ports handed to another department or a customer network
  • Preventing a lab or test switch from taking over the production root role
exam: The exam always tests these two together. The discriminator words are any BPDU (BPDU guard, port shuts down) versus superior BPDU (root guard, port blocks but stays up). The scenario 'prevent an external switch from becoming the root bridge' is root guard; 'prevent a switch from being connected at all' is BPDU guard.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is MSTP (802.1s) for?
answer: It maps groups of VLANs onto a small number of spanning-tree instances, so you get per-VLAN load balancing without the CPU cost of running a separate instance for every VLAN.
detail:
It is the middle ground between one instance for the entire switch (802.1D, no load sharing) and one instance per VLAN (PVST+, heavy on large VLAN counts).
How it works
  • One instance per VLAN does not scale: Cisco's PVST+ runs a full spanning tree per VLAN. With 300 VLANs that is 300 topologies to compute and 300 sets of BPDUs, which strains switch CPU.
  • MSTP groups VLANs into instances: VLANs 1-100 map to instance 1, VLANs 101-200 to instance 2. Only two topologies are computed regardless of how many VLANs exist.
  • Different instances get different roots: Making switch A the root for instance 1 and switch B the root for instance 2 sends half the VLANs up each uplink. Both redundant links carry traffic instead of one sitting idle.
  • All switches must share the MST region configuration: The region name, revision number and VLAN-to-instance mapping must match exactly on every switch. A mismatch causes switches to treat each other as being in different regions, producing an unexpected topology.
Where you see it
  • Campus networks with many VLANs and redundant uplinks
  • Load balancing VLAN traffic across two distribution uplinks
  • Replacing per-VLAN spanning tree where VLAN count is high
exam: N10-009 wants the standard number and the purpose: 802.1s = MSTP, which maps multiple VLANs to fewer spanning-tree instances and allows load balancing. Keep the standards straight: 802.1D STP, 802.1w RSTP, 802.1s MSTP, 802.1Q VLAN tagging, 802.1X authentication.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is DTP, and how does switch spoofing abuse it?
answer: Dynamic Trunking Protocol auto-negotiates whether a link becomes a trunk. In switch spoofing, an attacker's device sends DTP messages from a normal wall port, negotiates a trunk, and gains access to every VLAN on it.
detail:
DTP exists to save configuration effort. It also means an unconfigured port will happily become a trunk for anyone who asks, which is the vulnerability.
How it works
  • Dynamic auto and dynamic desirable both accept trunking: A port left in a dynamic mode will form a trunk if the far end asks for one. On many switches this is the default state of an unconfigured port.
  • A trunk exposes every VLAN at once: Once trunking, the attacker's device receives tagged traffic for all allowed VLANs and can send into any of them. VLAN segmentation is gone for that port.
  • The fix is to hardcode every port: Configure access ports explicitly as access and disable DTP negotiation on them. Configure uplinks explicitly as trunks with an explicit allowed VLAN list.
  • It is distinct from double tagging: Switch spoofing makes the port a real trunk and gives two-way access to all VLANs. Double tagging exploits native VLAN handling on an existing access port and is one-way only.
Where you see it
  • Hardening a switch configuration to a security baseline
  • Explaining an audit finding that access ports are in dynamic mode
  • Investigating a device that unexpectedly sees traffic from multiple VLANs
exam: This is a security-domain question that lives in the switching material. The exam names the attack VLAN hopping and expects both methods: switch spoofing (via DTP) and double tagging (via the native VLAN). The mitigation it wants is disable DTP and manually configure port modes.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: How does double-tagging VLAN hopping work?
answer: The attacker sends a frame with two 802.1Q tags. The first switch strips the outer tag (which matches the native VLAN) and forwards the frame over the trunk still carrying the inner tag, so the next switch delivers it into the victim VLAN.
detail:
The attack exploits the rule that exactly one VLAN crosses a trunk untagged, combined with the fact that a switch only removes one tag.
How it works
  • The outer tag must match the trunk's native VLAN: The attacker's access port must be in the same VLAN as the trunk's native VLAN. If they differ, the first switch does not strip the tag in the way the attack needs and it fails.
  • A switch removes only one tag: The first switch strips the outer tag as normal, sees an ordinary frame, and forwards it untagged onto the trunk because the frame is in the native VLAN. The inner tag is still attached and rides along.
  • The second switch acts on the inner tag: It reads what it believes is a single legitimate 802.1Q tag and delivers the frame into that VLAN — a VLAN the attacker was never permitted to reach.
  • The attack is one-way: The victim's replies follow normal switching rules and go back into the victim's own VLAN, never to the attacker. It is useful for injection — a DoS, a spoofed command — not for two-way conversation.
  • The mitigation is native VLAN hygiene: Set the native VLAN to a dedicated unused VLAN that no access port is in, and do not allow it on trunks where it is not needed. Some designs tag the native VLAN as well.
Where you see it
  • Explaining a penetration test finding about VLAN segmentation
  • Justifying changing the native VLAN away from VLAN 1
  • Reviewing trunk configuration during a security audit
exam: The exam expects that double tagging depends on the native VLAN and that the fix is to change the native VLAN to an unused one — not 'disable trunking' and not 'use a firewall'. Its other testable property is that the attack is unidirectional. Pair it with switch spoofing as the two forms of VLAN hopping.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is link aggregation, and what does LACP contribute?
answer: Bundling several physical links into one logical link for more bandwidth and redundancy — also called EtherChannel, port channel or LAG. LACP (802.3ad / 802.1AX) is the standard protocol that negotiates the bundle with the far end.
detail:
Aggregation solves the problem STP creates: instead of blocking a redundant link, make the two links look like one so spanning tree sees a single loop-free path and both cables carry traffic.
How it works
  • STP sees one logical link: Because the bundle presents itself as a single interface, there is no loop for STP to block. Both members forward simultaneously, which is the main reason to aggregate.
  • Traffic is hashed per flow, not per packet: The switch hashes source and destination addresses to pick a member link, so all packets of one conversation stay on one link and cannot arrive out of order. A single transfer therefore does not exceed one link's speed.
  • Failure of one member is transparent: The bundle stays up with reduced capacity, and existing sessions on the surviving links are unaffected. No STP recalculation is needed.
  • LACP negotiates and verifies: Both ends exchange LACP packets confirming they agree on the bundle before any member forwards. It also detects a member that is miswired or unidirectional and removes it.
Where you see it
  • Doubling a switch-to-switch uplink without leaving a link blocked by STP
  • Server NIC teaming to a switch
  • Providing uplink redundancy that fails over without STP convergence
exam: The exam wants the standard number 802.3ad (LACP) and the two benefits: increased bandwidth and redundancy. The nuance it sometimes tests is that a single flow does not get the aggregate speed — four bonded 1 Gbps links do not give one file transfer 4 Gbps. Do not confuse 802.3ad (aggregation) with 802.1AX naming or with 802.1Q.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What must match on both ends of a link aggregation bundle?
answer: Speed, duplex, VLAN mode (access or trunk), allowed VLAN list, native VLAN, and the aggregation mode itself. A mismatch causes the ports to be suspended rather than bundled.
detail:
A bundle is only safe if every member behaves identically. The switch refuses to form a bundle from mismatched links because inconsistent members would deliver traffic unpredictably.
How it works
  • Physical parameters must be identical: Every member must run the same speed and duplex. Mixing a 1 Gbps and a 100 Mbps link is rejected, because the hashing assumes equal-capacity members.
  • Layer 2 configuration must be identical: All members must be access ports in the same VLAN, or trunks with the same allowed list and the same native VLAN. Differences would put the same flow into different VLANs depending on which member it hashed to.
  • Modes must be compatible: Both ends must agree on the aggregation method. LACP active with LACP passive works; LACP on one side and static on the other does not.
  • The failure mode is suspension, not chaos: A properly configured switch detects the inconsistency and places the offending port in a suspended or err-disabled state instead of forwarding. That is protective — the symptom is a link that is up but passing nothing.
Where you see it
  • Troubleshooting an EtherChannel that will not come up
  • Verifying configuration before enabling a new uplink bundle
  • Explaining why one member of a bundle is suspended
exam: The exam scenario is 'a port channel was configured but one interface is suspended' or 'the bundle will not form'. The expected answer is a configuration mismatch — usually speed/duplex, VLAN or native VLAN. It is testing that you know the switch refuses to bundle mismatched ports rather than bundling them badly.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: Static aggregation vs LACP — what is the risk of static?
answer: Static bundles have no negotiation. If one end is bundled and the other is not, or a cable is patched wrongly, the result is a loop or black-holed traffic. LACP verifies both ends agree before forwarding anything.
detail:
Static aggregation forces the ports into a bundle by assertion. It works when everything is correct and fails badly when it is not.
How it works
  • Static assumes the far end is configured correctly: The switch just starts hashing traffic across the members. It has no way to confirm the other end is doing the same, or that the cables even go to the same device.
  • A half-configured static bundle is a loop: One side treats two links as one logical interface, so STP sees a single link and blocks nothing. The other side treats them as two independent ports. Two forwarding paths exist between the switches — that is a Layer 2 loop.
  • LACP catches the mismatch before forwarding: Members stay down until LACP packets confirm both ends agree on the bundle and on which links belong to it. Miswired or unidirectional links are excluded automatically.
  • Static still has a use: Some devices do not support LACP, and static removes the small negotiation delay. It requires disciplined configuration and verification.
Where you see it
  • Choosing an aggregation mode for a new uplink
  • Investigating a broadcast storm that appeared after adding a second uplink
  • Bundling to a device or NIC team that lacks LACP support
exam: The exam frames this as a best-practice question: use LACP over static because it negotiates and validates the bundle. The consequence to remember is that a misconfigured static bundle can create a Layer 2 loop that spanning tree cannot see, because STP believes the bundle is one link.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is a MAC flooding attack and what does it achieve?
answer: The attacker generates frames with thousands of fake source MAC addresses to fill the switch's CAM table. Once full, the switch cannot learn real addresses and floods traffic out every port, letting the attacker capture it.
detail:
The attack turns a switch back into a hub. It does not break the switch; it exhausts a finite resource so the switch falls back to its default behavior.
How it works
  • The CAM table is finite: A switch stores a fixed maximum number of MAC entries. Filling it with garbage leaves no room for legitimate learning.
  • Failing open is the design, not a bug: When the switch cannot look up a destination, it floods. That is correct behavior for an unknown unicast. The attacker has simply made every destination unknown.
  • The payoff is passive sniffing: Traffic destined for other hosts now arrives at the attacker's port, where a capture tool reads it. On an unencrypted protocol, credentials and data are exposed.
  • Port security is the direct mitigation: Limiting the number of MAC addresses learned per port means one port cannot consume the whole table. The port shuts down or drops the excess long before the CAM table fills.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why a packet capture from a user port shows other hosts' traffic
  • Justifying port security on all access ports
  • Investigating sudden switch-wide flooding with no topology change
exam: The exam pairs the attack with its mitigation: MAC flooding (also called CAM table overflow) is stopped by port security. The distractors are STP, BPDU guard and 802.1Q — none of which limit MAC addresses. The observable symptom to recognize is the switch flooding traffic out all ports, letting an attacker sniff.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What does port security do, and what are the violation modes?
answer: It limits which and how many MAC addresses may be learned on a port. Violation actions are protect (silently drop), restrict (drop and log/count) and shutdown (err-disable the port, the default).
detail:
A per-port control that binds physical access to specific devices. It is the mitigation for MAC flooding and a basic defense against unauthorized devices.
How it works
  • Maximum MAC count is the main knob: Setting a maximum of one means only the first device seen may use the port. A port serving a PC behind an IP phone needs at least two.
  • Sticky learning avoids manual entry: The switch learns the current MAC and writes it into the configuration as if it had been typed. That pins the port to whatever was plugged in when it was enabled.
  • Shutdown is the default and the most disruptive: The port enters err-disabled state and stays down until it is manually bounced or an auto-recovery timer expires. Protect and restrict keep the port up and just discard the extra traffic.
  • It is MAC-based, so it is spoofable: An attacker who reads a permitted MAC address can clone it. Port security raises the effort required; 802.1X is the real authentication control.
Where you see it
  • Locking a port to a specific printer, camera or kiosk
  • Preventing users from attaching unmanaged switches or extra devices
  • Mitigating MAC flooding on access ports
exam: Two exam angles. First, the mitigation pairing: port security stops MAC flooding. Second, the symptom: a port in err-disabled state after a user swapped devices, caused by the default shutdown violation mode. Distinguish port security (MAC-based, on the switch) from 802.1X (credential-based, uses a RADIUS server) — the exam contrasts them directly.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: What is MTU, and what are jumbo frames?
answer: MTU is the largest payload an interface will carry in one frame — 1500 bytes for standard Ethernet. Jumbo frames raise it to around 9000 bytes, and every device in the path must be configured for it.
detail:
Larger frames mean fewer headers and fewer per-packet interrupts for the same amount of data, which reduces CPU overhead on high-throughput links.
How it works
  • Efficiency comes from fewer frames, not faster ones: Moving a gigabyte in 9000-byte frames requires roughly a sixth as many frames as at 1500 bytes. The savings are in header overhead and per-frame processing, not in the wire speed.
  • Every hop must agree: If one switch in the path is left at 1500, oversized frames are dropped as giants. Jumbo frames are all-or-nothing across the whole Layer 2 path, including both endpoints.
  • The failure mode is confusing: Small packets like pings and TCP handshakes succeed because they are under 1500 bytes. Only large transfers fail or stall. 'Ping works but the application does not' is the signature of an MTU problem.
  • Tunnels reduce the usable MTU: VPN and GRE encapsulation adds headers, so the payload that fits inside shrinks. This is why MTU and MSS adjustments are routine on tunnel interfaces.
  • It is confined to controlled networks: Storage networks and data center fabrics use jumbo frames because every device is under one administration. The internet stays at 1500.
Where you see it
  • iSCSI and NFS storage networks
  • Data center server-to-server and backup traffic
  • Diagnosing large transfers that fail while ping succeeds
exam: Know the two numbers: standard Ethernet MTU 1500, jumbo frames 9000. The scenario CompTIA uses is 'small packets succeed but large transfers fail after a network change' — the answer is an MTU mismatch. The other testable requirement is that jumbo frames must be enabled end to end; enabling them on only some devices causes drops.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::07 Switching, VLANs & STP
front: You are told the whole network went down with no configuration change. What symptoms identify a spanning tree loop?
answer: Sudden network-wide slowness or total outage, switch CPU at or near 100%, all port LEDs blinking in unison, MAC address flapping between ports in the logs, and management access to switches becoming impossible.
detail:
A loop is a troubleshooting pattern with a distinctive fingerprint. Recognizing it quickly matters because it does not resolve on its own.
How it works
  • Simultaneous LED activity on every port: The same broadcast is being flooded out every port on every switch continuously. The physical indicators pulse together, which is not something normal traffic produces.
  • MAC flapping in the logs: The switch repeatedly relearns the same source MAC on different ports and logs the change. This log message is the clearest single indicator that frames are arriving from two directions.
  • Management access dies too: The CPU is saturated processing flooded frames, so SSH and the web interface become unresponsive. You often cannot log in to the switch to fix it, which is why console access matters.
  • The trigger is usually physical and recent: Someone patched two wall ports together, connected a small unmanaged switch in a loop, or a redundant link was enabled where STP was disabled. Ask what was plugged in, not what was configured.
  • The fix is to break the loop, then prevent it: Disconnect the offending cable to restore service, then enable or repair STP, and apply PortFast with BPDU guard on access ports so it cannot recur.
Where you see it
  • Responding to a sudden campus-wide outage
  • Interpreting MAC flapping messages in switch logs
  • Post-incident hardening after a user-caused loop
exam: CompTIA presents this as a symptom-matching question, so learn the fingerprint as a set: broadcast storm, MAC flapping, pegged CPU, LEDs blinking together. Distractors are duplex mismatch (slow but not a total outage, with late collisions), a failed uplink (partial outage) and DHCP exhaustion (new clients fail while existing ones work). The immediate action is to physically break the loop.

front: Describe the three-tier hierarchical network model.
answer:
Core: high-speed backbone, switches as fast as possible, no filtering.
Distribution/aggregation: routing between VLANs, ACLs, policy, redundancy.
Access/edge: where end devices plug in — port security, PoE, VLAN assignment.
detail:
A campus design pattern that assigns each layer one job, so you can scale and troubleshoot one layer without redesigning the others.
How it works
  • Core is built for speed and nothing else: Core switches forward as fast as the hardware allows. You deliberately do not put access lists, NAT or deep inspection there, because anything that adds per-packet work in the core slows the entire network.
  • Distribution is where policy lives: This is the boundary between Layer 2 and Layer 3. Inter-VLAN routing, ACLs, QoS marking, route summarisation and first-hop redundancy all belong here. It is the layer that isolates access-layer problems from the rest of the network.
  • Access is where users and risk arrive: Every untrusted device plugs in here, so this is where 802.1X, port security, DHCP snooping, PoE and VLAN assignment are enforced. Access switches are numerous and cheap; they are meant to be replaceable.
  • The point is fault and change isolation: A broadcast storm or a misconfigured device at the access layer is contained by the distribution layer. Adding a new building means adding an access and distribution block, not touching the core.
Where you see it
  • Campus LAN design for a multi-building organisation
  • Deciding at which layer to apply an ACL or a QoS policy
  • Explaining why the core switch configuration is deliberately minimal
exam: CompTIA tests this by function: which layer would you apply an access control list to — the answer is distribution, not core. Which layer provides PoE and connects end devices — access. The distractor is always putting filtering in the core, which reverses the design principle the model exists to express.

front: What is a collapsed core and when do you use it?
answer: A two-tier design where the core and distribution layers are combined into one pair of switches. Used when the network is not large enough to justify a separate core.
detail:
Most organisations do not have enough traffic or enough distribution blocks to need a dedicated core. Merging the two upper layers removes a whole tier of hardware and latency.
How it works
  • Two tiers instead of three: Access switches uplink directly to a redundant pair of core/distribution switches that do both the high-speed forwarding and all the routing and policy.
  • The economic argument: A dedicated core only pays for itself when you have many distribution blocks to interconnect. With two or three wiring closets, a separate core is expensive hardware doing almost nothing.
  • Redundancy still matters: A collapsed core is still built as a redundant pair with first-hop redundancy and dual uplinks from each access switch, because it is now a single tier carrying every function.
  • It limits growth: The trade-off is scaling. Adding many more access blocks eventually overloads the collapsed pair, and the migration path is to promote it to distribution and add a true core above it.
Where you see it
  • Single-building offices and small campuses
  • Branch sites with two or three wiring closets
  • Any network where a full three-tier core would sit mostly idle
exam: The exam usually gives you a size cue. A small or medium network with a couple of closets is a collapsed core; a large multi-building campus is three-tier. Know that collapsed core merges core and distribution, not core and access — that reversal is the standard distractor.

front: What is spine-and-leaf and why does it exist?
answer: Every leaf switch connects to every spine switch; leaves never connect to each other and spines never connect to each other. Every server is exactly the same number of hops from every other server.
detail:
The modern data centre topology. It exists because three-tier plus spanning tree handles server-to-server traffic badly.
How it works
  • Predictable, equal latency: Any leaf-to-leaf path is leaf, spine, leaf — two hops, always. In a three-tier design, two servers might be one hop apart or five, so application performance depended on where the VM happened to land.
  • It uses every link instead of blocking them: Spanning tree keeps a loop-free topology by disabling redundant links, which wastes half the bandwidth you paid for. Spine-and-leaf uses ECMP or a fabric protocol so all uplinks forward simultaneously, and total bandwidth scales by adding spines.
  • It scales horizontally: Need more server ports, add a leaf. Need more inter-rack bandwidth, add a spine and cable it to every leaf. Neither change requires redesigning anything else.
  • It was built for east-west traffic: Virtualisation, microservices, distributed storage and VM migration made server-to-server traffic dominant. A design optimised for traffic leaving the building was the wrong shape for that.
Where you see it
  • Modern data centre and cloud provider fabrics
  • Any environment with heavy virtualisation and VM mobility
  • Replacing a spanning-tree core that is wasting redundant links
exam: The exam asks why spine-and-leaf replaced three-tier in data centres. The two accepted answers are consistent low latency for east-west traffic and all links active via ECMP instead of STP blocking. Remember the structural rule: leaf-to-spine only, never leaf-to-leaf. A design where leaves interconnect is the wrong answer.

front: North-south versus east-west traffic.
answer:
North-south: traffic entering or leaving the data centre — client to server, or server to internet.
East-west: traffic between servers inside the data centre.
detail:
Two directions of flow drawn from the usual network diagram, where the internet is at the top and servers are in rows across the bottom.
How it works
  • North-south crosses the perimeter: This is the traffic a traditional firewall, IPS and load balancer at the edge inspect. It was the dominant volume when applications were monolithic and a client simply talked to one server.
  • East-west stays inside: A web tier calling an application tier calling a database, a VM migrating between hosts, a distributed storage cluster replicating. None of it crosses the perimeter, so none of it is inspected by an edge firewall.
  • East-west is now the larger share: Virtualisation and service-oriented architectures multiplied internal calls. That volume is what made the old three-tier data centre design inadequate and drove spine-and-leaf.
  • It is also a security argument: If an attacker compromises one server, all their lateral movement is east-west and invisible to a perimeter firewall. That is the reasoning behind microsegmentation and zero trust inside the data centre.
Where you see it
  • Justifying spine-and-leaf during a data centre refresh
  • Explaining why perimeter security alone misses lateral movement
  • Sizing inter-rack bandwidth versus internet bandwidth
exam: The exam uses these as vocabulary in topology and security questions. East-west equals server-to-server inside the data centre is the definition to lock in, and it is the answer to why spine-and-leaf exists. In security questions, east-west traffic is the argument for microsegmentation.

front: Describe the star topology and its trade-off.
answer: Every node connects to one central device. It is the normal Ethernet LAN. One cable failure isolates one node; the central device is a single point of failure.
detail:
The physical shape of essentially every wired network built in the last thirty years, because it matches how a switch works.
How it works
  • Failure is isolated per node: Each device has its own dedicated cable. A damaged cable takes out exactly one user, which is the decisive advantage over bus and ring designs where one break affected everyone.
  • The centre is the single point of failure: If the switch fails, everything attached to it fails. This is why distribution and core switches are deployed in redundant pairs while access switches often are not.
  • Physical star, logical star: With a switch, both the physical wiring and the logical forwarding are star-shaped. With a hub, the wiring was a star but the logical topology was a shared bus — every device shared one collision domain.
  • It scales by stacking stars: Connecting access switches up to a distribution switch produces an extended star or tree, which is what a real building network actually is.
Where you see it
  • Every wiring closet with a switch and drops radiating to offices
  • Home networks with a router at the centre
  • Explaining why a single failed patch cord affects only one user
exam: The exam tests star through its failure behaviour: which topology fails one node when a cable breaks but all nodes when the central device fails? The answer is star. The related trap is the physical-versus-logical distinction with a hub — physically a star, logically a bus.

front: Describe mesh topology and the full-mesh link formula.
answer: Nodes interconnect directly with redundant paths. A full mesh connects every node to every other node and requires n(n−1)/2 links. A partial mesh connects only the important pairs.
detail:
The maximum-redundancy topology. Any single link failure leaves an alternate path, at a cost that grows quadratically.
How it works
  • The formula matters because the growth is brutal: Five sites need 10 links. Ten sites need 45. Twenty sites need 190. That quadratic growth is precisely why full mesh is rare outside of small critical cores and wireless mesh.
  • Partial mesh is the practical compromise: You mesh the sites that carry heavy traffic to each other and hub the rest. Most real WANs are partial mesh, not full mesh.
  • Redundancy is the whole point: With no single point of failure, any one link or node can fail without partitioning the network. This is why critical WAN cores and wireless mesh backhauls use it.
  • Wireless mesh applies the same idea: Mesh access points relay for each other so only some need a wired uplink, which is how large outdoor and warehouse coverage is built without cabling every AP.
Where you see it
  • WAN designs between critical sites
  • Wireless mesh coverage in warehouses and outdoor areas
  • Calculating link count for an exam question about adding a site
exam: The n(n−1)/2 formula is directly calculated on the exam — expect to be handed a node count and asked for the number of links. The conceptual question contrasts cost against fault tolerance: mesh gives the highest redundancy at the highest cost, which is why partial mesh is usually the correct real-world answer.

front: Describe the bus and ring topologies and why they were abandoned.
answer:
Bus: all nodes share one cable with terminators at both ends — one break kills the whole segment.
Ring: each node connects to two neighbours in a loop, often with a token controlling who transmits.
detail:
The two legacy topologies. You learn them because the exam names them and because their failure modes explain why star won.
How it works
  • Bus was one shared collision domain: Every device shared one coaxial cable, so only one could transmit at a time and all of them heard every frame. Adding devices degraded everyone's performance.
  • A bus needs terminators: Without a resistor at each end, signals reflect back down the cable and corrupt everything. A missing or failed terminator took down the whole segment, which was a very common fault.
  • Ring passes a token: Token Ring and FDDI granted the right to transmit by circulating a token, which eliminated collisions entirely and made performance predictable under load — genuinely better than early Ethernet, but more expensive.
  • Ring survives as a dual counter-rotating loop: FDDI and SONET/metro rings use two rings running in opposite directions so a single cut wraps the traffic back and the ring keeps running. That is why ring topology persists in carrier and metro networks even though it vanished from the LAN.
Where you see it
  • Legacy 10BASE2/10BASE5 coaxial installations
  • Token Ring and FDDI in older enterprise and campus backbones
  • SONET and metro Ethernet rings still used by carriers
exam: The exam tests these by failure behaviour. One break takes down the entire network describes bus, and also a single (non-redundant) ring. A terminator is required is unique to bus. If a question mentions a token controlling transmission, it is ring. Do not confuse physical ring with logical ring — Token Ring was physically wired as a star through an MAU.

front: What are hybrid and point-to-point topologies?
answer:
Hybrid: any combination of the basic topologies — what real networks actually are.
Point-to-point: a dedicated link between exactly two nodes, with no contention and no other devices on it.
detail:
Two terms that describe real deployments rather than textbook shapes.
How it works
  • Real networks are hybrids: A building with star-wired access switches uplinking to a partial-mesh distribution layer is a hybrid — commonly called a star-bus or tree/extended star. The exam expects you to recognise that a diagram combining shapes is a hybrid.
  • Point-to-point has exactly two endpoints: A leased line between two offices, a wireless bridge across a car park, a serial WAN link, or a single fibre run between two switches. Bandwidth is not shared with anyone.
  • Point-to-multipoint is the contrast: One central device serving several remote endpoints — a wireless sector antenna serving multiple subscriber radios, or a hub-and-spoke WAN. Bandwidth is shared among the remote sites.
  • Point-to-point simplifies troubleshooting: With only two devices on the link, there is no contention, no shared media and no third party to blame. If it is broken, it is one of two endpoints or the medium between them.
Where you see it
  • A wireless bridge linking two buildings across a road
  • A leased line or dark fibre between a data centre and a DR site
  • Describing a real campus network that mixes star and mesh
exam: Point-to-point appears most often in wireless and WAN questions. The tested contrast is point-to-point versus point-to-multipoint: a bridge between two buildings is point-to-point; one antenna serving several remote sites is point-to-multipoint. Hybrid is usually the correct answer for any diagram that is not a textbook-pure shape.

front: Hub versus switch — what actually changes?
answer: A hub repeats every bit out every other port: one collision domain, half duplex, Layer 1. A switch forwards by MAC address to one port: one collision domain per port, full duplex, Layer 2. Both are one broadcast domain.
detail:
The upgrade that made Ethernet fast. It is not about speed rating — it is about how many devices are forced to share the wire.
How it works
  • A hub is an electrical repeater: It has no idea what a MAC address is. A signal arriving on one port is regenerated out every other port. Every attached device therefore contends for the same wire and must use CSMA/CD.
  • A switch learns and forwards: It reads the source MAC of every frame and records which port it came from in a MAC address table. When it later sees that address as a destination, it forwards only out that one port. Everything else stays quiet.
  • Full duplex becomes possible: Because a switch port has exactly one device on it, there is no contention, so both ends can transmit simultaneously. Collisions cease to exist on that segment, and CSMA/CD is no longer needed.
  • Neither breaks up broadcast domains: A switch floods broadcasts out every port in the VLAN, exactly as a hub would. Only a router — or a VLAN boundary, which is routed — separates broadcast domains.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why an old hub in a closet cripples a segment
  • Counting collision and broadcast domains in an exam diagram
  • Understanding why a hub is still occasionally used to tap traffic for a sniffer
exam: This is a guaranteed domain-counting question: given a diagram, how many collision domains and how many broadcast domains? A hub contributes one collision domain regardless of port count; a switch contributes one per port; a router creates a new broadcast domain per interface. The trap is thinking a switch separates broadcast domains — it does not, unless VLANs are involved.

front: Switch versus router — what is the real division of labour?
answer: A switch forwards frames by MAC address within one broadcast domain (Layer 2). A router forwards packets by IP address between networks and terminates broadcast domains (Layer 3).
detail:
The two forwarding devices, distinguished by which address they read and what they do with broadcasts.
How it works
  • Different addresses, different tables: A switch builds a MAC address table by learning source addresses it sees. A router builds a routing table from connected interfaces, static routes and routing protocols. One is learned from traffic, the other is configured or advertised.
  • A router drops broadcasts: Routers do not forward broadcasts. That is what makes each router interface a separate broadcast domain, and it is why broadcast storms are contained to one subnet.
  • A router rewrites Layer 2 on every hop: The IP source and destination stay the same end to end, but the router replaces the source and destination MAC addresses at every hop. Understanding this is what makes the difference between the two layers concrete.
  • A router makes a decision, a switch makes a lookup: Routers apply longest-prefix match, may choose between multiple paths by metric, and can apply NAT and ACLs. Switch forwarding is a straight table lookup on an exact MAC address.
Where you see it
  • Deciding whether a connectivity problem is a VLAN issue or a routing issue
  • Counting broadcast domains in a diagram
  • Explaining why two hosts in different subnets cannot reach each other on the same switch
exam: The reliable exam pattern: two hosts on the same switch but in different subnets cannot communicate — the answer is that a router or Layer 3 switch is needed, not a switch configuration change. Remember that a switch is a MAC/frame/Layer 2 device and a router is an IP/packet/Layer 3 device, and that only the router bounds a broadcast domain.

front: Router versus Layer 3 switch — when do you pick each?
answer: Both route. A Layer 3 switch has many high-speed LAN ports and routes in hardware (ASIC) — use it for inter-VLAN routing inside a campus. A router has fewer ports but supports WAN interfaces, NAT and richer WAN protocols — use it at the network edge.
detail:
A Layer 3 switch is a switch that also routes. The distinction is not capability at Layer 3, it is port density, port type and what else the box can do.
How it works
  • Hardware routing versus software features: A Layer 3 switch routes in an ASIC at line rate between VLANs. A router historically processed packets in software, which is slower per packet but allows far more complex per-packet handling.
  • Port types decide the placement: A Layer 3 switch has dozens of Ethernet ports and no serial, DSL, cellular or DOCSIS interfaces. A router has few Ethernet ports but takes WAN interface cards. You cannot terminate a carrier circuit on a Layer 3 switch.
  • Feature sets differ: NAT, extensive VPN termination, advanced QoS shaping, and complex WAN routing policy live on routers. Layer 3 switches focus on fast inter-VLAN forwarding and often support only a subset.
  • SVIs are the mechanism: A Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs using switched virtual interfaces — a virtual Layer 3 interface with an IP address for each VLAN. That replaces the old 'router on a stick' with a single trunk to a router.
Where you see it
  • Inter-VLAN routing in a campus distribution layer
  • Terminating an ISP circuit and performing NAT at the edge
  • Replacing a router-on-a-stick that has become a bottleneck
exam: The exam decides this by what the scenario needs. Inter-VLAN routing with high throughput inside a building is a Layer 3 switch. Anything mentioning a WAN link, NAT, or an ISP connection is a router. The distractor is assuming a Layer 3 switch cannot route at all — it can; it simply lacks WAN interfaces and edge features.

front: Stateful versus stateless firewall.
answer: Stateful: tracks connections in a state table, so return traffic for an allowed outbound session is permitted automatically. Stateless: evaluates each packet independently against rules — faster, but you must explicitly permit return traffic.
detail:
The difference is memory. One remembers which conversations it already approved; the other treats every packet as if it were the first.
How it works
  • The state table is the mechanism: When an inside host opens a TCP session outbound, the stateful firewall records the source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and protocol. Returning packets that match an existing entry are allowed without consulting the rule set.
  • Stateless needs mirrored rules: Without state, allowing web browsing means writing an outbound rule to port 80/443 and a matching inbound rule for the ephemeral return ports. That inbound rule is far broader than you want, which is why stateless ACLs are weaker.
  • Stateful catches protocol anomalies: Because it tracks the TCP handshake, a stateful device can drop a bare ACK or a mid-stream packet that belongs to no known session — traffic a stateless filter would happily forward if the ports matched.
  • Stateless is still used where speed dominates: Router ACLs are stateless and are applied at line rate for coarse filtering — blocking a whole subnet or bogon addresses. They complement rather than replace a stateful firewall.
Where you see it
  • Any modern perimeter or internal firewall (stateful by default)
  • Router ACLs performing fast coarse filtering
  • Explaining why an outbound-only rule set still allows replies to arrive
exam: The tested behaviour is return traffic. If a scenario says internal users can reach the internet with only an outbound rule configured, the device is stateful. If it says an administrator had to add an explicit inbound rule for replies, it is stateless. Router ACL is the usual example of a stateless filter.

front: What does a next-generation firewall do that a traditional firewall does not?
answer: It inspects at Layer 7. It identifies the actual application, ties traffic to user identity, decrypts and inspects TLS, and includes integrated IPS — instead of filtering only on IP, port and protocol.
detail:
Port-based filtering stopped working when everything moved to port 443. An NGFW makes decisions based on what the traffic actually is.
How it works
  • Port no longer identifies the application: A traditional firewall allowing TCP 443 allows a business SaaS application, a personal file-sharing site, and an attacker's command-and-control channel equally. All three look identical at Layer 4.
  • Application identification reads the payload: The NGFW inspects the traffic's behaviour and content to name the application regardless of port. That is what makes a rule like 'permit the corporate file service, deny consumer file sharing' possible on the same port.
  • User identity replaces IP addresses in rules: By integrating with a directory service, rules apply to users and groups rather than DHCP-assigned addresses, so policy follows the person across devices.
  • TLS inspection is the enabling requirement: Most traffic is encrypted, so the firewall must terminate and re-originate TLS to see inside. That means deploying an internal CA certificate to clients, and it creates real privacy, performance and certificate-pinning problems.
Where you see it
  • Allowing a social platform for the marketing team but blocking its games
  • Applying per-user policy that follows a person across devices
  • Replacing a separate firewall, IPS and web filter with one device
exam: The exam signals NGFW with the phrase application awareness or a scenario needing different rules for different applications on the same port. The distractor is a traditional/stateful firewall, which cannot distinguish them because it only sees port 443. Note that an NGFW is stateful too — next-generation adds Layer 7 on top, it does not replace state tracking.

front: What is a UTM appliance and what is its downside?
answer: Unified Threat Management — one box combining firewall, IPS, antivirus, content filtering, VPN, anti-spam and often DLP. Simple and cheap to manage, but a single point of failure and a performance bottleneck.
detail:
The consolidation appliance aimed at organisations without a dedicated security team. One vendor, one console, one licence, one box.
How it works
  • Consolidation is the selling point: A small organisation cannot staff separate firewall, IPS, proxy and mail-filtering platforms. A UTM gives an acceptable version of each in a single managed device.
  • Every enabled feature costs throughput: The rated firewall throughput on a datasheet assumes inspection is off. Turning on antivirus scanning, IPS and TLS inspection can cut real throughput by well over half. Undersizing a UTM is the most common deployment mistake.
  • It is one failure and one blast radius: If the box fails, you lose the firewall, the VPN, the web filter and the mail filter simultaneously. That argues for a redundant pair, which erases part of the cost advantage.
  • UTM versus NGFW is largely marketing: The distinction CompTIA draws is that UTM emphasises breadth of bundled security functions for SMB, while NGFW emphasises deep application and user awareness for enterprise. Modern products blur the line.
Where you see it
  • Small and medium businesses with no dedicated security staff
  • Branch offices needing firewall, VPN and content filtering in one shipment
  • Explaining why enabling every inspection feature halved internet throughput
exam: The exam presents UTM as the answer when a scenario asks for multiple security functions in a single device, usually for a small business or branch. The expected downsides to recognise are single point of failure and performance degradation when all features are enabled.

front: IDS versus IPS — how do they differ and where is each placed?
