answer: An IDS sits out of band on a SPAN port or network TAP and can only alert. An IPS sits inline in the traffic path and can drop the packet. Inline placement is what gives it the power to block.
detail:
Both inspect traffic for known attacks. The entire distinction is whether the traffic passes through the device or merely past it.
How it works
  • Placement determines capability: An IDS receives a copy of traffic. By the time it sees a malicious packet, the real packet has already reached the target — so it can only log and alert. An IPS sits in the forwarding path and can decide not to forward.
  • An IPS is a new failure point and a latency source: Every packet waits for inspection, and if the device fails, traffic stops unless it is configured to fail-open. That trade-off — fail-open loses protection, fail-closed loses the network — is a genuine design decision.
  • False positives cost differently: A false positive on an IDS creates a noisy alert. A false positive on an IPS blocks legitimate business traffic. That is why an IPS is often deployed in detect-only mode first and tuned before blocking is enabled.
  • Signature versus anomaly detection: Signature-based matches known attack patterns and misses anything new. Anomaly/behaviour-based flags deviations from a learned baseline, catching novel attacks at the cost of far more false positives.
Where you see it
  • An IDS on a SPAN port for monitoring without touching the traffic path
  • An IPS inline behind the perimeter firewall to block known exploits
  • Running a new IPS in alert-only mode during a tuning period
exam: This is a mandatory contrast card and CompTIA tests it constantly. The trigger words: out of band, passive, SPAN/TAP, alert only = IDS; inline, active, blocks/prevents = IPS. The classic scenario asks which device could have stopped an attack rather than just recording it — the answer is IPS. A follow-up trap is that an IDS on a SPAN port cannot block no matter how it is configured.

front: What does a load balancer do beyond distributing traffic?
answer: It presents one virtual IP to clients and distributes connections across a pool of servers, performs health checks to remove failed members, maintains session persistence, and commonly terminates TLS.
detail:
A reverse-proxy device that makes many servers look like one and keeps a failed server from ever being sent a request.
How it works
  • Health checking is the availability function: The balancer probes each pool member — a TCP connect, an HTTP request, or an application-specific check. A member that fails is pulled from rotation automatically, so a crashed server never receives traffic. This matters more than the distribution algorithm.
  • Distribution algorithms: Round robin sends each new connection to the next server. Least connections favours the least busy. Weighted variants account for servers of different capacity. Source-IP hashing sends the same client to the same server.
  • Session persistence, also called stickiness: If an application keeps state in server memory, a user bounced to a different server loses their shopping cart or session. Persistence pins a client to one server by cookie or source address.
  • TLS offload centralises certificates: Terminating TLS at the balancer removes the encryption cost from the servers and means the certificate is installed and renewed in one place instead of on every pool member.
Where you see it
  • A web farm behind a single public address
  • Draining a server out of rotation for patching without downtime
  • Handling a traffic spike by adding servers to the pool
exam: The exam's favourite load-balancer detail is session persistence: users are randomly logged out or lose their cart, and the answer is that persistence/stickiness must be enabled. The other common one is health checks — traffic is still being sent to a failed server, so health checking is misconfigured. Also know that a load balancer provides high availability and scalability, not security.

front: Forward proxy versus reverse proxy — which side does each protect?
answer: A forward proxy sits in front of the clients and makes requests on their behalf — filtering, logging and caching outbound traffic. A reverse proxy sits in front of the servers and accepts requests on their behalf — hiding, protecting and offloading them.
detail:
Both are intermediaries for HTTP. The difference is entirely which end of the conversation they represent.
How it works
  • Forward proxy is the corporate web gateway: Clients are configured, by browser setting or by policy, to send all web requests to the proxy. It enforces acceptable-use categories, authenticates users, scans downloads, caches popular content, and produces the browsing log an auditor asks for.
  • Forward proxying gives visibility you otherwise lose: Because clients terminate TLS at the proxy rather than at the site, the organisation can inspect content that would otherwise be an opaque encrypted stream leaving the network.
  • Reverse proxy is the server front door: External clients connect to the reverse proxy, which forwards to internal servers. Clients never learn the real server addresses. It commonly adds TLS termination, caching, compression and a web application firewall.
  • A load balancer is a reverse proxy: Functionally they overlap heavily — a reverse proxy that distributes across multiple backends is a load balancer. The label depends on which function is emphasised.
Where you see it
  • A forward proxy enforcing web filtering and logging for staff
  • A reverse proxy publishing internal applications to the internet
  • Caching at either end to reduce bandwidth
exam: CompTIA tests this by direction. Filtering and logging what employees browse = forward proxy. Protecting and publishing internal web servers = reverse proxy. The scenario wording almost always names whose traffic is being handled, so read for whether the protected party is the client or the server.

front: NAS versus SAN.
answer:
NAS: file-level storage over the existing Ethernet LAN using SMB or NFS — appears as a shared folder.
SAN: block-level storage on a dedicated high-speed fabric using Fibre Channel or iSCSI — appears to the server as a local disk.
detail:
Two ways to put storage on a network, distinguished by whether the network carries files or raw disk blocks.
How it works
  • File level means the NAS owns the filesystem: The client asks for a named file and the NAS device manages the underlying disk layout. That makes it simple, easy to share between many clients, and dependent on a network file protocol.
  • Block level means the server owns the filesystem: A SAN presents raw storage volumes. The server formats them with its own filesystem and treats them exactly like an internal drive. That is what makes SAN suitable for databases and VM datastores, which need direct block access.
  • The transport differs: NAS rides the ordinary LAN. A SAN traditionally uses a separate Fibre Channel fabric with its own switches and HBAs; iSCSI is the cheaper option that carries SCSI commands over ordinary Ethernet, usually on an isolated VLAN with jumbo frames.
  • Cost and complexity follow: NAS is inexpensive and can be installed by a generalist. Fibre Channel SAN requires dedicated hardware, zoning, LUN masking and specialised skills, which is the price of the performance.
Where you see it
  • A NAS holding department file shares
  • A SAN providing datastores for a virtualisation cluster
  • iSCSI as a middle ground on existing Ethernet
exam: The exam distinguishes them with the phrase file-level versus block-level — that is the discriminator to memorize. A scenario needing shared folders for users is NAS; a scenario needing storage for database or virtual machine datastores is SAN. Remember iSCSI is a SAN technology despite running on Ethernet.

front: What does a wireless LAN controller do?
answer: Centrally manages lightweight access points — pushes configuration, coordinates channel and power assignment, handles fast roaming, aggregates or tunnels client traffic, and enforces policy from one place.
detail:
The device that turns dozens of individual access points into one manageable wireless system.
How it works
  • Configuration comes from one place: Lightweight APs hold almost no local configuration. Adding an SSID or changing security settings is done once on the controller and applied to every AP, instead of being configured on each one.
  • Radio resource management: The controller sees the whole RF environment and assigns non-overlapping channels and transmit power automatically. When one AP fails, neighbouring APs can increase power to fill the coverage hole.
  • It makes roaming fast: Because the controller holds the client's session and security context, a client moving between APs does not have to fully re-authenticate. Without that, a voice call drops during every handoff.
  • Deployment models vary: The controller may be a hardware appliance, a virtual machine, or a cloud service. Traffic may be tunnelled back through the controller (centralised) or forwarded locally at the AP (local switching / FlexConnect).
Where you see it
  • Enterprise wireless across many floors or buildings
  • Deploying a new SSID to two hundred access points at once
  • Supporting seamless voice roaming across a campus
exam: Expect a management scenario: an organisation with many access points needs consistent configuration and coordinated channel assignment. The answer is a WLC. The related vocabulary is lightweight/thin AP (needs a controller) versus autonomous/fat AP (standalone, configured individually) — that contrast is frequently the actual question.

front: What is a VPN headend or concentrator?
answer: The device that terminates many VPN tunnels on the corporate side — handling the encryption workload, authenticating remote users or peers, and applying access policy to tunnelled traffic.
detail:
The single point where remote users and remote sites land on the internal network. It exists because encryption and tunnel state are expensive and belong in dedicated hardware.
How it works
  • It does the cryptographic work: Establishing and maintaining thousands of encrypted sessions is computationally heavy. Concentrators use hardware crypto acceleration, which is why a general-purpose router struggles where a headend does not.
  • It is where authentication is enforced: Remote-access tunnels authenticate against RADIUS or a directory, usually with multi-factor. The headend is therefore the enforcement point for who may connect at all.
  • Split tunnel versus full tunnel is configured here: Full tunnel sends all client traffic through the corporate network, giving full inspection at the cost of bandwidth. Split tunnel sends only corporate-destined traffic through, which is faster but leaves the client's internet traffic uninspected.
  • It is a capacity and availability chokepoint: Every remote worker depends on it. Headends are deployed redundantly and sized for peak concurrent sessions, because when it saturates, the entire remote workforce is offline.
Where you see it
  • Terminating remote-access client VPNs for a workforce
  • Terminating site-to-site IPsec tunnels from branch offices
  • Enforcing MFA and posture checks before granting network access
exam: The exam uses concentrator and headend interchangeably; recognise both as the device that terminates multiple VPN tunnels. The associated tested concept is split tunnel versus full tunnel — if a scenario requires all remote traffic to be inspected by corporate security, the answer is full tunnel.

front: LAN, WLAN, WAN, MAN, CAN, PAN, SAN — define each by scope.
answer:
LAN: one building or floor.
WLAN: a wireless LAN.
CAN: a campus of nearby buildings you own.
MAN: city-scale.
WAN: geographically separated sites.
PAN: personal range — Bluetooth, USB, NFC.
SAN: a dedicated storage network.
detail:
A vocabulary set defined by geographic scope, plus two that are defined by purpose rather than size.
How it works
  • Scope is the ordering principle: PAN (metres) to LAN (a building) to CAN (a campus) to MAN (a city) to WAN (any distance). Memorize them as a ladder and the definitions follow.
  • The CAN and MAN distinction is ownership: A campus area network spans buildings the organisation owns, usually on its own fibre. A metropolitan area network spans a city and normally uses a carrier's infrastructure.
  • The internet is the largest WAN: Any link between sites that crosses a public or carrier network is a WAN link, regardless of distance. Two buildings across the street connected by a leased line is a WAN.
  • SAN is the odd one out: It is defined by what it carries — block storage — not by how far it reaches. A SAN normally lives inside one data centre.
Where you see it
  • Describing a network's scope accurately in documentation
  • Identifying which acronym a scenario is describing
  • Distinguishing a campus fibre link from a carrier metro service
exam: These appear as straight definition questions and as scenario labels. The two most-missed are CAN (multiple owned buildings on one site) and MAN (city-scale, carrier-provided). Watch for SAN in a list of geographic terms — it is a storage network and is the odd item out, which the exam sometimes exploits.

front: Client-server versus peer-to-peer architecture.
answer:
Client-server: resources centralised on dedicated servers — easier to secure, back up and audit; costs more and the server is a single point of failure.
Peer-to-peer: every node both offers and consumes resources — cheap and simple, but no central control and it does not scale.
detail:
Two ways to organise where resources live and who controls them.
How it works
  • Centralisation buys control: One directory holds accounts, one backup job protects the data, one set of permissions governs access. That is why every organisation past a handful of people uses client-server.
  • Peer-to-peer distributes administration to users: Each machine holds its own accounts and its own shares. With five machines that is workable. With fifty, granting one person access to everything means fifty separate changes, and nobody knows where data actually lives.
  • Backup and audit are the real breaking point: In a peer-to-peer network, business data sits on individual workstations that are not backed up and not monitored. Losing a machine loses the data on it.
  • Peer-to-peer still has legitimate uses: Small home and workgroup networks, and distributed protocols like BitTorrent and blockchain networks, deliberately use peer-to-peer for cost or for resilience against a central failure.
Where you see it
  • A small office workgroup sharing a printer and folders
  • A domain with centralised authentication and file servers
  • Explaining why a growing company must move off workgroup sharing
exam: The exam tests this through growth and control scenarios: a company outgrowing a workgroup needs client-server for centralised administration, security and backup. The tested weakness of peer-to-peer is lack of central administration and poor scalability, not raw performance.

front: What are SCADA, ICS and OT, and why do they concern a network technician?
answer: Systems that monitor and control physical processes — utilities, manufacturing, building services. They often run unpatchable legacy software with weak or no authentication, so the control is strict network segmentation, not endpoint hardening.
detail:
Operational technology networks that were designed for reliability and safety in an isolated environment, then connected to corporate IT networks without being redesigned.
How it works
  • The terms nest: OT is the broad category of technology controlling physical processes. ICS is the industrial control system category within it. SCADA is a specific ICS architecture for supervising geographically distributed sites — pipelines, power grids, water systems.
  • Availability outranks confidentiality: In IT, the priority order is roughly confidentiality, integrity, availability. In OT it inverts: a process that stops can destroy equipment or endanger people. That is why you cannot patch and reboot a controller during business hours.
  • The devices cannot be hardened conventionally: PLCs and RTUs may run firmware from a decade ago, have hardcoded credentials, speak unauthenticated protocols like Modbus, and be unsupported by their vendor. No agent can be installed on them.
  • Segmentation is the compensating control: Because the endpoints cannot be secured, the network must be. OT sits in its own segment behind a firewall with a tightly restricted rule set, often with a jump host or data diode as the only permitted path from IT.
Where you see it
  • Manufacturing plant floors and process control networks
  • Utility SCADA supervising remote substations and pumping stations
  • Building management systems for HVAC, lighting and access control
exam: The exam wants one answer here: the correct control for legacy industrial systems that cannot be patched is network segmentation and restricted access. Distractors are 'install antivirus', 'apply the latest patches' and 'enforce a password policy' — all of which are impossible or unsupported on the devices themselves.

front: Why are IoT and IIoT devices segmented, and what does an IoT gateway do?
answer: IoT devices are numerous, rarely patched, and often shipped with weak defaults, so they are placed on their own VLAN with restricted access. An IoT gateway aggregates them, translates their protocols, and forms a controlled boundary to the rest of the network.
detail:
Consumer- and industrial-grade connected devices added to networks that were never designed to hold thousands of unmanageable endpoints.
How it works
  • The devices are the weak link: Smart cameras, sensors, thermostats, badge readers and displays commonly ship with default credentials, no update mechanism, and firmware nobody maintains. They are the easiest foothold on a network.
  • Segmentation limits the blast radius: Putting them on a dedicated VLAN with an ACL that permits only their controller and blocks lateral movement means a compromised camera cannot reach a file server. This is the same reasoning as OT segmentation.
  • IIoT is the industrial version: Industrial IoT sensors on production equipment sit at the intersection of IoT and OT, and inherit the security problems of both — internet-connected and unpatchable.
  • A gateway translates and filters: Constrained devices often speak Zigbee, Z-Wave, BLE, MQTT or CoAP rather than plain IP. The gateway converts those to standard protocols, may perform local processing to reduce upstream traffic, and is the single controlled crossing point into the main network.
Where you see it
  • A separate VLAN and SSID for cameras, sensors and smart displays
  • A gateway bridging Zigbee sensors onto the IP network
  • Preventing a compromised device from reaching corporate systems
exam: The exam answer for securing IoT is almost always segmentation onto a separate VLAN with restricted access, mirroring the SCADA/OT answer. The related tested item is changing default credentials, which is the one endpoint hardening step that is actually possible. Recognise the gateway's role as protocol translation and a controlled boundary.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: Cat 5e — rated speed, distance and bandwidth?
answer: 1 Gbps at 100 m, 100 MHz. Unshielded twisted pair, 4 pairs, RJ45.
detail:
The baseline modern copper cable. The 'e' means enhanced: it is Cat 5 retested and tightened for crosstalk so that all four pairs can carry data at once.
How it works
  • Why four pairs matter: Original Cat 5 at 100BASE-TX used two pairs. 1000BASE-T uses all four pairs simultaneously in both directions, which made near-end crosstalk between pairs the limiting problem. Cat 5e is the same physical cable with tighter crosstalk specifications.
  • 100 MHz of usable bandwidth: Bandwidth here means signalling frequency, not throughput. 1 Gbps is achieved inside 100 MHz by using all four pairs and a dense encoding scheme, not by signalling faster.
  • The 100 m limit is a channel limit: The 100 m figure is 90 m of solid-core horizontal run plus roughly 10 m total of stranded patch cable at both ends. Exceeding it causes attenuation-driven errors, not a hard refusal to link.
  • Also carries 2.5GBASE-T: 802.3bz defined 2.5 Gbps over existing Cat 5e at 100 m specifically so buildings could feed Wi-Fi 6 access points without recabling.
Where you see it
  • Existing office horizontal runs installed from roughly 2000 onward
  • Voice and low-speed device drops where 1 Gbps is plenty
  • Feeding 2.5 Gbps access points over cable already in the walls
exam: Cat 5e is the anchor of the category table, so memorize it as the reference point everything else is compared against. The trap is the exam asking for the cheapest cable that supports a stated requirement — if the requirement is 1 Gbps at 100 m, the answer is Cat 5e, not Cat 6. Plain Cat 5 is a valid distractor and tops out at 100 Mbps.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: Cat 6 — rated speed and distance, and what changed from Cat 5e?
answer: 1 Gbps at 100 m, 10 Gbps only to 55 m. 250 MHz. Adds a plastic spline separating the pairs.
detail:
The first category that can do 10 Gbps, but only on a short run. It is Cat 5e with a physical separator and tighter twist tolerances.
How it works
  • The spline is the change: Cat 6 typically has a plastic cross-shaped spine running down the cable that holds the four pairs apart. Physical separation reduces crosstalk between pairs, which is what buys the extra bandwidth.
  • 250 MHz, not 250 percent faster: The jump from 100 MHz to 250 MHz is what allows 10GBASE-T to run at all. Throughput at 1 Gbps is unchanged from Cat 5e.
  • 55 m is an alien crosstalk limit: Beyond about 55 m the coupling between adjacent Cat 6 cables in the same bundle, called alien crosstalk, overwhelms 10GBASE-T. In a loose or well-separated bundle the practical limit can drop as low as 37 m.
  • Backward compatible: Cat 6 terminates on the same RJ45 and runs everything Cat 5e runs. Upgrading a patch cord to Cat 6 changes nothing if the horizontal run is Cat 5e — the weakest link sets the channel rating.
Where you see it
  • Building runs installed in the mid-2000s
  • Short 10 Gbps links between a switch and a nearby server
  • New drops where 10 Gbps might be needed later but the run is short
exam: The 55 m figure is the single most tested Cat 6 fact and the most common distractor pair on the exam is Cat 6 versus Cat 6a. If a scenario says 10 Gbps over a full 100 m run, Cat 6 is wrong and Cat 6a is right. If it says 10 Gbps to a server two racks away, Cat 6 is sufficient and is the cheaper correct answer.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: Cat 6a — rated speed and distance, and what changed from Cat 6?
answer: 10 Gbps at the full 100 m, 500 MHz. Thicker, usually shielded, heavier to pull.
detail:
The category that makes 10GBASE-T work at normal building distances. The whole design goal was defeating alien crosstalk.
How it works
  • Doubles the frequency: 500 MHz versus Cat 6's 250 MHz. That headroom is what carries 10 Gbps across 100 m instead of 55 m.
  • Attacks alien crosstalk directly: Cat 6a is built with foil shielding around the pairs or around the whole bundle (F/UTP or S/FTP), a larger overall diameter, and tighter twists. All three reduce coupling into neighbouring cables in the same tray.
  • It is physically harder to install: The cable is roughly twice the diameter of Cat 5e and much stiffer, so it has a larger bend radius, fills conduit faster, and needs shielded jacks with a bonded path back to ground.
  • Shielding only helps if it is grounded: An F/UTP run terminated on unshielded jacks, or shielded jacks with no bonding to the rack ground, performs no better than UTP and can act as an antenna.
Where you see it
  • New commercial building cabling standard for horizontal runs
  • 10 Gbps to the desktop or to a workgroup switch
  • 802.3bt PoE++ runs, where the thicker conductors also run cooler
exam: Cat 6a is the answer to almost any exam scenario phrased as '10 Gbps over copper at 100 metres'. The trap is a question offering both Cat 6 and Cat 6a where the stated distance is under 55 m — then Cat 6 is the cost-correct answer. Also expect the shielding-and-grounding angle: if a scenario has a run beside industrial machinery, shielded Cat 6a plus proper bonding is the fix.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: Cat 7 and Cat 8 — speeds, distances and what makes them different?
answer:
Cat 7: 10 Gbps at 100 m, 600 MHz, fully shielded, GG45/TERA connectors.
Cat 8: 25 or 40 Gbps but only 30 m, 2000 MHz.
detail:
The two categories past Cat 6a. Cat 7 is a shielding-focused standard that never displaced Cat 6a; Cat 8 is a deliberate short-reach data centre cable.
How it works
  • Cat 7 shields every pair individually: S/FTP construction: foil around each of the four pairs plus an overall braid. That gives 600 MHz and excellent noise immunity, but it is thick, stiff and expensive.
  • Cat 7 is not a TIA category: It is an ISO/IEC standard. Its native GG45 and TERA connectors are not RJ45, which is a large part of why North American installers stayed on Cat 6a.
  • Cat 8 trades distance for speed: 2000 MHz of bandwidth carries 25GBASE-T and 40GBASE-T, but only across 30 m. That is not a building cable — it is a top-of-rack cable.
  • Cat 8 keeps the RJ45: Cat 8.1 terminates on a normal RJ45 and is backward compatible; Cat 8.2 uses the Cat 7-style GG45/TERA connectors. Cat 8 is always shielded.
Where you see it
  • Cat 7 in European installations and in high-EMI industrial plants
  • Cat 8 for switch-to-server and switch-to-switch links inside a single rack
  • Cat 8 as a copper alternative to short fibre or DAC in the data centre
exam: The exam tests these two by their limits. 30 m is the Cat 8 number to memorize, and the classic wrong answer is choosing Cat 8 for a long building run because it is 'the fastest'. For Cat 7, the testable oddity is that it is fully shielded and may not use a standard RJ45.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: UTP versus STP/shielded cable — when does shielding actually earn its cost?
answer: Only where external electrical noise is present. Shielding adds cost, stiffness, and a bonding requirement — and does nothing if the shield is not grounded at the termination.
detail:
Twisting the pairs already cancels most noise. Shielding is the extra layer you add when twisting is not enough because the environment is electrically hostile.
How it works
  • Twisting is the primary defence: Two conductors twisted together pick up the same interference. Because the signal is read as the difference between them, common noise cancels. This is why UTP works at all.
  • Shielding stops what twisting cannot: A foil or braid around the pairs blocks strong external fields from reaching the conductors. It is the answer for runs near motors, welders, fluorescent ballasts, elevator equipment and high-voltage feeds.
  • Naming: F/UTP, S/FTP, U/FTP: The letters before the slash describe the overall shield, the letters after describe the per-pair shield. F is foil, S is braid, U is none. F/UTP is an overall foil around unshielded pairs; S/FTP is a braid outside foiled pairs.
  • An ungrounded shield is worse than none: The shield must be bonded at the jack and carried back to a grounded rack. A shield grounded at both ends of a run between two differently grounded buildings can carry a ground loop current, which injects noise instead of removing it.
Where you see it
  • Factory floors and elevator machine rooms
  • Cable trays sharing a path with electrical conduit
  • Cat 6a and Cat 8 runs, where shielding is effectively standard
exam: The exam frames this as a symptom question: intermittent errors on one run that passes beside machinery is EMI, and the fix is shielded cable or rerouting away from the source. The distractor is 'replace with a higher category' — a higher category alone does not fix external interference. Remember that CompTIA expects you to know the shield must be grounded.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What is plenum-rated cable and where is it required?
answer: Cable with a fire-resistant, low-smoke jacket (usually FEP), required by building code in any air-handling space — above a drop ceiling used as a return-air plenum, or under a raised floor.
detail:
A fire-safety rating, not a performance rating. Plenum cable does not run faster; it fails to poison people when it burns.
How it works
  • The hazard is smoke, not flame: Ordinary PVC jacket gives off dense, toxic smoke when it burns. In a plenum that air is being circulated through the building, so a small ceiling fire distributes lethal smoke everywhere in minutes.
  • CMP, CMR, CM: CMP is plenum, CMR is riser, CM is general purpose. The rating is printed along the jacket, so you can identify an existing run by reading it.
  • Riser is for vertical shafts: CMR-rated cable resists carrying fire from floor to floor up a vertical shaft. Plenum may substitute for riser; riser may never substitute for plenum.
  • It is a code violation, not a preference: An inspector who finds PVC cable in a return-air plenum will fail the installation, and the whole run has to be pulled and replaced.
Where you see it
  • Horizontal runs above suspended ceilings in commercial offices
  • Cable under raised floors in data centres and trading floors
  • Any run an inspector or fire marshal will look at
exam: This appears as a straightforward scenario: cable is being run above a drop ceiling that is used for air return, which type is required? The answer is plenum. The distractors are riser and shielded. Note the direction of the substitution rule — plenum can replace riser, never the reverse.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: Single-mode versus multimode fibre — core size, light source, jacket colour and reach?
answer:
SMF: 8–10 micron core (usually stated as 9), laser at 1310/1550 nm, yellow jacket, tens of kilometres.
MMF: 50 or 62.5 micron core, LED or VCSEL at 850 nm, orange or aqua jacket, hundreds of metres.
detail:
The two families of optical fibre. The only physical difference that matters is core diameter, and every other difference follows from it.
How it works
  • Core size decides everything: A 9 micron core is so narrow that light can only travel one path down it — one mode. A 50 or 62.5 micron core lets light enter at many angles and take many paths of different lengths.
  • Modal dispersion is what limits multimode: Rays taking longer paths arrive later. Over distance a sharp pulse smears until it overlaps the next pulse and the receiver cannot tell them apart. That smearing, not attenuation, is the multimode distance limit.
  • Single-mode costs more at the ends, not in the glass: The fibre itself is comparable in price. The transceivers are what cost more, because aiming a laser into a 9 micron core demands much tighter tolerances than flooding a 62.5 micron core with an LED.
  • Neither is affected by EMI: Glass carries light, not current. Fibre is immune to electromagnetic interference and does not conduct, which makes it the answer for runs between buildings where ground potential differs.
Where you see it
  • Single-mode for campus backbones, building-to-building runs and carrier links
  • Multimode for switch-to-switch and switch-to-server inside a data centre
  • Fibre anywhere a copper run would exceed 100 m or cross a lightning-prone gap between buildings
exam: Expect a distance-driven choice. Any requirement over a few hundred metres, or between buildings, points at single-mode. Inside one data centre at 100–400 m, multimode is the cost-correct answer. CompTIA also tests the colour codes directly: yellow is single-mode, orange is OM1/OM2, aqua is OM3/OM4, lime green is OM5.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: OM1 through OM5 — core size, colour and 10 Gbps reach for each?
answer:
OM1: 62.5 µm, orange, 33 m
OM2: 50 µm, orange, 82 m
OM3: 50 µm, aqua, 300 m
OM4: 50 µm, aqua/violet, 400 m
OM5: 50 µm, lime green, 400 m
detail:
The grading system for multimode fibre. Higher OM number means the glass was manufactured to a tighter refractive-index profile, so modal dispersion is lower and the same 10 Gbps signal travels further.
How it works
  • OM1 and OM2 are legacy LED-era fibre: They were designed for LED sources at 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps. Their 10 Gbps reach of 33 m and 82 m is short enough that they are effectively unusable for 10G and cannot do 40G or 100G at all.
  • OM3 and OM4 are laser-optimised: Both are 50 micron and both are tuned for 850 nm VCSEL lasers. OM4 is the same design with a better index profile, which is the whole reason it reaches 400 m instead of 300 m.
  • OM5 adds wavelength division: OM5 is specified across 850–953 nm so short-wavelength division multiplexing can run four colours down one pair of fibres. Its advantage only appears with SWDM transceivers; with ordinary 850 nm optics it behaves like OM4.
  • Mixing grades in one link is a real fault: An OM3 patch cord spliced into an OM1 run creates a core-size mismatch at the joint. Light from a 50 micron core entering a 62.5 micron core is mostly fine; going the other way loses a large fraction of the power and the link runs hot on errors or will not come up.
Where you see it
  • OM3 aqua as the common existing data centre fibre
  • OM4 for 40G and 100G runs across a large data hall
  • Identifying legacy orange OM1 in an old riser that will not support a 10G upgrade
exam: Colour identification is directly testable: a scenario describing existing orange fibre that will not support a 10 Gbps upgrade is OM1/OM2, and the answer is to pull OM4 or single-mode. The distractor is 'change the transceivers' — new optics cannot rescue fibre whose modal bandwidth is too low.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: LC, SC and ST fibre connectors — how do you tell them apart?
answer:
LC: small form factor, latching, usually duplex — the modern default on SFPs.
SC: large square body, push-pull, 'stick and click'.
ST: round with a bayonet twist lock, 'stick and twist'.
detail:
Three connector bodies you have to recognise by description on the exam. They terminate the same fibre; they differ only in size and locking mechanism.
How it works
  • LC won because of density: The LC ferrule is 1.25 mm, half the size of SC and ST. That is what lets a duplex LC pair fit into an SFP cage, and why a 48-port switch can be all fibre.
  • SC is square and pushes in: A 2.5 mm ferrule in a square plastic housing that clicks when seated. Common on older equipment, GBICs, and telco/ISP hand-offs.
  • ST is round and twists: A 2.5 mm ferrule with a bayonet coupling, like a BNC. Almost entirely legacy — you find it on old multimode runs and patch panels installed in the 1990s.
  • Polish type matters more than body: UPC (blue) and APC (green) describe the angle of the polished end face, not the connector shape. Mating an APC to a UPC damages the ferrules and causes heavy reflection loss, so the colour of the connector body is a genuine field check.
Where you see it
  • LC on every SFP, SFP+ and 10G/25G switch port
  • SC on ISP demarcation points and older core equipment
  • ST on legacy multimode patch panels in older buildings
exam: CompTIA tests these by physical description rather than by picture. Memorize the mnemonics: SC = stick and click (square), ST = stick and twist (round bayonet), LC = little connector. If a question says the connector fits a small form-factor pluggable transceiver, the answer is LC.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What is an MPO/MTP connector and why does it exist?
answer: A single rectangular connector carrying 12, 16 or 24 fibres in one ferrule. Used for 40G and 100G links that transmit across multiple fibre lanes in parallel.
detail:
The connector for parallel optics. It exists because some high-speed standards do not send one serial stream — they split the data across several fibres at once.
How it works
  • Parallel lanes, not one stream: 40GBASE-SR4 sends four lanes of 10 Gbps out four transmit fibres and receives on four more, using eight of the twelve fibres in an MPO. 100GBASE-SR4 does the same with four lanes at 25 Gbps.
  • MTP is a brand of MPO: MTP is US Conec's higher-precision implementation of the MPO standard. They intermate; MTP is specified to tighter tolerances.
  • Polarity is a real installation problem: Because twelve fibres must land in the right order at the far end, MPO cabling defines Type A, B and C polarity methods. Getting it wrong means transmit meets transmit and the link never comes up, with no error message that says why.
  • Breakout cassettes: An MPO trunk is commonly landed on a cassette that fans it out to six duplex LC ports, so one high-fibre-count trunk feeds many ordinary connections.
Where you see it
  • 40G and 100G spine-to-leaf links in a data centre
  • High-density trunk cabling between racks and rows
  • Breaking one 40G port out into four 10G server connections
exam: The exam angle is recognition and purpose: which connector is used for 40/100 Gbps multi-fibre connections — the answer is MPO/MTP. Distractors are LC and SC, which are one- or two-fibre connectors. Knowing that the connector implies parallel transmission over multiple strands is enough.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: RJ45 versus RJ11 — what is the actual difference?
answer:
RJ45: 8 positions, 8 conductors (8P8C), 4 twisted pairs — Ethernet.
RJ11: 6 positions, usually 2 or 4 conductors (6P4C), narrower body — analogue telephone and DSL.
detail:
Two modular connectors that look similar enough to be confused in a wall plate but differ in width and conductor count.
How it works
  • Count the positions: RJ45 is wider and has eight gold contacts. RJ11 is visibly narrower with four or six. An RJ11 plug will physically slide into an RJ45 jack and make no useful contact.
  • RJ45 carries four pairs because Ethernet needs them: 1000BASE-T and everything above use all four pairs bidirectionally. RJ11 was only ever designed for one or two analogue voice circuits.
  • RJ11 is where the DSL line lands: A DSL modem takes an RJ11 from the phone line and presents an RJ45 to the LAN. That is the most common place a technician sees both connectors on one device.
  • Neither name is strictly correct: The formal names are 8P8C and 6P2C/6P4C. CompTIA uses RJ45 and RJ11, so answer in those terms.
Where you see it
  • RJ45 on every Ethernet patch cord, wall plate and switch port
  • RJ11 on analogue phones, fax lines and the WAN side of a DSL modem
  • Identifying a mislabelled wall plate that is actually a voice drop
exam: This appears in device-connection scenarios: which connector attaches the DSL line to the modem — RJ11 — and which attaches the modem to the router — RJ45. The trap is a question describing a wall jack a user plugged their laptop into with no link; a voice drop wired for RJ11 is a valid cause.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: F-type versus BNC connectors, and where is coax still used?
answer:
F-type: threaded screw-on, used on RG-6 for cable internet and TV.
BNC: bayonet twist-lock, used on RG-59 for CCTV, video and legacy 10BASE2.
detail:
Coaxial cable survives in two niches: the cable-television plant that delivers broadband, and analogue video runs.
How it works
  • Coax carries one signal on a centre conductor: A single copper core, a dielectric, a braided shield and a jacket. The braid is both the shield and the return path, which is why coax resists EMI well without twisting.
  • F-type screws on: A threaded barrel that tightens with fingers or a wrench, using the cable's own centre conductor as the pin. Standard on cable modems, splitters and TV outlets.
  • BNC twists and locks: A quarter-turn bayonet mount. It is faster to mate and unmate than a threaded connector, which is why it dominated lab and video equipment.
  • RG-6 versus RG-59: RG-6 has a thicker centre conductor and better shielding, so it carries the higher frequencies of modern cable broadband. RG-59 is thinner, lower bandwidth, and now mostly analogue CCTV.
Where you see it
  • The cable modem coax feed at a home or branch office
  • Analogue CCTV camera runs terminated in BNC
  • Legacy lab and broadcast video equipment
exam: The exam pairs these with the media: RG-6 with F-type for cable internet, RG-59 with BNC for video. Expect a straightforward question about which connector terminates the coax entering the building from the ISP — F-type. Do not confuse BNC with the fibre ST connector; both twist, but ST is fibre.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: T568A versus T568B — what is different, and does it matter?
answer: Only the orange and green pairs are swapped. Either standard works. What matters is using the same one on both ends.
detail:
Two pin-out standards for terminating four pairs into an eight-pin RJ45. They are electrically equivalent; the difference is purely which pair lands on which pins.
How it works
  • The swap is orange and green: In T568B, pins 1-2 are the orange pair and pins 3-6 are green. T568A reverses those two. Blue on 4-5 and brown on 7-8 are identical in both.
  • Pins 3 and 6 must be the same pair: Notice that in both standards, pin 3 and pin 6 belong to one pair even though pin 4 and pin 5 sit between them. Splitting that pair — wiring 3 and 4 as a pair, for example — produces a cable that passes a simple continuity test but fails badly under load with crosstalk.
  • Same standard both ends is straight-through: A straight-through cable is A-to-A or B-to-B. It connects unlike devices: PC to switch, switch to router.
  • Different standards is a crossover: A-on-one-end, B-on-the-other swaps transmit and receive. That is what a crossover cable is — there is no separate 'crossover wire'.
Where you see it
  • Terminating keystone jacks and patch panels in a new build
  • Making patch cords in the field
  • Diagnosing a cable that links but performs badly because pairs were split
exam: The exam wants two facts: that only orange and green change, and that mixing A and B ends produces a crossover. A common scenario describes a technician terminating one end to A and the other to B by accident — the result is a crossover, which on modern auto-MDI-X gear still works, and on old gear does not. B is the more common choice in North America but neither is 'correct'.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: When do you still need a crossover cable?
answer: Almost never. Auto-MDI-X on modern interfaces detects the pinout and flips transmit and receive in silicon. Crossovers are only needed on old gear connecting like devices — switch to switch, PC to PC, router to router.
detail:
A crossover exists because early Ethernet devices had fixed transmit and receive pin assignments, so connecting two of the same kind of device put transmit against transmit.
How it works
  • The original problem: A NIC transmits on pins 1-2 and listens on 3-6. A hub or switch port is wired the opposite way, so a straight cable works between them. Two NICs, or two switch ports, both transmit on the same pins and neither hears anything.
  • Auto-MDI-X negotiates it away: During auto-negotiation each side can detect the mismatch and internally swap its transmit and receive pairs. It is mandatory in the 1000BASE-T standard, which is why any gigabit port handles either cable.
  • Gigabit uses all four pairs anyway: 1000BASE-T transmits and receives on all four pairs simultaneously with echo cancellation, so the notion of a dedicated transmit pair barely applies.
  • Rollover is a different cable entirely: A rollover, or console cable, reverses all eight conductors end for end and connects a PC serial port to a router or switch console port. It carries no Ethernet at all.
Where you see it
  • Very old switches or hubs without auto-MDI-X
  • Directly connecting two laptops with legacy 100 Mbps NICs
  • Explaining why an accidental A/B termination still works today
exam: The exam still asks about crossovers, so know the like-to-like rule: switch to switch, PC to PC, router to router historically needed a crossover; PC to switch did not. But if the question mentions modern or gigabit equipment, the correct answer is that auto-MDI-X makes it unnecessary. Do not confuse a crossover with a rollover/console cable — that is a favourite distractor.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What is a DAC cable and what is twinaxial cable?
answer: DAC (Direct Attach Copper): a fixed assembly with the transceivers permanently attached to both ends. Twinax: the two-conductor shielded copper cable inside it. Typical reach 1–7 m (passive), up to about 15 m active.
detail:
The cheap short link between boxes in the same rack. You buy the cable and the optics as one non-separable unit.
How it works
  • Transceivers are moulded on: A DAC has an SFP+ or QSFP body at each end that slots into the switch cage exactly like an optic, but there is no optical component inside — it is copper end to end.
  • It is far cheaper and lower latency: No electrical-to-optical conversion means no transceiver cost and slightly lower latency. For a 3 m link between a top-of-rack switch and a server, DAC is the obvious choice over two optics plus a fibre patch.
  • Passive versus active: A passive DAC is plain twinax and is limited to roughly 7 m. An active DAC includes signal conditioning electronics and reaches about 15 m, at higher cost and slightly more power.
  • Vendor coding can block it: The transceiver ends carry an EEPROM identifying the vendor. Switches that enforce vendor matching will refuse a third-party DAC, which looks like a dead cable and is a genuine field trap.
Where you see it
  • Server-to-top-of-rack connections inside one cabinet
  • Switch stacking and short uplinks between adjacent racks
  • Any 10G/25G/40G link short enough to avoid the cost of optics
exam: The exam contrasts DAC against fibre-plus-transceivers on cost and distance. If a scenario asks for the most cost-effective 10 Gbps connection between two devices in the same rack, the answer is DAC. If the distance is 200 m, DAC is wrong and multimode fibre with SR optics is right. Remember twinax is the media, DAC is the assembly.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: SFP, SFP+, SFP28, QSFP+, QSFP28 — what speed does each carry?
answer:
SFP: 1 Gbps
SFP+: 10 Gbps
SFP28: 25 Gbps
QSFP+: 40 Gbps (4 × 10)
QSFP28: 100 Gbps (4 × 25)
detail:
The pluggable transceiver families. A switch ships with empty cages and you choose the optic that matches the media and distance you need.
How it works
  • Q means quad: QSFP is physically wider and carries four independent lanes. 40G QSFP+ is four 10G lanes; 100G QSFP28 is four 25G lanes. That is why a QSFP port can often be broken out into four smaller ports with a breakout cable.
  • The form factor sets the speed, the optic sets the distance: SFP+ is the 10 Gbps slot. Whether that link goes 300 m or 40 km depends on whether you fit an SR, LR or ER optic — the cage is the same.
  • They are hot-swappable: You can pull and replace a transceiver on a live switch without rebooting it, which is the entire reason modular optics replaced fixed ports.
  • Backward fit is limited: A 1G SFP will usually seat and run in an SFP+ cage. An SFP+ will not run at 10G in a 1G-only cage, and QSFP will not fit an SFP cage at all.
Where you see it
  • Choosing optics when specifying a new switch uplink
  • Breaking a 40G QSFP+ port into four 10G server links
  • Matching an existing far-end optic when adding a new site link
exam: This is a memorization item CompTIA tests directly. The reliable rule is SFP = 1G, SFP+ = 10G, QSFP+ = 40G, QSFP28 = 100G, with the Q meaning four lanes. The distractor is confusing form factor with reach — SFP+ does not mean short distance, it means 10 Gbps.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What is a transceiver mismatch and what does it look like?
answer: The two ends do not agree on wavelength, fibre type or distance rating. The link stays down, flaps, or comes up with very high error counts and abnormal light levels.
detail:
The most common reason a brand-new fibre link will not come up. Everything is plugged in, the fibre is good, and the two optics are simply not the same standard.
How it works
  • Wavelength must match end to end: An 850 nm SR optic cannot talk to a 1310 nm LR optic. The receiver is tuned for a different colour of light and sees nothing usable, so the link never establishes.
  • Fibre type must match the optic: An LR single-mode optic firing into multimode fibre, or an SR multimode optic on single-mode fibre, loses most of its power at the launch. Short runs may limp up with heavy errors; longer runs stay down.
  • Too much light is also a fault: Putting a 40 km ER optic on a 10 m patch overdrives the far-end receiver and saturates it. The fix is an attenuator, not a longer cable. This is why 'more powerful optic' is not a safe default.
  • Diagnose it with the optic itself: Modern transceivers report DOM/DDM data — transmit power, receive power and temperature. show interface transceiver tells you whether light is arriving and at what level, which separates a dead optic from a dead fibre.
Where you see it
  • Turning up a new inter-building fibre link
  • Replacing a failed optic with whatever was in the spares drawer
  • Troubleshooting a link that comes up but drops under load
exam: Look for scenarios where a fibre link will not come up despite good cabling. The exam answer is mismatched transceivers — check that both ends are the same standard, wavelength and fibre type. The distractor is 'bad cable'. Also remember an attenuator is the fix for excessive receive power on a short run.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: 1000BASE-T, 1000BASE-SX, 1000BASE-LX — media and distance?
answer:
1000BASE-T: Cat 5e copper, 100 m
1000BASE-SX: multimode, 850 nm, 220 m on OM1 and 550 m on OM2
1000BASE-LX: 1310 nm, 550 m on multimode, up to 5 km on single-mode (10 km on common vendor optics)
detail:
The three gigabit Ethernet physical layers you are expected to be able to place by media and reach.
How it works
  • T is copper and uses all four pairs: 1000BASE-T runs 250 Mbps on each of four pairs simultaneously in both directions, using echo cancellation to separate its own transmission from what it receives. That is why it needs all eight conductors and why a damaged pair kills gigabit but may leave 100 Mbps working.
  • S means short wavelength: SX uses an 850 nm source into multimode. Cheap optics, cheap fibre, limited reach. The exact reach depends on the fibre grade, which is why the exam quotes a range.
  • L means long wavelength: LX uses 1310 nm and is designed for single-mode. Longer wavelengths suffer less attenuation in glass, which is what buys the kilometres.
  • LX on multimode needs a conditioning cable: Launching a single-mode-oriented 1310 nm signal into a multimode core excites a strong centre mode and causes differential mode delay. A mode-conditioning patch cord offsets the launch to avoid it.
Where you see it
  • 1000BASE-T for every ordinary desktop and access port
  • 1000BASE-SX for building risers and short data centre links
  • 1000BASE-LX for campus and building-to-building backbones
exam: The exam tests the letter conventions as much as the numbers: in any xBASE-y name, T is twisted pair copper, S is short-wavelength multimode, L is long-wavelength single-mode. If you forget a specific distance, you can still eliminate wrong answers with that rule. The reliable anchors are 100 m for copper and 'kilometres' for single-mode.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: 10GBASE-T versus 10GBASE-SR versus 10GBASE-LR — media and distance?
answer:
10GBASE-T: copper — 55 m on Cat 6, 100 m on Cat 6a
10GBASE-SR: multimode — 300 m on OM3, 400 m on OM4
10GBASE-LR: single-mode 1310 nm — 10 km
detail:
The three ways to move 10 Gbps that the exam expects you to distinguish, and the distances that decide which one a scenario needs.
How it works
  • 10GBASE-T is power-hungry: Pushing 10 Gbps through copper takes far more digital signal processing than 1 Gbps, so 10GBASE-T ports draw noticeably more power and run hotter than SFP+ optics. That is part of why data centres favour DAC and fibre.
  • SR is the data centre default: Short reach on multimode with 850 nm VCSELs. Cheap optics, and 300–400 m covers essentially any distance inside one building.
  • LR reaches 10 km, ER reaches 40 km: Long reach at 1310 nm on single-mode is the standard campus and metro choice. Extended reach at 1550 nm goes further but the optics are expensive and can overdrive a short link.
  • Copper category sets the copper distance: 10GBASE-T is not one distance. Cat 6 gives roughly 55 m, Cat 6a gives the full 100 m. The cable, not the interface, is the limit.
Where you see it
  • 10GBASE-T uplinks from an access switch on existing Cat 6a
  • 10GBASE-SR between top-of-rack and aggregation switches
  • 10GBASE-LR between two buildings on a campus
exam: The tested contrast is Cat 6 at 55 m versus Cat 6a at 100 m for 10GBASE-T, and SR for inside a building versus LR for kilometres. A scenario asking for 10 Gbps over 2 km rules out every copper option immediately — the answer is LR on single-mode. Watch for questions that give a distance just over 55 m to force the Cat 6a answer.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: 802.3af, 802.3at and 802.3bt — power at the switch port and power at the device?
answer:
802.3af (PoE, Type 1): 15.4 W at the port → 12.95 W at the device
802.3at (PoE+, Type 2): 30 W → ~25.5 W
802.3bt Type 3 (PoE++): 60 W → 51 W
802.3bt Type 4: 90 W → ~71 W
detail:
Delivering DC power and data over the same twisted pair, so a camera or access point needs only one cable and no local outlet.
How it works
  • The two numbers differ because of cable loss: The higher figure is what the power sourcing equipment supplies at the port. The lower figure is what the powered device is guaranteed at the far end of a 100 m run after resistive loss in the copper. The exam quotes both, and the device figure is the one that must cover the device's rating.
  • Two pairs versus four: 802.3af and 802.3at power over two pairs. 802.3bt uses all four pairs, which is how it roughly doubles and then triples the deliverable power without raising voltage past the safety limit.
  • Devices are classified before power is applied: The PSE performs a resistance-based detection to confirm a real powered device is present, then a classification handshake that tells it how much power to reserve. Nothing is energised until detection passes, so plugging a laptop into a PoE port is harmless.
  • PoE and PoE+ negotiation: 802.3at devices can request the higher power tier through LLDP after the link comes up. A PoE+ device on an 802.3af switch will typically power up in a reduced mode or not at all rather than browning out the switch.
Where you see it
  • IP phones and basic cameras on 802.3af
  • Wi-Fi 6 access points and PTZ cameras on 802.3at
  • Multi-radio APs, video conferencing endpoints and LED lighting on 802.3bt
exam: These four numbers are heavily tested and easily confused. Anchor on 15.4 / 30 / 60 / 90 watts at the port and remember the device always gets less. The classic scenario is an access point that requires more than 12.95 W — the switch must support at least 802.3at. Do not confuse the standard names: af is PoE, at is PoE+, bt is PoE++.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: A new access point will not power up on a PoE switch. What do you check?
answer: The switch's total power budget, whether the port supports the required PoE standard, whether PoE is enabled on that port, and the cable run itself. Start with show power inline.
detail:
PoE failures are usually about budget arithmetic or standard mismatch, not about a broken device.
How it works
  • The budget is shared across all ports: A 48-port switch does not supply 30 W to every port. It has a fixed power supply — perhaps 370 W — shared across all PoE ports. Adding one more access point to a nearly full budget causes the switch to deny power to the newest device, or to shed a lower-priority port.
  • Standard mismatch is silent: An 802.3at device on an 802.3af-only switch may not power at all, or may boot into a degraded mode with a radio disabled. Nothing on the switch reports 'wrong standard' — you have to compare the device datasheet with the port capability.
  • Cable length and quality reduce delivered power: Resistive loss over 100 m is exactly why the device-side figure is lower. A long run using thin 28 AWG patch cords or a run with a damaged pair can drop delivered power below what the device needs to boot.
  • Check that PoE is administratively on: Ports can be configured with PoE disabled, or with a static power limit lower than the device requires. show power inline shows admin state, class, allocated watts and consumed watts per port.
Where you see it
  • Adding access points to an existing switch during a Wi-Fi upgrade
  • Diagnosing a camera that reboots in a loop at the end of a long run
  • Sizing a switch and its power supply before a deployment
exam: The exam favours the power budget exhausted answer when a scenario adds devices to an already-populated switch. If the scenario instead says the device is new and requires more wattage than the others, the answer is a PoE standard mismatch and the fix is a PoE+ or PoE++ switch or a single-port injector. 'Bad access point' is the distractor.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What does a media converter do?
answer: Converts between physical media at Layer 1 — most often copper Ethernet to fibre, to extend a run past the 100 m copper limit.
detail:
A small, cheap box that changes the medium a signal travels on without touching the frame.
How it works
  • It is a Layer 1 device: It regenerates the signal onto different media. It does not read MAC addresses, does not learn, does not filter, and does not create a new collision domain boundary in the way a switch does.
  • The usual job is breaking the 100 m limit: A camera 400 m from the closet cannot be reached with copper. A pair of converters plus multimode fibre bridges the gap, with copper at each end where the devices are.
  • It also handles media type differences: Multimode to single-mode conversion, or old coax to Ethernet, are the other common uses in retrofits.
  • Power and troubleshooting: Each converter needs its own power, which puts a small active device in the middle of the run. When a link fails, the converters are the first thing to check because they are the only powered element between the two switches.
Where you see it
  • Reaching a remote building, gate or camera beyond 100 m
  • Connecting a copper-only legacy device to a fibre backbone
  • Retrofitting old coax runs into an Ethernet network
exam: The exam presents this as a distance problem: a device is 250 m from the switch, what do you use? The answer is fibre with media converters. Distractors are a repeater, a longer Cat 6a cable, or 'use a switch in the middle' — the last is technically workable but the exam is testing that you know converters exist and that 100 m is the copper ceiling.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What is attenuation and what causes it?
answer: Signal loss over distance, measured in dB. On copper it comes from resistance and cable length; on fibre from absorption, scattering, splices and connectors.
detail:
The reason every cable standard has a maximum length. The signal weakens until the receiver can no longer distinguish it from noise.
How it works
  • It is why 100 m exists: The 100 m copper limit is set so the received signal is still strong enough relative to noise at the far end. Exceeding it does not immediately break the link — it produces intermittent errors and slowdowns that get worse under load, which is harder to diagnose than a dead cable.
  • On fibre it is measured as a loss budget: Every connector adds roughly 0.3–0.75 dB and every splice adds a smaller amount. A link budget adds up fibre loss per kilometre plus all connector and splice losses, and the total must stay under what the optic can tolerate.
  • Dirty connectors are the usual fibre cause: A single dust particle on a ferrule end face can add several dB. Cleaning fibre connectors before mating is standard practice precisely because contamination looks identical to a failing optic.
  • Symptoms are gradual, not binary: Rising CRC error counters, throughput that collapses under load, and a link that comes up and stays up but performs badly. A link that is simply dead is more likely a break than attenuation.
Where you see it
  • A run measured at 120 m that works fine at idle and fails during backups
  • A fibre link with rising errors after new patch cords were added
  • Calculating whether a proposed fibre span will work before installing it
exam: The tested contrast is attenuation versus interference. Attenuation is distance-driven and predictable — a too-long run. Interference is environment-driven — a run beside a motor. If the scenario emphasises cable length, answer attenuation; if it emphasises what the cable passes near, answer EMI. The fix for attenuation is a shorter run, a repeater, or fibre.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What is EMI and how do you fix it?
answer: Electromagnetic interference — outside electrical noise coupling into the cable and corrupting the signal. Fix by rerouting away from the source, using shielded cable properly bonded, or switching to fibre.
detail:
Copper cable is an antenna. Any strong changing magnetic field nearby induces current in it, and that current is indistinguishable from signal.
How it works
  • Sources are anything with a motor or a ballast: Fluorescent lighting ballasts, elevator motors, HVAC units, welders, large transformers and parallel electrical conduit are the classic culprits.
  • The symptom is localised and intermittent: One or two drops show CRC errors while everything else is clean, and the errors correlate with something turning on — the lift running, the compressor cycling. That correlation is the diagnostic clue.
  • Distance and angle both help: Separating data cable from power conduit, and crossing power at 90 degrees rather than running parallel to it, dramatically reduces coupling. Rerouting is often cheaper than recabling.
  • Fibre is immune: Glass carries no current, so no external field can induce anything into it. Where the environment is genuinely hostile, fibre is the definitive answer rather than a mitigation.
Where you see it
  • A drop that errors only when the freight lift runs
  • Cable trays sharing a path with high-voltage feeds in a plant
  • Choosing fibre for a run between two buildings with different grounds
exam: CompTIA gives EMI away through the environment description: near motors, near fluorescent lights, running alongside power. The expected answers, in order, are reroute the cable, use shielded cable, or use fibre. The distractor is upgrading to a higher category — that changes bandwidth, not noise immunity.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What is crosstalk, and what are NEXT, FEXT and alien crosstalk?
answer: Signal bleeding from one pair into another. NEXT is measured at the transmitting end, FEXT at the far end, and alien crosstalk is bleed between separate cables in a bundle.
detail:
Noise generated inside the cabling itself rather than by the outside world. It is the reason pairs are twisted and the reason higher categories exist.
How it works
  • Untwisting at termination is the field cause: Every pair must stay twisted right up to the punch-down point. Stripping back 50 mm and untwisting the pairs to make them easier to seat destroys the cancellation and produces near-end crosstalk. TIA allows about 13 mm of untwist for Cat 5e and less for Cat 6.
  • NEXT is measured near the transmitter: The transmitted signal is strongest at the point it leaves, so that is where it couples most strongly into the neighbouring pair and interferes with the weak incoming signal. This is why near-end crosstalk is the dominant copper impairment.
  • Alien crosstalk is a bundle problem: Coupling between different cables lying against each other in a tray. It is not measurable by testing one cable alone, and it is the specific limit that caps 10GBASE-T on Cat 6 at 55 m.
  • A split pair passes continuity but fails crosstalk: Wiring pin 3 with pin 4 instead of pin 6 produces end-to-end continuity on every conductor. A cheap continuity tester says the cable is good; a certifier fails it on NEXT, and the link performs terribly.
Where you see it
  • Certifying newly terminated jacks with a cable certifier
  • Diagnosing a drop that links but errors constantly after a rushed termination
  • Explaining why Cat 6 cannot do 10 Gbps at 100 m in a full bundle
exam: The exam links crosstalk to termination quality. A scenario where a technician terminated jacks and the links now show errors points at untwisting too much pair at the punch-down. The split pair case is a favourite because it explains why a basic tester shows pass but the link misbehaves — the fix is re-terminating to the correct standard, not a new cable.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What do runts, giants and CRC errors in an interface counter tell you?
answer:
Runts: frames under 64 bytes — collisions or duplex mismatch.
Giants: frames over the configured MTU — MTU or jumbo-frame mismatch.
CRC errors: frames whose checksum failed — bad cable, EMI, a failing transceiver, or duplex mismatch.
detail:
The three counters an interface shows that turn a vague 'the network is slow' complaint into a specific physical-layer diagnosis.
How it works
  • A runt is a truncated frame: Ethernet's minimum frame is 64 bytes. Anything shorter was cut off mid-transmission, usually because a collision aborted it or because a half-duplex side stopped transmitting when it heard the other end.
  • A giant exceeds the MTU the port will accept: If one switch is configured for 9000-byte jumbo frames and its neighbour is not, the neighbour counts every jumbo frame as a giant and drops it. Small frames still pass, so ping works and large transfers fail — a very characteristic symptom.
  • CRC errors mean the bits changed in flight: The sender computes a frame check sequence; the receiver recomputes it and finds a mismatch. Something corrupted the frame on the wire. That is cabling, connectors, noise or an optic — it is not a routing or configuration problem.
  • Read them as a rate, not a total: A counter that has accumulated a few hundred errors over a year of uptime is noise. Errors climbing while you watch, or climbing in proportion to traffic, is a live fault. Clear the counters and re-check.
Where you see it
  • Running show interface on a switch port a user complains about
  • Distinguishing a bad patch cord from a configuration problem
  • Confirming a jumbo-frame mismatch on a storage network
exam: Match the counter to the cause. CRC errors plus a specific cable means a physical problem — swap the cable first. Runts and late collisions together means duplex mismatch. Giants means MTU mismatch, and the exam pairs that with iSCSI or storage scenarios where jumbo frames were enabled on only one side.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What is a duplex mismatch and how do you recognise it?
answer: One end is full duplex and the other is half duplex. The link comes up and works at low load, then collapses under load with late collisions on the half-duplex side and CRC/runt errors on the other.
detail:
The classic misconfiguration that produces a working-but-terrible link. It is not a broken cable and it does not take the interface down, which is exactly what makes it hard to spot.
How it works
  • Why it happens: Auto-negotiation on one side and a hard-coded setting on the other. If one end is forced to 100/full and the other is left on auto, the auto side cannot detect duplex, falls back to half duplex by the parallel-detection rule, and the mismatch is created.
  • The half-duplex side sees late collisions: Half duplex uses CSMA/CD and expects any collision to occur within the first 64 bytes. The full-duplex partner transmits whenever it wants, so collisions arrive after that window. A late collision counter that is non-zero is almost always duplex mismatch, not a genuinely oversized network.
  • The full-duplex side sees FCS and runt errors: It receives frames the other end aborted mid-transmission, so it counts them as runts and CRC failures. The two ends therefore show different symptoms — which is why you must look at both.
  • Fix by matching both ends: Either set both ends to auto-negotiate, or hard-code both ends identically. Half-configured is the failure mode. Modern practice is auto on both sides.
Where you see it
  • A server link that saturates at a fraction of its rated speed
  • A port hard-coded years ago that now faces a replacement switch
  • Backups that take hours longer than expected with no obvious errors
exam: Late collisions are the giveaway CompTIA uses. If a scenario mentions late collisions, or 'the link is up but throughput is terrible and gets worse under load', the answer is duplex mismatch. The trap is answering 'bad cable' — a bad cable normally produces CRC errors symmetrically and often drops the link, and it does not produce late collisions.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: Toner probe versus cable tester — which question does each answer?
answer:
Toner probe (tone generator + inductive probe): which cable is this — traces and identifies an unlabelled run.
Cable tester: is this cable wired correctly — continuity and pin-to-pin map.
detail:
Two tools people conflate. One finds a cable; the other verifies a cable. They do not substitute for each other.
How it works
  • The toner injects an audible signal: Clip the tone generator onto one end of an unknown cable, then wave the inductive probe over the bundle at the other end. The probe squeals over the right one. It works without any connection at the far end.
  • A basic cable tester checks continuity and mapping: It confirms all eight conductors are connected end to end and that pin 1 goes to pin 1. It detects opens, shorts, reversed pairs and crossed pairs.
  • A basic tester does not detect a split pair reliably: A split pair is continuous on every conductor, so a continuity tester passes it. Only a wiremap tester that checks pair association, or a certifier that measures NEXT, catches it.
  • A certifier is a third tool: A cable certifier measures against the TIA standard — NEXT, return loss, attenuation, delay skew — and issues a pass or fail for a category rating. That is what a contractor uses to prove an installation meets Cat 6a, and it costs far more than a tester.
Where you see it
  • Identifying which of 48 unlabelled patch panel ports serves a given office
  • Verifying a freshly terminated jack before handing it over
  • Proving a new installation certifies to Cat 6a for a customer
exam: The exam distinguishes these by the question being asked. 'A technician needs to locate a specific cable in a bundle' is always the toner probe. 'A technician needs to verify the cable was terminated correctly' is a cable tester or wiremap tester. Do not answer 'cable tester' for the locating scenario — that is the intended distractor.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: TDR, OTDR, visual fault locator, light meter — which tool for which fibre or copper question?
answer:
TDR: distance to a copper fault.
OTDR: distance to a fibre fault plus a loss profile of the whole span.
Visual fault locator: a red laser that makes breaks and bad bends glow.
Light meter / power meter: measures actual dB loss end to end.
detail:
The four tools for finding where a run is broken and how much signal it is losing.
How it works
  • TDR and OTDR measure by echo timing: They send a pulse and time the reflection from the fault. Because the propagation speed of the cable is known, time converts directly to distance — so the tool reports 'open at 47 metres' and you know exactly where to open the ceiling.
  • An OTDR also profiles the whole link: Its trace shows every connector, splice and bend as a step or spike of loss along the span. That is how you find the one dirty connector in a 3 km run rather than just confirming the run is lossy.
  • A VFL is cheap and immediate: It injects visible red light. Light escaping at a break, a crushed section or a bad splice is visible with the naked eye through the jacket. It only works over short distances but needs no interpretation.
  • A power meter with a light source measures real loss: An OTDR estimates loss from backscatter. A light source at one end and a power meter at the other measures the actual delivered power in dB, which is what you compare against the link budget.
Where you see it
  • Locating a cut in a buried fibre run between buildings
  • Finding a break in a copper run inside a wall without opening the whole wall
  • Confirming a new fibre span meets its loss budget before turn-up
exam: Match tool to question. 'How far along the cable is the break' is a TDR for copper, OTDR for fibre. 'Is there light and how much' is a light/power meter. 'Is this short patch cord broken' is a VFL. The exam's favourite trap is offering a cable tester when the scenario asks for the distance to the fault — a tester says the cable failed, only a TDR/OTDR says where.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::05 Cables, Connectors & Media
front: What is a patch panel for, and what is the difference between a 110 block and a 66 block?
answer: A patch panel terminates permanent horizontal cable runs so you can rearrange connections with short patch cords. 110 blocks are the modern punch-down standard for data; 66 blocks are legacy analogue voice.
detail:
Structured cabling separates the permanent cable in the walls from the flexible connections in the rack. The patch panel is the boundary between them.
How it works
  • Solid core in the wall, stranded in the rack: Horizontal runs use solid-core conductors, which punch down cleanly but crack if flexed repeatedly. Patch cords use stranded conductors that tolerate movement. Terminating solid core into RJ45 plugs and plugging them directly into switches is why old installations fail intermittently.
  • A punch-down tool cuts and seats in one motion: The blade pushes the conductor into an insulation-displacement contact that slices the insulation and grips the copper, and the other side of the blade trims the excess. That is why the tool has a cut and a non-cut side.
  • 110 blocks carry data-grade specifications: 110 is rated for Cat 5e and Cat 6 performance and is what a patch panel's rear side actually is. 66 blocks were designed for analogue telephone and have no data category rating.
  • The panel enables moves without re-terminating: Changing which switch port serves an office becomes moving a patch cord, not re-punching a wall run. That is the entire economic argument for structured cabling.
Where you see it
  • Wiring closets and MDF/IDF racks in any commercial building
  • Moving a user to a different VLAN by moving a patch cord
  • Identifying legacy 66 blocks in an old telephone room during an upgrade
exam: The testable facts are the roles: the patch panel is where permanent runs terminate, and 66 = legacy voice, 110 = data. Expect a scenario about a technician finding an old block in a closet, or a question on which tool is used — the answer is a punch-down tool, and the distractor is a crimper, which is for attaching RJ45 plugs to patch cords.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: RPO versus RTO — define and contrast.
answer: RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data you can afford to lose, measured backwards from the failure — it drives backup frequency. RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long you can be down, measured forwards — it drives recovery capability.
detail:
Both are business decisions expressed as time, and they point in opposite directions from the moment of failure. Confusing them is the single most common error in this topic.
How it works
  • RPO looks backwards and is answered by backups: If the RPO is four hours, you must capture data at least every four hours, because the worst case is a failure immediately before the next capture. An RPO near zero requires synchronous replication, not backups, and that costs bandwidth and latency.
  • RTO looks forwards and is answered by infrastructure: If the RTO is one hour, restoring 40 TB from tape is not a plan. Meeting a short RTO requires standby hardware, pre-staged data and a rehearsed procedure — a hot or warm site, or a cloud failover region.
  • They are set per service, not per company: Payroll can tolerate a day; the transaction database cannot tolerate a minute. Applying one figure to everything either wastes money on unimportant systems or under-protects critical ones.
  • Tighter objectives cost disproportionately more: Going from a 24-hour to a 4-hour RTO is often an operational change. Going from 4 hours to 15 minutes usually means duplicating the environment. The business must state what the downtime actually costs before the number is chosen.
  • They must be validated, not just written: An RTO is a claim until a test proves it. Untested plans routinely miss stated RTOs by an order of magnitude because of forgotten dependencies such as DNS, licensing and authentication.
Where you see it
  • Choosing hourly snapshots versus nightly backups for a database
  • Justifying a warm standby site to management with a cost-of-downtime figure
  • Auditing whether last quarter's failover test actually met the stated RTO
exam: This contrast is guaranteed to appear. The reliable mnemonic is RPO = Point in time = data loss, RTO = Time to restore = downtime. Watch for scenarios that give you a backup schedule and ask for the RPO — nightly backups mean an RPO of up to 24 hours. Distractors swap the two definitions verbatim.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: MTTR versus MTBF — and how do they relate to availability?
answer: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair): average time to restore a failed component. MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures): average working time between failures. Availability ≈ MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
detail:
RPO and RTO are targets you set. MTTR and MTBF are measurements you take. One describes how reliable a thing is, the other how quickly you fix it.
How it works
