  • MTBF is a reliability figure from the vendor: Manufacturers publish MTBF for drives, power supplies and fans, often as a very large number of hours derived from population testing. It predicts failure rates across a fleet; it does not promise that any individual unit will last that long.
  • MTTR is an operational figure you control: It includes detection, diagnosis, obtaining the part, and the repair itself. Spare hardware on the shelf, current configuration backups and good documentation cut MTTR far more than better components do. MTTF, mean time to failure, is the related figure used for non-repairable items.
  • The formula shows where to spend: Because availability is MTBF over MTBF plus MTTR, halving MTTR improves availability exactly as much as doubling MTBF, and it is usually far cheaper. That is the argument for cold spares and out-of-band access.
  • Redundancy attacks the problem differently: A redundant pair does not make either device more reliable; it makes the failure of one invisible, which turns a long MTTR into a non-event for users.
Where you see it
  • Justifying a spare switch on the shelf by its effect on MTTR
  • Comparing vendor MTBF figures when choosing hardware for a remote site
  • Reporting availability against an SLA using measured MTBF and MTTR
exam: The exam tests the definitions and the direction of each: MTBF between failures is uptime, MTTR to repair is downtime. The distractor expands MTTR as 'mean time to respond' or 'to recovery', which sounds plausible; on N10-009 treat it as repair. If a question asks which metric a stock of spare parts improves, the answer is MTTR.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Business continuity versus disaster recovery?
answer: BC is keeping the business operating during a disruption, by any means including manual workarounds. DR is the technical subset that restores the failed IT systems.
detail:
DR is about systems. BC is about the organization. Every DR plan lives inside a BC plan, and the BC plan has to cover what people do while the systems are still down.
How it works
  • Scope is the difference: BC covers staff, facilities, suppliers, communications and alternate ways of taking orders. DR covers restoring servers, data, network and applications. A company can survive a disaster with a good BC plan and a slow DR plan; the reverse is rarely true.
  • The BIA comes first: A business impact analysis identifies critical processes, what they depend on, and what an hour of outage costs each one. The RPO and RTO for every system are outputs of that analysis, not guesses made by IT.
  • Both need a communication plan: Who declares the disaster, who is called, in what order, and over what channel when the corporate phone system and email are part of the outage. Contact trees that live only on an internal file server are a documented classic failure.
  • Testing differs in kind: BC is exercised with tabletop and functional exercises across departments. DR is validated by actually failing systems over. Both must be scheduled, because plans decay as systems and staff change.
Where you see it
  • Running the warehouse on paper picking lists while the WMS is restored
  • A business impact analysis that sets RTO per application
  • An out-of-band conference bridge and printed contact list for incident coordination
exam: The exam tests scope. If the question is about restoring servers, data and network services, that is disaster recovery. If it is about keeping the business functioning, including non-technical workarounds and staff relocation, that is business continuity. Remember that DR is a component of BC, not a synonym or an alternative.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Cold, warm and hot sites — what is in each and how fast is recovery?
answer: Cold: space, power and cooling only — cheapest, days to weeks. Warm: hardware and connectivity installed, data restored from backup — hours to days. Hot: a fully running duplicate with current data — minutes, most expensive.
detail:
All three are alternate facilities. They differ in how much is already there and therefore in how much of the recovery clock is spent building versus switching.
How it works
  • Cold means an empty room with utilities: There is floor space, power, cooling and usually a network drop. Everything else — servers, storage, switches, data, staff — arrives after the disaster is declared. It is cheap to hold and unusable for anything with a short RTO.
  • Warm means hardware waiting but data behind: Equipment is racked, configured and connected, but the data is whatever the last backup or periodic replication delivered. Recovery is a restore plus a cutover, so the RTO is hours and the RPO is whatever the replication interval was.
  • Hot means it is already running: The environment is live, data is replicated continuously or near-continuously, and failover is a switch rather than a build. This is what a short RTO with a near-zero RPO requires, and it costs roughly a second full environment.
  • Cloud has blurred the middle: A DR region with infrastructure-as-code templates and replicated storage behaves like a warm site at close to cold-site cost, because compute is only paid for when it is started. Expect the exam to still use the three classic terms.
Where you see it
  • A regulated business holding a hot site to meet a sub-hour RTO
  • A small firm with a cold-site contract and offsite backups
  • A warm site kept in sync with nightly replication for a 12-hour RTO
exam: The exam maps site type to RTO and cost, so anchor on those two axes. If a scenario states recovery within minutes, the answer is a hot site; days and lowest cost is a cold site. The distractor is picking hot whenever the scenario sounds important — read for the stated recovery time and budget constraint, because the cheapest option that meets the requirement is usually the intended answer.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Active-active versus active-passive high availability?
answer: Active-active: all nodes carry production traffic; a failure reduces capacity but not availability. Active-passive: a standby node idles until failover, so full capacity survives but there is a switchover delay.
detail:
Both are two-node designs against single-device failure. They differ in whether the second node is working or waiting, and each has a distinct failure mode.
How it works
  • Active-active uses everything you paid for: Both nodes carry load, so the pair is also a capacity play. The catch is that each node must be able to absorb the whole load alone, or a failure turns into an overload — a pair running at 70 percent each has no headroom to survive one loss.
  • Active-passive is simpler and more predictable: The standby holds a synchronized configuration and takes over on failure. State is easier to reason about because only one node is authoritative at a time, which matters for firewalls and databases.
  • Failover is not instant: Detection plus convergence takes seconds. Existing sessions may drop unless the pair synchronizes state — a stateful firewall pair replicates its connection table specifically so established sessions survive the switch.
  • The passive node's real risk is that it is untested: A standby that has never carried traffic can have a bad configuration, expired licence or failed disk that nobody notices until the day it is needed. Scheduled failovers are what convert a theoretical standby into a real one.
  • Split brain is the shared danger: If the nodes lose their heartbeat link but both stay alive, both may claim the active role and the shared address. Dedicated heartbeat paths and quorum mechanisms exist to prevent this.
Where you see it
  • A firewall pair failing over with session synchronization
  • Two load balancers sharing a VIP with VRRP
  • A scheduled failover test to prove the standby is actually viable
exam: Expect a definition contrast plus a capacity trap: in active-active, a single node failure means the survivor carries all the traffic, so each must be sized for the full load. If a scenario says both devices process traffic simultaneously, that is active-active. If it says one sits idle awaiting failure, that is active-passive. Split brain is the term for both nodes going active at once.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Tabletop exercise versus validation testing?
answer: Tabletop: a discussion-based walkthrough of the plan with the people who would execute it — no systems are touched. Validation test: actually performing the failover or restore and proving the result.
detail:
One tests whether the plan and the people make sense. The other tests whether the technology does what the plan claims. Both are required, and they catch different failures.
How it works
  • The tabletop finds process and people gaps: A facilitator presents a scenario and the participants talk through what they would do. It reliably surfaces missing contact details, unclear decision authority, unstated dependencies and assumptions that two teams held differently. It is cheap, causes no outage, and can be run often.
  • Validation finds technical gaps: Actually restoring the database, actually failing the site over, actually booting from the backup image. This is where you learn that the backup has been silently failing for six weeks, that a licence is tied to a MAC address, or that the DR environment's certificates expired.
  • An untested backup is not a backup: Backup success in a console means the job ran, not that the data is restorable. Periodic test restores to a scratch environment are the only proof, and they are what separate a real RPO from an aspirational one.
  • Escalating levels of realism: Between the two sit walkthroughs, simulations and parallel tests where the DR environment runs alongside production without taking over. Full interruption testing is the most convincing and the most disruptive, so it is scheduled deliberately.
Where you see it
  • An annual tabletop covering a ransomware scenario with IT, legal and communications
  • A quarterly restore of a random backup set to prove recoverability
  • A scheduled failover to the DR site during a maintenance window
exam: The discriminator is whether systems are touched. If the description says the team meets and talks through the plan, it is a tabletop. If it says they perform the failover and verify results, it is validation. A frequent scenario says backups reported success but the restore failed during a real incident — the corrective action is regular test restores, not more frequent backups.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is an SLA, and how much downtime is 99.9%?
answer: A contractual commitment covering uptime, response and resolution times, and the remedy when missed. 99.9% ≈ 8.76 hours per year (about 43.8 minutes a month). 99.99% ≈ 52.6 minutes a year; 99.999% ≈ 5.26 minutes a year.
detail:
Uptime percentages sound similar and mean wildly different things. Converting them to time is the only way to judge whether a commitment is meaningful.
How it works
  • The arithmetic is simple: A year is 8,760 hours. One percent of that is 87.6 hours, so 99% allows about 3.65 days of downtime. Each additional nine divides the allowance by ten: 99.9% is 8.76 hours, 99.99% is 52.6 minutes, 99.999% is 5.26 minutes.
  • Five nines is an engineering commitment, not a promise: Roughly five minutes a year is less than one reboot. It cannot be met with any design that requires a human to notice and act, which is why it implies full redundancy and automated failover throughout the path.
  • The measurement window matters as much as the number: 99.9% measured monthly allows 43.8 minutes each month. Measured annually it allows one 8.76-hour outage. Read whether the SLA states availability per month or per year before agreeing to it.
  • Exclusions are where SLAs are won and lost: Scheduled maintenance windows, force majeure and customer-caused faults are normally excluded from the calculation. An SLA credit is also a refund, not compensation for the business impact, so it is rarely a substitute for redundancy.
  • End-to-end availability is worse than any single link: Chaining services multiplies their availabilities. Two 99.9% components in series give roughly 99.8%, so a provider SLA is a ceiling on your own, not a floor.
Where you see it
  • Comparing two ISP contracts on measured availability, not marketing wording
  • Calculating whether a monthly maintenance window fits inside the committed uptime
  • Reporting last quarter's availability against a 99.9% commitment
exam: The number to memorize is 99.9% = about 8.76 hours per year, and CompTIA does ask for it. Distractors offer 8.76 minutes or 87.6 hours, so keep the scale straight. Also know that an SLA specifies remedies and response times, not just uptime, and that scheduled maintenance is typically excluded from the calculation.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: In SNMP, what are the manager, agent, MIB and OID?
answer: Manager: the monitoring system that queries devices on UDP 161. Agent: software on the managed device that answers. MIB: the catalogue of what can be queried. OID: the dotted-number address of one specific value.
detail:
SNMP is a simple question-and-answer protocol over UDP. Its whole structure is a naming scheme for device values plus two verbs for reading and writing them.
How it works
  • The manager polls, the agent answers: The manager sends GET or GETNEXT requests to the agent on UDP 161 and receives the current value. GETBULK, added in v2c, retrieves a whole table in one exchange, which matters when walking hundreds of interfaces.
  • The MIB is the schema, the OID is the address: A MIB file defines a tree of manageable objects with names, types and descriptions. An OID such as 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10 is the numeric path to one leaf — in that case the inbound octet counter on an interface. Loading a vendor MIB is what turns raw numbers into readable names in the monitoring tool.
  • SET is why write access is dangerous: SNMP can write as well as read: an SNMP SET can shut an interface or change a configuration. A read-write community string on v1 or v2c, sent in cleartext, is effectively an administrative credential broadcast across the network.
  • Counters, not gauges, drive most graphs: Interface statistics are ever-increasing counters. The manager subtracts consecutive polls and divides by the interval to produce a rate. That is why a device reboot, which resets counters, produces a spike or a gap on the graph.
Where you see it
  • Adding a new switch to a monitoring platform and walking its interface table
  • Loading a vendor MIB so temperature and PSU status appear by name
  • Restricting SNMP to read-only with an ACL limiting which managers may poll
exam: The port pair is heavily tested: 161 for polling, 162 for traps. Know that the agent runs on the managed device and the manager runs on the NMS — the distractor reverses them. If a question asks what defines the objects a device exposes, the answer is the MIB; if it asks how a single value is identified, the answer is the OID.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: SNMP polling versus traps — when do you use each?
answer: Polling is the manager asking on a schedule (UDP 161) — good for trending and graphs. Traps are the agent pushing an alert the moment something happens (UDP 162) — good for immediate notification. Use both.
detail:
The two directions answer different questions. Polling tells you what normal looks like over time; traps tell you the instant something abnormal occurred.
How it works
  • Polling has a resolution limit: A five-minute poll interval cannot see a 30-second saturation event; it averages it away. Shortening the interval increases fidelity and also increases load on both the manager and the devices, so intervals are a deliberate trade.
  • Traps are immediate but unreliable: A trap is a single unacknowledged UDP datagram. If it is lost, nobody retransmits it and nobody knows. An inform, added in v2c, is an acknowledged trap that the agent retries — more reliable, more overhead.
  • A dead device sends nothing: This is the reason polling cannot be dropped. A device that has lost power cannot send a trap announcing it. The absence of a poll response is what generates the 'device down' alert.
  • The practical combination: Poll for interface utilization, CPU, memory, temperature and error counters to build baselines and capacity trends. Configure traps for link down, power supply failure, fan failure, high temperature and authentication failures so they arrive without waiting for the next poll cycle.
Where you see it
  • Five-minute polling for capacity graphs plus link-down traps for immediate alerting
  • Switching to informs where trap loss across a WAN has been a problem
  • Explaining why a brief outage never appeared on the utilization graph
exam: The exam contrast is scheduled pull versus event-driven push, with ports 161 and 162 as the tell. The scenario trap: relying on traps alone means a failed device is never reported, because it cannot send anything. If a question asks how to detect that a device has stopped responding, the answer is polling, not traps.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Why use SNMPv3 instead of v1 or v2c?
answer: v1 and v2c authenticate with a community string sent in cleartext. v3 adds real user authentication, message integrity and encryption of the payload.
detail:
SNMP was designed when the management network was assumed to be trusted. v3 is the version that stopped assuming that.
How it works
  • A community string is a password in the clear: Anyone capturing traffic reads it, and the default values 'public' and 'private' are still found in production. With a read-write string an attacker can reconfigure devices; with a read-only string they can inventory your entire network.
  • v2c improved efficiency, not security: The 'c' means community-based. GETBULK and informs came from v2c, but the authentication model is identical to v1. Choosing v2c over v1 buys performance and nothing else.
  • v3 has three security levels: noAuthNoPriv is neither authenticated nor encrypted, authNoPriv authenticates each message with HMAC using SHA, and authPriv adds encryption with AES. Only authPriv protects the contents, and it is the level to configure.
  • Defence in depth still applies: Even with v3, restrict SNMP with an ACL naming the permitted managers, keep it off untrusted VLANs and internet-facing interfaces, and use read-only views unless write access is genuinely required.
Where you see it
  • Replacing 'public' community strings across a switch estate during a security audit
  • Configuring authPriv with SHA and AES on a new core switch
  • Blocking UDP 161 inbound at the perimeter
exam: The tested sentence is that v1 and v2c send the community string in cleartext and v3 adds authentication, integrity and encryption. Distractors claim v2c added encryption — it did not, it added GETBULK and informs. If a scenario says a security assessment found network management credentials visible in a packet capture, the fix is SNMPv3 with authPriv.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is syslog, and why centralize logs?
answer: A standard for devices to send event messages to a collector, traditionally UDP 514. Centralizing means the logs survive the device that failed, can be correlated across systems, and can be retained and searched.
detail:
Every device generates events locally, into a small buffer that is lost on reboot. Syslog moves those events somewhere they can outlive the device and be read alongside everyone else's.
How it works
  • A message carries facility, severity and text: The facility says which subsystem generated the event and the severity says how bad it is. The collector uses both to file and filter. Timestamps come from the device, which is why NTP is a prerequisite for logs that can be compared.
  • Local buffers are small and volatile: A switch keeps a few thousand lines in RAM. The exact evidence you need — the log line from the moment before a crash — is the line most likely to be lost. Shipping it off the box as it happens is the only way to keep it.
  • Correlation is the real payoff: An authentication failure on a server, a firewall deny, and a link flap are three unrelated lines until they are in one place with synchronized timestamps. Then they are an incident timeline.
  • Transport choices: Plain syslog is UDP 514 and is fire-and-forget, so messages can be silently lost under load. TCP 514 adds delivery reliability and TLS on 6514 adds confidentiality and integrity for logs crossing untrusted links.
  • Retention has to be deliberate: Volume is large and legal or contractual requirements often set a minimum. Storage sizing, rotation and tamper-resistance are part of the design, not an afterthought.
Where you see it
  • Pointing every switch, router, firewall and server at one collector
  • Investigating an outage using logs from a device that has since been rebooted
  • Meeting an audit requirement for one year of retained security logs
exam: Know UDP 514 and the reason for centralizing: correlation plus survival of the source device. The exam scenario is an investigation blocked because the evidence was on a device that rebooted or failed — the answer is a centralized syslog server / log aggregation. Remember that syslog depends on accurate time, which makes NTP a common paired answer.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: The syslog severity levels 0–7, in order?
answer:
0 Emergency · 1 Alert · 2 Critical · 3 Error · 4 Warning · 5 Notice · 6 Informational · 7 Debug
Mnemonic: Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice-cream Daily.
detail:
A memorized list. The counter-intuitive part is that the scale runs downwards in urgency: 0 is the worst and 7 is the most trivial.
How it works
  • Lower number means more severe: Emergency at 0 means the system is unusable. Debug at 7 is developer-level detail. Everyone's instinct is that a higher number is worse, and it is not — this inversion is exactly what the exam tests.
  • Configuring a level includes everything below it: Setting logging to level 4 sends severities 0 through 4 and suppresses 5, 6 and 7. Levels are a threshold, not a selection.
  • The middle of the scale is where operations lives: Errors at 3 and warnings at 4 are the actionable day-to-day traffic. Critical at 2 and above should page somebody. Notice and informational are useful for context during an investigation but generate large volume.
  • Debug is dangerous in production: Level 7 on a busy device can generate enough messages to load the CPU and flood the collector, and on a console session it can make the device effectively unmanageable. Turn it on deliberately, and turn it off again.
Where you see it
  • Setting logging trap 4 so only warnings and worse leave the device
  • Filtering a collector's dashboard to severity 3 and below for an incident view
  • Temporarily enabling debug on one device to capture a specific fault
exam: This table is asked directly, most often as 'which severity is most critical' or 'what is level 0'. The answer is 0 = Emergency, and the trap is candidates picking 7 because higher sounds worse. Know also that Debug is 7 and that configuring a level captures everything at or below that number.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: NetFlow, sFlow and IPFIX — what do they do and how do they differ?
answer: All three export traffic flow data — who talked to whom, on what ports, how much. NetFlow is Cisco's, exporting metadata about complete flows. sFlow samples packets in hardware, 1-in-N, and is multi-vendor. IPFIX is the IETF standard based on NetFlow v9.
detail:
SNMP tells you a link is at 90 percent. Flow data tells you which conversations are consuming it. That is the difference between knowing there is a problem and knowing what to do about it.
How it works
  • A flow is a conversation, keyed by a tuple: Source and destination IP, source and destination port, protocol, and usually input interface and type of service. The device accumulates packet and byte counts for that tuple and exports a record when the flow ends or a timer expires.
  • sFlow samples rather than accounting: Because it grabs one packet in N in the forwarding ASIC, sFlow scales to very high speeds with negligible CPU cost, and it is statistical by nature. It is excellent for proportions and for spotting the top talkers, and less exact for small flows and precise byte counts.
  • IPFIX is the standardized successor: It is NetFlow v9's template-based format turned into an IETF standard, so vendors other than Cisco can export a compatible format and add their own fields. Treat it as the vendor-neutral version of the same idea.
  • What it is actually used for: Answering 'what is saturating the WAN link', finding an infected host beaconing to an unusual destination, validating that traffic is taking the path the design intended, and producing per-application or per-department usage reports.
Where you see it
  • Finding the host responsible for a saturated internet circuit
  • Detecting an internal machine making repeated outbound connections to a suspicious address
  • Producing a monthly report of application mix across the WAN
exam: The exam asks what flow data is for and how it differs from SNMP: SNMP gives interface totals, flow gives per-conversation detail. Know that sFlow is sampled and multi-vendor while NetFlow is Cisco and flow-based, and that IPFIX is the IETF standard version. If a scenario asks who or what is using bandwidth, the answer is flow data, not SNMP and not a packet capture.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is a SIEM?
answer: Security Information and Event Management — a platform that aggregates logs from across the environment, normalizes and correlates them, alerts on patterns, and retains them for investigation and compliance.
detail:
A syslog server stores lines. A SIEM turns lines from many different systems into a single searchable model and applies rules that no individual device could apply.
How it works
  • Normalization makes sources comparable: A firewall, a domain controller and a proxy all describe a login or a connection in different formats. The SIEM parses each into common fields — user, source, destination, action — so one query can span all of them.
  • Correlation is the point: The value is in rules that combine events: a failed VPN login from an unusual country followed by a success, then a burst of file-server access. No single device sees that sequence; the SIEM does. This is what generates an actionable alert instead of a million log lines.
  • Retention serves audits and investigations: Regulations frequently require months or years of security logs, and intrusions are often discovered long after the initial compromise. The SIEM is where that history lives, ideally on write-once or otherwise tamper-resistant storage.
  • Tuning is the ongoing cost: An untuned SIEM produces enough false positives that analysts stop reading it, which is worse than having none. Baselines, suppression rules and periodic review are what keep it useful.
Where you see it
  • Correlating VPN, firewall and Active Directory logs to spot a compromised account
  • Meeting a PCI or HIPAA requirement for centralized log review and retention
  • Investigating an incident by searching six months of normalized logs from one console
exam: The distinction the exam draws is between plain log aggregation (collect and store) and a SIEM (collect, normalize, correlate and alert). If a scenario needs alerting on patterns across multiple systems, or compliance-driven retention and review, the answer is SIEM. A syslog server is the distractor and is right only when the requirement is simply to collect logs centrally.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Metric versus log versus trace?
answer: Metric: a number sampled over time (CPU %, throughput, error rate). Log: a timestamped record of a discrete event. Trace: the path of one request through multiple systems, with timing at each hop.
detail:
Three different shapes of telemetry answering three different questions: how is it behaving, what happened, and where did this specific request spend its time.
How it works
  • Metrics are cheap, aggregated and good for alerting: They compress well, graph naturally and support thresholds and trends. What they cannot tell you is why — a CPU graph shows the spike but never the cause.
  • Logs are detailed, expensive and good for explanation: Each line carries context: which user, which error, which file. Volume is the constraint, which is why logs are usually retained for a shorter period at full fidelity than metrics.
  • Traces answer 'which component is slow': A request that touches a load balancer, three microservices and a database is one trace with a span per hop. When a page is slow, the trace shows whether the time went to the database or to a downstream API. Without it, every team's own metrics look fine.
  • They are complementary, not competing: The normal workflow is a metric alert, logs to find out what the errors were, and a trace to locate which component caused them. Modern observability platforms ingest all three and cross-link them.
Where you see it
  • A dashboard alerting on latency, with logs and traces linked from the same view
  • Diagnosing a slow web application that spans several services
  • Deciding retention: metrics for a year, full logs for thirty days
exam: This appears as vocabulary. The discriminator for a trace is that it follows one request across multiple systems, which neither metrics nor logs do. If a question describes a numeric value sampled at intervals, that is a metric. If it describes an event record with a timestamp, that is a log. Expect it in the context of observability and monitoring tool selection.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is a baseline, and what is configuration drift?
answer: A baseline is the documented known-good state: the standard configuration and the normal performance profile. Drift is the accumulation of undocumented changes that move a device away from it.
detail:
Without a recorded normal, you cannot identify abnormal. Every monitoring threshold, every capacity decision and every 'the network is slow' complaint depends on having one.
How it works
  • A performance baseline captures normal, including its rhythm: Utilization, latency, error counters, CPU and memory recorded over enough time to include the Monday morning peak, the nightly backup window and month-end. 'Slow' is meaningless without knowing what Tuesday at 10am usually looks like.
  • It is what makes threshold alerting possible: Alerting at a fixed 80 percent utilization produces noise on a link that normally runs at 85. Baselines let thresholds be set relative to observed normal, and they are how you spot a gradual trend before it becomes an outage.
  • A configuration baseline is the golden standard build: The agreed VLAN scheme, SNMP and syslog settings, NTP servers, AAA, banner, hardening options. New devices are built from it and existing devices are compared against it.
  • Drift is how a network becomes unmaintainable: An emergency change here, a temporary ACL there, a test setting never removed. Six months later no two switches are alike, an outage cannot be reasoned about, and a replacement device built from the standard behaves differently. Automated configuration comparison against the baseline is the countermeasure.
  • Re-baseline after significant change: Adding a major application or a new site makes the old baseline misleading. Recording a new one is part of closing out the project.
Where you see it
  • Capturing a week of interface statistics before and after a WAN upgrade to prove the benefit
  • Nightly configuration diffs that flag any device deviating from the standard
  • Answering 'is the network slow' with data instead of opinion
exam: The exam angle is diagnostic: the answer to 'how do you know current performance is abnormal' is a baseline. Expect a scenario where an upgrade is claimed to have made no difference and the correct answer is comparing against the pre-change baseline. Configuration drift is tested as the reason for standardizing and for automated configuration comparison.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: The change management process, in order?
answer: Request → assess risk and impact → approval (CAB) → schedule a maintenance window → document the plan and the rollback → implement → test and validate → document the result.
detail:
Change management exists because most outages are caused by planned changes, not by hardware failing. The process makes changes visible, reviewed, reversible and recorded.
How it works
  • The request states the why and the blast radius: What is changing, which systems and users are affected, why it is needed, and what happens if it is not done. A change nobody can justify in writing does not get scheduled.
  • The CAB is the approval body: The Change Advisory Board reviews risk, checks for conflicts with other scheduled work, and approves, defers or rejects. It exists so the person making the change is not the only person judging its risk. Low-risk repetitive work is often pre-approved as a standard change so the board is not a bottleneck.
  • Emergency changes are a separate, documented path: Genuine emergencies bypass the normal lead time but not the record. They are reviewed retrospectively, and a high volume of emergency changes is itself a signal that planning is failing.
  • The maintenance window is the agreed time to be disruptive: A pre-approved, communicated period — chosen against the organization's real low-impact hours and against month-end and peak events — during which the work may be done. It is sized by how long the rollback takes, not by how long the change takes, and the service desk and affected users are notified in advance.
  • Validation and documentation close the loop: A change is not finished when the command is entered. It is finished when a test defined in advance proves the intended outcome, the configuration backup and diagram are updated, and the record says what was actually done — which is what makes the next outage diagnosable.
  • Unauthorized change is the thing being prevented: The most expensive outages are frequently traced to a change nobody knew about. The process is worth more for what it makes visible than for what it blocks.
Where you see it
  • A firewall rule change reviewed at the weekly CAB and applied in a Sunday 02:00 window
  • Correlating a Monday-morning outage with Friday's change record
  • Discovering during review that two teams planned conflicting work on the same night
exam: The exam tests order and vocabulary. Approval comes before implementation and documentation comes after validation. Know that CAB stands for Change Advisory Board. The most common scenario is troubleshooting an outage where the first step is to check recent changes — that is also step one of the troubleshooting methodology's 'what changed' question.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is a rollback plan, and when do you decide to use it?
answer: The documented, tested steps to return to the previous known-good state. The abort criteria and the deadline are decided before the change starts — not in the middle of a failing one.
detail:
Every change plan needs an exit. Deciding what failure looks like while you are inside it, tired and over time, is how a short outage becomes a long one.
How it works
  • Abort criteria are written in advance and are objective: 'If the core is not passing traffic by 04:00, we roll back' is a criterion. 'If it looks like it is not going well' is not. The criteria remove judgement from the moment when judgement is worst.
  • The deadline is the most important criterion: There must be a wall-clock time at which rollback begins regardless of how close the fix feels, chosen so that the rollback itself completes inside the window. This is what prevents overrunning into business hours.
  • The rollback must be tested or at least known to work: A plan that says 'restore the previous configuration' is worthless if nobody has confirmed the backup exists, is current and loads onto the replacement hardware. Some changes are genuinely one-way — a filesystem upgrade, a schema migration — and that has to be identified before starting, because the fallback is a restore from backup instead.
  • Not every change can be reversed by reversing it: Rolling back a firmware upgrade may require a downgrade path the vendor does not support. Where that is true, the real rollback is replacing the device or restoring an image, and the window must be sized for that.
Where you see it
  • A firmware upgrade with a stated 'revert by 05:00' deadline
  • Confirming the previous configuration file loads onto a spare before starting
  • Identifying a one-way database migration and planning a restore instead of a revert
exam: The tested idea is that the rollback plan and its trigger conditions exist before implementation, as part of the approved change. If a scenario describes an engineer improvising during a failed change, the missing control is the documented rollback plan with abort criteria. It is also the standard correct answer to 'what should be prepared before applying a risky change'.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Full, incremental and differential backups — how do they differ on backup and on restore?
answer: Full: everything; restore needs one set. Incremental: changes since the last backup of any type — fastest to back up, restore needs the full plus every incremental in order. Differential: changes since the last full — grows daily, restore needs the full plus only the latest differential.
detail:
The three schemes trade backup time against restore time. Which one is right depends entirely on which of those two you are optimizing.
How it works
  • Incremental is cheapest to write and dearest to read: Each job copies only what changed since yesterday, so nightly windows are short and storage is small. A restore on Friday needs Sunday's full plus Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday — and one corrupt or missing link in that chain breaks everything after it.
  • Differential is dearer to write and cheaper to read: Each job copies everything changed since the full, so Thursday's differential contains Monday through Thursday. Backups grow through the week, but a restore needs exactly two sets: the full and the most recent differential.
  • The archive bit is the classic mechanism: An incremental backup clears the archive bit, so the next job only sees new changes. A differential does not clear it, so changes keep accumulating. That single difference is the whole distinction and it is a favourite exam detail.
  • A typical schedule mixes them: Weekly full plus daily incremental for the shortest nightly window, or weekly full plus daily differential when restore time matters more. Synthetic fulls and image-based snapshot chains achieve similar tradeoffs in modern products.
  • The restore is what is actually being bought: Backup success rates are irrelevant if the restore does not meet the RTO. Test the restore, not the backup job.
Where you see it
  • Choosing differential for a system with a tight RTO and a long nightly window
  • Explaining a Friday restore that needs five separate tape sets
  • Sizing a backup window against a nightly incremental versus a growing differential
exam: This is a guaranteed question and the discriminator is always the restore. Full plus all incrementals since the full; full plus only the latest differential. Distractors swap those two. Remember incremental clears the archive bit and differential does not, and that incremental gives the fastest backup while differential gives the faster restore.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
answer: 3 copies of the data, on 2 different media or platforms, with 1 stored off-site.
detail:
A rule of thumb designed so that no single event — a failed disk, a failed array, a fire, a ransomware encryption pass — can take every copy at once.
How it works
  • Three copies means production plus two backups: The live data counts as one. Two additional independent copies mean a backup can itself fail or be found corrupt and you still have another.
  • Two media types defeats a common-mode failure: Two backups on the same storage array share a controller, a firmware version and a room. Disk plus tape, or on-premises disk plus cloud object storage, removes that shared fate.
  • One off-site copy defeats site loss: Fire, flood, theft and building power events destroy everything in the room, including the backup server. Off-site can be a second datacentre, a vaulting service or cloud storage in a different region.
  • Ransomware forced an update to the idea: Modern guidance adds that one copy should be offline, air-gapped or immutable, because ransomware deliberately encrypts reachable backups and network-attached backup shares are a primary target. Object-lock or write-once storage is the usual answer.
  • Verification is implied: Three copies of an unrestorable backup is one number and no protection. Periodic test restores are what make the rule mean something.
Where you see it
  • Nightly disk backup, weekly copy to immutable cloud storage, quarterly test restore
  • Explaining why a backup NAS in the same rack does not satisfy the rule
  • Recovering after a ransomware event from an offline copy
exam: The numbers are asked directly: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site. The scenario version describes backups stored beside the servers and asks what is wrong — the missing element is the off-site copy. Expect ransomware framing on N10-009, where the expected answer adds an offline or immutable copy that the attacker cannot reach.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Why are configuration backups critical in a network context?
answer: A failed switch or router is replaced in under an hour if you can push last night's configuration onto a spare, and takes a day of rebuilding if you cannot. Back them up automatically and after every change.
detail:
Network devices hold almost no data but a great deal of state. That state is the product of years of decisions, and none of it is recoverable by reasoning it out at 2am.
How it works
  • The configuration is the device's real value: VLANs, trunk allowed-lists, ACLs, routing policy, QoS classes, AAA, port descriptions. Recreating it from memory during an outage produces a device that is nearly right, which is worse than obviously broken because the faults appear later.
  • Automate the collection: A configuration management tool, or scheduled TFTP/SCP exports, pulls the running configuration from every device nightly and on change. A manual process is one that stops the week somebody is on leave.
  • Versioned copies give you a diff: Storing each night's configuration lets you compare today against yesterday. That answers 'what changed' in seconds, catches unauthorized changes, and shows configuration drift against the standard build.
  • Restoring is not always a straight paste: A replacement device may have different interface names, module positions or a different software version. Licences may be node-locked. Knowing that in advance — and having the licence details in the asset record — is part of the plan.
  • Off-box storage is the point: A configuration saved only to the device's own flash is lost with the device. It has to live on a server that is backed up.
Where you see it
  • Restoring a dead access switch onto a spare from last night's saved configuration
  • Nightly configuration diffs alerting on an undocumented ACL change
  • Rebuilding a site after a power event without reverse-engineering the design
exam: The exam frames this as an MTTR and preparedness question: the fastest way to restore service after a device failure is a current configuration backup plus a spare. The distractors are 'restore from the vendor's default' or 'recreate from the network diagram'. Also expect the pairing with change management, where saving the configuration before and after a change is part of the process.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Patch versus firmware update versus feature update?
answer: Patch: a targeted fix, usually security or a specific bug — small, frequent, low risk. Firmware: the device's low-level operating code — riskier, usually needs a reboot and a maintenance window. Feature update: new functionality, which can change behaviour and requires testing and possibly retraining.
detail:
All three are 'updates' and the exam separates them by risk and by what they can break. That difference decides how each one is scheduled.
How it works
  • Patches are the routine security cycle: Small, well-defined, and applied on a regular cadence with a short test period. The risk of applying them is normally lower than the risk of not applying them, which is why patch management is measured in days from release.
  • Firmware sits below the operating system: Switch and router software, BIOS/UEFI, NIC, drive and controller firmware, PDU and UPS controllers. A failed firmware update can leave the device unbootable, so it needs a window, a rollback image, out-of-band access and, for anything critical, a spare device on hand.
  • Feature updates change behaviour: New capability can alter defaults, deprecate configuration syntax or change how existing settings are interpreted. These need lab validation and are the ones most likely to break an integration that has worked for years.
  • Sequence and dependencies matter: Vendors frequently specify an upgrade path — you cannot always jump directly from a very old release to the newest, and a chassis may require its supervisor, line cards and modules to be at compatible versions. Read the release notes before scheduling, not during.
  • Test, stage, then deploy: Lab first, then a pilot group or a single non-critical device, then the fleet. Upgrading every core switch on the same night removes your ability to compare a working device with a broken one.
Where you see it
  • A monthly OS patch cycle contrasted with a quarterly, windowed firmware upgrade
  • Staging a switch code upgrade on one access switch before the whole floor
  • Deferring a feature release until an integration has been tested in the lab
exam: The exam separates these by risk: firmware is the one that needs the maintenance window, the rollback image and out-of-band access because a failure can brick the device. A patch is the routine security fix. If a scenario describes applying an update that could render a switch unbootable, the correct precautions are a window, a verified rollback and console access.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: EOL versus EOS?
answer: End-of-life: the vendor stops selling the product. End-of-support: the vendor stops issuing patches, firmware and technical assistance — this is the security-critical date.
detail:
Vendors announce both years in advance. The one that creates risk is the support date, because after it a newly published vulnerability will never be fixed.
How it works
  • EOL is a purchasing problem: Once a product is end-of-sale you cannot buy more of it, so expanding a site or replacing a failed unit means the second-hand market or a mixed-model estate. Plan spares before the date, not after.
  • EOS is a security and compliance problem: After the last support date there are no security patches. A device with a published, unpatchable vulnerability facing any untrusted network is a finding in every audit, and many compliance frameworks prohibit it outright.
  • The dates are staggered deliberately: There is normally a multi-year gap: end of sale, then end of software maintenance, then end of vulnerability support, then last date of support. Track them per model in the asset inventory so budget lands in the right year.
  • Discovering it during an outage is the failure mode: Finding out that a failed core switch is unsupported, unavailable and unpatchable while the site is down is the scenario asset lifecycle management exists to prevent.
  • Compensating controls buy time, not safety: If replacement genuinely cannot happen before the date, segment the device, restrict management access and monitor it closely — and record the accepted risk formally.
Where you see it
  • Budgeting a refresh cycle from the vendor's published support dates
  • An audit finding against a firewall past its last-date-of-support
  • Buying spares for a model that has gone end-of-sale but is still supported
exam: The exam tests which date matters and why. End-of-support is the one that creates security risk, because patches stop. The distractor treats EOL as the critical date because 'life' sounds final. If a scenario says a device can no longer receive security updates and asks for the risk, the answer is unpatchable vulnerabilities and the action is replacement.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is asset lifecycle management, and what belongs in a decommissioning process?
answer: Tracking hardware and software from procurement through deployment, maintenance, support dates and disposal. Decommissioning: remove from monitoring and documentation, revoke credentials and certificates, reclaim IP addresses and licences, sanitize or destroy storage, and update the diagrams and inventory.
detail:
The inventory is what turns a network from a collection of surprises into something that can be planned. Decommissioning is the step everyone skips, and it is where data and addresses leak.
How it works
  • The inventory record has to carry dates: Serial number, location, purchase date, warranty expiry, support contract, software version and the vendor's end-of-support date. Without those fields you cannot build a refresh budget or answer an auditor, and you discover coverage gaps only when something fails.
  • Sanitization is a legal obligation, not a courtesy: Devices hold configurations with credentials and pre-shared keys, and many hold storage with cached data. Wipe to the applicable standard or physically destroy, and keep the certificate of destruction — disposal of an un-wiped device is a reportable data breach in many jurisdictions.
  • Credentials and trust must be revoked, not just abandoned: Certificates, RADIUS entries, service accounts, SNMP and API keys, monitoring agents, VPN peer configurations and firewall rules referencing the device all persist after it is unplugged. Each one left behind is a stale path into the network.
  • Reclaim addressing and licences: Return IP addresses, DNS records and DHCP reservations to the pool in IPAM, and release licences that are node-locked so they can be reassigned. Stale DNS records pointing at reused addresses cause faults months later.
  • Update the documentation as the last step: A diagram that still shows a decommissioned device sends the next engineer to a rack that is empty, during an incident.
Where you see it
  • A refresh plan built from warranty and end-of-support dates in the inventory
  • Wiping and certifying disposal of returned branch firewalls
  • Removing DNS records, monitoring entries and firewall rules for a retired server
exam: Two things get tested. First, that lifecycle tracking is how you avoid discovering a critical device is out of support — expect it paired with EOL/EOS. Second, that decommissioning includes data sanitization and revoking credentials, not just unracking. The distractor is 'power it off and remove it from the rack', which leaves data, certificates and DNS records behind.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is IPAM and what problem does it solve?
answer: IP Address Management — a system that tracks subnet allocation and individual address assignments, and usually integrates with DHCP and DNS so all three stay consistent.
detail:
Addressing is the one piece of network state that every team touches and nobody owns. IPAM is what stops it from becoming a spreadsheet that is wrong.
How it works
  • It records the whole address plan, not just what is in use: Which subnets are allocated to which sites, VLANs and purposes, which are free, and how much room is left. That is what makes the next allocation a decision instead of a guess, and it is what keeps summarization possible in the routing design.
  • The failure it prevents is duplication and conflict: Two engineers assigning the same static address, or a subnet reused at two sites that are later joined by a VPN, produce faults that are painful to diagnose. A shared authoritative record is the only defence.
  • Integration with DHCP and DNS is where the value is: Creating a host in IPAM can create the DHCP reservation and the forward and reverse DNS records in one action. Doing them separately by hand is how reverse records go missing and how stale entries accumulate.
  • It is also a reporting and audit tool: Utilization per subnet drives the decision to renumber or expand before exhaustion, and a searchable record of what owns each address is invaluable during an incident.
  • IPv6 makes it mandatory rather than optional: Nobody tracks 128-bit addresses in a spreadsheet. Structured allocation and automated record-keeping are the only workable approach.
Where you see it
  • Allocating a new site's subnets from a documented plan rather than picking a free-looking range
  • Finding which subnets are near exhaustion before users are affected
  • Preventing an address conflict when two acquired networks are joined
exam: The exam asks what IPAM is and what it prevents: overlapping subnets, duplicate assignments and stale records. If a scenario describes address conflicts, or a merger where both companies used 192.168.1.0/24, the underlying answer is a lack of IPAM and central address planning. Note the DHCP and DNS integration — that pairing is frequently the correct option.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Physical versus logical network diagram — and what else belongs in the documentation set?
answer: Physical: what is where and what is plugged into what — racks, devices, ports, cable runs. Logical: how traffic flows — IP subnets, VLANs, routing, trust zones. Also expected: rack diagrams, cable maps, floor plans, wiring schematics, inventory and IDF/MDF layouts.
detail:
The two diagrams answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other. One tells you where to put your hands; the other tells you why the traffic went that way.
How it works
  • The physical diagram is for the person in the room: Rack elevations showing every device by unit position, patch panel port numbers, uplink cabling, media types and fibre strand assignments. This is what lets a technician who has never been on site find the right cable, and it is the difference between a five-minute and a two-hour repair.
  • The logical diagram is for the person reasoning about traffic: Subnets, VLAN numbers, SVIs and gateways, routing protocols and areas, firewall zones and the paths between them. It has no relationship to physical position — two VLANs can live in one switch and one VLAN can span a campus.
  • A cable map is its own document: Which patch panel port lands on which wall jack in which room, and which switch port serves it. Without it, tracing a single user's drop means a toner and a wiring closet.
  • Diagrams are only useful if they are current: An out-of-date diagram is worse than none because it is trusted. Updating them is the last step of the change management process, which is exactly why that step is in the process.
  • Label the physical world to match: Ports, patch panels, cables and racks labelled consistently with the documentation is what makes the documentation usable at 3am.
Where you see it
  • A rack elevation used to plan where a new switch will physically fit and be powered
  • A logical diagram used to work out why two VLANs cannot reach each other
  • Tracing a user's dead network drop from the cable map to the patch panel
exam: The tested split is that physical shows cabling and equipment placement, logical shows addressing and traffic flow. If a scenario asks which document helps determine why traffic between two subnets is blocked, the answer is the logical diagram; if it asks which cable to unplug or where a device is racked, the answer is physical. Rack diagram and cable map are physical documents.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: MDF versus IDF?
answer: MDF (Main Distribution Frame): the building's primary termination point, where the carrier circuit enters and the core equipment lives. IDF (Intermediate Distribution Frame): a floor or wing closet holding access switches and patch panels, uplinked back to the MDF.
detail:
This is the classic hierarchical building cabling design: one main room, several satellite closets, and backbone cable between them.
How it works
  • The MDF is where outside meets inside: The demarcation point, the carrier's equipment, the core or distribution switches and often the server room. Everything in the building ultimately traces back to it, which makes it the single most physically sensitive room in the site.
  • IDFs exist because copper stops at 100 metres: Horizontal runs to a work area are limited to 100 m of twisted pair. A large floor cannot be served from one room, so closets are placed so that every desk is within that distance, and the closet is uplinked to the MDF over fibre backbone.
  • The backbone between them is usually fibre: It exceeds copper distance limits, carries higher aggregate bandwidth, and is immune to the ground-potential differences between floors that make copper between buildings a hazard.
  • Both need environment and access control: Power, UPS, cooling, and locks. An IDF is often a small closet where heat and physical security are neglected, and it is a frequent source of intermittent faults that look like a network problem.
  • Document each closet: Rack diagram, patch panel to jack mapping, uplink fibre strands and switch port assignments. That documentation is what makes an unfamiliar closet workable.
Where you see it
  • Placing floor IDFs so no desk exceeds the 100 m horizontal limit
  • Fibre backbone from each floor closet down to the MDF
  • Investigating intermittent errors traced to an unventilated IDF closet
exam: The exam asks for the role of each and often pairs it with the 100 m copper limit as the reason IDFs exist. The MDF is where the ISP circuit and demarc terminate — that is the reliable discriminator. Distractors describe the IDF as the building entry point; it is not, it is an intermediate closet uplinked to the MDF.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is a wireless site survey, and what is a heat map used for?
answer: A survey measures the RF environment to decide AP placement, channels and power. A heat map is its visual output, showing measured signal strength across the floor plan. After installation the survey is the validation record.
detail:
Wireless design cannot be done on paper alone because buildings absorb and reflect RF unpredictably. The survey is how the design becomes measurement rather than assumption.
How it works
  • Three kinds, done at different times: A predictive survey models coverage from floor plans and wall materials before anything is installed. A passive survey walks the site listening, mapping signal and interference from existing APs. An active survey associates to the network and measures actual throughput, retries and roaming behaviour.
  • The survey sets more than placement: It determines channel plan and non-overlapping reuse, transmit power, whether to enable 2.4 GHz at all, AP density for capacity as opposed to coverage, and where interference sources such as microwaves, cordless equipment and neighbouring networks sit.
  • Coverage and capacity are different problems: A warehouse needs few APs for coverage. A lecture theatre needs many APs at low power for capacity, because the constraint is clients per radio rather than distance. Designing for coverage alone is the standard cause of a network that works when empty and fails when full.
  • The post-install survey is the proof: It validates that the deployment meets the design, and it becomes the record that the next engineer compares against when users complain. Without it, 'the Wi-Fi is worse than it used to be' cannot be tested.
  • Re-survey after the building changes: New walls, new shelving, a warehouse filled with stock, or a neighbour's new network all change the RF environment. The heat map is a snapshot, not a permanent truth.
Where you see it
  • Deciding AP count and placement for a new floor before ordering hardware
  • Diagnosing a dead zone by comparing current measurements to the installation heat map
  • Planning channels around a neighbouring tenant's overlapping network
exam: The exam uses the heat map as the answer to 'how do you identify coverage gaps or dead zones'. Know that a survey happens both before deployment (design) and after (validation and documentation). The distractor is a protocol analyzer or a spectrum analyzer — the spectrum analyzer finds non-Wi-Fi interference, while the heat map shows coverage.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: Traffic shaping versus policing?
answer: Shaping buffers excess traffic and releases it at the configured rate — smooths bursts, adds delay, no loss. Policing drops or re-marks traffic above the rate immediately — no delay, causes loss.
detail:
Both enforce a rate limit. The difference is what happens to the packets that exceed it: shaping delays them, policing discards them.
How it works
  • Shaping is used on the sending side: A branch router with a 10 Mbps circuit shapes its outbound traffic to just under 10 so that queuing happens in its own buffers, where QoS policy can prioritize, rather than in the carrier's, where it cannot. This is the standard fix for a link where voice degrades under load.
  • Policing is used on the receiving or ingress side: A carrier polices your traffic to what you paid for. An enterprise polices an untrusted class — guest Wi-Fi or backup traffic — to a hard ceiling. It is cheap because it needs no buffer.
  • TCP reacts very differently to each: Shaping delays a burst and TCP adapts smoothly. Policing drops packets, which triggers retransmission and congestion-window collapse, so a policed TCP flow can end up delivering considerably less than the policed rate.
  • Buffering has its own cost: Shaping adds latency and jitter, and an oversized buffer produces bufferbloat, which is bad for real-time traffic. Voice and video are usually placed in a priority queue that is policed rather than deeply buffered.
  • Where the classification happens matters: Traffic must be identified and marked before either mechanism can treat it differently, which is why marking is done as close to the source as possible.
Where you see it
  • Shaping a branch router's WAN output to the carrier's committed rate
  • Policing guest wireless to a fixed ceiling so it cannot starve corporate traffic
  • Diagnosing voice quality that degrades only when a large file transfer runs
exam: The exam contrast is buffer versus drop, and the consequence pair is delay versus loss. If a scenario wants to smooth bursts without losing data, the answer is shaping. If it wants a hard limit enforced immediately on traffic that must not exceed a rate, the answer is policing. Shaping is outbound; policing is typically inbound.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: How is traffic marked for QoS, and what does a priority queue do?
answer: DSCP is 6 bits in the IPv4/IPv6 header (64 values, Layer 3, survives routing) — EF (46) is the standard voice marking. 802.1p CoS is 3 bits inside the 802.1Q VLAN tag (8 values, Layer 2 only). A priority/low-latency queue is serviced before all others, which is what protects voice.
detail:
QoS is two separate jobs: labelling traffic so devices can tell it apart, and then treating the labels differently when there is congestion. Marking alone changes nothing.
How it works
  • DSCP is the durable marking: It lives in the differentiated services field of the IP header, so it survives routing between subnets and across a WAN if the carrier honours it. Common values: EF 46 for voice, AF41 (34) for interactive video, CS6 for network control, default 0 for everything else.
  • CoS dies at the first router: The 802.1p bits are in the VLAN tag. Strip the tag — which happens at an access port or when routing between VLANs — and the marking is gone. Devices therefore map CoS to DSCP at the boundary so the classification survives.
  • The trust boundary decides who may mark: Mark as close to the source as possible, and do not trust markings from user devices — a workstation that marks its own traffic EF would be prioritized ahead of the phones. Switches are configured to trust the phone and re-mark or clear everything from the PC behind it.
  • Queues are where the marking finally matters: On a congested interface, a scheduler decides which queue is served next. A strict-priority or low-latency queue is emptied before any other, giving voice minimal delay and jitter. It is bandwidth-limited on purpose so it cannot starve everything else.
  • QoS only acts under congestion: On an uncongested link every packet goes straight out and markings are irrelevant. QoS is how you choose what suffers when there is not enough bandwidth — it does not create capacity.
Where you see it
  • Marking voice EF at the access switch and giving it a low-latency queue on the WAN
  • Mapping CoS to DSCP where a trunk terminates so priority survives routing
  • Explaining why QoS changed nothing on a link that was never congested
exam: The tested facts are DSCP is Layer 3 in the IP header, CoS is Layer 2 in the 802.1Q tag, and that voice is marked EF / DSCP 46. The scenario trap: QoS is configured but voice quality is unchanged, because markings were not trusted end to end or the link is not actually congested. Remember that QoS prioritizes; it never adds bandwidth.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What is a jump box (jump host / bastion host)?
answer: A hardened, tightly controlled system that is the only permitted entry point into a sensitive network segment. All administrative access passes through it, so access is funnelled, logged and monitored in one place.
detail:
It converts many possible paths into one. That single path is then the thing you harden, log and watch.
How it works
  • It exists to collapse the attack surface: Instead of every administrator's laptop being able to reach every management interface, only the jump host can. Firewall rules become simple: management interfaces accept connections from one address, and that address is heavily controlled.
  • It is the audit choke point: Session recording, keystroke logging, command approval and MFA are applied once, on the jump host, and cover every administrative action. Reconstructing who did what becomes a single log source rather than a correlation exercise.
  • Hardening it is not optional: Minimal installed software, no user browsing or email, aggressive patching, MFA required, and no shared accounts. A weakly maintained jump host is a single point of total compromise, because everything of value is reachable from it.
  • It is also the point of failure to plan around: If the jump host is down, nobody administers anything. Production designs make it redundant and keep a documented, controlled out-of-band alternative for the case where it is unavailable.
  • Related terms: A bastion host is the same idea placed in a DMZ. Privileged access management systems are the enterprise product version, adding credential vaulting and just-in-time access.
Where you see it
  • Administering a PCI or OT segment only through a recorded jump host
  • Restricting all switch and firewall management interfaces to one source address
  • Providing contractors controlled access without giving them network-level reach
exam: The exam presents it as the answer to 'how do you control and monitor administrative access to a secure segment'. The distractors are a VPN, which gets you onto the network but does not funnel or record administrative sessions, and a proxy, which is about client web traffic. Note the pairing with out-of-band management and with the principle of least privilege.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: In-band versus out-of-band management?
answer: In-band: managing devices over the production network — simple, and it fails exactly when the network fails. Out-of-band: a separate path — console server, dedicated management port and VLAN, cellular modem or lights-out card — that works when production is down.
detail:
The question is whether you can still reach a device after you have broken it. In-band management cannot answer yes.
How it works
  • The failure it is designed for is self-inflicted: An ACL, a VLAN change, a routing mistake or a firmware upgrade that removes your own access. With in-band management only, the fix requires somebody physically at the site with a console cable.
  • Console servers aggregate serial access: A terminal server with serial connections to every device's console port, reachable over its own path, gives access at a level below the network stack — you can watch a device boot and interrupt it, which no in-band method can do.
  • Truly separate means separate in every layer: An out-of-band path that traverses the same WAN circuit, the same switch or the same power feed is not out-of-band for the failures that matter. A cellular modem or a second carrier is what makes it genuinely independent.
  • Dedicated management ports and lights-out cards: Many switches and routers have a management interface in its own VRF, and servers have iDRAC, iLO or IPMI processors that run on standby power. These allow power cycling and console access when the operating system is gone.
  • The management path must be secured like a crown jewel: It bypasses the production network's controls by design. Strong authentication, encryption, and strict access control are mandatory, because a compromised out-of-band network is total access.
Where you see it
  • Recovering a remote branch router after a bad ACL locked out SSH
  • A console server plus a 4G modem at each unmanned site
  • Power-cycling a hung server through its lights-out interface
exam: The exam scenario is always a remote device made unreachable by a change or an outage, and the answer is out-of-band management. The distractors are SSH and a VPN, both of which are in-band and depend on the production network being up. Remember the examples — console/terminal server, dedicated management port, cellular modem, lights-out card.

deck: CompTIA Network+ N10-009::11 Network Operations, DR & HA
front: What environmental and power factors do you monitor and provide in a closet or datacentre?
answer: Monitor temperature, humidity, airflow, water and smoke, door access, and power quality. Provide a UPS — battery ride-through and power conditioning for minutes, not for a long outage — and rack PDUs, where a managed PDU adds per-outlet metering and remote power cycling.
detail:
The most common cause of unexplained hardware failure is not the network — it is the room and the power feeding it.
How it works
  • Heat is the silent killer: Switches throttle, power supplies fail early and optics produce errors as temperature rises. A closet with blocked ventilation or a failed air conditioner produces intermittent faults for days before anything dies outright, and those faults get diagnosed as network problems. Humidity matters at both ends: too high condenses and corrodes, too low allows static discharge.
  • Airflow direction and containment: Equipment is front-to-back or back-to-front, and mixing directions in one rack makes one device exhaust into another's intake. Hot-aisle/cold-aisle layout and blanking panels in empty rack units are what stop hot air recirculating. Water sensors under raised floors and smoke detection buy time before damage.
  • A UPS covers the gap, not the outage: Typical runtime at full load is five to twenty minutes — enough to ride out a brief interruption or to start a generator and transfer to it. Extended outages are a generator's job, not a bigger battery's. Batteries degrade over three to five years and fail silently, so self-tests and battery health monitoring are mandatory.
  • UPS topologies differ in protection: Standby switches to battery when the mains fails, with a brief transfer time. Line-interactive adds automatic voltage regulation for sags and surges without draining the battery. Online double-conversion always runs the load from the inverter, so there is no transfer time and the output is fully conditioned — that is what critical equipment uses.
  • A managed PDU turns power into a remote tool: Per-outlet switching hard power-cycles a hung device at an unstaffed site without a truck roll, and per-outlet metering shows actual draw so a circuit is not overloaded. True redundancy means two independent feeds into dual-corded equipment; a single-PSU device on one PDU is a single point of failure regardless of the UPS.
Where you see it
  • Sensors alerting when an IDF closet exceeds a temperature threshold
  • Investigating intermittent switch reboots traced to a failed closet air conditioner
  • Remotely power-cycling a locked-up switch at an unmanned branch through a managed PDU
exam: Two framings appear. Diagnostic: intermittent, unexplained hardware failures at one site point to an environmental cause, usually heat — do not answer 'replace the switch' when the scenario mentions a warm closet. Definitional: a UPS provides short-term battery power and conditioning and the distractor claims it covers a long blackout, which needs a generator. The managed PDU is the answer to rebooting an unresponsive remote device, alongside out-of-band management.

front: How long is an IPv6 address and how is it written?
answer:
128 bits, written as eight groups (hextets) of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons.
Example: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329
Each hextet is 16 bits. Hex digits are case-insensitive but conventionally written lowercase.
detail:
A vastly larger address space — 2^128 addresses — created because 32-bit IPv4 space ran out. The hexadecimal, colon-separated format exists because writing 128 bits in dotted decimal would be unreadable.
How it works
  • Four times the bits, not four times the addresses: IPv4 has 2^32 addresses, about 4.3 billion. IPv6 has 2^128, which is roughly 3.4 × 10^38. The increase is exponential, not proportional.
  • Hexadecimal keeps it compact: Each hex digit encodes exactly 4 bits, so 32 hex digits cover 128 bits. Decimal would need 39 digits with no clean bit alignment.
  • The prefix is still written with a slash: 2001:db8:acad::/64 works exactly like CIDR in IPv4 — the number is how many leading bits identify the network.
  • The header is a fixed 40 bytes: IPv4's header is 20 bytes minimum but variable because of options. IPv6 fixed the base header at 40 bytes and moved options into optional extension headers, which makes router processing simpler.
Where you see it
  • Reading ipconfig or ip -6 addr output on any modern OS
  • Entering an IPv6 address in a firewall rule or DNS AAAA record
  • Recognizing 2001:db8:: as the documentation prefix in examples
exam: Straight recall of 128 bits and eight groups of four hex digits. The distractors are 64 bits, 128 bytes, and 'four groups of eight'. Also be ready for the AAAA record: an IPv6 host record in DNS is AAAA (quad-A), not A and not AA.

front: State the two IPv6 compression rules, and compress 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329.
answer:
Rule 1: drop leading zeros within any hextet (0042 → 42; 0000 → 0).
Rule 2: replace one contiguous run of all-zero hextets with :: — only once per address.
Result: 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329
detail:
Two rules that shorten IPv6 addresses without changing their value. They exist because most addresses contain long runs of zeros.
How it works
  • Only leading zeros go, never trailing: ff00 stays ff00. 0042 becomes 42. Dropping trailing zeros would change the value — 4200 and 0042 are entirely different hextets.
  • The double colon can appear only once: 2001:0:0:1:0:0:0:1 could be written 2001:0:0:1::1 or 2001::1:0:0:0:1, but never 2001::1::1. With two double colons a parser cannot tell how many zero hextets belong to each, so the address becomes ambiguous.
  • When runs tie, compress the longest one: In 2001:0:0:1:0:0:0:1 there is a run of two and a run of three. Convention compresses the longer run: 2001:0:0:1::1. If two runs are equal length, compress the leftmost.
  • Expanding is the reverse: Count the hextets present, subtract from 8, and that is how many zero hextets the :: stands for. fe80::1 has two hextets shown, so :: represents six zero hextets: fe80:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001.
Where you see it
  • Typing an address into a router or firewall without transcription errors
  • Comparing a logged address against a configured one that is written differently
  • Reading fe80::1 and knowing it is the fully-expanded fe80:0:0:0:0:0:0:1
exam: CompTIA tests this both directions: compress a given address, or pick the correct expansion of a compressed one. The single most common trap is an answer containing two double colons — eliminate it immediately. The second trap is an answer that dropped trailing zeros, such as writing ff00 as ff. Count hextets in every candidate answer; the total must reconstruct to eight.

front: What is the IPv6 global unicast prefix, and how is such an address structured?
answer:
2000::/3 — addresses whose first hextet begins with 2 or 3. Globally routable on the public internet, the IPv6 equivalent of a public IPv4 address.
Typical structure: 48-bit global routing prefix + 16-bit subnet ID + 64-bit interface ID.
detail:
The public, internet-routable IPv6 address type. Every host that talks to the internet over IPv6 has one, and unlike IPv4 it is usually a genuine globally unique address with no NAT involved.
How it works
  • The /3 covers a huge but specific slice: Three leading bits fixed as 001 means the first hextet runs from 2000 to 3fff. That is one eighth of the total space, deliberately reserved to be handed out first.
  • A site typically receives a /48: An ISP assigns a /48 to an organization, leaving 16 bits of subnet ID — 65,536 subnets — each a /64. There is no pressure to size subnets tightly the way there is in IPv4.
  • 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation: RFC 3849 set it aside so examples and training material never collide with real addresses. If you see 2001:db8 in a question, it is an example address.
