  • A host commonly holds several addresses at once: A link-local fe80:: address always, plus one or more global unicast addresses, plus possibly a temporary privacy address. Multiple simultaneous addresses per interface is normal in IPv6, not a misconfiguration.
Where you see it
  • Any host communicating over the public IPv6 internet
  • Reading an ISP allocation letter granting a /48 or /56
  • Recognizing a 2001: or 2600: address in a log as internet-facing
exam: Recall the prefix as 2000::/3 and the practical test as 'starts with 2 or 3'. CompTIA gives you an address and asks its type: 2001:db8::1 is global unicast, fe80::1 is link-local, fd00::1 is unique local, ff02::1 is multicast, ::1 is loopback. The distractor is 2000::/16 or 2001::/3 — the correct prefix length is /3.

front: What is the IPv6 link-local prefix, and what is it used for?
answer:
fe80::/10 — in practice every link-local address begins fe80::.
Automatically configured on every IPv6-enabled interface, always present, and never routed off the local link. Used for Neighbor Discovery, Router Advertisements, and as the next-hop address in routing protocols.
detail:
A mandatory, self-generated address scoped to one link. It exists so that IPv6 can bootstrap itself — neighbour discovery and router discovery must work before any global address exists.
How it works
  • It is mandatory, not optional: Enabling IPv6 on an interface creates a link-local address automatically. A device with no global address and no DHCPv6 server still has a working link-local address.
  • Routers drop it at the boundary: A packet with a link-local source or destination is never forwarded. Its scope is exactly one link, which is why the same fe80::1 can exist on every segment without conflict.
  • This is why link-local addresses need a zone index: Because fe80::1 is ambiguous across interfaces, you must specify which one: ping fe80::1%eth0 on Linux or %12 on Windows.
  • Routing protocols peer over it: OSPFv3 and EIGRP for IPv6 form adjacencies using link-local addresses and install link-local next hops. Renumbering the global addressing does not disturb the routing adjacencies.
Where you see it
  • Every IPv6 interface on every host, whether or not IPv6 is otherwise configured
  • A default gateway learned via Router Advertisement, which is a link-local address
  • Troubleshooting IPv6 on a segment with no router present at all
exam: Recall fe80::/10 and know it is the direct counterpart of IPv4's APIPA 169.254.0.0/16. CompTIA's likely trap is offering fe80::/8, fe80::/16 or fe80::/64 — the prefix length is /10. Also expect a scenario where a host shows only an fe80:: address: that is normal for link-local and does not by itself indicate a failure, unlike APIPA in IPv4.

front: What is the IPv6 unique local address (ULA) prefix, and what is it for?
answer:
fc00::/7, which in practice means addresses beginning fd (fd00::/8).
Private, site-scoped addressing — the rough IPv6 equivalent of RFC 1918. Routable inside an organization, not routed on the public internet.
detail:
Private IPv6 space for networks or devices that should never be internet-reachable. It exists so internal addressing can be stable and independent of whichever ISP prefix a site currently holds.
How it works
  • The fc00::/7 splits into two halves: The eighth bit is the L flag. With L=1 the prefix is fd00::/8, meaning locally assigned — this is what everyone actually uses. fc00::/8 with L=0 was reserved for a central assignment scheme that never materialized.
  • A random 40-bit global ID prevents collisions: You generate 40 random bits after fd, giving fdxx:xxxx:xxxx::/48. Randomizing makes it very unlikely that two organizations merging will collide — the problem that plagues 192.168.1.0/24 in IPv4.
  • It does not imply NAT: In IPv4, private addressing forces NAT to reach the internet. A ULA is simply not advertised externally; hosts that need internet access carry a global unicast address as well.
  • Good for infrastructure that must never leave the site: Management interfaces, storage networks, industrial controllers. Their addressing stays constant even if the ISP-assigned global prefix changes.
Where you see it
  • Addressing an internal management VLAN that must not be internet-reachable
  • Keeping stable internal addressing when a site's ISP prefix changes
  • Lab and test networks with no external connectivity
exam: Know both forms: the formal prefix is fc00::/7, and the practical one you will see is fd00::/8. Either may be the keyed answer, so read the choices. The exam's framing is 'the IPv6 equivalent of RFC 1918 private addresses'. The distractor is fe80::/10, which is link-local, not private site addressing — the difference is scope: ULA is routable within the site, link-local is not routable at all.

front: What is the IPv6 multicast prefix, and which well-known groups should you know?
answer:
ff00::/8 — any address starting ff is multicast.
ff02::1 all nodes on the link · ff02::2 all routers on the link
ff02::5 / ff02::6 OSPFv3 · ff02::1:2 all DHCPv6 servers and relays
ff02::1:ff00:0/104 solicited-node multicast, used by Neighbor Discovery
detail:
IPv6's replacement for broadcast. Instead of interrupting every host, traffic goes only to the hosts that belong to the relevant group.
How it works
  • The second hex digit encodes scope: ff02 is link-local scope — never forwarded off the link. ff05 is site scope and ff0e is global. Almost everything you meet in practice is ff02.
  • Solicited-node multicast makes address resolution efficient: It is formed by appending the last 24 bits of a unicast address to the ff02::1:ff00:0/104 prefix. Neighbor Solicitation goes to that group instead of to everyone, so typically only the intended host's NIC processes it.
  • ff02::1 is the closest thing to a broadcast: It reaches every IPv6 node on the link. It is used sparingly, mainly for Router Advertisements and diagnostics, not for routine traffic.
  • Switches use MLD snooping: Multicast Listener Discovery is the IPv6 counterpart of IGMP. Switches snoop it to forward multicast only out ports with interested listeners, exactly as IGMP snooping does for IPv4.
Where you see it
  • ping ff02::1%eth0 to discover every IPv6 host on a segment
  • Reading a capture and identifying Router Advertisements sent to ff02::1
  • Recognizing Neighbor Solicitation traffic to a solicited-node group
exam: The recall item is ff00::/8, and the two named groups worth memorizing are ff02::1 (all nodes) and ff02::2 (all routers). The conceptual item, which CompTIA cares about more, is that IPv6 uses multicast wherever IPv4 used broadcast. If broadcast appears as an IPv6 address type in a list, it is the wrong answer.

front: What are the IPv6 loopback and unspecified addresses?
answer:
Loopback: ::1 (fully written 0000:...:0001) — equivalent to IPv4's 127.0.0.1. Tests the local stack only.
Unspecified: :: (all 128 bits zero) — means 'I have no address yet'. Used as the source address before an address is configured. It is never a valid destination.
detail:
Two special all-zero-ish addresses with fixed meanings. IPv6 collapsed IPv4's entire 127.0.0.0/8 loopback range down to a single address.
How it works
  • One loopback address, not sixteen million: IPv4 reserved a whole /8 for a function needing one address. IPv6 reserved exactly ::1, which is why you will never see ::2 used as a loopback.
  • The unspecified address appears during DAD: In Duplicate Address Detection, a host sends a Neighbor Solicitation for the address it wants to claim, sourced from :: because it has nothing else yet. A reply means the address is taken.
  • They are structurally similar but semantically opposite: :: means no address at all; ::1 means this machine. Writing one when you mean the other is a common configuration error.
  • :: also appears as a wildcard bind: A service listening on :::443 is bound to all IPv6 interfaces, the counterpart of IPv4's 0.0.0.0. Compare with IPv4: 0.0.0.0 is both the unspecified address and the default route.
Where you see it
  • ping ::1 to verify the local IPv6 stack is functioning
  • Reading netstat -an output showing a service bound to :::80
  • Interpreting a capture where a booting host sources packets from ::
exam: Both are direct recall, and they are almost always asked together with the other prefixes. The trap is offering ::0 or 127.0.0.1 as the IPv6 loopback, or confusing :: with ::1. Remember: ::1 is loopback, :: is unspecified. Also note IPv6's default route is written ::/0, the equivalent of 0.0.0.0/0.

front: Why does IPv6 have no broadcast address, and what replaced it?
answer:
Broadcast forces every host on a segment to process a frame it usually does not need, wasting CPU on every device. IPv6 removed it entirely.
Replaced by multicast (only subscribed hosts) and anycast (nearest member of a group). ff02::1 reaches all nodes when that is genuinely required.
detail:
A deliberate design decision. Every job IPv4 gave to broadcast, IPv6 gave to a scoped multicast group instead.
How it works
  • Broadcast interrupts every NIC and every CPU: In IPv4 an ARP request must be processed up the stack by every host on the segment, even the 999 that are not the target. On a large VLAN that is continuous wasted work.
  • Solicited-node multicast is the direct fix: IPv6 address resolution sends a Neighbor Solicitation to a group derived from the target's last 24 bits. Statistically only the intended host is listening, so the other hosts' NICs filter it out in hardware without waking the CPU.
  • IPv6 defines three address types, not four: Unicast, multicast and anycast. Broadcast is simply not one of them, which is a favourite exam fact.
  • Anycast is formalized: Multiple interfaces share one address and routing delivers to the topologically nearest. In IPv4 anycast is a routing convention; in IPv6 it is a defined address type.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why large IPv6 VLANs suffer far less background chatter than IPv4 ones
  • Reading a capture and seeing Neighbor Solicitation to a solicited-node group instead of ARP broadcast
  • Answering 'what are the IPv6 address types?' correctly
exam: This is one of the most reliably tested IPv6 facts. IPv6 address types are unicast, multicast and anycast — there is no broadcast. Any answer listing broadcast as an IPv6 type is wrong. The follow-up question is what replaced it: multicast, specifically solicited-node multicast for address resolution.

front: What is NDP, and which four ICMPv6 messages does it use?
answer:
Neighbor Discovery Protocol, carried in ICMPv6. It replaces ARP, ICMP Router Discovery and ICMP Redirect.
NS Neighbor Solicitation — 'who has this address?'
NA Neighbor Advertisement — 'I do, here is my MAC'
RS Router Solicitation — 'are there routers here?'
RA Router Advertisement — 'I am a router, here is the prefix'
detail:
The protocol that does address resolution, router discovery and reachability testing on an IPv6 link. It exists because IPv6 has no broadcast, so ARP could not be carried forward.
How it works
  • NS and NA replace ARP request and reply: The solicitation is sent to the target's solicited-node multicast group rather than to a broadcast address, so uninterested hosts never process it. The result is stored in the neighbor cache, the IPv6 equivalent of the ARP table.
  • RS and RA replace static gateway configuration: A booting host multicasts an RS to ff02::2; routers reply with an RA to ff02::1 carrying the /64 prefix, the router's link-local address as default gateway, and flags describing how to configure addresses. This is how IPv6 hosts learn their gateway automatically.
  • Duplicate Address Detection is built in: Before using any address, a host sends an NS for that address sourced from ::. Any reply means the address is in use. IPv4 has no equivalent mandatory step.
  • Blocking all ICMPv6 breaks IPv6 entirely: In IPv4 you can filter ICMP and mostly get away with it. In IPv6, ICMPv6 carries NDP, so blanket blocking prevents address resolution, router discovery and PMTUD. IPv6 firewall policy must permit the necessary ICMPv6 types.
Where you see it
  • Reading ip -6 neigh or netsh interface ipv6 show neighbors
  • Writing an IPv6 firewall policy that permits the required ICMPv6 types
  • Diagnosing a host that gets a link-local address but no global one — no RA is being received
exam: Two guaranteed items. First, NDP replaces ARP in IPv6, and the distractor is 'IPv6 uses ARP' or 'IPv6 uses ARPv6'. Second, NDP runs over ICMPv6, which is why you cannot block ICMPv6 the way administrators habitually block ICMP. Know the four message names by their initials — CompTIA abbreviates them as NS, NA, RS and RA.

front: What is SLAAC, and how does it differ from DHCPv6?
answer:
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration. The host multicasts a Router Solicitation, receives a Router Advertisement containing a /64 prefix, and generates its own 64-bit interface ID. No server, no lease, no record kept anywhere.
DHCPv6 (UDP 546 client / 547 server) is stateful: a server assigns and tracks each address.
detail:
Address configuration with no server at all. The router supplies the network half; the host invents its own host half.
How it works
  • Stateless means nobody records the assignment: The router advertises a prefix and forgets about it. There is no lease database and no way to look up which host holds which address — which is exactly why some organizations prefer DHCPv6 despite the extra infrastructure.
  • The interface ID comes from EUI-64 or randomization: Older stacks derive it from the MAC using EUI-64. Modern operating systems generate random privacy addresses instead, and rotate them, because an EUI-64 address exposes the MAC to every site you visit.
  • Flags in the RA steer the host: The M (managed) flag tells hosts to use stateful DHCPv6 for addressing. The O (other) flag tells them to use SLAAC for the address but DHCPv6 for extra information such as DNS servers. A common deployment sets O only.
  • SLAAC alone historically supplied no DNS server: That gap is filled either by the RDNSS option inside the RA or by stateless DHCPv6. A host with a working SLAAC address and no DNS server is a classic partial-configuration failure.
Where you see it
  • Any IPv6 network where hosts configure themselves from a router with no DHCP server
  • Diagnosing a host with a global IPv6 address that cannot resolve names
  • Choosing DHCPv6 over SLAAC because the organization requires an address-to-host audit trail
exam: The keyword mapping is direct: 'stateless' and 'no DHCP server needed' → SLAAC; 'the server tracks assignments' → DHCPv6. Know that SLAAC depends on Router Advertisements, so a scenario where hosts only obtain fe80:: addresses points to no RA being received. The DHCPv6 ports are UDP 546 and 547, not 67 and 68 — that is a favourite distractor.

front: How does EUI-64 build a 64-bit interface ID from a 48-bit MAC? Work through 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E.
answer:
Result: 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E, giving fe80::21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e with a link-local prefix.
Steps: split the MAC in half → insert FFFE in the middle → flip the seventh bit of the first byte.
detail:
The original method for turning a 48-bit MAC into the 64-bit interface ID that SLAAC needs. It guarantees uniqueness on the link without any coordination.
How it works
  • Step 1 — split the MAC into two halves: 00:1A:2B (the OUI) and 3C:4D:5E (the device-specific half).
  • Step 2 — insert FFFE between them: 00:1A:2B:FF:FE:3C:4D:5E. That is 16 added bits, taking 48 up to 64. FFFE was chosen because it never appears in a real MAC in that position.
  • Step 3 — flip the seventh bit from the left of the first byte: This is the Universal/Local bit. 0x00 is binary 0000 0000; flipping bit 7 gives 0000 0010 = 0x02. The address becomes 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E.
  • Why the bit flip exists: In a MAC the U/L bit means 0 = globally unique, 1 = locally administered. In an EUI-64 interface ID the sense is inverted, so 1 means globally unique. Flipping it preserves the meaning across the two formats.
Where you see it
  • Recognizing ff:fe in the middle of an IPv6 address as an EUI-64 giveaway
  • Deriving a host's MAC address from its IPv6 address during an investigation
  • Explaining why privacy extensions were added — EUI-64 tracks a device across every network it joins
exam: The two testable mechanics are insert FFFE in the middle and flip the 7th bit. The single most useful recognition shortcut for the exam: an IPv6 address containing ff:fe in the middle of the interface ID was built by EUI-64. Watch for a distractor that inserts FFFF instead of FFFE, or that appends FFFE to the end rather than inserting it in the middle. The common first-byte results are 00→02 and 0c→0e.

front: Why is /64 the standard IPv6 subnet size, even for a link with two hosts?
answer:
Because SLAAC and EUI-64 both require the interface ID to be exactly 64 bits. A prefix longer than /64 leaves too few host bits and breaks autoconfiguration.
A /64 provides 2^64 addresses per subnet — deliberately far more than any segment will use.
detail:
The convention that IPv6 subnets are all the same size. It exists because the protocol's autoconfiguration mechanisms assume a fixed 64-bit boundary.
How it works
  • The 64-bit boundary is structural: IPv6 unicast addresses are designed as 64 bits of network plus 64 bits of interface ID. SLAAC, EUI-64 and privacy addressing all generate 64-bit interface IDs and have nowhere to put them in a longer prefix.
  • Address conservation is not a goal: Assigning 2^64 addresses to a two-host link would be absurd in IPv4 thinking. In IPv6 there is no shortage, and uniform subnet size removes an entire class of design decisions and errors.
  • A /48 site gives 65,536 subnets: 48 bits of routing prefix plus 16 bits of subnet ID leaves the 64-bit interface ID intact. That is the standard site allocation, and every subnet inside is a /64.
  • Point-to-point links are the recognized exception: /127 is defined for router-to-router links because there is no SLAAC there and a /64 on a point-to-point link enables a neighbour-cache exhaustion attack. It is a deliberate exception that proves the /64 rule.
Where you see it
  • Every LAN and VLAN in a conventionally designed IPv6 network
  • Reading an ISP allocation of a /56 or /48 and knowing how many /64s it contains
  • Explaining why you do not 'subnet down' an IPv6 LAN to save addresses
exam: The exam wants the reason, not just the number: /64 is required because SLAAC and EUI-64 need a 64-bit interface ID. The distractor is a justification based on address conservation, which is backwards — IPv6 has no conservation pressure. If a question asks how many /64 subnets a /48 contains, the answer is 65,536 (2^16).

front: Contrast dual stack, tunneling and NAT64 as IPv6 transition methods.
answer:
Dual stack — run IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously on the same interfaces. The preferred and most common method.
Tunneling — encapsulate IPv6 packets inside IPv4 to cross an IPv4-only path (6to4, Teredo, ISATAP, GRE).
NAT64 — translate between IPv6-only clients and IPv4-only servers, usually paired with DNS64.
detail:
Three answers to the same problem: IPv4 and IPv6 do not interoperate directly, and both must coexist for years.
How it works
  • Dual stack avoids translation entirely: Each host has both an IPv4 and an IPv6 address and picks whichever the destination supports. Nothing is encapsulated or rewritten, so nothing breaks. The cost is running and securing two complete stacks, including two sets of firewall rules.
  • Tunneling carries IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure: The IPv6 packet becomes the payload of an IPv4 packet, crosses the IPv4-only network, and is unwrapped at the far end. It works, but adds header overhead, reduces effective MTU, and complicates troubleshooting.
  • NAT64 is for one-way access to legacy servers: An IPv6-only client needs to reach an IPv4-only server. DNS64 synthesizes an AAAA record pointing at the NAT64 gateway, which rewrites the packet into IPv4. This is common on IPv6-only mobile carrier networks.
  • They solve different directions of the problem: Dual stack means you speak both. Tunneling means your IPv6 traverses IPv4 transit. NAT64 means IPv6-only clients reach IPv4-only content. Matching the mechanism to the scenario is the skill.
Where you see it
  • An enterprise enabling IPv6 alongside existing IPv4 with no cutover event
  • A branch office whose ISP is IPv4-only tunneling IPv6 to headquarters
  • A mobile carrier running IPv6-only handsets with NAT64/DNS64 for legacy websites
exam: Objective 1.8 names these three explicitly, so expect a scenario-to-method match. The signals: 'run both protocols at once' → dual stack; 'the transit network only supports IPv4' → tunneling; 'IPv6-only clients must reach IPv4-only servers' → NAT64. Dual stack is the expected answer when a question asks for the recommended or least disruptive migration approach.

front: What does administrative distance actually rank, and when does a router use it?
answer: It ranks how much the router trusts the source of a route, not how good the path is. Lowest AD wins. It is only consulted when two different sources offer the same prefix length.
detail:
A tiebreaker for believability. When two routing protocols both claim to know how to reach the identical network, the router has no way to compare their metrics, so it falls back on a preconfigured trust ranking.
How it works
  • Metrics are not comparable across protocols: An OSPF cost of 65 and a RIP hop count of 3 measure different things. There is no arithmetic that converts one into the other, so the router cannot pick on metric. AD exists to break exactly that deadlock.
  • Lower is more trusted: A directly connected interface is AD 0 because the router can see the link itself. A hand-typed static route is AD 1 because an administrator asserted it. Dynamic protocols rank below both.
  • It is a local value, never advertised: AD lives only in the router that holds it. It is not carried in routing updates, so two routers can legitimately have different AD settings for the same protocol.
  • Only one route reaches the routing table: Each protocol picks its own best path first, then offers that single candidate to the routing table. AD decides which candidate is installed; the loser sits unused in its own protocol database.
Where you see it
  • Deciding whether a backup static route or the OSPF-learned route is used
  • Making a WAN link preferred over a DSL link by adjusting AD
  • Diagnosing why show ip route shows a path you did not expect
exam: CompTIA words this as 'which route will the router install' or 'what determines route preference'. The reliable trap is offering a route with a better metric but higher AD as a distractor — metric never beats AD across protocols. The second trap is forgetting that longest prefix match is evaluated before AD, so AD only matters when the prefix lengths are identical.

front: Give the default administrative distance for each route source.
answer: Connected 0 · Static 1 · eBGP 20 · EIGRP internal 90 · OSPF 110 · IS-IS 115 · RIP 120 · EIGRP external 170 · iBGP 200 · Unknown/unreachable 255
detail:
The standard trust ranking every Cisco-style router ships with. This table is memorized as a unit and appears on the exam as raw recall.
How it works
  • The pattern is confidence in the information: Connected (0) is observed firsthand. Static (1) is asserted by a human. eBGP (20) is trusted highly because a route learned from outside your AS is the only way to reach that destination at all.
  • EIGRP is split in two: Internal EIGRP is 90. Routes redistributed into EIGRP from another protocol are external EIGRP at 170 — deliberately worse than OSPF and RIP, because they are second-hand information.
  • BGP is split the opposite way: eBGP is 20 (very trusted) but iBGP is 200 (barely trusted, worse than every IGP). Inside your own AS your IGP knows the topology better, so iBGP must lose.
  • 255 means never install: A route with AD 255 is considered unreachable and is not placed in the routing table at all. Setting AD to 255 is a way to administratively kill a route.
Where you see it
  • Predicting which protocol wins when two of them advertise the same network
  • Configuring a floating static route with an AD above the dynamic protocol's
  • Reading the bracketed value in show ip route output such as [110/65]
exam: Expect a bare recall question ('what is the default AD of OSPF?') and a comparison question ('a network is learned via both EIGRP and OSPF — which is installed?', answer EIGRP at 90). The two values people miss are IS-IS 115, which sits between OSPF and RIP, and iBGP 200, which people wrongly assume matches eBGP's 20. In [110/65] the first number is AD, the second is metric — CompTIA has asked which is which.

front: In what order does a router choose between candidate routes to a destination?
answer:
1) Longest prefix match — the most specific route wins outright.
2) Lowest administrative distance, if prefix lengths tie.
3) Lowest metric, if AD also ties (same protocol).
4) Equal-cost load balancing if metrics tie too.
detail:
The forwarding decision is a strict cascade. Each step is only reached when the previous step produced a tie, and that ordering is what makes most exam questions solvable.
How it works
  • Longest prefix match is first and absolute: The router compares the destination IP against every route and keeps only those whose network portion matches. Of those, the one with the most mask bits wins immediately. Protocol and AD are never consulted.
  • Specificity beats trust because specificity means better information: A /24 describes 256 addresses; a /8 describes 16 million. Whoever advertised the /24 demonstrably knows more about that exact destination, no matter which protocol carried it.
  • AD only breaks a prefix-length tie: Two protocols must be offering the identical prefix — same network and same mask — before AD is examined at all.
  • Metric only compares inside one protocol: Once AD has picked a protocol, that protocol's own metric (OSPF cost, RIP hops, EIGRP composite) chooses among its paths. Metrics are never compared across protocols.
  • Ties at the end become load balancing: Equal prefix, equal AD, equal metric produces multiple entries and traffic is shared across them. This is equal-cost multipath.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why a specific host route overrides the default gateway
  • Predicting the effect of adding a more specific static route to steer traffic
  • Troubleshooting traffic that takes an unexpected exit interface
exam: This is the single highest-yield routing concept on N10-009. CompTIA builds questions where the specific route comes from the worse protocol precisely so that candidates who reach for AD first get it wrong. Read the masks before you read the protocol names. Also note the default route 0.0.0.0/0 has a prefix length of zero, so it is the shortest possible match and is used only when nothing else matches.

front: A router has 172.16.0.0/16 via OSPF and 172.16.5.0/24 via RIP. Which is used for a packet to 172.16.5.10?
answer: The RIP /24. Longest prefix match is evaluated before administrative distance, so OSPF's better AD of 110 is never considered.
detail:
A worked example built to defeat the instinct of comparing administrative distances first. The naive answer here is OSPF, and it is wrong.
How it works
  • Both routes match the destination: 172.16.5.10 falls inside 172.16.0.0/16 and also inside 172.16.5.0/24. The router therefore has two candidates and must choose.
  • The /24 is more specific: 24 mask bits beat 16 mask bits. The lookup stops there — the router installs and uses the RIP route for this destination.
  • Both routes stay in the table: This is not a competition one route wins permanently. Both entries coexist. The /16 still serves every other 172.16.x.x destination outside 172.16.5.0/24.
  • AD would only matter if the masks matched: If RIP had advertised 172.16.0.0/16 as well, then AD 110 versus 120 would apply and OSPF would win.
Where you see it
  • Reading a routing table and predicting the exit interface
  • Understanding why injecting a more specific prefix hijacks traffic
  • Explaining suboptimal routing caused by a leaked specific prefix
exam: The distractor CompTIA offers is 'OSPF, because 110 is lower than 120'. That reasoning only applies to identical prefixes. Watch for the same trap phrased as 'the router prefers the more reliable protocol' — the exam wants you to say most specific match first.

front: A router has a static route to 192.168.10.0/24 and an EIGRP route to 192.168.10.128/25. Where does a packet to 192.168.10.200 go, and where does one to 192.168.10.50 go?
answer: .200 takes the EIGRP /25. .50 takes the static /24. The same table sends the two packets different ways.
detail:
A second worked example, this time with the most trusted possible dynamic competitor losing to a less trusted route on one packet and winning on another.
How it works
  • 192.168.10.200 falls inside the /25: The /25 covers 192.168.10.128 through 192.168.10.255. The destination matches both routes, so the more specific /25 wins even though the static route has AD 1 and EIGRP has AD 90.
  • 192.168.10.50 does not fall inside the /25: It is below .128, so the /25 does not match at all and is never a candidate. The only matching route is the static /24, which is used.
  • Specificity is per-packet, not per-route: The routing table is evaluated fresh for every destination address. One entry does not permanently defeat another; it only wins for the addresses it actually covers.
  • AD 1 losing feels wrong and is correct: A static route is the second most trusted source there is, and it still loses on the .200 packet. That is the whole point of the ordering.
Where you see it
  • Deliberately overriding part of a static route's range with a dynamic route
  • Diagnosing 'half the subnet works and half does not'
  • Understanding how a /32 host route pulls a single address off the normal path
exam: CompTIA likes two-part scenarios like this because a candidate who memorized 'static beats EIGRP' answers both halves the same way and gets one wrong. If the exam gives you a destination address and a table, always compute which prefixes actually contain that address before comparing anything else.

front: IGP vs EGP — what is the dividing line, and which protocols are which?
answer:
IGP routes within one autonomous system: OSPF, EIGRP, RIP, IS-IS.
EGP routes between autonomous systems: BGP is the only one in use.
detail:
The classification is about administrative boundaries, not about technology. An autonomous system is a network under one routing policy, and the two protocol families are optimized for opposite problems.
How it works
  • IGPs optimize for speed and accuracy: Inside your own network you control every router, you want the shortest path, and you want convergence in seconds. IGPs compute paths from a metric like cost or hop count.
  • EGPs optimize for policy and scale: Between organizations the shortest path is often the wrong path — you may be contractually required to avoid a competitor's transit. BGP selects on attributes and policy, and holds the full internet table.
  • The AS number is the boundary marker: A globally assigned AS number identifies each independently routed network. BGP records the list of AS numbers a route has crossed as the AS-path, and rejects any route already containing its own AS — that is its loop prevention.
  • They coexist inside one network: A service provider edge router typically runs an IGP internally for its own links and BGP externally for customer and peer routes.
Where you see it
  • Deciding what protocol a multi-homed enterprise runs to two ISPs
  • Reading a diagram where routers are grouped into AS 65001 and AS 65002
  • Explaining why an ISP's core does not run OSPF for internet routes
exam: The exam usually gives a list of protocols and asks which is the exterior gateway protocol — the answer is always BGP. The distractor is EIGRP, because its name contains 'Enhanced Interior' and candidates skim it; EIGRP is an IGP. Also expect the scenario framing 'a company connects to two different ISPs and needs to influence inbound and outbound path selection' — that is BGP.

front: How does OSPF work as a link-state protocol, and what is its AD?
answer: Every router floods descriptions of its own links, builds an identical link-state database of the whole area, then runs SPF (Dijkstra) on it to compute its own shortest-path tree. AD 110, metric is cost, open standard.
detail:
Link-state means each router independently holds a full map of the topology and calculates paths itself. This is fundamentally different from distance-vector, where a router only knows what neighbors told it.
How it works
  • Neighbors first, then database, then routes: OSPF forms adjacencies with directly connected neighbors using Hello packets, synchronizes link-state databases with them, and only then runs SPF. A stuck adjacency means no routes at all.
  • Every router in an area has the identical database: The LSDB is not per-router information — it is a shared map. Each router runs SPF against that same map from its own position, which is why every router arrives at a consistent, loop-free result.
  • Changes trigger flooding, not periodic dumps: When a link fails, the attached router originates an updated LSA and floods it through the area. Routers rerun SPF. This is why OSPF converges in seconds rather than minutes.
  • Open standard and multi-vendor: OSPF runs on any vendor's equipment. That is the practical reason it is chosen over EIGRP in mixed environments.
Where you see it
  • Enterprise campus and WAN routing in mixed-vendor networks
  • Any design that needs fast reconvergence after a link failure
  • Data center underlay routing alongside or instead of IS-IS
exam: The exam tests OSPF by category and number: it is the link-state option, it is the open standard alternative to Cisco's EIGRP, and its AD is 110. The classic scenario is 'a multi-vendor network needs a fast-converging interior routing protocol' — answer OSPF, distractor EIGRP (Cisco-oriented) or RIP (too slow).

front: Why does OSPF use areas, and what is special about area 0?
answer: Areas bound the size of the link-state database and confine LSA flooding, so SPF stays cheap. Area 0 is the backbone — every other area must connect to it, directly or through a virtual link.
detail:
SPF cost grows with the size of the database, and a flood in a flat OSPF domain reaches every router. Areas are the containment mechanism that lets OSPF scale past a few dozen routers.
How it works
  • Flooding stops at the area border: An LSA describing a link inside area 10 is flooded only within area 10. Routers in area 20 never see it, never store it and never rerun SPF because of it. That is the entire scaling win.
  • Area border routers summarize between areas: An ABR sits in two areas and injects summarized reachability from one into the other, rather than the raw topology. Other areas learn 'this prefix is reachable through me', not the full link detail.
  • Area 0 is the transit hub: All inter-area traffic passes through the backbone. Area 1 cannot talk to area 2 directly — the path goes area 1 → area 0 → area 2. This hub-and-spoke rule is what prevents inter-area routing loops.
  • A detached area needs a virtual link: If an area ends up not physically touching area 0, a virtual link tunnels its ABR back to the backbone through an intervening area. It is a repair, not a design choice.
Where you see it
  • Segmenting a large campus OSPF domain by building or region
  • Reducing router CPU and memory on small branch routers via stub areas
  • Explaining why an isolated area cannot reach the rest of the network
exam: N10-009 asks the conceptual version: what is the OSPF backbone area, or why does OSPF use areas. The answer is area 0 and limiting the scope of flooding and the size of the database. The distractor to avoid is 'areas provide security' or 'areas assign IP addresses' — they do neither.

front: What is the OSPF metric and how is a link's cost derived?
answer: The metric is cost, calculated as reference bandwidth ÷ interface bandwidth. Costs are added along the path and the lowest total wins.
detail:
OSPF's metric is bandwidth-based, which means it naturally prefers fast links. It ignores hop count entirely, so a four-hop gigabit path beats a one-hop T1.
How it works
  • Cost is inversely proportional to bandwidth: Faster interface, lower cost, more preferred. With the traditional 100 Mbps reference bandwidth, FastEthernet is cost 1 and a 10 Mbps link is cost 10.
  • Costs accumulate hop by hop: The path cost is the sum of the outbound interface costs along the route. SPF picks the lowest total from the router to each destination.
  • The reference bandwidth must be raised on modern links: With the default reference, every interface at or above 100 Mbps computes to cost 1, so gigabit and 10-gigabit links look identical to OSPF. Administrators raise the reference bandwidth consistently on all routers to restore differentiation.
  • Cost can also be set directly: An interface cost can be hardcoded to steer traffic without changing bandwidth statements. This is how a link is made a deliberate backup.
Where you see it
  • Making a router prefer the fiber uplink over the backup circuit
  • Explaining why OSPF picks a longer but faster path than RIP would
  • Interpreting the second value in [110/65] in a routing table
exam: The exam pairs metrics with protocols: OSPF = cost (bandwidth), RIP = hop count, EIGRP = bandwidth and delay, BGP = AS-path and policy attributes. The trap is answering 'hop count' for OSPF, or claiming OSPF measures latency — it does not measure anything live, it computes from configured bandwidth.

front: What is an LSA and what does flooding accomplish in OSPF?
answer: A Link-State Advertisement is one router's description of its own links and neighbors. Flooding reliably pushes each LSA to every router in the area so all of them build the same database.
detail:
The LSA is the unit of OSPF information, and flooding is the distribution mechanism. Together they are how a distributed set of routers arrives at one identical map.
How it works
  • Each router originates only its own LSAs: A router describes its own interfaces, costs and adjacencies. It never invents information about a distant router — it just relays that router's LSA unchanged. This is why the database is trustworthy.
  • Flooding is reliable and acknowledged: OSPF acknowledges LSAs and retransmits unacknowledged ones. A router that receives an LSA it already holds does not re-flood it, which stops the flood from circulating forever.
  • Sequence numbers and ageing keep it fresh: Each LSA carries a sequence number so routers can tell newer from older, and an age that causes it to be refreshed periodically or expire if the originator disappears.
  • A topology change triggers a targeted flood plus SPF: Only the changed LSA is flooded, not the whole database. Receiving routers install it and rerun SPF, which is the actual convergence event.
Where you see it
  • Diagnosing why one router has routes another does not (database mismatch)
  • Explaining OSPF CPU spikes during a flapping link
  • Understanding why an area boundary limits the blast radius of a failure
exam: N10-009 does not test individual LSA types. It tests the idea: OSPF routers share link-state information so every router builds the same topology map, then each computes its own shortest path. The distractor is describing OSPF like a distance-vector protocol — 'routers exchange their routing tables with neighbors'. That is RIP, not OSPF.

front: What kind of protocol is EIGRP, and what are its administrative distances?
answer: Cisco's advanced distance-vector (often called hybrid) IGP. AD 90 for internal routes, 170 for external (redistributed) routes. Uses DUAL for loop-free path calculation.
detail:
EIGRP behaves like a distance-vector protocol — it learns from neighbors rather than building a full topology map — but it adds neighbor discovery, incremental updates and a formal loop-free path algorithm.
How it works
  • It learns from neighbors, not from a map: Unlike OSPF, an EIGRP router never sees the whole topology. It knows what its neighbors reported plus the cost to reach each neighbor. That is what makes it distance-vector at heart.
  • Updates are incremental and triggered: EIGRP sends the full table once when an adjacency forms, then only changes. RIP, by contrast, rebroadcasts its whole table on a timer forever.
  • Neighbor relationships are explicit: Hello packets establish and maintain adjacencies. Loss of hellos removes the neighbor immediately, which is a large part of why EIGRP converges quickly.
  • External routes are deliberately distrusted: Anything redistributed into EIGRP from another protocol becomes AD 170 — worse than OSPF at 110 and RIP at 120 — so a native route from almost any protocol beats a second-hand EIGRP one.
Where you see it
  • Cisco-only enterprise networks wanting fast convergence with simple configuration
  • Branch WAN designs where per-link bandwidth varies widely
  • Networks migrating between routing protocols where redistribution is in play
exam: The exam's discriminator is vendor: EIGRP is Cisco-proprietary, OSPF is the open standard. A scenario naming a multi-vendor environment rules EIGRP out. The commonly missed number is external EIGRP 170 — candidates memorize 90 and assume it always applies.

front: In EIGRP, what are a successor and a feasible successor, and what does DUAL do with them?
answer: The successor is the current best path installed in the routing table. A feasible successor is a precomputed, guaranteed loop-free backup. DUAL is the algorithm that picks them and guarantees no loop.
detail:
This is EIGRP's headline feature. Because a verified backup path is already computed and stored, losing the primary link is a table swap rather than a network-wide recalculation.
How it works
  • The successor is the lowest-metric path: It is the route that actually appears in show ip route and forwards traffic. Its metric is the feasible distance.
  • A feasible successor must pass the feasibility condition: The neighbor's own reported distance to the destination must be strictly less than the local router's current feasible distance. That test proves the neighbor is not routing back through you, which is what makes the backup provably loop-free.
  • Failover is instant when a feasible successor exists: The router promotes the backup out of its topology table with no queries and no recomputation. Convergence is sub-second.
  • No feasible successor means the route goes active: DUAL sends queries to neighbors asking for an alternative and waits for replies. This is slower, and a query that never gets answered is the classic 'stuck in active' failure.
Where you see it
  • Explaining EIGRP's sub-second failover on a redundant branch link
  • Reading the EIGRP topology table to see backup paths
  • Troubleshooting slow EIGRP convergence caused by no feasible successor
exam: N10-009 tests the vocabulary, not the math: successor = best path in use, feasible successor = precomputed backup, DUAL = the algorithm guaranteeing loop-free paths. The distractor is describing a feasible successor as 'the second-best path' — it is only a feasible successor if it satisfies the feasibility condition, and a second-best path often does not.

front: What is EIGRP's composite metric built from?
answer: By default, bandwidth and delay. Reliability, load and MTU exist in the formula but are switched off by default via the K values.
detail:
EIGRP does not reduce a path to one dimension. It combines the slowest link's bandwidth with the cumulative delay of the path, which produces better decisions than hop count alone.
How it works
  • Bandwidth is the minimum along the path: EIGRP uses the lowest-bandwidth link in the path, because that link is the bottleneck. Adding fast links after a slow one does not improve the bandwidth term.
  • Delay is cumulative: The delay values of every outgoing interface along the path are added. This is what distinguishes two paths that share the same bottleneck bandwidth.
  • K values enable or disable each term: The default K values turn on bandwidth and delay only. Reliability and load are available but almost never enabled, because a metric that changes with live traffic causes route flapping.
  • Delay is the safe tuning knob: Administrators adjust interface delay rather than bandwidth to steer EIGRP, because the bandwidth statement also affects QoS and other features.
Where you see it
  • Making EIGRP prefer a low-latency circuit over a higher-bandwidth but slower one
  • Explaining why EIGRP and RIP pick different paths across the same topology
  • Interpreting the large metric numbers in EIGRP routing table output
exam: The exam wants the pairing: EIGRP uses bandwidth and delay. The distractors are 'hop count' (that is RIP), 'cost' (that is OSPF) and 'bandwidth, delay, reliability and load' — the last one is tempting because all four appear in the formula, but only the first two are used by default.

front: Describe RIP: type, metric, administrative distance and its hard limit.
answer: Distance-vector IGP. Metric is hop count. AD 120. Maximum 15 hops — a metric of 16 means unreachable.
detail:
The oldest and simplest IP routing protocol. It is on the exam as the baseline against which every other protocol's improvements are described.
How it works
  • Hop count ignores everything that matters: A one-hop 1.5 Mbps link beats a two-hop 10 Gbps path. RIP has no concept of bandwidth or latency, which is the core reason it was superseded.
  • 15 hops is the loop-prevention mechanism, not a design limit: Because distance-vector routers can count to infinity when a loop forms, RIP defines infinity as 16. A route that reaches 16 hops is declared unreachable and discarded, which caps how long a loop can persist.
  • Periodic full-table broadcasts: RIP re-advertises its entire routing table every 30 seconds whether anything changed or not. On a large network that is constant background traffic.
  • Slow convergence by design: It relies on hold-down and invalidation timers measured in minutes rather than on explicit neighbor loss detection, so a failure can take several minutes to propagate.
Where you see it
  • Very small or lab networks where simplicity outweighs efficiency
  • Legacy equipment that supports nothing else
  • Exam contrast questions against OSPF and EIGRP
exam: Two guaranteed exam facts: the metric is hop count and the maximum is 15 hops. The classic trap is answering '16' for the maximum — 16 is the value that means unreachable, so the largest usable path is 15. Any scenario mentioning a network larger than 15 router hops, or one needing fast convergence, rules RIP out.

front: What makes BGP a path-vector protocol, and what is an AS number?
answer: BGP advertises the full list of autonomous systems a route has traversed — the AS-path. An AS number is a globally assigned identifier for a network under one routing policy.
detail:
BGP does not compute a shortest path from a metric. It records the sequence of networks a route passed through and selects using that path plus administrative policy.
How it works
  • The AS-path is both metric and loop prevention: A shorter AS-path is generally preferred. More importantly, a router that receives a route whose AS-path already contains its own AS number discards it — that is how BGP guarantees loop freedom without any timers.
  • Policy beats shortest path: Attributes such as local preference and AS-path prepending let an operator make a longer path preferred because of cost or contract. This is the main reason BGP is not an IGP.
  • It runs over TCP 179: BGP peers are explicitly configured and establish a TCP session. Neighbors are not discovered automatically, which is appropriate between organizations that must agree to peer.
  • It scales to the full internet table: BGP carries the complete set of internet prefixes, which is why it converges slowly and why peers exchange only incremental updates after the initial full table.
Where you see it
  • Multi-homing an enterprise to two ISPs with failover and traffic engineering
  • ISP-to-ISP peering and transit
  • Advertising a company's own provider-independent address space
exam: The exam asks for BGP's classification — path-vector, and the only EGP — and for the scenario 'connect to multiple ISPs and control which one is used'. Distractors are 'link-state' and 'distance-vector'. Also expect the framing 'the routing protocol of the internet'.

front: eBGP vs iBGP — what is the difference, and why are their ADs so far apart?
answer: eBGP peers sit in different AS numbers, AD 20. iBGP peers sit in the same AS, AD 200. Same protocol, different relationship.
detail:
The distinction is purely whether the two peers declare the same AS number. That one difference changes trust level, loop prevention behavior and how routes are propagated.
How it works
  • eBGP is trusted because there is no alternative: A route to an external network can only be learned from outside. Nothing inside your AS knows it, so AD 20 makes eBGP beat every IGP.
  • iBGP is distrusted because your IGP knows better: For destinations inside your own AS, OSPF or EIGRP has real topology knowledge. AD 200 puts iBGP below every IGP so it can never override them.
  • iBGP does not re-advertise between iBGP peers: A route learned from one iBGP peer is not passed to another, because the AS-path does not change inside an AS and would not catch a loop. This is why iBGP traditionally requires a full mesh of peers, or route reflectors.
  • The AS-path only grows at eBGP hops: A router prepends its AS number when advertising to an eBGP peer. Inside the AS the path stays untouched.
Where you see it
  • Two border routers in one enterprise AS carrying internet routes to each other
  • Peering with an upstream ISP that has its own AS number
  • Explaining why an internal BGP route lost to an OSPF route
exam: The exam mostly wants the AD pair: eBGP 20, iBGP 200. Candidates routinely answer 200 for both or 20 for both. Remember the logic — external routes must win, internal BGP must lose to your IGP.

front: What is convergence, and what determines how fast a protocol achieves it?
answer: The time from a topology change until every router again holds a consistent, correct view of the network. During convergence, traffic can loop or be black-holed.
detail:
Convergence is the real measure of a routing protocol's quality. Everything else — link-state versus distance-vector, hello timers, feasible successors — exists to shorten it.
How it works
  • How the failure is detected sets the floor: Physical link-down detection is immediate. Waiting for missed hello packets takes seconds. Waiting for a route invalidation timer to expire, as RIP does, takes minutes.
  • How the news propagates sets the ceiling: OSPF floods a single changed LSA and every router recomputes in parallel. RIP passes changes hop by hop on its update timer, so each router adds delay.
  • Precomputed backups eliminate recomputation entirely: EIGRP's feasible successor is already validated, so failover is a table swap. This is why EIGRP can converge faster than protocols that must rerun an algorithm.
  • The network is genuinely broken until convergence finishes: Different routers hold different views. Packets can be forwarded back and forth between two routers that each think the other has the path — a transient routing loop.
Where you see it
  • Justifying OSPF or EIGRP over RIP in a design decision
  • Explaining a brief outage after a WAN link failure
  • Tuning hello and dead timers to trade CPU for faster failure detection
exam: The exam phrases this as 'which protocol converges fastest' or 'a company needs minimal downtime after a link failure'. Rank them: EIGRP and OSPF fast, RIP slow, BGP slowest. The trap is choosing BGP for an internal design because it is 'the internet's protocol' — BGP is deliberately slow and policy-driven, and is wrong for an interior fast-failover requirement.

front: What is a routing loop, and what four mechanisms prevent or limit it?
answer: Packets circulating between routers that each believe the other has the path. Prevented by split horizon, route poisoning, hold-down timers, and ultimately the IP header's TTL.
detail:
Distance-vector protocols are vulnerable to loops because a router believes what its neighbor tells it without knowing where that neighbor learned it. These four mechanisms exist to contain that.
How it works
  • Split horizon: Never advertise a route back out the interface you learned it on. If B learned network X from A, B does not tell A about X. This stops the simplest two-router loop.
  • Route poisoning and poison reverse: When a network fails, the router advertises it with an infinite metric (16 in RIP) rather than silently removing it. Poison reverse sends that poisoned route back toward the source deliberately, overriding split horizon, so the neighbor is explicitly told the route is dead instead of just not hearing about it.
  • Hold-down timers: After a route is marked unreachable, the router refuses updates about it for a period. This prevents a stale advertisement still circulating in the network from reinstalling the dead route.
  • Counting to infinity is the failure mode being prevented: Without these, two routers each increment the metric using the other's stale information, ratcheting the hop count upward forever. Defining infinity as 16 caps how long that can go on.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why RIP takes minutes to fully drop a failed network
  • Diagnosing traffic that ping-pongs between two routers during convergence
  • Justifying link-state protocols in a redundant topology
exam: Expect a definition-matching question: which technique prevents advertising a route back out the interface it was learned on — split horizon. Do not confuse route poisoning (advertising an infinite metric) with split horizon (staying silent). Both appear as options in the same question.

front: How does TTL stop a Layer 3 loop, and why is there no equivalent at Layer 2?
answer: The IP header carries a TTL that each router decrements; at zero the packet is dropped. The Ethernet header has no such field, so a looping frame circulates forever until a switch is powered off or STP blocks the port.
detail:
This contrast explains why a routing loop degrades a network while a switching loop destroys it, and it is the reason spanning tree has to exist at all.
How it works
  • TTL is a hop budget in the IP header: Every router decrements TTL by one before forwarding. A packet stuck in a loop burns its budget — typically 64 or 128 hops — and is discarded, then an ICMP Time Exceeded is returned.
  • This is also how traceroute works: Traceroute sends packets with TTL 1, then 2, then 3, collecting the ICMP Time Exceeded message from each router in turn. The loop-limiting field doubles as a discovery tool.
  • The Ethernet frame header has no hop counter: There is a destination MAC, a source MAC, a type field and a checksum. Nothing counts hops and nothing expires. A frame that enters a loop is copied around it indefinitely.
  • Broadcasts make it exponential, not just persistent: A looping broadcast is flooded out every port at every switch, so each pass multiplies the number of copies. Link utilization and switch CPU saturate within seconds.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why a routing loop causes slow traffic but a switching loop causes total outage
  • Reading traceroute output and understanding what generated each line
  • Justifying why STP cannot simply be turned off on redundant links
exam: CompTIA tests this as a why-question: 'why is a Layer 2 loop more damaging than a Layer 3 loop?' The answer is no TTL in the Ethernet frame. It is also tested through traceroute — the tool that manipulates TTL to map a path. Do not answer 'switches are faster' or 'Layer 2 has no addressing'.

front: Static vs dynamic routing — what does each buy you and cost you?
answer:
Static: exact control, no CPU or bandwidth overhead, no automatic failover, and manual work that scales badly.
Dynamic: automatic adaptation and scale, at the cost of CPU, memory, bandwidth and design complexity.
detail:
The tradeoff is control versus adaptability. A static route is a hand-typed instruction that never changes; a dynamic route is recalculated whenever the topology does.
How it works
  • A static route survives a failure it should not: If the next hop becomes unreachable but the local interface stays up, the static route remains in the table and traffic is black-holed. Nothing tells the router the far end died.
  • Static routes have AD 1 and usually win: That is deliberate — an administrator's explicit instruction should override a protocol's calculation. It also means a wrong static route is very hard to override accidentally.
  • Dynamic routing costs resources continuously: Neighbor keepalives, database storage and recomputation all consume CPU and memory. On a small stub site that overhead buys you nothing.
  • The common design uses both: A branch runs a static default route to headquarters because there is only one way out, while the core runs OSPF because it has real choices to make.
Where you see it
  • A single-homed branch office pointing a default route at its one WAN link
  • A campus core running OSPF across redundant paths
  • Pointing a specific prefix at a firewall or VPN appliance regardless of protocol
exam: The exam scenario is usually 'a small office with a single connection to the internet' — the answer is a static default route, not a routing protocol. The reverse scenario, 'redundant paths with automatic failover', is dynamic routing. The trap is choosing dynamic routing for a topology that has no alternate path to choose between.

front: What is a floating static route and what makes it float?
answer: A static route configured with an administrative distance higher than the dynamic route it backs up, so it stays out of the routing table until the primary route disappears.
detail:
A cheap, protocol-free backup path. The AD is deliberately raised so that the static route loses under normal conditions and only surfaces when the winner is gone.
How it works
  • The default AD of 1 would break this: A normal static route beats every dynamic protocol, so it would always be used and the primary path would never be preferred. Raising its AD inverts that.
  • Pick an AD above the protocol being backed up: Backing up an OSPF route (AD 110) requires an AD above 110 — commonly 200 or 250. Backing up EIGRP (90) requires above 90.
  • Installation is automatic on failure: When the dynamic route is withdrawn, the routing table has no candidate left except the floating static, which is then installed. When the dynamic route returns, it wins again and the static drops out.
  • It has no health awareness of its own: The floating static is installed the moment the dynamic route disappears, whether or not the backup path actually works. Pairing it with a reachability check is what makes it reliable.
Where you see it
  • A cellular or broadband backup that activates when the MPLS circuit fails
  • A secondary VPN tunnel used only if the primary drops
  • Backing up a dynamic default route with a manually configured one
exam: The exam gives you the scenario — 'a backup link that should only be used if the primary fails' — and wants floating static route. The specific detail it tests is that you achieve this by increasing the administrative distance, not by changing the metric. Metric is a distractor here; static routes have no metric to compare.

front: What is a default route, how is it written, and when is it used?
answer: The gateway of last resort, written 0.0.0.0/0 in IPv4 and ::/0 in IPv6. It is used only when no more specific route matches the destination.
detail:
A route with a mask of zero bits matches every possible destination address. Because longest prefix match runs first, it is always the last route to be selected.
How it works
  • Zero mask bits means it always matches, and always loses: Every destination falls inside 0.0.0.0/0, so it is a candidate for every packet. But any other matching route has more mask bits and wins, which is exactly the behavior wanted.
  • It is what makes small routing tables possible: An edge router does not need internet routes. It needs its own local networks plus 'everything else goes to the ISP'. That single entry replaces hundreds of thousands.
  • Gateway of last resort is the same concept: A host's 'default gateway' setting is the host's version of this route: send anything not on my own subnet to this address.
  • No default route means unmatched traffic is dropped: The router returns ICMP Destination Unreachable rather than guessing. If a routing table has no 0.0.0.0/0 and the destination is not listed, the packet dies there.
Where you see it
  • A branch router forwarding all non-local traffic to the corporate WAN
  • An edge router sending all internet-bound traffic to the ISP
  • A host's default gateway configuration
exam: The exam wants the notation 0.0.0.0/0 (equivalently 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0) recognized on sight, and it asks 'what happens to traffic with no matching route' — it uses the default route, or is dropped if none exists. In a routing-table question, remember the default route is only chosen after every specific prefix has failed to match.

front: Distinguish static NAT, dynamic NAT and PAT.
answer:
Static NAT: one private address permanently mapped to one public address.
Dynamic NAT: private addresses take a public address from a pool as needed.
PAT (NAT overload): many private addresses share one public address, distinguished by source port.
detail:
All three rewrite addresses in the IP header at the network boundary. They differ in how many public addresses are needed and whether inbound connections are possible.
How it works
  • Static NAT supports inbound connections: Because the mapping is permanent and one-to-one, an outside host can initiate a connection to the public address and reach the internal server. This is how a DMZ web server is published.
  • Dynamic NAT is one-to-one but temporary: The mapping is created when an inside host sends traffic and released afterward. If the pool is exhausted, additional hosts simply cannot get out. Inbound connections are not possible because no mapping exists until the inside host starts one.
  • PAT multiplexes on the transport port: The router rewrites both the source IP and the source port, and records the pairing in a translation table. A reply arriving for that public IP and port is mapped back to the correct inside host. Thousands of hosts fit behind one address.
  • PAT is what every home router does: Your entire household shares one ISP-assigned public IP. It is also the reason IPv4 has survived address exhaustion as long as it has.
Where you see it
  • Publishing an internal mail or web server on a public address (static)
  • Sharing a single ISP-assigned address across an entire office (PAT)
  • A legacy design with a small block of public addresses assigned on demand (dynamic)
exam: The exam scenario 'many internal hosts must share a single public IP address' is always PAT, also called NAT overload. The scenario 'an internal server must be reachable from the internet' is static NAT (or port forwarding). The trap is answering plain 'NAT' when the question is specifically counting addresses — read whether it says one public address or a pool.

front: Define inside local, inside global, outside local and outside global.
answer:
Inside local: your host's private address.
Inside global: the public address it is translated to.
Outside global: the destination's real public address.
Outside local: how the destination appears to your inside hosts (usually identical to outside global).
detail:
Two words, each with a fixed meaning. Inside/outside says whose network the host belongs to; local/global says which side of the NAT device you are looking from.
How it works
  • Inside means your network, outside means theirs: The first word never changes based on where you stand. Your web browser is always an inside host; the remote server is always an outside host.
  • Local means as seen inside, global means as seen outside: The second word is the viewpoint. Inside local 192.168.1.10 and inside global 203.0.113.5 are the same machine described from the two sides of the NAT router.
  • Outside local usually equals outside global: Unless you are doing destination NAT, the remote server has one address and both inside and outside hosts see it the same way. That is why this term is the one people forget.
  • The translation table stores the pairing: The NAT router keeps inside local ↔ inside global (plus ports, under PAT) so return traffic can be reversed correctly.
Where you see it
  • Reading show ip nat translations output
  • Troubleshooting why an inbound connection reaches the wrong internal host
  • Documenting a NAT design for a firewall change request
exam: This is pure terminology recall and CompTIA tests it by giving an address and asking which term applies. Anchor on the two most-tested: inside local = private address of your host, inside global = the public address it becomes. The distractor swaps local and global, since 'global' sounds like it might mean 'the far end'.

front: What problem does an FHRP solve, and how do VRRP and HSRP solve it?
answer: Hosts have exactly one default gateway address, which is a single point of failure. An FHRP lets two or more routers share a virtual IP and virtual MAC, so one can fail without any host reconfiguring. VRRP is the open standard; HSRP and GLBP are Cisco.
detail:
First Hop Redundancy Protocol. It exists because the default gateway is configured statically or by DHCP on every host, and changing it across a subnet during an outage is not feasible.
How it works
  • Hosts point at a virtual IP, not a real one: The gateway address configured on every host belongs to the FHRP group, not to any single router. Whichever router is currently active answers for it.
  • The virtual MAC is what makes failover invisible: Hosts have ARP entries mapping the gateway IP to a MAC. The standby router takes over the same virtual MAC, so existing ARP caches stay valid and no host needs to re-ARP.
  • Routers elect an active/master by priority: One router forwards; the others listen to its hello messages. If those stop, the highest-priority standby takes over within seconds. VRRP calls them master and backup, HSRP calls them active and standby.
  • GLBP adds load balancing: Plain HSRP and VRRP leave the standby router idle. GLBP hands out different virtual MACs to different hosts so multiple routers forward simultaneously.
Where you see it
  • Dual routers or firewalls providing a redundant default gateway for a VLAN
  • Multilayer switch pairs providing redundant SVIs for user subnets
  • Maintaining connectivity through a planned router reboot
exam: The exam scenario is 'the default gateway must remain available if a router fails' — the answer is FHRP, or specifically VRRP or HSRP. The discriminator it tests is vendor: VRRP is the open standard, HSRP and GLBP are Cisco. Distractors are load balancers, STP and link aggregation — none of which protect a gateway address.

front: What is a subinterface, and how does router-on-a-stick route between VLANs?
answer: A subinterface is a logical division of one physical router interface, each assigned a VLAN ID and an IP address. Router-on-a-stick uses one 802.1Q trunk to the switch, with one subinterface per VLAN acting as that VLAN's gateway.
detail:
A design for routing between VLANs when you have a router with few interfaces and a switch that cannot route. One physical link carries every VLAN, tagged.
How it works
  • One physical link, many logical gateways: Interface Gi0/0 is subdivided into Gi0/0.10, Gi0/0.20 and so on. Each subinterface is configured with its VLAN's 802.1Q tag and holds the gateway IP for that subnet.
  • The link must be a trunk on both ends: The switch port is configured as an 802.1Q trunk carrying all the routed VLANs. If it stays an access port, only one VLAN arrives and the other subinterfaces never see traffic.
  • Traffic crosses the link twice: A packet from VLAN 10 to VLAN 20 travels up the trunk to the router, gets routed, and comes back down the same trunk. The single link is the bandwidth bottleneck of the whole design.
  • Tag handling must match: Each subinterface is told which VLAN ID to expect. A mismatch between the subinterface's VLAN and the switch's trunk configuration silently breaks that VLAN only.
Where you see it
  • A small office with one router and a Layer 2 switch serving several VLANs
  • Adding inter-VLAN routing without buying a Layer 3 switch
  • Firewalling between VLANs by routing them all through one firewall interface
exam: The exam names this scenario directly: 'inter-VLAN routing using a single router interface'. The answer is router-on-a-stick with subinterfaces on an 802.1Q trunk. Its stated drawback is that all inter-VLAN traffic shares one physical link. The contrasting answer, when the question mentions a multilayer switch or higher performance, is an SVI.

front: What is route summarization, and what does it require?
answer: Advertising several contiguous networks as one shorter prefix — for example 192.168.0.0/24 through 192.168.3.0/24 becoming 192.168.0.0/22. It requires the networks to be contiguous and correctly aligned on a block boundary.
detail:
Also called supernetting or aggregation. It shrinks routing tables and, more importantly, hides instability inside one part of the network from all the others.
How it works
  • Fewer entries means less memory and faster lookups: Four routes become one. Across a large network with hundreds of subnets, that is the difference between a manageable table and an unmanageable one.
  • It contains flapping: If one of the four subnets goes up and down, the summary stays valid the whole time and is never withdrawn. Routers outside the summarizing router never see the churn and never recompute.
  • The blocks must be contiguous and aligned: 192.168.0.0/22 covers exactly 0, 1, 2 and 3. You cannot summarize 192.168.1.0/24 through 192.168.4.0/24 into one clean prefix because the range does not start on a /22 boundary.
  • Over-summarizing black-holes traffic: If the summary advertises addresses you do not actually have, traffic for those addresses is drawn to you and then dropped. The summary must not be larger than the real address space behind it.
Where you see it
  • Advertising a whole branch site as one prefix to the WAN core
  • Designing an IP addressing plan so each region is summarizable
  • Reducing OSPF inter-area or BGP advertisement size
exam: The exam usually gives four contiguous /24s and asks for the single summary prefix, so be able to do the arithmetic: four /24s aggregate to a /22, two to a /23, eight to a /21. It also asks for the benefit — the answer is smaller routing tables and reduced update traffic, not increased speed of individual packets.

front: What is asymmetric routing, and why does it break stateful firewalls?
answer: Traffic leaves by one path and returns by a different one. A stateful firewall on either path sees only half the conversation, has no matching session entry for the return traffic, and drops it.
detail:
Asymmetric paths are normal and harmless on the internet. They become an outage the moment a device in the path needs to see both directions.
How it works
  • A stateful firewall builds a session on the first packet: It records source, destination, ports and TCP state when the outbound SYN passes. Return packets are permitted because they match that session.
  • A return packet arriving at a different firewall matches nothing: The second firewall never saw the SYN. It sees an unsolicited SYN-ACK or mid-stream data, which fails its state check, and drops it silently. The user sees a connection that opens and then hangs.
  • Other stateful devices break the same way: IPS and IDS inspection, NAT translation tables, WAN optimizers and load balancers all depend on seeing both directions. NAT in particular has no translation entry to reverse.
  • It usually appears after a redundancy change: Adding a second internet circuit, a second firewall or an FHRP pair frequently introduces asymmetry. Fixes are pinning routes so both directions use one path, or clustering the firewalls so they share state.
Where you see it
  • Troubleshooting sessions that establish and then stall after adding a second WAN link
  • Explaining why a firewall pair must be state-synchronized
  • Diagnosing intermittent failures in a dual-homed data center
exam: CompTIA presents this as a symptom-to-cause question: after adding a redundant path, some connections fail while ping still works. The answer is asymmetric routing. The reason is that the firewall is stateful — that word is the key to the question. Distractors are MTU mismatch and duplex mismatch, which produce different symptoms.

front: 802.11a, 802.11b and 802.11g — band and maximum data rate for each?
detail:
The three original generations. 802.11a and 802.11b were released together in 1999 in different bands; 802.11g arrived in 2003 and brought the faster 5 GHz encoding down into the 2.4 GHz band.
How it works
  • a and b are the same age, not a progression: The letters are allocation order, not speed order. 802.11a is the faster of the two even though it comes first alphabetically. They use different bands, so an 802.11a radio and an 802.11b radio cannot hear each other at all.
  • The speed difference is the modulation: 802.11b uses DSSS and tops out at 11 Mbps. 802.11a and 802.11g use OFDM, which packs far more bits into the same 20 MHz, giving 54 Mbps.
  • 802.11g is backward compatible with 802.11b: Both live in 2.4 GHz, so a g AP will serve a b client. The cost is protection mechanisms: when a legacy b client associates, the AP adds overhead frames so the slow radio can hear the medium, and the whole cell slows down.
  • All three are single-stream, 20 MHz: No MIMO, no channel bonding. One radio chain, one 20 MHz channel. That is the ceiling on all of them.
Where you see it
  • Legacy barcode scanners, handheld terminals and building-control devices still on 802.11b/g
  • Explaining why one old client can drag an entire 2.4 GHz cell down
  • Deciding whether a device can use 5 GHz at all
exam: CompTIA loves the a-versus-b band trap. If a question says a client can only see the 2.4 GHz SSID, 802.11a is the wrong answer because 802.11a is 5 GHz only. The other reliable pattern is a scenario where 'the wireless got slower after a new device joined' — that is an 802.11b client forcing protection mode on a 2.4 GHz cell.

front: 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) — bands, maximum rate, and the feature that defines it?
answer: 2.4 and 5 GHz, up to 600 Mbps. Defined by MIMO and channel bonding to 40 MHz.
detail:
The first generation to break past 54 Mbps. It did that by transmitting several independent data streams at once over multiple antennas, and by doubling the channel width.
How it works
  • MIMO with spatial streams: Multiple transmit and receive antennas send different data simultaneously on the same channel. The receiver separates the streams using the fact that each took a slightly different path. 802.11n allows up to four spatial streams.
  • Channel bonding to 40 MHz: Two adjacent 20 MHz channels are joined into one 40 MHz channel, roughly doubling capacity. This is workable on 5 GHz and destructive on 2.4 GHz, where it consumes most of the usable band.
  • The 600 Mbps figure is theoretical: 600 Mbps requires four spatial streams, a 40 MHz channel and the short guard interval, all at once. Real 802.11n clients were typically two-stream and saw a fraction of that.
  • Dual band, and the first to be so: 802.11n operates in both 2.4 and 5 GHz. This is what made dual-band APs and, later, band steering meaningful.
Where you see it
  • The oldest generation still commonly found in production networks
  • Printers, IP cameras and IoT devices that are 2.4 GHz 802.11n only
  • Explaining why a '300 Mbps' consumer router never delivers 300 Mbps
exam: Two facts get tested: 802.11n is the first dual-band standard, and it introduced MIMO. If a question asks which standard first allowed multiple spatial streams, the answer is n, not ac — ac introduced multi-user MIMO, which is a different thing. Watch for a distractor claiming 802.11n is 5 GHz only; that is 802.11ac.

front: 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) — band, maximum rate, and the features that define it?
answer: 5 GHz only, up to roughly 6.9 Gbps. Defined by 80/160 MHz channels, 256-QAM, and downlink MU-MIMO.
detail:
A 5 GHz-only speed upgrade. It scaled the same ideas 802.11n introduced — wider channels, more streams, denser modulation — and added the ability to talk to several clients at once in the downstream direction.
How it works
  • 5 GHz only, by design: There is no 802.11ac radio in 2.4 GHz. A dual-band 'ac' access point is running 802.11ac on 5 GHz and 802.11n on 2.4 GHz. This surprises people troubleshooting slow 2.4 GHz clients on a new AP.
  • Wider channels: 80 MHz is the practical norm and 160 MHz is optional. Bandwidth is the single biggest contributor to the headline rate, which is why the peak number is only reachable in a clean, empty spectrum.
  • 256-QAM: Denser modulation packs 8 bits per symbol instead of 802.11n's 6. It only works at high signal quality, so the top rates require the client to be close to the AP.
  • Downlink MU-MIMO: The AP can transmit to multiple clients simultaneously on different spatial streams. Uplink is still one client at a time — that limitation is what 802.11ax fixed.
  • Beamforming standardized: 802.11n had several incompatible beamforming schemes. 802.11ac defined one, so beamforming actually works between vendors.
Where you see it
  • The most common AP generation in existing office deployments
  • Justifying a move to 5 GHz for laptops and video traffic
  • Explaining why a phone reports 866 Mbps (two streams, 80 MHz, 256-QAM)
exam: The exam's favourite 802.11ac fact is that it is 5 GHz only. Expect a scenario where a 2.4 GHz-only IoT device cannot join a new 'Wi-Fi 5' network. Also know that 802.11ac's MU-MIMO is downlink only — if a question contrasts ac with ax, uplink MU-MIMO and OFDMA are the ax answers.

front: 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) — bands, maximum rate, and what it was actually designed to fix?
answer: 2.4 and 5 GHz (6 GHz as Wi-Fi 6E), up to 9.6 Gbps. Designed for efficiency in dense environments, not peak speed: OFDMA, uplink and downlink MU-MIMO, 1024-QAM, BSS coloring, TWT.
detail:
The first generation whose headline goal was capacity per area rather than speed per client. It targets rooms full of devices — lecture halls, stadiums, open offices — where the problem is contention, not link rate.
How it works
  • OFDMA is the centrepiece: A channel is divided into resource units so the AP can serve several clients inside one transmission instead of giving each the whole channel in turn. This is what cuts latency and airtime waste with many small packets.
  • MU-MIMO in both directions: 802.11ax extends multi-user MIMO to the uplink, so multiple clients can transmit simultaneously under AP scheduling rather than contending.
