  • 1024-QAM: 10 bits per symbol, about 25% more than 256-QAM, but only at very high signal quality and short range.
  • It works in 2.4 GHz too: Unlike 802.11ac, 802.11ax is defined for both legacy bands, which is why Wi-Fi 6 improves crowded 2.4 GHz IoT deployments as well.
  • BSS coloring and TWT: Coloring reduces unnecessary deferral between overlapping cells; Target Wake Time schedules when battery devices must be awake. Both are about efficiency, not raw rate.
Where you see it
  • High-density deployments: auditoriums, classrooms, conference centres, warehouses
  • IoT and sensor fleets where battery life matters
  • Networks where per-client experience degrades as the client count climbs
exam: The trap is answering 'faster' when the question describes a density problem. If a scenario says an auditorium has adequate signal but terrible performance when 300 devices connect, the answer is 802.11ax/OFDMA, not a wider channel or more transmit power. Know the pairing: OFDMA solves many-small-clients; MU-MIMO solves simultaneous streams; 1024-QAM only raises the ceiling for close clients.

front: What is Wi-Fi 6E, and how is it different from Wi-Fi 6?
answer: The same 802.11ax standard extended into the 6 GHz band (5.925–7.125 GHz in the US, about 1200 MHz of new spectrum). Not a new standard — a new band.
detail:
A regulatory event more than a technical one. Regulators opened 6 GHz for unlicensed use, and 6E is 802.11ax operating there.
How it works
  • It is spectrum, not protocol: A Wi-Fi 6E AP runs identical 802.11ax mechanics. What changed is that there is suddenly room for many wide, clean channels — enough for multiple non-overlapping 160 MHz channels.
  • No legacy devices exist there: Nothing older than 6E can transmit in 6 GHz, so there are no 802.11b/g/n/ac clients forcing protection mechanisms and no legacy interference. That is a large part of the performance benefit.
  • Range is shorter: Higher frequency means more free-space loss and worse wall penetration than 5 GHz. Expect to need more APs for the same coverage.
  • Power classes replace DFS: 6 GHz uses low-power indoor and standard-power classes with automated frequency coordination rather than the DFS radar-avoidance scheme used at 5 GHz.
Where you see it
  • Greenfield high-density deployments where clean spectrum matters more than range
  • Offloading modern laptops and phones off congested 5 GHz
  • Wireless backhaul and AR/VR traffic needing wide channels
exam: The exam wants you to know 6E is 802.11ax in 6 GHz and requires 6E-capable clients — an existing Wi-Fi 6 laptop cannot use it. If a scenario says new APs were installed but only two devices can see the new fast SSID, missing 6E client support is the cause. Do not confuse Wi-Fi 6E with Wi-Fi 7.

front: What is Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) and what defines it?
answer: The newest generation, across 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. Defined by 320 MHz channels, 4096-QAM, and Multi-Link Operation (MLO).
detail:
An extension of the Wi-Fi 6 approach with wider channels, denser modulation, and the ability for one client to use several bands at the same time instead of picking one.
How it works
  • 320 MHz channels: Double the widest Wi-Fi 6 channel. Only 6 GHz has enough contiguous spectrum for this, so the headline rates are 6 GHz rates.
  • 4096-QAM: 12 bits per symbol instead of 1024-QAM's 10 — about 20% more throughput at very high signal quality, and only at short range.
  • Multi-Link Operation is the real change: A client can associate over 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz simultaneously and either aggregate them for throughput or use the best one per frame for latency and reliability. Previous generations forced a single band choice.
  • Peak numbers vary by how they are counted: Vendors quote figures from roughly 23 Gbps on one link up to about 46 Gbps aggregated. Treat the features, not the number, as the exam-relevant part.
Where you see it
  • Low-latency use cases: wireless VR, real-time video production, cloud gaming
  • Roaming and reliability improvements where a single band is unreliable
  • New builds where clients are expected to be 6 GHz-capable
exam: N10-009 expects recognition, not depth. Know that 802.11be = Wi-Fi 7, that it uses all three bands, and that MLO is its distinguishing feature. The likely distractor is attributing MLO or 320 MHz to Wi-Fi 6E, which is still 802.11ax with 160 MHz channels.

front: What channel widths does Wi-Fi use, and what is the trade-off in widening one?
answer: 20, 40, 80, 160 MHz (320 MHz in Wi-Fi 7). Wider channels give more throughput but leave fewer non-overlapping channels and raise the noise floor, so cells interfere with each other.
detail:
Channel width is bandwidth in the literal sense: more spectrum per transmission means more bits per second. The spectrum is finite, so every doubling halves the number of distinct channels available.
How it works
  • Throughput scales roughly with width: Doubling from 20 to 40 MHz roughly doubles the data rate for a single client with a strong signal. This is why consumer routers ship bonded by default.
  • Reuse collapses as width grows: 5 GHz has roughly 24 non-overlapping 20 MHz channels in the US. At 80 MHz that becomes about six, and at 160 MHz only one or two once DFS restrictions are applied. In a multi-AP deployment you then cannot avoid reusing channels.
  • Wider channels also hear more noise: A wider receiver takes in more of the noise floor, so a 160 MHz link needs a stronger signal than a 20 MHz link to reach the same modulation. Range effectively shortens.
  • 2.4 GHz should stay at 20 MHz: The whole band is only about 80 MHz wide. A single 40 MHz channel consumes most of it and destroys the 1/6/11 plan for every neighbour.
Where you see it
  • Choosing 20 or 40 MHz on 5 GHz for a dense multi-AP office
  • Diagnosing a network that got slower after someone enabled 80 MHz everywhere
  • Planning 160 MHz only where 6 GHz spectrum is available
exam: Expect a scenario where an administrator widens channels to 'improve speed' in a dense office and performance drops. The answer is that wider channels reduced channel reuse and increased co-channel interference; the fix is to go back to narrower channels. On 2.4 GHz, 20 MHz is always the correct answer.

front: Why are only channels 1, 6 and 11 used on 2.4 GHz?
answer: The band holds 11 usable channels in the US spaced 5 MHz apart, but each channel is 20 MHz wide. Only channels five apart do not overlap — so 1, 6 and 11 are the only three that fit without partially covering each other.
detail:
The 2.4 GHz channel numbering describes centre frequencies, not separate slots. The channels were defined to overlap, and the 1/6/11 plan is the workaround.
How it works
  • Centre frequencies are 5 MHz apart: Channel 1 is centred at 2412 MHz, channel 2 at 2417, and so on to channel 11 at 2462. The numbering suggests eleven independent channels.
  • Each transmission is 20 MHz wide: A 20 MHz signal extends about 10 MHz either side of its centre. Channel 1 therefore occupies roughly 2402–2422 MHz, which covers channels 2, 3 and 4 entirely.
  • Five channels apart is the minimum separation: 5 MHz × 5 = 25 MHz between centres, which just clears two 20 MHz signals. That gives 1, 6 and 11 — three non-overlapping channels total.
  • Region matters: Some regulatory domains permit channels 12–14, which changes the plan. North America is 1–11, and the exam assumes it.
Where you see it
  • Assigning channels across APs on a floor so neighbouring cells never share or overlap
  • Explaining why a neighbour's AP on channel 3 harms your channel 1 and channel 6 cells
  • Justifying a policy of never bonding channels on 2.4 GHz
exam: This is a guaranteed exam item, usually phrased as 'which channels are non-overlapping in the 2.4 GHz band'. The answer is 1, 6, 11. The trap is a distractor like 1, 5, 9 or 1, 6, 12. Be ready for the follow-up asking why: channels are 5 MHz apart but 20 MHz wide.

front: Co-channel vs adjacent-channel interference — what does each actually do?
answer:
Co-channel (CCI): APs on the same channel hear each other and take turns — throughput is shared, not corrupted.
Adjacent-channel (ACI): APs on partially overlapping channels cannot decode each other, so they transmit over each other and frames are corrupted.
detail:
Both are contention problems, but only one of them destroys frames. Understanding the difference is what makes 1/6/11 non-negotiable.
How it works
  • Wi-Fi is CSMA/CA — devices listen before transmitting: A radio senses the medium and defers if it hears another Wi-Fi transmission it can decode. Co-channel neighbours are decodable, so they politely queue behind each other.
  • Co-channel costs airtime: Two APs on channel 6 in earshot each get roughly half the airtime. Latency rises and throughput falls, but frames still arrive intact. It is degradation, not failure.
  • Adjacent-channel causes corruption: An AP on channel 3 overlaps channels 1 and 6 but is not decodable by either, so neither defers. The signals collide, the CRC fails, and the frame is retransmitted — burning airtime twice and raising the noise floor.
  • This is why ACI is worse: Co-channel interference degrades gracefully; adjacent-channel interference produces retries, low data rates and unexplained packet loss. It is the classic symptom of a rogue or consumer AP set to channel 3 or 9.
Where you see it
  • Reading a site survey and deciding whether a neighbouring AP is a nuisance or a real problem
  • Explaining unexplained retransmissions to an application team
  • Justifying a channel plan of 1/6/11 rather than 'spread them out'
exam: The exam contrasts these directly. Remember: co-channel = shared airtime, still works; adjacent-channel = collisions and retries, worse. If a scenario describes high retransmission counts and a rogue AP found on channel 4, the answer is adjacent-channel interference. If it describes slow speeds with many APs all on channel 1, that is co-channel.

front: 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz vs 6 GHz — the trade-offs.
answer:
2.4 GHz: best range and wall penetration, only 3 clean channels, heavily polluted.
5 GHz: ~24 channels, much faster, shorter range, some channels need DFS.
6 GHz: ~1200 MHz of clean spectrum, shortest range, 6E/7 clients only.
detail:
Lower frequencies travel further and through more material; higher frequencies carry more data and have more room. Every wireless design decision sits somewhere on that line.
How it works
  • Range and penetration fall as frequency rises: A 2.4 GHz signal will cross two interior walls where a 6 GHz signal will not. This is physics, not vendor implementation, and no amount of transmit power fixes the asymmetry — the client still has to reply.
  • 2.4 GHz shares its band with everything: Microwave ovens, Bluetooth, cordless phones, wireless cameras, Zigbee and baby monitors all sit in 2.4 GHz. Non-Wi-Fi interference does not defer politely; it simply raises the noise floor.
  • 5 GHz has channels but also rules: Roughly half of the 5 GHz channels are DFS channels that must vacate when radar is detected. Some client devices will not use DFS channels at all, which quietly shrinks the usable plan.
  • 6 GHz is clean but exclusive: No legacy clients, no legacy protection overhead, wide channels available. The cost is coverage area and that only Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 devices can use it.
Where you see it
  • Deciding which band an IoT sensor fleet should live on
  • Explaining why a warehouse keeps 2.4 GHz enabled despite congestion
  • Sizing AP count when moving a design from 5 GHz to 6 GHz
exam: Scenario questions usually give you a symptom and expect a band choice. 'Devices far from the AP keep dropping' points to keeping or using 2.4 GHz. 'Interference from a microwave / Bluetooth headsets' is always 2.4 GHz. 'Many channels available, need throughput' is 5 or 6 GHz. The common trap is treating 5 GHz as strictly better — its shorter range is a real design constraint.

front: What is CSMA/CA, and why does Wi-Fi use it instead of CSMA/CD?
answer: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance. A station listens, waits a random backoff, transmits, and waits for an ACK. Wireless radios cannot hear while transmitting, so collisions cannot be detected — only avoided.
detail:
The wireless medium is half-duplex and shared, and a transmitting radio is deaf to everything else. That single fact forces a different access method than wired Ethernet used.
How it works
  • A radio cannot listen while it transmits: Its own signal is millions of times stronger than any incoming one. Collision detection, which Ethernet used, is physically impossible, so Wi-Fi has to avoid collisions in advance.
  • Listen, backoff, transmit: A station senses the channel idle, waits an interframe space plus a random backoff counter, then transmits. The randomness is what keeps two waiting stations from firing simultaneously.
  • Every unicast frame is acknowledged: The receiver sends an ACK. No ACK means the sender assumes a collision and retransmits with a longer backoff. This is why interference shows up as retransmissions and falling data rates.
  • Optional RTS/CTS for hidden nodes: Two clients may hear the AP but not each other. RTS/CTS makes the AP announce the reservation so both defer. It costs overhead, which is why it is used selectively.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why airtime, not bandwidth, is the scarce resource on Wi-Fi
  • Diagnosing the hidden node problem in a long corridor or warehouse
  • Understanding why one slow client consumes disproportionate airtime
exam: The exam tests the contrast: wired Ethernet used CSMA/CD, wireless uses CSMA/CA. The reason — a radio cannot detect collisions while transmitting — is frequently the actual question. Also know that Wi-Fi is half-duplex; a distractor claiming full-duplex operation for an AP is wrong.

front: MIMO vs MU-MIMO — what is the difference?
answer:
MIMO: multiple antennas send multiple spatial streams to one client at a time, raising that client's rate.
MU-MIMO: the AP sends different streams to several clients simultaneously, raising total cell capacity.
detail:
Both use multiple antennas, but they solve different problems. MIMO makes one conversation faster; MU-MIMO lets several conversations happen at once.
How it works
  • Spatial streams exploit multipath: Signals bouncing off walls arrive by different paths. A multi-antenna receiver uses those path differences to separate simultaneous streams that share the same channel. Multipath, historically a problem, becomes the mechanism.
  • Notation is TX×RX:streams: A 4×4:4 AP has four transmit chains, four receive chains and four spatial streams. A client capped at two streams cannot use more than two, regardless of the AP.
  • MU-MIMO needs spatial separation: Clients must be far enough apart, direction-wise, for the AP to aim distinct streams at them. Clients sitting together get little benefit.
  • Direction matters by generation: 802.11ac added downlink MU-MIMO only. 802.11ax added uplink MU-MIMO, so multiple clients can transmit at once under AP scheduling.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why a 4×4 AP does not make a 1×1 IoT device faster
  • Reading AP datasheets when sizing a high-density deployment
  • Deciding whether MU-MIMO or OFDMA addresses a given density problem
exam: The exam separates these two cleanly: MIMO is one client, more streams; MU-MIMO is multiple clients at once. Remember 802.11n introduced MIMO, 802.11ac introduced downlink MU-MIMO, and 802.11ax added uplink MU-MIMO. A common distractor swaps MU-MIMO and OFDMA — MU-MIMO separates clients by space, OFDMA separates them by frequency.

front: What is OFDMA and what problem does it solve?
answer: Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access — introduced in Wi-Fi 6. It splits a channel into resource units so the AP can serve several clients inside one transmission instead of giving each the entire channel in turn.
detail:
In earlier generations, every transmission occupied the whole channel no matter how small the payload. OFDMA ends that waste by subdividing the channel in frequency.
How it works
  • Before OFDMA, small frames wasted the channel: A 100-byte sensor reading took the entire 80 MHz channel for its turn. With hundreds of small-packet devices, most airtime went to overhead and turn-taking rather than data.
  • Resource units are frequency subdivisions: The AP allocates portions of the channel's subcarriers to different clients within the same transmit opportunity, then tells each client which portion is theirs.
  • The AP schedules, it does not just contend: OFDMA makes the AP a coordinator. Downlink and, with Wi-Fi 6, uplink allocations are scheduled, which is why latency and jitter improve so much in dense cells.
  • It improves efficiency, not peak rate: A single client alone with the AP sees no OFDMA benefit. The gains appear as client count rises.
Where you see it
  • Lecture halls, stadiums, and open-plan offices with hundreds of clients
  • IoT and sensor networks generating constant small packets
  • Latency-sensitive traffic like voice on a busy cell
exam: The contrast CompTIA uses is OFDMA divides by frequency, MU-MIMO divides by space. If a question describes many clients each sending small amounts of data with rising latency, the answer is OFDMA. If it describes wanting to send full streams to several distant clients at once, that is MU-MIMO. Do not confuse OFDMA with OFDM, which is the underlying modulation used since 802.11a.

front: What is beamforming?
answer: Shaping the transmitted signal so the copies arriving at a specific client's location add constructively, instead of radiating power evenly in all directions. Result: stronger signal and a higher data rate for that client.
detail:
An antenna array can control the relative phase of each element. Adjusting those phases steers where the energy concentrates without physically moving anything.
How it works
  • It is phase control, not more power: Total transmit power is unchanged. The AP times each antenna's transmission so the waves reinforce at the target and partially cancel elsewhere. Regulatory power limits are not exceeded.
  • It requires knowing the channel: The AP sends sounding frames; the client replies with feedback describing how the signal arrived. The AP uses that to compute the phases. This is explicit beamforming, standardized in 802.11ac.
  • Both ends must support it: The beamformer (usually the AP) and the beamformee (the client) both need the capability. A legacy client gets no benefit.
  • The gain is rate, not coverage area: Beamforming typically lets an existing client sustain a higher modulation rather than dramatically extending the edge of the cell.
Where you see it
  • Improving throughput to clients at the edge of a cell
  • Multi-user MIMO, which depends on beamforming to aim streams at separate clients
  • Reducing retransmissions in environments with heavy multipath
exam: Keep beamforming distinct from a directional antenna. Beamforming is dynamic and per-client, done in software by an antenna array; a directional antenna is a fixed physical shape. The exam uses that contrast. Also know that 802.11ac standardized beamforming — 802.11n's versions were vendor-specific and rarely interoperable.

front: What do BSS coloring and TWT do in Wi-Fi 6?
answer:
BSS coloring: tags frames with a short BSS identifier so a radio can tell 'my cell' from 'a neighbour's cell' and stop deferring unnecessarily — it recovers airtime lost to co-channel interference.
TWT (Target Wake Time): the AP schedules when each client must be awake, so battery devices sleep far longer.
detail:
Two Wi-Fi 6 efficiency features. One reclaims wasted airtime between overlapping cells; the other reclaims battery life on low-power clients.
How it works
  • Coloring changes the deferral threshold: Under plain CSMA/CA a radio defers to any decodable Wi-Fi transmission, including a distant neighbouring AP on the same channel. With a different BSS color, the radio can apply a more aggressive threshold and transmit anyway.
  • The color is a small field in the PHY header: It is read before decoding the rest of the frame, so the decision to defer or not is made immediately and cheaply.
  • Coloring mitigates co-channel interference; it does not remove it: It reduces unnecessary waiting when channels must be reused. A good channel plan is still required.
  • TWT is negotiated scheduling: The client and AP agree on a wake schedule. Between those times the radio is fully off rather than periodically waking to check for buffered traffic — a large difference for a sensor expected to run for years.
Where you see it
  • Dense deployments where channel reuse is unavoidable and cells overlap
  • Battery-powered IoT: sensors, badges, medical telemetry, asset tags
  • Explaining why Wi-Fi 6 helps even when clients are not faster
exam: Both appear as 'which Wi-Fi 6 feature' items. Match them to the symptom: battery life or device sleep → TWT; overlapping cells wasting airtime → BSS coloring. The distractors are usually OFDMA and MU-MIMO, which are about capacity and simultaneity, not deferral or power.

front: SSID vs BSSID vs ESSID
answer:
SSID: the network name clients see.
BSSID: the MAC address of one AP radio serving that name — unique per radio per SSID.
ESSID: the same SSID advertised by multiple APs so clients can roam between them.
detail:
Three terms that sound interchangeable and are not. One is a name, one is a hardware address, and one describes a group of APs sharing the name.
How it works
  • The SSID is just a label: Up to 32 characters, carried in beacons. It has no security value at all — hiding it only removes it from beacons, and the name still appears in client probe requests.
  • The BSSID identifies the actual radio: It is normally derived from the AP's MAC address. An AP with 2.4 and 5 GHz radios and three SSIDs presents six different BSSIDs. This is how a client knows which specific AP it is associated to.
  • ESSID is the roaming domain: When several APs advertise the same SSID with the same security settings, a client can move between them without the user noticing. Each AP still has its own BSSID.
  • Tools show all three: A wireless survey tool lists SSID (name), BSSID (which radio), channel and signal. Identifying a rogue AP means matching BSSIDs, not names, because names can be copied.
Where you see it
  • Reading a site survey or netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid output
  • Tracking which physical AP a complaining user is actually attached to
  • Detecting an evil twin by finding an unfamiliar BSSID advertising your SSID
exam: The exam asks this as a definition-matching item. Anchor on the word MAC: BSSID is a MAC address. A frequent scenario is 'a client reports the right SSID but poor performance — how do you tell which AP it is on?' — the answer is the BSSID. Also expect the point that disabling SSID broadcast is not a security control.

front: Why are WEP and TKIP deprecated?
answer: WEP uses RC4 with a 24-bit IV that repeats quickly, letting the key be recovered from captured traffic in minutes. TKIP (WPA) was a software-compatible patch on the same RC4 hardware and inherits its weaknesses. Both are broken; use AES-based WPA2 or WPA3.
detail:
The first two attempts at wireless encryption. Both were designed under constraints that made them weak, and both are now trivially attacked.
How it works
  • WEP's initialization vector is too small: The 24-bit IV is sent in cleartext and repeats after a modest amount of traffic. Reused IVs with a static key let an attacker statistically recover the key from passively captured frames.
  • WEP has no real integrity check: It uses a CRC-32 checksum, which an attacker can adjust to match a modified packet. Frames can be altered in flight without detection.
  • TKIP was a compatibility bridge: WPA with TKIP added per-packet key mixing and a proper integrity check (Michael) so existing WEP hardware could be firmware-upgraded. It kept RC4, and it has since been broken as well.
  • Enabling TKIP also caps your speed: 802.11n and later refuse to negotiate high data rates when TKIP is in use, so a legacy setting silently forces the whole network down to legacy rates.
Where you see it
  • Auditing old APs, printers and industrial equipment still configured for WEP
  • Explaining why a Wi-Fi 6 AP runs at 54 Mbps after someone enabled WPA/TKIP compatibility
  • Wireless security assessments and compliance findings
exam: WEP appears as a wrong answer and as an audit finding. If a question asks for the weakest option, WEP is it. Know the chain in order: WEP (RC4, broken) → WPA/TKIP (RC4, deprecated) → WPA2/AES-CCMP → WPA3/SAE. The performance detail — TKIP forcing legacy data rates — is a favourite scenario twist.

front: WPA2 vs WPA3 — encryption and handshake.
answer:
WPA2: AES-CCMP, and a 4-way handshake from a pre-shared key — captureable and crackable offline.
WPA3: SAE replaces the PSK handshake, adds forward secrecy, mandates Protected Management Frames, and adds AES-GCMP-256 in the 192-bit Enterprise mode.
detail:
WPA3's improvements are mostly about the handshake and management frames, not about AES being broken. AES was and remains fine.
How it works
  • CCMP vs GCMP: Both are AES modes providing confidentiality plus integrity. CCMP-128 is WPA2's cipher and remains the WPA3-Personal baseline. GCMP-256 is faster in hardware and is required in WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode. The exam usually states this simply as CCMP for WPA2 and GCMP for WPA3.
  • The WPA2 4-way handshake leaks a crackable value: Anyone who captures the handshake — or forces a reconnection to capture one — can guess passphrases offline at full CPU or GPU speed with no further contact with the network. A weak PSK falls quickly.
  • SAE removes the offline attack: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals proves knowledge of the passphrase without exposing anything crackable offline. Every guess costs an online exchange, so a weak passphrase is dramatically harder to break.
  • Protected Management Frames are mandatory in WPA3: Management frames are authenticated, so forged deauthentication frames are rejected. That closes the deauth flood used to kick clients off and to force handshake captures.
  • Forward secrecy: Each session derives fresh keys. Traffic captured today cannot be decrypted later even if the passphrase is discovered.
Where you see it
  • Choosing the security mode when standing up a new SSID
  • Explaining why the same passphrase is more dangerous on WPA2 than WPA3
  • Transition mode SSIDs that accept both WPA2 and WPA3 clients
exam: The single most tested pairing is WPA2 = AES/CCMP with a 4-way handshake, WPA3 = SAE. If a question says an attacker captured the handshake and cracked the passphrase offline, the fix is WPA3/SAE, not a longer WEP key or hidden SSID. Watch for a distractor claiming WPA3 stopped using AES — it did not.

front: What is SAE and what attack does it stop?
answer: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (the Dragonfly handshake), used by WPA3-Personal. It proves both sides know the passphrase without transmitting anything an attacker can crack offline, defeating the offline dictionary attack against captured handshakes.
detail:
WPA2-Personal's weakness was never the encryption — it was that the key exchange gave an eavesdropper enough material to guess passwords at leisure. SAE removes that material.
How it works
  • The WPA2 problem it replaces: In WPA2-PSK, the 4-way handshake contains a value derived from the passphrase. Capture it once and you can test billions of candidate passphrases offline, entirely disconnected from the network.
  • SAE is a password-authenticated key exchange: Both sides run a commit-and-confirm exchange over elliptic-curve maths. The messages do not contain anything that can be tested against a guessed password after the fact.
  • Every guess must be made online: An attacker has to attempt an actual association per guess, which is slow, rate-limitable and visible in logs. A short passphrase is still weaker, but attacks become practically detectable.
  • It also gives forward secrecy: Session keys are freshly derived, so learning the passphrase later does not decrypt previously captured traffic.
Where you see it
  • Deploying WPA3-Personal on a network where the passphrase is widely known
  • Responding to a penetration test finding about captured WPA2 handshakes
  • Explaining why WPA3 helps even with an unchanged passphrase
exam: CompTIA asks this as 'what replaces the pre-shared key handshake in WPA3'. The answer is SAE, sometimes written as Dragonfly. The distractors are usually AES, EAP or 802.1X — note that 802.1X is the Enterprise alternative, a different axis entirely, while SAE is the Personal-mode improvement.

front: Personal (PSK) vs Enterprise (802.1X) wireless authentication.
answer:
Personal: one shared passphrase for every device. Simple; revoking access means changing it everywhere.
Enterprise: each user or device authenticates individually to a RADIUS server using EAP, with per-user credentials or certificates.
detail:
The difference is whether the network can distinguish one user from another. That determines whether you can revoke, log or differentiate access.
How it works
  • PSK gives everyone the same key: Any device holding the passphrase is equivalent to any other. There is no per-user identity, so logs show MAC addresses at best.
  • Revocation is the practical failure of PSK: When an employee leaves or a phone is lost, the only remedy is to change the passphrase and reconfigure every remaining device. This is why PSK does not scale.
  • Enterprise authenticates each identity: The client presents credentials or a certificate; the RADIUS server validates them against a directory. Revoking one account or certificate affects only that user.
  • Enterprise enables per-user policy: RADIUS can return attributes that place the user in a specific VLAN, apply an ACL, or limit session time. PSK cannot do any of this on a single SSID.
  • Both still encrypt the same way: The cipher (CCMP/GCMP) is unchanged. Personal versus Enterprise is about authentication, not encryption strength.
Where you see it
  • Corporate SSIDs backed by Active Directory or a certificate authority
  • Guest SSIDs, where PSK or an open network with a captive portal is normal
  • Onboarding and offboarding processes where access must be revoked per person
exam: The scenario is nearly always about revocation or accountability: 'the company must be able to disable one employee's wireless access without affecting others' — that is WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and RADIUS. The distractor is 'change the pre-shared key', which technically works but fails the 'without affecting others' clause.

front: In 802.1X, what are the three roles and what does each do?
answer:
Supplicant: the client device requesting access.
Authenticator: the AP or switch port that blocks traffic until authentication succeeds.
Authentication server: the RADIUS server that actually validates the credentials.
detail:
802.1X is port-based network access control. The device in the middle does not decide anything — it just enforces the answer it gets back.
How it works
  • The authenticator is a gate, not a judge: An AP or switch port in 802.1X mode passes only EAPOL frames until authentication completes. It forwards the EAP conversation to RADIUS and enforces the accept or reject it receives.
  • EAP is the conversation, RADIUS is the transport: EAP messages travel from supplicant to authenticator as EAPOL (EAP over LAN), and from authenticator to server inside RADIUS. Common methods are EAP-TLS (certificates both ways), PEAP and EAP-TTLS (server certificate plus inner credentials).
  • Success can carry policy: A RADIUS Access-Accept can include attributes assigning a VLAN or an ACL, which is how dynamic VLAN assignment by user identity works.
  • It is not wireless-only: The same three roles apply to a wired switch port. Wired 802.1X is the standard control for preventing unauthorized devices in network jacks.
Where you see it
  • Corporate Wi-Fi authenticating users against Active Directory
  • Wired port authentication in conference rooms and lobbies
  • Dynamic VLAN assignment based on user or device identity
exam: Role identification is the exam item: 'the switch acts as the ___' → authenticator. The common trap is calling the RADIUS server the authenticator. Also remember the protocol pairing: 802.1X uses EAP, carried over RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813). TACACS+ is device administration, not 802.1X network access.

front: What is WPS and why is it disabled?
answer: Wi-Fi Protected Setup — joining a network with a button press or an 8-digit PIN instead of the passphrase. The PIN is validated in two halves, which collapses the search space to a few thousand attempts, so it must be disabled.
detail:
A convenience feature for consumers that introduced a far weaker credential alongside a strong one. The weakest path in is the one attackers use.
How it works
  • The PIN is checked in two parts: The AP reveals whether the first four digits are correct before the rest is checked, and the last digit is a checksum. That reduces roughly 10 million combinations to about 11,000 — brute-forceable in hours.
  • Pixie Dust makes it worse: Weak nonce generation in many chipsets allows the PIN to be derived offline from a single exchange, in seconds.
  • It bypasses your good passphrase: A 30-character WPA2 passphrase is irrelevant if WPS is enabled, because WPS hands out the passphrase to anyone who guesses the PIN.
  • Push-button mode is safer but still a window: PBC requires physical access during a short window, which is acceptable at home and unacceptable in a public or shared building.
Where you see it
  • Hardening checklists for consumer and small-business APs
  • Vulnerability scan findings on branch office equipment
  • Explaining a wireless compromise where the passphrase was strong
exam: This appears as a hardening question: 'which feature should be disabled on the wireless router'. The answer is WPS. The reason CompTIA wants is the PIN brute force, not the push button. Expect it alongside other hardening answers — disable WPS, disable WEP/TKIP, change default credentials, disable remote management.

front: Antenna types, antenna gain, and EIRP.
answer:
Omnidirectional: coverage in all directions.
Directional (Yagi, parabolic, patch/panel): focused energy for range or point-to-point.
EIRP = transmit power + antenna gain − cable loss, and regulators cap it per band.
detail:
An antenna does not create energy; it redistributes it. Gain is a description of that reshaping, and EIRP is the number regulators actually limit.
How it works
  • Gain is shape, not amplification: A high-gain omni squashes the sphere of coverage into a flatter disc — more range horizontally, less above and below. Mounting a high-gain omni on a high ceiling can leave the floor beneath it poorly covered.
  • Directional types differ in beamwidth: A patch or panel antenna covers a wide sector and is used to push coverage away from a wall. A Yagi is narrower. A parabolic dish is narrowest and reaches furthest, and requires precise aiming.
  • EIRP is what leaves the antenna: Expressed in dBm: radio output power plus antenna gain minus loss in the cable and connectors. Two systems with very different transmit powers can have identical EIRP.
  • The cap forces a trade-off: Because the regulatory limit is on EIRP, adding a high-gain antenna usually means turning transmit power down. You are choosing the shape of the coverage, not simply getting more of it.
  • Link budget is bidirectional: A big antenna on the AP does not help if the client's small antenna cannot be heard on the return path. Coverage is limited by the weaker direction.
Where you see it
  • Building-to-building point-to-point bridges using parabolic or Yagi antennas
  • Patch antennas on a warehouse wall aiming coverage inward rather than into the car park
  • Calculating whether a proposed antenna and power setting stays legal
exam: Expect an antenna-selection scenario: 'connect two buildings 500 m apart' → a directional antenna at each end, usually parabolic or Yagi. 'Cover an open office floor from a central ceiling mount' → omnidirectional. For EIRP, know the formula and the implication that higher antenna gain generally requires lower transmit power to stay within limits.

front: Why is turning transmit power down sometimes the fix for a slow wireless network?
answer: High power makes cells too large. Cells overlap and create co-channel interference, distant clients associate at very low data rates and consume disproportionate airtime, and clients stop roaming. Smaller, cleaner cells usually perform better.
detail:
The instinct is that more power means better Wi-Fi. In a multi-AP deployment the opposite is often true, because coverage is not the same as capacity.
How it works
  • A slow client steals airtime from everyone: The medium is shared and time-based. A client transmitting at 6 Mbps occupies the channel far longer for the same data than one at 400 Mbps. One distant, weakly connected client can degrade the entire cell.
  • Oversized cells overlap: If every AP shouts, cells that should be separate hear each other, and co-channel interference forces them to take turns. Effective capacity drops even though signal bars look excellent.
  • Power is asymmetric: The AP may transmit at 20 dBm while a phone transmits at far less. Cranking AP power creates a cell where clients can hear the AP but the AP cannot hear them — the client shows full signal and still fails.
  • Low power encourages roaming: Clients roam when the current AP's signal degrades. If the old AP is still loud across the building, a sticky client never leaves it.
Where you see it
  • Remediating a high-density office where all APs were left at maximum power
  • Designing cell size deliberately in a site survey rather than accepting defaults
  • Fixing roaming complaints in a building with good coverage everywhere
exam: This is a favourite scenario reversal. The symptom is 'strong signal everywhere but poor throughput and clients not roaming'; the answer is reduce transmit power, not add APs or raise power. Watch for the asymmetry point too: full signal bars with failing uploads points to the client being unable to reach the AP.

front: RSSI vs SNR — which one actually determines your data rate?
answer:
RSSI: received signal strength, in dBm, always negative (−40 is strong, −80 is weak).
SNR: the gap in dB between the signal and the noise floor. SNR determines the achievable rate — a strong signal in a noisy environment still performs badly.
detail:
Signal strength alone does not tell you whether a receiver can decode anything. What matters is how far the signal stands above the noise.
How it works
  • RSSI is measured in negative dBm: Closer to zero is stronger. Roughly: −30 dBm is next to the AP, −67 dBm is a common design target for voice and video, −70 dBm is adequate for data, below −80 dBm is unusable.
  • The noise floor sets the baseline: A typical clean noise floor is around −95 dBm. Interference from non-Wi-Fi sources raises it. When the floor rises, the same RSSI yields a lower SNR and a lower data rate.
  • SNR is simply signal minus noise: An RSSI of −65 with a −95 noise floor gives 30 dB SNR — excellent. The same −65 with a −70 floor gives 5 dB — barely usable. Both clients report 'good signal'.
  • Rates step down as SNR falls: The radio picks a modulation it can decode reliably. Dense modulations like 1024-QAM need high SNR; as it falls the client drops to slower, more robust rates. This is why throughput degrades gradually rather than cutting out.
Where you see it
  • Interpreting site survey output and heat maps
  • Diagnosing a client with strong signal bars and poor performance
  • Setting design targets, commonly −67 dBm with 25 dB SNR for voice
exam: The exam sets up the trap explicitly: a user has a strong signal but a slow, unreliable connection. The answer is low SNR from interference, not weak signal. Remember RSSI is negative and closer to zero is better — a distractor offering '−40 dBm is a weak signal' is testing exactly that.

front: What is a wireless site survey and what does a heat map show?
answer: Measuring real RF conditions — signal strength, noise, channel usage and interference — so APs are placed, powered and channelled correctly. A heat map renders that as colour over a floor plan, exposing coverage holes and overlapping cells.
detail:
Wireless design cannot be done from a drawing alone, because walls, shelving, glass and metal change propagation in ways no formula predicts reliably.
How it works
  • Predictive survey comes first: Software models coverage from a floor plan with wall materials to produce a proposed AP count and placement. It is a starting point, not a result.
  • Passive and active surveys measure reality: A passive survey listens to what is on the air. An active survey associates and measures actual throughput, retries and roaming behaviour. Walking the site with a survey tool is what turns a prediction into a design.
  • Post-installation validation closes the loop: A survey after deployment confirms the design and finds what changed — a stacked warehouse aisle, a new glass partition, a neighbour's AP.
  • A spectrum analyzer finds non-Wi-Fi interference: Wi-Fi survey tools only see Wi-Fi. A microwave, a wireless camera or a bad power supply appears as a raised noise floor with no visible SSID. Identifying it needs a spectrum analyzer.
Where you see it
  • Planning AP count and placement before a build or office move
  • Diagnosing complaints of dead zones in a specific area
  • Documenting coverage after a change to shelving, walls or occupancy
exam: Two exam angles. First, the sequence: predictive → validation survey after install. Second, the tool choice: if the scenario says a non-Wi-Fi source is suspected, the answer is a spectrum analyzer, not a Wi-Fi analyzer. A heat map answers 'where is coverage weak', not 'what is causing interference'.

front: Autonomous vs lightweight access points, and what a WLC does.
answer:
Autonomous (fat) AP: self-contained, configured one at a time.
Lightweight (thin) AP: gets configuration and RF decisions from a wireless LAN controller. The WLC centralizes config, channel and power assignment, roaming and monitoring.
detail:
Managing twenty APs individually is tedious; managing two hundred is impossible, and individually configured APs cannot coordinate their radios with each other.
How it works
  • Autonomous APs are independent: Each holds its own SSIDs, security settings and radio configuration. A change means touching every unit, and each AP picks its channel and power without knowing what its neighbours chose.
  • Lightweight APs get everything from the controller: On boot, the AP discovers a controller, downloads its configuration, and builds a tunnel to it. Adding an AP is close to plug and play.
  • Centralized RF management is the real benefit: The WLC sees the whole deployment and can assign channels and power to minimize overlap, then adjust automatically when an AP fails by raising the power of its neighbours.
  • Roaming and policy become coherent: The controller can hold client state, coordinate fast roaming, apply consistent per-SSID policy and enforce client load balancing across APs.
  • Cloud-managed is the third model: The controller function lives in the provider's cloud. Configuration and monitoring are centralized; data forwarding usually stays local at the AP.
Where you see it
  • Campus and multi-floor deployments with dozens or hundreds of APs
  • Small offices where one or two autonomous APs are entirely appropriate
  • Explaining why a single AP outage is partly self-healing under a controller
exam: Scale is the trigger word. If a scenario describes many APs needing consistent configuration and coordinated channel or power management, the answer is lightweight APs with a WLC. Also know the failure implication: in a centrally switched design, losing the controller can disrupt wireless service, which is why controller redundancy is a standard exam-worthy design point.

front: Infrastructure vs ad hoc vs mesh vs point-to-point wireless.
answer:
Infrastructure: clients connect through an AP.
Ad hoc (IBSS): devices connect directly, no AP.
Mesh: APs relay to each other wirelessly, so only some need a cable.
Point-to-point: a directional link joining two locations.
detail:
Four arrangements of the same radios. What distinguishes them is whether there is a central AP and whether the APs use radio for backhaul.
How it works
  • Infrastructure is the default (BSS): One AP forms a basic service set. Clients talk to the AP, never directly to each other, even in the same room. Multiple APs sharing an SSID form an extended service set.
  • Ad hoc has no coordinator: Peer-to-peer with no AP and no central management, which means no controller-based security or roaming. Used for direct device-to-device transfers and some legacy equipment.
  • Mesh trades throughput for cabling: Mesh APs forward traffic to each other over the air. Every wireless hop shares airtime with client traffic, so throughput drops with each hop. Use it where running cable is impossible — outdoors, historic buildings, temporary sites.
  • Point-to-point is a wireless cable: Two directional antennas aimed at each other bridge two networks, typically between buildings. It needs clear line of sight and precise alignment.
Where you see it
  • Mesh APs across a campus courtyard or a warehouse yard
  • A point-to-point bridge linking a main office to an annex across a road
  • Ad hoc / direct connections for device pairing and file transfer
exam: Match topology to scenario wording. 'Two buildings, line of sight, no fibre available' → point-to-point with directional antennas. 'Extend coverage outdoors where running cable is not feasible' → mesh. 'Devices connect directly with no access point' → ad hoc. The trap on mesh is forgetting that each wireless hop cuts available throughput.

front: What is a captive portal and how is a guest network normally built?
answer: A captive portal intercepts a new client's first web request and redirects it to a page requiring acceptance of terms, a login, or a voucher before granting internet access. Guest networks pair it with a separate VLAN isolated from the internal network.
detail:
The requirement is to let visitors online without letting them onto the corporate network, and to establish that they accepted the acceptable-use policy.
How it works
  • Interception happens before routing is allowed: Until the client authorizes, the gateway permits only DNS and traffic to the portal, and redirects HTTP requests to it. This is why HTTPS-only devices sometimes fail to see the login page.
  • Isolation is the security control, not the portal: The guest SSID maps to its own VLAN with an ACL permitting internet only. The portal handles identity and terms; the VLAN and ACL prevent access to internal resources.
  • Client isolation stops guest-to-guest traffic: Also called AP isolation. It prevents wireless clients on the same SSID from reaching each other, which matters when strangers share a network.
  • Bandwidth limits protect the business: Per-client or per-SSID rate limiting keeps a guest streaming video from consuming the internet circuit that production traffic depends on.
Where you see it
  • Hotel, airport, café and conference-centre Wi-Fi
  • Corporate visitor SSIDs with terms-of-use acceptance for legal cover
  • Vendor and contractor access separated from the production network
exam: The exam pairs captive portal with guest network design. When asked how to give visitors internet access without exposing internal systems, the full answer is a separate guest VLAN/SSID with client isolation and an ACL, fronted by a captive portal. A portal alone is not an isolation control, and that is the distractor.

front: What is band steering?
answer: The AP nudges dual-band-capable clients onto 5 GHz (or 6 GHz) rather than letting them settle on the crowded 2.4 GHz band — usually by delaying or withholding responses to the client's 2.4 GHz probes.
detail:
Many clients default to whichever band they find first, and 2.4 GHz travels further so it is often found first. Band steering corrects that default.
How it works
  • The AP influences the client's choice: The client always decides which AP and band to associate with. The AP can only make 2.4 GHz look less attractive — typically by not answering, or answering slowly, on 2.4 GHz for clients it has seen on 5 GHz.
  • It requires the same SSID on both bands: If 2.4 and 5 GHz are advertised as separate SSIDs, there is nothing to steer; the user picks manually. One SSID across both bands is the prerequisite.
  • It relieves 2.4 GHz for devices that need it: Moving laptops and phones to 5 GHz leaves the three 2.4 GHz channels for IoT and legacy devices that have no alternative.
  • It can misfire at the cell edge: A client steered to 5 GHz at the edge of coverage may perform worse than it would have on 2.4 GHz. Aggressive steering thresholds cause sticky and unstable clients.
Where you see it
  • Mixed offices where laptops and phones should not sit on 2.4 GHz
  • Reducing 2.4 GHz congestion without disabling the band entirely
  • Troubleshooting a client that keeps landing on the wrong band
exam: Recognition-level item: band steering moves capable clients to the higher band. The distractor is client load balancing, which spreads clients across APs rather than across bands. Also remember the prerequisite that both bands share one SSID.

front: What is roaming, what is a sticky client, and why does roaming fail?
answer: Roaming is a client moving its association from one AP to another on the same ESSID. A sticky client holds onto a distant AP at a poor data rate instead of switching. Roaming fails from coverage gaps, excessive cell overlap, over-powered APs, or missing fast-roaming support.
detail:
The client, not the network, decides when to roam. Everything the network can do is indirect: shape coverage so the decision is obvious, and make the switch cheap when it happens.
How it works
  • The client owns the decision: Each vendor's driver uses its own signal thresholds and hysteresis. That is why two laptops in the same seat behave differently, and why network-side fixes are about influencing conditions.
  • Sticky clients are usually a power problem: If the original AP is still audible at a reasonable level across the building, the client's roam threshold is never crossed. Reducing transmit power shrinks cells so the old AP fades and the decision becomes clear.
  • Too little overlap creates gaps: Cells need enough overlap — commonly cited around 15–20% — for the client to find the next AP before losing the current one. Too little and the client disconnects instead of roaming.
  • Re-authentication is the delay: Without fast-roaming support, each roam on an 802.1X network repeats the full EAP exchange with RADIUS. That can take hundreds of milliseconds, which drops a voice call.
  • Same channel on both APs hides the alternative: If neighbouring APs share a channel, the client sees interference rather than a clearly better target, and roaming behaviour becomes erratic.
Where you see it
  • Voice-over-Wi-Fi handsets and warehouse scanners moving through a building
  • Complaints that Wi-Fi 'drops' when walking between floors or wings
  • Post-deployment tuning of transmit power and cell overlap
exam: The classic scenario: a user walks across the office and stays connected to the far AP with poor throughput. The answer is a sticky client, and the remediation is to lower transmit power and/or enable 802.11k/v so the client is told where to go. 'Increase transmit power' is the tempting wrong answer.

answer:
802.11r: Fast BSS Transition — pre-establishes keys so a roam does not repeat the full authentication.
802.11k: neighbour reports — tells the client which APs are nearby and on what channel.
802.11v: BSS Transition Management — lets the network suggest that a client move to a specific AP.
detail:
Three amendments that together make roaming fast and informed. Each fixes a different part of the problem: the delay, the client's ignorance, and the client's stubbornness.
How it works
  • 802.11r removes the re-authentication delay: Key material is derived in advance and shared, so the client can transition in a few milliseconds instead of running a fresh EAP/RADIUS exchange. This is what keeps a voice call alive across a roam.
  • 802.11k tells the client where to look: Without it, a roaming client must scan all channels to find candidates, which interrupts traffic. A neighbour report hands it a short list, so the scan is fast and targeted.
  • 802.11v lets the network ask the client to move: A BSS transition management frame suggests a better AP. The client can still refuse — this is a request, not a command — but most modern clients cooperate.
  • They are complementary, not alternatives: k informs, v suggests, r accelerates. Deployments usually enable all three, though some older clients misbehave with 802.11r and may need it disabled per SSID.
Where you see it
  • Voice over Wi-Fi, where roam times above roughly 50 ms are audible
  • Handheld scanners and medical devices moving continuously through a facility
  • Reducing sticky-client behaviour without lowering power further
exam: Memorize the letter-to-function mapping — it is asked directly. The mnemonic that works: k = know your neighbours, v = move (steering), r = re-authenticate fast. The exam's scenario framing is usually a dropped VoIP call while walking, where 802.11r is the answer.

front: What are DFS and TPC, and what is 802.11h?
answer: 802.11h added two mechanisms so 5 GHz Wi-Fi can share spectrum with radar. DFS (Dynamic Frequency Selection): the AP listens for radar and vacates the channel if it hears any. TPC (Transmit Power Control): the AP uses no more power than needed, limiting interference.
detail:
Parts of the 5 GHz band are also used by weather, military and aviation radar. Regulators allowed Wi-Fi in only on the condition that it yields.
How it works
  • A DFS channel must be checked before use: The AP performs a channel availability check — typically 60 seconds, and 10 minutes on the weather-radar channels — listening for radar before it may transmit. That is why a DFS channel is not instantly available after a reboot or channel change.
  • A radar detection forces an immediate move: If radar is detected, the AP must stop transmitting and change channel. Clients are disconnected or moved, and the channel is marked unusable for a non-occupancy period, typically 30 minutes.
  • False detections cause mystery outages: Nearby radar, or a radar-like signal, can trigger a channel change with no error a user would recognise. The symptom is all clients on one AP dropping simultaneously, then reconnecting.
  • Some clients avoid DFS channels entirely: Older and cheaper devices will not associate on DFS channels. Building a channel plan that depends on them can leave those clients unable to see the network.
  • TPC is a regulatory obligation, not a tuning feature: It reduces power to the minimum required, which also happens to be good design practice for cell sizing.
Where you see it
  • Choosing whether to enable DFS channels to widen a 5 GHz channel plan
  • Explaining a whole-AP disconnect near an airport, coastline or weather radar
  • Reading controller logs for radar-detected channel change events
exam: The exam scenario is a wireless network near an airport or coastline where all clients on one AP drop at once and the channel changes. The answer is a DFS radar event. Know that 802.11h = DFS + TPC and that it applies to the 5 GHz band. A distractor may attribute DFS to 2.4 GHz, which has no radar-sharing requirement.

front: The seven steps of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology, in order.
answer:
1. Identify the problem
2. Establish a theory of probable cause
3. Test the theory to determine the cause
4. Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem and identify potential effects
5. Implement the solution or escalate as necessary
6. Verify full system functionality and, if applicable, implement preventive measures
7. Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned
detail:
A fixed, ordered procedure that CompTIA treats as a single memorized unit. It exists so that troubleshooting is repeatable by someone who is not the person who built the network, and so that the fix is proven rather than guessed.
How it works
  • The order is the content: Every step consumes the output of the one before it. You cannot test a theory you have not formed, and you cannot plan a change whose cause you have not confirmed. Questions are built entirely on this dependency.
  • Theory and test are separate steps: Step 2 produces a hypothesis. Step 3 proves or disproves it. Most wrong exam answers collapse these two, or jump from theory straight to implementing a fix.
  • Step 3 has a failure branch: If the test does not confirm the theory, you do not proceed. You establish a new theory, or escalate. Escalation is a legitimate answer at step 3 and again at step 5, never earlier.
  • Plan comes before implement: Step 4 is where you decide the change window, the rollback, and what else the change might break. A scenario that has just confirmed a cause is at step 4, not step 5.
  • Verification is not the same as the fix: Step 6 means confirming with the user and testing the whole system, not just the one symptom. Preventive measures are folded into this step.
Where you see it
  • Answering any exam question phrased as what should the technician do next
  • Structuring an incident write-up so a colleague can follow it
  • Deciding when escalation is defensible rather than lazy
exam: This list is memorized verbatim and is the single highest-yield item in Domain 5. The exam tests it almost entirely through next-step questions, so know both the step names and their order. The most common distractor is offering the fix itself when the scenario has only reached step 3 or 4.

front: Step 1 — Identify the problem. What actually happens in this step?
answer: Gather information, question users, identify symptoms, determine if anything has changed, duplicate the problem if possible, and approach multiple problems individually.
detail:
The information-gathering step. Nothing is diagnosed here — the goal is an accurate, specific statement of what is broken, for whom, and since when.
How it works
  • Question the user, and question the report: Users report interpretations, not observations. The internet is down usually means one site failed to load. Ask what exact error appeared, on what device, and what they were doing.
  • Determine if anything changed: This is the highest-yield question in the whole methodology. A patch, a config push, a cable move, a new device or an expired certificate explains far more outages than spontaneous hardware failure.
  • Duplicate the problem: If you can reproduce it on demand you can test a theory in seconds. If you cannot reproduce it, you cannot verify a fix in step 6 either, so establishing reproduction is worth real time.
  • Approach multiple problems individually: If three symptoms are reported, treat them as three problems until evidence links them. Assuming a single root cause too early is how technicians chase the wrong thing for an hour.
  • Scope the problem: Establish how many users, which subnet, which building, which application. Scope alone often points at the cause — one user is an endpoint, one floor is a switch, everyone is the core or the WAN.
Where you see it
  • Opening ticket questions that make the rest of the ticket fast
  • Comparing a broken machine against a working one on the same segment
  • Establishing whether the fault started at a change window
exam: The exam wording for this step is gather information and question the user. If a scenario opens with a vague report and asks what the technician should do first, the answer is a question-the-user or identify-symptoms option, not running a tool. Do not confuse determine if anything has changed (step 1) with question the obvious (step 2).

front: Step 2 — Establish a theory of probable cause. What does it involve?
answer: Form a hypothesis about the cause. Question the obvious first, and consider multiple approaches: top-down, bottom-up, or divide-and-conquer.
detail:
The step where symptoms become a candidate cause. It produces a statement that can be proven false, which is what makes the next step possible.
How it works
  • Question the obvious: Check the trivial causes before the clever ones: is it plugged in, is it powered on, is the wireless switch off, is the account locked, is caps lock on, was the cable moved. Most outages have boring causes.
  • A theory must be testable: The cable is bad is a theory because swapping it proves or disproves it. The network is broken is not. If you cannot state the test, you do not yet have a theory.
  • Choose an OSI approach here: This is where you pick top-down, bottom-up or divide-and-conquer. The choice is driven by the symptom: one broken application points down from Layer 7, one dead port points up from Layer 1.
  • Rank multiple theories: You are allowed more than one candidate. Order them by likelihood divided by cost to test, so the cheap common causes are eliminated first.
  • Escalation is not yet appropriate: If you have no theory, gather more information. Escalation belongs at step 3 when a theory cannot be confirmed, or step 5 when the fix is outside your authority.
Where you see it
  • Deciding whether to walk to the wiring closet or open a packet capture
  • Writing a short list of candidate causes on the ticket before touching anything
  • Explaining to a manager why you are checking the cable on a Layer 7 complaint
exam: The tested phrase is question the obvious, and CompTIA uses it to justify checking power and cabling on a scenario that sounds sophisticated. The classic trap: a scenario where the technician has just gathered symptoms and the options include both establish a theory and test a theory — the answer is establish, because there is no theory yet to test.

front: Step 3 — Test the theory to determine the cause. What are the two outcomes?
answer: Confirmed: proceed to determine the next steps to resolve the problem. Not confirmed: establish a new theory, or escalate.
detail:
The proof step. Its whole purpose is to stop you from fixing something that was never broken, which is the most common way a technician creates a second outage.
How it works
  • Test cheaply and reversibly: Swap the patch cable, move the laptop to a known-good port, query a different DNS resolver. Good tests are fast, non-destructive and give an unambiguous answer.
  • Test the theory, not the symptom: If the theory is duplex mismatch, the test is reading interface counters on both ends, not asking the user if it feels faster. A test that cannot falsify the theory has proved nothing.
  • The not-confirmed branch is examinable: When a test fails to confirm, you loop back to step 2 with a new theory or you escalate. You never proceed to a plan of action on an unproven theory.
  • Confirming the cause is not fixing it: Proving the transceiver is bad is step 3. Deciding when to swap it, who to notify, and what the swap will interrupt is step 4.
Where you see it
  • Moving a failing device to a known-good switch port to isolate the port
  • Querying 8.8.8.8 directly to prove the internal resolver is at fault
  • Escalating to the carrier once your tests prove the fault starts past the demarc
exam: Expect scenarios that end with the theory disproved. The correct answer is then establish a new theory or escalate — never implement a fix and never document. Also watch for scenarios that end with a confirmed theory: the answer is establish a plan of action, one step forward only.

front: Step 4 — Establish a plan of action. What does the full step name include, and why?
answer: Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem and identify potential effects. You decide the change, the window, the rollback, and what else the change may break.
detail:
The step between knowing the cause and touching production. It exists because a correct fix applied at the wrong time or without a rollback can cost more than the original fault.
How it works
  • Identify potential effects: Rebooting the core switch fixes the loop and drops every user. Changing the subnet mask fixes one host and orphans the printers. The step name explicitly requires thinking this through before the change.
  • It connects to change management: In a managed environment this plan becomes a change request: the reason, the steps, the maintenance window, the backout plan, and the approver. Domain 3 change control and Domain 5 step 4 are the same activity.
  • Define the rollback first: A plan without a defined way back is not a plan. Save the running configuration, note the previous setting, or take a snapshot before you begin.
  • Scope who is affected: Notify the affected users and the service desk before the window, not after the outage. Unannounced fixes generate a second wave of tickets.
Where you see it
  • Writing the change request after a root cause is confirmed
  • Scheduling a switch firmware upgrade for a maintenance window
  • Backing up a running config before editing an ACL
exam: The examinable half of this step is identify potential effects, which CompTIA uses to make plan-of-action the right answer over implement. A scenario where the cause is known but the fix would interrupt a production service is asking for step 4. Distractors offer implement the solution immediately.

front: Step 5 — Implement the solution or escalate as necessary. When is escalation the right answer?
answer: When the fix is outside your authority, your access, or your expertise — a carrier circuit, a vendor firmware bug, another team's firewall, or a change you are not approved to make.
detail:
The step where the plan is actually executed. Escalation is written into the step name because handing a problem to the right owner is a legitimate resolution, not a failure.
How it works
  • Escalate for ownership, not difficulty: If the evidence shows the fault is past the demarc, the carrier owns it. If it is a bug in the vendor operating system, the vendor owns it. Escalating with evidence is correct and fast.
  • Escalate with your findings attached: A good escalation includes what you tested, what you ruled out, and the traceroute or counter output that proves it. That is what stops the other team from repeating your first hour.
  • Follow the plan, do not improvise: Deviating from step 4 mid-change is how a small fix becomes an incident. If the plan turns out to be wrong, stop and go back to step 4.
  • Implement one change at a time: Changing three things at once means you cannot tell which one worked, and cannot roll back cleanly. Single changes preserve the ability to verify in step 6.
Where you see it
  • Handing a proven circuit fault to the ISP with traceroute evidence
  • Applying a configuration change inside an approved maintenance window
  • Passing a suspected application defect to the software vendor
exam: The tested distinction is that escalation lives at step 5 (and as the failure branch of step 3), never at step 1 or 2. A scenario where the technician has proven the fault is on the provider side is answered by escalate, not by continuing to test. Escalating before forming a theory is always a wrong answer.

front: Step 6 — Verify full system functionality. Why is this more than checking the original symptom?
answer: Because a fix can resolve the reported symptom and break something else. You test the whole system, confirm with the user, and if applicable implement preventive measures.
detail:
The quality gate. It converts it seems to work into it is confirmed working, and it is where prevention is added so the same ticket does not return next month.
How it works
  • Confirm with the user who reported it: The technician's test and the user's workflow are not the same test. The user is the only one who can say the original task now completes.
  • Test around the change, not just the change: If you fixed a VLAN assignment, also check that printing, the file share and the phone on that desk still work. Collateral damage found now is cheap.
  • Preventive measures are part of this step: Adding a DHCP reservation after a duplicate IP, enabling BPDU Guard after a loop, or shortening a lease after scope exhaustion belongs here. It is the difference between fixing the incident and fixing the cause.
  • Verification requires reproduction: This is why duplicating the problem in step 1 pays off. If you never reproduced it, you cannot prove it is gone.
Where you see it
  • Calling the user back to confirm the application now loads
  • Re-running the failing test from the client rather than from the switch
  • Adding a monitoring alert so the same condition is caught automatically next time
exam: CompTIA attaches implement preventive measures to this step, and that phrasing is examinable — preventive measures are not step 7. A scenario where the fix is applied and the technician is asked what comes next is answered by verify, not document.

front: Step 7 — Document findings, actions and outcomes. Why is documentation always last, and why is it never optional?
answer: Last because it records what actually happened, which is only known once the fix is verified. Never optional because the ticket is the only artifact that survives — it is what makes the next occurrence a five-minute fix instead of a fresh investigation.
detail:
The step everyone skips because the pain has stopped. It converts one person's hour of work into organizational knowledge.
How it works
  • It has to be last: Documenting a theory before it is verified records a guess. Only after step 6 do you know the true cause, the true fix and the true side effects.
  • Record the cause, not just the action: Rebooted the switch is useless. Uplink to SW3 was err-disabled by BPDU Guard after a user connected an unmanaged switch to jack 214 is a document that solves the problem next time in minutes.
  • N10-009 adds lessons learned: The current objectives extend this step to outcomes and lessons learned — what would have caught this sooner, what monitoring was missing, what documentation was wrong.
  • It feeds the knowledge base and the baseline: Ticket documentation updates the network diagram, the IP address management records and the configuration baseline. Those artifacts are what makes step 1 fast on the next incident.
Where you see it
  • Writing the root cause into the ticket before closing it
  • Updating the network diagram after a cable or VLAN change
  • Building a knowledge base article for a recurring vendor fault
exam: Documentation is the correct answer only when the scenario states the fix has been applied and verified. If verification has not happened, document is the classic trap answer. Remember the order: verify, then document — never the reverse.

front: How do you answer a what should the technician do NEXT question?
answer: Locate exactly where the scenario stopped in the seven steps, then choose the very next step — not the eventual fix, and not two steps ahead.
detail:
The dominant question format in Domain 5. The scenario is written to end precisely on a step boundary, and every wrong answer is a real step placed at the wrong point in the sequence.
How it works
  • Read the last sentence of the scenario: The final action described is the step just completed. Everything before it is context. Map that action to a step number, then answer with the step number plus one.
  • Common stopping points and their answers: Symptoms gathered means establish a theory. Theory formed means test it. Theory confirmed means establish a plan of action. Theory disproved means new theory or escalate. Fix applied means verify. Fix verified means document.
  • The fix is almost never the answer: Distractor sets are built from plausible technical actions — replace the cable, reboot the switch, reconfigure DHCP. If the scenario has not reached step 5, none of them can be correct.
  • Take exactly one step: Skipping ahead is the most common error. Even when the correct fix is obvious and listed, if the scenario stopped at step 3 the answer is the plan of action.
Where you see it
  • Parsing any Domain 5 scenario question under time pressure
  • Distinguishing a methodology question from a technical-knowledge question
  • Deciding between test the theory and establish a plan of action
exam: This is the single most reliable point-scoring technique on the exam. When two options are both real methodology steps, the answer is the earlier of the two, because scenarios stop early far more often than they stop late. When one option is a step and the others are technical actions, the step wins.

front: Top-down, bottom-up and divide-and-conquer — what are they and when is each correct?
answer: Three ways of walking the OSI model. Bottom-up starts at Layer 1, best when a physical fault is likely. Top-down starts at Layer 7, best when one application is broken and everything else works. Divide-and-conquer starts in the middle (usually Layer 3) and eliminates half the stack per test.
detail:
Search strategies over the seven layers. The point is to eliminate the largest number of possibilities per test, so the right choice depends entirely on what the symptom already tells you.
How it works
  • Bottom-up when nothing works: One user with a dead port, no link light, a new cable run, or a whole floor down. Physical causes are the most common and the cheapest to rule out, so starting at Layer 1 eliminates the likely answer immediately.
  • Top-down when one application is broken: If web browsing works and only the accounting application fails, Layers 1 through 4 are already proven by the traffic that does work. Starting at the cable wastes time on a link you know is good.
  • Divide-and-conquer when you have no clue: Ping the default gateway or a remote IP. Success proves Layers 1 through 3 in one test and pushes you upward. Failure proves the problem is at or below Layer 3 and pushes you downward. Each test halves the search space.
  • The approach is chosen in step 2: This choice belongs to establishing a theory of probable cause, not to identifying the problem. CompTIA lists top-to-bottom, bottom-to-top and divide-and-conquer as sub-bullets of step 2.
Where you see it
  • Choosing to open a packet capture instead of walking to the wiring closet
  • Starting with ping when a scenario gives you no useful symptoms
  • Justifying skipping a cable test on a single-application failure
exam: The exam gives you a scenario and asks which approach is most efficient. The signal is in the scope: a physical or total failure means bottom-up, a single application means top-down, an ambiguous slow or intermittent complaint means divide-and-conquer. Do not pick bottom-up reflexively — CompTIA specifically builds top-down questions where checking the cable is the wrong first move.

front: What is question the obvious guarding against?
answer: Skipping the trivial cause. Before any sophisticated theory, confirm it is plugged in, powered on, the correct cable, the correct port, the account is not locked, and nothing was moved.
detail:
A deliberate discipline inserted into step 2 because technical people systematically underweight boring explanations.
How it works
  • The base rate favours boring causes: Unplugged cables, disabled adapters, wrong SSID, expired passwords and accidentally kicked power strips outnumber routing and firewall faults by a wide margin.
  • Cheap tests come first regardless of likelihood: Even if a physical cause is only somewhat likely, checking it takes ten seconds. A theory that takes an hour to test should not be checked first unless it is far more likely.
  • It applies to changes too: The obvious cause of a fault that started this morning is whatever was changed last night. Check the change log before theorizing about hardware.
  • It does not mean ignoring the symptoms: Question the obvious means rule out the trivial, not assume the trivial. You still confirm it rather than telling the user to reboot and hanging up.
Where you see it
  • Checking the link light before opening a packet capture
  • Confirming the laptop wireless radio switch before blaming the access point
  • Reading the change log as the first move on a fault that started overnight
exam: This phrase appears verbatim in the objectives under step 2, so recognise it as a methodology term, not general advice. Exam scenarios that describe an elaborate symptom and offer one mundane check among sophisticated options are usually testing this — the mundane check wins.

front: Why is determine if anything has changed the highest-yield question in step 1?
answer: Because most incidents are caused by a change. A patch, a config push, a firmware upgrade, a cable move, a new device or an expired certificate explains far more outages than spontaneous failure.
detail:
Working networks do not usually break by themselves. Something acted on them. Finding that action collapses the search space from the whole network to one change.
How it works
  • Correlate the fault with a timestamp: If the fault started at 02:00 and the patch window is 01:00 to 03:00, you have a candidate cause before you have run a single command. Ask when it last worked, not just what is broken.
  • Changes include things that expire: A certificate, a DHCP lease, a licence, a password or a scheduled task can change state with nobody touching anything. These are the changes people forget to look for.
  • Ask the user, not just the change log: Users make undocumented changes: a new monitor with a dock, a moved desk, a personal switch under the desk, an unapproved app. These never appear in change management.
  • It is what makes rollback possible: If the cause is a change, the fastest fix is often reverting it. That is available only if you identified the change rather than working the symptom forward.
Where you see it
  • Asking when it last worked as the second question on every ticket
  • Checking last night's change window against this morning's ticket surge
  • Finding an expired certificate behind a sudden wave of connection errors
exam: This is a step 1 activity, so it is the correct answer in scenarios where the technician has only just received the report. The contrast pair CompTIA uses is question the obvious, which is step 2. If the question asks what to do first on a fault that appeared overnight, determining what changed beats running any tool.

front: What does ping actually prove, and what does a failed ping not prove?
answer: It proves bidirectional Layer 3 reachability and reports round-trip latency and loss. A failed ping does not prove the host is down — ICMP is routinely filtered.
detail:
ping sends an ICMP echo request and waits for an echo reply. It is the cheapest test in networking and the most frequently over-interpreted.
How it works
  • It tests the whole path, not one thing: A reply means addressing, routing, ARP, the physical path and the return path all worked. That is why a successful ping eliminates so much at once — and why a failure tells you so little about where it broke.
