  • Latency and loss come free: The round-trip time and the summary line (packets sent/received/lost) are often more useful than the pass/fail. Rising or wildly varying RTT points at congestion; intermittent loss points at a marginal link.
  • ICMP is commonly blocked: Many hosts and firewalls drop inbound echo requests by policy. A server can be happily serving HTTPS while refusing every ping. Never conclude 'the server is down' from ping alone — test the actual service port.
  • Useful flags: ping -t (Windows) runs continuously so you can watch a link while someone reseats a cable. ping -l / -s sets payload size, which is how you probe for MTU problems. ping -f plus a size tests with Don't Fragment set.
Where you see it
  • Confirming a newly configured host can reach its gateway
  • Watching a flapping link continuously while someone works on it
  • Establishing a latency baseline to a remote site
exam: CompTIA uses ping in two ways. As a diagnostic sequence: loopback, then own IP, then gateway, then a remote IP, then a name — each step eliminates a layer. And as a trap: a scenario where ping fails but the service works, testing whether you know ICMP filtering is common. If a question says 'ping fails but users can browse the site', the answer is that ICMP is blocked, not that the host is offline.

front: How does traceroute work, and what is the difference between traceroute and tracert?
answer:
It manipulates TTL. Send a packet with TTL 1, the first router decrements it to 0 and returns an ICMP Time Exceeded — that reveals hop 1. TTL 2 reveals hop 2, and so on.
Linux/macOS traceroute sends UDP probes by default. Windows tracert sends ICMP echo requests.
detail:
traceroute maps the path a packet takes and shows where latency or loss enters it. It is the tool that turns 'the network is slow' into 'it is slow starting at hop 7'.
How it works
  • The TTL trick: TTL exists to kill looping packets. traceroute abuses it: each router that decrements TTL to zero must send back an ICMP Time Exceeded, and that message's source address is the router's identity.
  • Three probes per hop: Each hop is probed three times, so you see three RTTs. Compare them — one slow probe among three is noise; three consistently slow probes is a real problem at that hop.
  • Asterisks are usually not failures: A * means no reply to that probe. Many routers rate-limit or suppress ICMP Time Exceeded, so a hop that shows all asterisks while later hops respond is simply a quiet router, not a break.
  • Latency at one hop is not the problem hop: A router may deprioritize responding to you while forwarding traffic fine. What matters is latency that rises at a hop and stays high for every hop after it.
  • The UDP/ICMP difference matters at firewalls: A firewall that permits ICMP but blocks high UDP ports will let tracert through and stop traceroute. That is a real cause of platform-dependent results.
Where you see it
  • Finding where added latency enters a path to a cloud service
  • Proving a fault is inside the carrier network rather than yours
  • Discovering an unexpected asymmetric or suboptimal route
exam: Two exam items. The mechanism — traceroute is built on TTL and ICMP Time Exceeded; questions ask what field is manipulated. And the platform difference — tracert is Windows and uses ICMP, traceroute is Linux/macOS and uses UDP by default. Also know that pathping (Windows) and mtr (Linux) combine traceroute with sustained ping to measure per-hop loss over time.

front: What do ipconfig / ifconfig / ip show, and which flags matter?
answer:
Local interface configuration: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, MAC address, and with /all the DNS servers, DHCP server and lease times.
ipconfig /all · /release · /renew · /flushdns · /displaydns
Linux modern: ip addr, ip route, ip neigh (ifconfig is deprecated).
detail:
This is the first command in almost every client-side investigation, because it tells you what the machine believes about itself.
How it works
  • The four values that matter: IP, mask, gateway and DNS. A wrong mask makes remote hosts look local. A wrong gateway breaks everything off-subnet. Wrong DNS breaks names but not IPs. A 169.254 address means DHCP failed entirely.
  • /all is where the DHCP evidence lives: It shows which DHCP server issued the lease and when it expires — that is how you catch a rogue DHCP server handing out addresses from the wrong scope.
  • release and renew force a fresh lease: ipconfig /release then /renew makes the client redo DORA. It fixes a stale or wrong lease and confirms whether the DHCP path works at all.
  • /flushdns clears the resolver cache: After a DNS record changes, a client can keep using the cached old answer until the TTL expires. Flushing proves whether you are fighting a cache or a real DNS problem.
  • ip replaced ifconfig: On modern Linux, ifconfig may not even be installed. ip addr show is the equivalent, and ip route replaces route -n.
Where you see it
  • Confirming a workstation got the addressing you expected
  • Catching a rogue DHCP server by reading the issuing server address
  • Clearing a stale DNS answer after a cutover
exam: Expect a scenario with ipconfig /all output where you must spot the wrong value — a gateway outside the subnet, a mask that does not match the rest of the LAN, or an APIPA address. Also expect the /flushdns answer when a site was recently moved and one client still reaches the old server.

front: nslookup and dig — what do they prove, and how do you use them to isolate a DNS fault?
answer:
They query DNS directly, bypassing the application. Point them at a known-good public resolver to split 'DNS is broken' from 'my DNS is broken':
nslookup host 8.8.8.8 · dig @8.8.8.8 host
detail:
If the name resolves correctly against a public resolver but not against yours, the fault is your resolver, its cache, or your zone data — not the internet.
How it works
  • Query a specific server: Both tools let you name the server to ask. That single capability is what makes them diagnostic rather than merely informative.
  • Query a specific record type: dig MX example.com or nslookup -type=MX example.com. Mail problems are usually MX or PTR problems, and you cannot see those from a browser.
  • dig gives you the full picture: Its output separates QUESTION, ANSWER, AUTHORITY and ADDITIONAL sections, and shows the TTL remaining on the cached record. That TTL tells you how long a stale answer will persist.
  • Authoritative vs cached answers: nslookup labels a response 'Non-authoritative' when it came from a cache. To see the truth, query the zone's authoritative name server directly.
  • Reverse lookups: nslookup 8.8.8.8 or dig -x 8.8.8.8 checks the PTR record. Mail servers reject senders with missing or mismatched reverse DNS.
Where you see it
  • Proving whether a failing website is a DNS problem or a connectivity problem
  • Checking that a new MX or CNAME record has actually propagated
  • Diagnosing mail rejection caused by a missing PTR record
exam: The reliable pattern is the 'can ping by IP but not by name' scenario — the answer is always a name-resolution tool. Know that dig is the Linux/macOS tool with richer output and nslookup works on both. Also expect a question where the fix is flushing a cache rather than changing a record.

front: What does netstat tell you that no other tool does?
answer:
Which ports this machine is listening on and which connections are established, with their states.
netstat -an all connections, numeric · netstat -r routing table · netstat -b (Windows) the owning program
detail:
netstat answers the question 'is the service actually running and accepting connections here?' — which ping and traceroute cannot touch.
How it works
  • LISTENING means the service is up: If a service should be on 3389 and netstat -an shows nothing listening on 3389, the problem is the application or its configuration, not the network.
  • ESTABLISHED means a session exists: Seeing an established connection from the client address proves traffic reached the server and was accepted — so any remaining fault is above Layer 4.
  • Lots of SYN_RECV or TIME_WAIT is a signal: A pile of half-open connections can indicate a SYN flood; a pile of TIME_WAIT usually just means a busy server cycling short connections.
  • -n avoids a trap: Without -n, netstat tries to resolve every address to a name. On a broken-DNS host that makes the command hang, which is itself a clue.
Where you see it
  • Confirming a newly installed service is bound and listening
  • Finding which process holds a port you need
  • Checking the local routing table without a separate command
exam: The exam framing is usually 'verify the service is listening' or 'determine which ports are open on this host'. Distinguish it from Nmap: netstat inspects the local machine from the inside; Nmap probes a remote machine from the outside.

front: What does arp -a show, and what problems does it expose?
answer: The local IP-to-MAC cache — which hardware address this host currently believes owns each IP on its subnet.
detail:
ARP resolves Layer 3 addresses to Layer 2 addresses. The cache is small, local, and revealing when something is impersonating another host.
How it works
  • It only covers the local subnet: ARP never crosses a router. Every off-subnet destination resolves to the gateway's MAC, which is why a poisoned gateway entry is so damaging.
  • Two IPs sharing one MAC is a red flag: That is the signature of ARP poisoning — the attacker has claimed the gateway's address as well as its own, putting itself on-path.
  • It exposes duplicate IPs: When two hosts claim the same address, the cache entry flaps between two MACs. Take the MAC to show mac-address-table on the switch to find the physical port.
  • Clearing it forces re-resolution: arp -d removes entries. Useful after replacing hardware, when the cache still holds the old NIC's MAC.
Where you see it
  • Tracking down a duplicate IP address to a physical port
  • Detecting ARP poisoning by spotting a changed gateway MAC
  • Confirming a device is present on the local segment at all
exam: Two angles. Duplicate IP scenarios — arp is how you identify the offender. And security — recognizing that a changed or duplicated gateway MAC means an on-path attack, with Dynamic ARP Inspection as the mitigation.

front: tcpdump, Wireshark and 'protocol analyzer' — when is a capture the right move, and what do you need to see other hosts' traffic?
answer: When you must prove what is actually on the wire rather than what a device claims. To capture traffic that is not to or from your own NIC you need a SPAN/mirror port or a network TAP.
detail:
A packet capture is the ground truth of networking. It is also slow to read, so it is the tool you reach for after cheaper tests have narrowed the problem.
How it works
  • It settles arguments: Is the client actually sending the request? Is the server replying and the reply being dropped? Is the DHCP offer present but ignored? Only a capture answers these.
  • Filter or drown: Capture filters (tcp port 443 and host 10.1.1.5) limit what is recorded; display filters narrow what you view. An unfiltered capture on a busy link is unreadable within seconds.
  • Retransmissions and resets are the fast wins: Wireshark flags TCP retransmissions, duplicate ACKs and RSTs in colour. Heavy retransmission means loss; an immediate RST means something actively refused or terminated the connection.
  • A switch hides traffic by design: A switch forwards frames only to the destination port, so your NIC sees almost nothing else. That is why SPAN or a TAP is mandatory, and why the old hub trick worked.
  • tcpdump for servers, Wireshark for analysis: Capture on the remote host with tcpdump -i eth0 -w file.pcap, then open the file in Wireshark where you have a GUI.
Where you see it
  • Proving whether a firewall or the application dropped a connection
  • Diagnosing DHCP failures by watching for Discover, Offer, Request and Ack
  • Investigating unexplained traffic or a suspected compromise
exam: Expect the phrase 'protocol analyzer' as the correct answer when a question asks how to inspect the actual contents of traffic. The commonly missed follow-up is SPAN port vs TAP — a TAP is passive inline hardware that cannot drop frames; a SPAN port is configured on the switch, costs nothing, but can drop frames under load and hides physical-layer errors.

front: What is Nmap for, and how does it differ from netstat?
answer: Host discovery and port scanning from the outside — which hosts are alive, which ports are open, what service and version answers, and often what OS it is.
detail:
Nmap tells you what an attacker would see. That makes it an inventory and audit tool, and it is also why unexplained scans in your logs are worth investigating.
How it works
  • Discovery before scanning: A ping sweep across a subnet finds live hosts. That alone catches devices nobody documented — the rogue switch, the forgotten test server.
  • Open, closed, filtered: Open means something is listening. Closed means the host replied but nothing is listening. Filtered means no reply at all, which usually means a firewall is dropping the probe.
  • Service and version detection: Nmap can fingerprint the software behind a port. That turns 'port 22 is open' into 'an outdated OpenSSH version is exposed', which is what a vulnerability finding looks like.
  • Outside-in, not inside-out: This is the netstat contrast. Nmap probes a remote target across the network; netstat reads the local kernel's own tables.
Where you see it
  • Auditing which services a server actually exposes
  • Finding undocumented devices on a subnet
  • Verifying a firewall rule change actually closed a port
exam: The exam contrast is Nmap (remote scan) vs netstat (local sockets). Also expect Nmap named as the tool for port scanning or discovering unauthorized devices, and appearing on the attacker's side as reconnaissance.

front: What do LLDP and CDP give you, and how do they differ?
answer:
Layer 2 neighbor discovery — the name, model, remote port, VLAN and capabilities of whatever is plugged into each port.
CDP is Cisco-proprietary. LLDP (802.1AB) is the vendor-neutral standard.
detail:
In an undocumented network these protocols rebuild the map for you without walking to the wiring closet.
How it works
  • They advertise, they do not route: Each device periodically multicasts a frame describing itself. Neighbors record it. Nothing forwards these frames beyond one hop, so what you see is genuinely directly connected.
  • The remote port number is the payoff: Knowing that your uplink lands on GigabitEthernet1/0/24 of a specific switch is what lets you troubleshoot the far end without guessing.
  • LLDP-MED extends it to phones: The media extension carries voice VLAN assignment and PoE power negotiation, which is how an IP phone learns its VLAN automatically.
  • They are also an information leak: Both broadcast device model and software version to anyone on the segment. Standard hardening disables them on ports facing untrusted users.
Where you see it
  • Mapping an inherited network with no documentation
  • Confirming which switch port a device is really on before making a change
  • Automatic voice VLAN and PoE negotiation for IP phones
exam: Know the pair: CDP = Cisco, LLDP = open standard (802.1AB). Expect them as the answer to 'how do you determine what device is connected to this interface' and as a hardening item on untrusted ports.

front: The show commands — what does each reveal that nothing else does?
answer:
show interface — status, speed/duplex, errors, discards, utilization
show mac-address-table — MAC to port and VLAN
show ip route — the routing table and gateway of last resort
show arp — IP to MAC bindings on the device
show vlan — VLAN membership per port
show running-config — the live configuration
show power inline — PoE budget and per-port draw
show spanning-tree — root bridge, port roles and states
detail:
These are the device's own view of reality. When a client-side symptom and the device's counters disagree, the counters win.
How it works
  • show interface is the workhorse: Line protocol status separates a physical problem from a protocol one. 'Up/down' means the cable is fine but the encapsulation or protocol is not. 'Down/down' means physical. The error counters then tell you which physical fault.
  • show mac-address-table finds anything: Any MAC you have — from an ARP cache, a DHCP log, a security alert — becomes a physical port through this command.
  • show ip route explains reachability: It shows what the router will actually do with a destination, including whether a default route exists. 'Gateway of last resort is not set' explains an enormous number of outages.
  • show power inline answers PoE questions: It gives the total budget, the consumed watts and the draw per port. A device that will not power on is usually explained here.
  • show spanning-tree catches the wrong root: If an access-layer switch has become root because someone plugged in cheap gear with a low priority, your traffic is taking bizarre paths. This is where you see it.
Where you see it
  • Diagnosing a link that is up but performing badly
  • Tracing a rogue device to a wall jack
  • Explaining why a new AP will not power up
exam: CompTIA lists these commands explicitly in objective 5.5, so expect direct matching: given a symptom, choose the command. The mapping to memorize — errors → show interface, find a device → show mac-address-table, reachability → show route, PoE → show power, loop or wrong path → show spanning-tree.

front: The hardware tools — which one answers which question?
answer:
Toner probe — which cable is this?
Cable tester — is it wired correctly end to end?
Cable certifier — does it meet the Cat spec under load?
TDR / OTDR — how far away is the break?
Visual fault locator — where is the fiber broken or badly spliced?
Wi-Fi analyzer — what is on the air and how strong?
Spectrum analyzer — what non-Wi-Fi interference is present?
Network TAP — give me a lossless copy of this traffic.
detail:
Each of these answers exactly one question. Picking the right one is most of the exam's physical-layer content.
How it works
  • Toner vs tester: A toner locates — it injects an audible tone you chase with a probe through a bundle. A tester validates — it checks continuity and pin mapping. They are not interchangeable and the exam pairs them as distractors.
  • Tester vs certifier: A basic tester says the eight wires connect correctly. A certifier measures attenuation, NEXT and return loss against the TIA standard and prints a pass/fail — that is what you need to prove a run supports 10 Gbps.
  • TDR is copper, OTDR is fiber: Both send a pulse and time the reflection to compute distance to the fault. TDR for copper, OTDR (optical) for fiber. This letter is the whole distinction.
  • Visual fault locator is the cheap fiber check: It shoots visible red laser light down the fiber. A break, a sharp bend or a bad splice glows. It finds faults in the first few hundred metres without an OTDR.
  • Wi-Fi analyzer vs spectrum analyzer: A Wi-Fi analyzer shows SSIDs, channels and signal strength — other Wi-Fi. A spectrum analyzer shows all RF energy including microwaves, cordless phones and video senders, which a Wi-Fi analyzer cannot see at all.
Where you see it
  • Finding one cable in an unlabeled bundle of two hundred
  • Proving a contractor's cabling meets Cat 6a before you accept the job
  • Locating a buried fiber cut without digging up the whole run
  • Explaining Wi-Fi problems that no amount of channel changing fixes
exam: This is a straight tool-to-scenario match, and CompTIA leans on two pairs. Toner locates / tester validates. Wi-Fi analyzer sees Wi-Fi / spectrum analyzer sees everything else. If a question describes interference with no visible competing access points, the answer is a spectrum analyzer.

front: What do a speed tester and iperf actually measure, and where do you run them?
answer: Achievable throughput between two points — not the link's rated bandwidth. iperf runs client-to-server between two hosts you control, so you choose exactly which segment is under test.
detail:
A speed test is only meaningful when you know which path it crossed. Testing to the internet measures your ISP, your firewall, your NAT and your Wi-Fi all at once.
How it works
  • Bisect the path: Test LAN-to-LAN first. If internal throughput is good and internet throughput is bad, the problem is at the edge or beyond. If internal throughput is bad, stop looking at the ISP.
  • Test at the demarc: Running a test directly at the provider's handoff removes your firewall, switching and Wi-Fi from the result. That is the number the carrier will accept as evidence.
  • TCP vs UDP mode: iperf's TCP mode measures realistic throughput with congestion control. Its UDP mode lets you push a fixed rate and measure loss and jitter — which is how you validate a link for VoIP.
  • Wireless clients are not a valid test point: Wi-Fi rates vary with signal, contention and client capability. Never benchmark a WAN circuit over Wi-Fi.
Where you see it
  • Proving a circuit is not delivering the contracted bandwidth
  • Validating a link for VoIP by measuring jitter and loss under load
  • Isolating whether a bottleneck is internal or the carrier's
exam: Expect this as the evidence-gathering step in a 'the internet is slow' scenario. The exam-worthy idea is where you test determines what you measured — testing at the demarc versus from a desk isolates responsibility.

front: An interface shows rising errors on one port and rising discards on another. What is different about these two problems?
answer:
Errors = the frame arrived damaged. That is a physical problem.
Discards = the frame was fine but the interface had no buffer or queue space for it. That is a congestion problem.
detail:
These two counters look similar in the output and point at completely different fixes. Confusing them sends you replacing cables when you needed more bandwidth.
How it works
  • Errors mean the bits changed in flight: The CRC no longer matches. Causes: damaged or wrong cable, exceeding distance, EMI, a failing transceiver or NIC, or a duplex mismatch.
  • Discards mean the queue was full: Nothing is broken. The interface simply received more than it could forward or buffer. Causes: an oversubscribed uplink, a speed mismatch (gigabit feeding a 100 Mbps port), or microbursts.
  • The fix differs completely: Errors → replace the cable, check the distance, match the duplex, swap the transceiver. Discards → increase capacity, apply QoS, or shape the traffic.
  • Both can rise together: A saturated link with a marginal cable shows both. Fix the physical fault first, because errors cause retransmissions that make congestion worse.
Where you see it
  • Deciding whether a slow link needs a new cable or a bigger pipe
  • Interpreting show interface output on a complaint call
exam: This is a favourite discriminator. If a scenario mentions CRC errors, think physical. If it mentions output drops or discards with no errors, think congestion. Answering 'replace the cable' to a discard problem is the trap.

front: What are runts, giants and late collisions telling you?
answer:
Runt — a frame under 64 bytes. Usually a collision or a duplex mismatch truncating it.
Giant — a frame over the interface MTU. Usually an MTU or jumbo-frame mismatch, or a VLAN tag the far end did not expect.
Late collision — a collision detected after the first 64 bytes. On modern gear this means a duplex mismatch or a cable run beyond spec.
detail:
These three counters each point at a specific misconfiguration rather than a general fault.
How it works
  • Runts come from truncation: A frame cut short mid-transmission. In a duplex mismatch the half-duplex side detects a 'collision' while the full-duplex side is still sending, and aborts.
  • Giants come from size disagreement: One side is sending jumbo frames or adding a tag the other side does not account for. The receiver sees an oversized frame and drops it.
  • Late collisions are never normal: A normal collision is detected within the first 64 bytes. A late one means the two ends disagree about duplex, or the segment is physically too long for collision detection to work.
  • Full duplex should have zero collisions: Any collision counter on a full-duplex link is evidence the other end is running half duplex.
Where you see it
  • Diagnosing a link that works but crawls under load
  • Confirming an MTU mismatch on a tunnel or storage network
exam: Map each counter to its cause: runts and late collisions → duplex mismatch, giants → MTU/jumbo mismatch. If a scenario gives you late collisions, duplex is the answer and no other option is close.

front: Port status: what do err-disabled, administratively down and suspended each mean, and how do you clear them?
answer:
Err-disabled — the switch shut the port down after a violation. Find the cause in the log, fix it, then shutdown / no shutdown.
Administratively down — someone issued shutdown. Issue no shutdown.
Suspended — the port was removed from a bundle or VLAN because settings do not match on both ends.
detail:
Three different states that all look like 'the port is off' but have three different causes and fixes.
How it works
  • Err-disable has many triggers: Port security violation, BPDU Guard receiving a BPDU, link flapping, unidirectional link detection, or an EtherChannel misconfiguration. The log entry names which.
  • Clearing it without fixing it just repeats: Bouncing the port brings it up until the same violation happens again. Read the reason first — if BPDU Guard fired, someone plugged a switch into a user port.
  • Errdisable recovery can auto-restore: You can configure the switch to re-enable after a timeout. Convenient, but it hides recurring problems.
  • Suspended means a mismatch, not a fault: An EtherChannel member whose speed, duplex, VLAN list or native VLAN differs from its peers is suspended rather than bundled. Align the settings and it joins.
Where you see it
  • A user's port goes dead every time they plug in their own switch
  • A new link aggregation bundle that will not come up
exam: The high-value one is err-disabled from BPDU Guard — the scenario describes a user plugging in a personal switch or hub and their port dying. Also know that clearing the state requires addressing the cause, which is often the second half of the answer.

front: Latency, jitter and packet loss — define each and say what each one breaks.
answer:
Latency — delay in transit. Breaks interactive work; voice becomes a walkie-talkie conversation.
Jitter — variation in latency. The main killer of VoIP quality: choppy, robotic audio.
Packet loss — packets never arrive. TCP retransmits and throughput collapses; UDP voice and video simply drop out.
detail:
All three feel like 'the network is slow' to a user, but they have different causes and different fixes.
How it works
  • Latency is often distance and hops: Physics sets a floor: roughly 1 ms per 100 km each way in fiber, plus per-hop processing. You cannot fix geography, only reduce hops, use a closer endpoint, or add a CDN.
  • Jitter comes from variable queuing: Packets queue behind bursts of other traffic, so each one waits a different amount of time. A jitter buffer absorbs some of it; QoS with a priority queue for voice is the real fix.
  • Loss punishes TCP disproportionately: TCP treats loss as congestion and backs off. Even 1-2% loss can cut throughput dramatically — far more than the raw percentage suggests.
  • They point at different layers: High latency with low loss is usually distance or an overloaded device. High loss with normal latency is usually a physical fault. Both high together usually means saturation.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why a video call is unusable while file transfers seem fine
  • Deciding whether QoS, more bandwidth, or a cable replacement is the fix
exam: The exam's most reliable pairing is jitter → choppy or robotic VoIP audio → QoS. If a scenario describes inconsistent voice quality, the metric is jitter, not latency and not bandwidth.

front: Bandwidth vs throughput vs goodput — and why the numbers never match.
answer:
Bandwidth — the link's theoretical maximum capacity.
Throughput — what you actually achieve, including protocol overhead and retransmissions.
Goodput — only the useful application data that arrived, excluding headers and retransmissions.
detail:
A gigabit link never delivers a gigabit of application data. Understanding why prevents chasing a number that was never achievable.
How it works
  • Overhead is unavoidable: Ethernet, IP and TCP headers, plus interframe gaps and acknowledgements, all consume capacity. Throughput below bandwidth is normal, not a fault.
  • Retransmissions eat goodput twice: A lost segment consumes bandwidth going out, and again on retransmission, while delivering useful data only once.
  • The bottleneck sets the ceiling: End-to-end throughput equals the slowest element in the path, whether that is a 100 Mbps switch port, a saturated WAN link, or the server's disk.
  • Wireless rates are negotiated, not delivered: An advertised 'up to' rate is a modulation rate under ideal conditions, shared among all clients on the channel. Real throughput is a fraction of it.
Where you see it
  • Answering a user who says their gigabit link only gets 940 Mbps
  • Setting realistic expectations before a circuit upgrade
exam: Expect a definition-matching question. The one worth internalizing is that throughput is measured and bandwidth is rated, and a gap between them is expected rather than evidence of a problem.

front: Congestion, contention and bottleneck — how do they differ?
answer:
Congestion — more traffic offered than a link can carry, so queues fill and packets drop.
Contention — multiple devices competing for shared media, so each waits its turn.
Bottleneck — the single slowest element that caps the whole path.
detail:
Three words that all describe 'not enough capacity' but at different places and with different remedies.
How it works
  • Congestion is about volume on a link: The classic case is many gigabit access ports feeding one gigabit uplink. Fixes: a faster uplink, link aggregation, or QoS to protect what matters.
  • Contention is about shared access: A wireless channel is shared media — only one device transmits at a time, so thirty clients on one AP each get a slice. Fixes: more APs, smaller cells, band steering.
  • A bottleneck is a single choke point: Upgrading anything except the bottleneck changes nothing. Find it by testing segment by segment.
  • Oversubscription is a design choice, not always a fault: Access layers are deliberately oversubscribed because not everyone transmits at once. It becomes a problem only when the assumption breaks.
Where you see it
  • Explaining why adding bandwidth to the wrong segment changed nothing
  • Diagnosing poor Wi-Fi in a full conference room with strong signal
exam: The one the exam most often tests is contention on wireless — strong signal, many clients, poor performance. The answer is more APs or channel planning, never more transmit power.

front: A workstation has 169.254.22.9 and cannot reach anything. Walk the diagnosis.
answer: DHCP failed and APIPA self-assigned. Work outward: link → switch port/VLAN → DHCP relay → DHCP server → scope.
detail:
APIPA is not a fault in itself. It is the client telling you it never received a DHCP acknowledgement.
How it works
  • 1. Is the link actually up?: No link means the client never sent a Discover at all. Check the link light, the cable and the switch port status before anything else.
  • 2. Is the port in the right VLAN?: A port in the wrong VLAN reaches a segment with no DHCP service. show vlan and compare with a working neighbour.
  • 3. Is there a relay on this subnet?: DHCP Discover is a broadcast and routers do not forward broadcasts. If the DHCP server is on another subnet, the router interface needs an ip helper-address. A recently added VLAN that was never given a helper is a classic cause.
  • 4. Is the scope exhausted?: Check the server for free leases. Guest and wireless networks with long lease times run out. Shorten the lease or widen the scope.
  • 5. Is the DHCP service running?: Obvious and frequently the answer — the service stopped, the server was patched and did not come back, or the scope was disabled.
  • Also consider a rogue server: If some clients get correct addresses and others get addresses from an unknown range, a rogue DHCP server is competing. ipconfig /all names the issuing server.
Where you see it
  • A single user offline after a desk move
  • A whole new VLAN where nobody can get an address
exam: APIPA is one of the most frequently tested symptoms on the entire exam. Memorize 169.254.0.0/16 means DHCP failure, and that the fix for a whole subnet failing is usually the relay agent / ip helper-address, not the server.

front: A user can reach internal file servers but no websites. What splits the possibilities?
answer: ping 8.8.8.8. If the IP works but names do not, it is DNS. If the IP also fails, it is the default route, NAT or the ISP link.
detail:
One command divides the problem cleanly in half. That is why divide-and-conquer is the right approach here.
How it works
  • IP works, name fails → DNS: Check the configured DNS servers, query a public resolver directly with nslookup host 8.8.8.8, flush the client cache, and verify the internal resolver is running and can recurse.
  • IP also fails → routing or edge: Check the default route on the router, NAT on the firewall, and the WAN interface. Traceroute shows how far you get before it stops.
  • Internal works, so the LAN is fine: Reaching internal servers proves Layer 1 through 3 on the local network, the switch port, VLAN and gateway ARP all work. Do not re-test them.
  • Watch for a partial DNS failure: If the internal zone resolves and external names do not, the internal resolver cannot reach the internet or its forwarders are wrong.
Where you see it
  • The single most common help-desk call in any organization
  • Diagnosing after a firewall or DNS server change
exam: Expect this exact scenario. The tell is 'by IP but not by name' or its inverse. Also expect the follow-up asking which tool confirms it — nslookup or dig.

front: A host can reach some devices on its own LAN but not others, and cannot reach anything remote. Wrong mask or wrong gateway?
answer: Wrong subnet mask. A wrong gateway breaks everything off-subnet but leaves the whole local subnet reachable. Partial local failure is the signature of a mask error.
detail:
The mask decides which destinations a host treats as local. Get it wrong and the host makes the wrong routing decision for a subset of addresses.
How it works
  • How a host decides local vs remote: It ANDs the destination with its own mask. Same result as its own network → ARP for the destination directly. Different → send to the gateway.
  • A mask that is too long shrinks the local view: A host with /26 on a /24 network treats three quarters of its own subnet as remote and sends that traffic to the gateway, which may or may not route it back.
  • A mask that is too short is worse: The host ARPs for addresses that are actually on other subnets, gets no reply, and those destinations simply fail while the gateway itself still works.
  • Wrong gateway looks different: Everything local works perfectly. Nothing remote works at all. There is no partial pattern within the LAN.
  • Confirm with the numbers: Compare the host's mask against a known-good neighbour, and check the gateway address is inside the subnet the mask describes.
Where you see it
  • A statically addressed printer or server that half the office cannot reach
  • A host configured by hand during a rushed change
exam: CompTIA tests the difference by the pattern of what fails. Partial failure within the LAN → mask. Total failure outside the LAN with the LAN fine → gateway. Read the scenario for which pattern it describes.

front: Two hosts have the same IP. What are the symptoms and how do you find the offender?
answer: Symptoms: intermittent connectivity for both, sessions that drop and reconnect, an OS conflict warning. Find it with arp -a (which MAC owns the IP, and does it change?) then show mac-address-table to map that MAC to a switch port.
detail:
Whichever host answered the last ARP request wins traffic, so both hosts work erratically rather than one failing cleanly.
How it works
  • The flapping ARP entry is the tell: The IP-to-MAC binding changes back and forth. Run arp -a twice a few seconds apart and compare.
  • Trace the MAC to a port: Take the unexpected MAC to the switch and run show mac-address-table address . That gives you a physical port and, with CDP/LLDP, the downstream device.
  • The usual causes: A static address assigned inside a DHCP scope without an exclusion, a device cloned or restored from an image, or two DHCP servers with overlapping scopes.
  • The permanent fix: Use DHCP reservations instead of static addressing, and exclusions for anything that must stay static. Document the static ranges.
Where you see it
  • A server that becomes unreachable whenever a particular laptop is on site
  • Intermittent printing failures after a new device was installed
exam: Expect either the symptom ('intermittent connectivity for two devices') or the tool ('which command identifies a duplicate IP'). The answer chain is arp → show mac-address-table → physical port, and the prevention is reservations plus exclusions.

front: A new VLAN works on the switch where it was created but not on any other switch. What is wrong?
answer: The VLAN is almost certainly not allowed on the trunk between the switches, or was never created in the second switch's VLAN database.
detail:
VLANs are local to a switch unless they are explicitly created everywhere and permitted on the links between.
How it works
  • Check the allowed VLAN list: A trunk configured with an explicit allowed list carries only those VLANs. Adding a VLAN without updating every trunk in the path is the single most common cause.
  • Check the VLAN exists on both switches: Some environments require the VLAN to be created in each switch's database. If it does not exist there, tagged frames arriving for it are dropped.
  • Check the native VLAN matches: A native VLAN mismatch on the two ends of a trunk silently merges traffic between two VLANs and generates errors — a different symptom, but the same place to look.
  • Check for an SVI or router interface: If devices in the VLAN can reach each other but nothing else, the VLAN exists and trunks fine — it simply has no gateway. That is an SVI or subinterface problem, not a trunking one.
  • Check DHCP for the new VLAN: A new VLAN with no scope and no ip helper-address gives every client APIPA even when the Layer 2 path is perfect.
Where you see it
  • A new department VLAN that works in one building only
  • Devices in a new VLAN that see each other but nothing beyond
exam: This is a standard multi-part scenario. Learn the checklist in order: VLAN exists on every switch → allowed on every trunk → SVI or router subinterface for routing → DHCP scope and relay. The exam usually removes exactly one of these.

front: The whole network slows to a crawl, switch CPUs hit 100%, and all the port LEDs blink in unison. What is happening?
answer: A Layer 2 switching loop. Broadcast frames circulate endlessly because Ethernet frames have no TTL, multiplying at every switch until the network saturates.
detail:
This is the single most destructive Layer 2 failure and it escalates in seconds, which is why spanning tree exists at all.
How it works
  • Why it never stops on its own: An IP packet has a TTL that decrements and eventually kills a looping packet. An Ethernet frame has no such field. A looped broadcast is forwarded forever and duplicated at every junction.
  • The diagnostic signature: MAC address flapping messages in the log — the same MAC appearing on different ports repeatedly — plus CPU saturation and synchronized LED activity.
  • Common causes: Two switch ports patched together, a user plugging both ends of a cable into wall jacks, an unmanaged switch that does not participate in STP, or STP disabled on a link.
  • The immediate action: Physically break the loop — unplug the redundant link — then investigate. Waiting for STP to reconverge does not help if STP was not running on that path.
  • The prevention: Keep STP enabled everywhere, use BPDU Guard on access ports so a user-added switch shuts the port down, and set the root bridge priority explicitly so your core is root.
Where you see it
  • A network outage minutes after someone tidied a patch panel
  • Recurring brief outages in one wiring closet
exam: The symptom triad — broadcast storm, MAC flapping, high CPU — is the exam's way of describing a loop, and it appears often. The preventive answers are BPDU Guard on access ports and correct root bridge placement.

front: A new access point will not power on from a PoE switch, though the port shows link. What do you check?
answer: In order: the switch's total PoE budget, the PoE standard the device needs versus what the port provides, whether PoE is enabled on that port, and the cable.
detail:
PoE failures usually come down to arithmetic — the switch has a finite power budget and the last device added exceeds it.
How it works
  • 1. Total budget: show power inline gives available and consumed watts. A 370 W switch fully populated with 30 W devices runs out long before the ports do.
  • 2. Standard mismatch: 802.3af delivers 15.4 W at the port, 802.3at 30 W, 802.3bt Type 3 60 W and Type 4 90 W. A Wi-Fi 6 AP or a PTZ camera that needs PoE+ will not start on an af-only switch.
  • 3. PoE disabled on the port: Some deployments disable inline power by default. The port passes data and no power at all.
  • 4. The cable: PoE uses the same pairs as data. A run with damaged pairs, poor terminations, or beyond 100 m can pass data at a reduced rate while failing to deliver stable power.
  • 5. A power injector as the workaround: A midspan injector supplies power for one device when the switch cannot. Useful as a test to prove the device itself is fine.
Where you see it
  • Deploying a new generation of APs onto older switches
  • Cameras that reboot intermittently under load
exam: The exam's PoE questions are mostly budget exhaustion and standard mismatch. Know the wattage tiers, and know that show power inline is the command that answers the question.

front: A newly installed fiber link stays down at both ends. What are the likely causes in order?
answer:
1. TX and RX transposed — swap one end.
2. Transceiver mismatch — single-mode optic on multimode fiber, or different wavelengths.
3. Dirty or damaged connectors.
4. Distance beyond the optic's rating.
detail:
Fiber links are either up or hard down, and the causes are a short, ordered list. TX/RX transposition is by far the most common on a fresh install.
How it works
  • Transmit must reach receive: The strand leaving your TX must arrive at the far end's RX. Duplex fiber assemblies are usually crossed for you; individual strands patched by hand frequently are not. Swapping one end is a five-second test.
  • Optics must match the fiber and each other: A 1310 nm single-mode optic will not work over multimode fiber, and two optics of different wavelengths will not talk. Both ends must be the same type.
  • Contamination is invisible and common: A single dust particle on a fiber end face blocks a meaningful fraction of the light. Clean with proper tools before assuming hardware failure.
  • Verify with light, not guesses: A visual fault locator shows breaks and bad splices in the first few hundred metres. An optical power meter tells you whether light is arriving at the right level. An OTDR gives distance to the fault on a long run.
  • Too much light is also a fault: On a very short run with long-haul optics, the receiver can be overdriven. That is what inline attenuators are for.
Where you see it
  • Commissioning a new building-to-building link
  • A link that came up on the bench but not in the rack
exam: Objective 5.2 names TX/RX transposed explicitly, and it is the expected first answer for a fiber link that will not come up. Transceiver mismatch is the expected second.

front: Small pings succeed and web pages load, but large file transfers and VPN traffic hang. What is happening?
answer: An MTU mismatch, usually combined with ICMP being blocked so Path MTU Discovery cannot work.
detail:
This is one of the few problems where the symptom is size-dependent, which makes it distinctive once you have seen it.
How it works
  • Why size matters: Small packets fit through every link. Large ones need fragmentation somewhere. If the packet has Don't Fragment set and a router cannot forward it, the router must send back an ICMP 'Fragmentation Needed' message.
  • Blocking ICMP breaks the feedback: If that ICMP message is filtered, the sender never learns to send smaller packets. It keeps retransmitting the same oversized packet, which keeps being dropped. The connection hangs rather than failing cleanly — a black hole.
  • Tunnels shrink the usable MTU: GRE, IPsec and VXLAN all add headers, reducing the payload that fits. A tunnel over a 1500-byte path may only carry ~1400 bytes of original packet.
  • Test it with sized pings: ping -f -l 1472 host on Windows or ping -M do -s 1472 host on Linux sends a 1500-byte frame with Don't Fragment. Reduce the size until it succeeds to find the real path MTU.
  • The fixes: Permit ICMP type 3 code 4, lower the MTU on the tunnel interface, or clamp the TCP MSS at the edge.
Where you see it
  • Users who can browse but cannot upload attachments over the VPN
  • A new site-to-site tunnel where some applications work and others stall
exam: The signature to recognize is 'small packets work, large ones do not'. Also know that jumbo frames must be configured consistently end to end — enabling them on a server but not the switch produces giants and drops.

front: Traffic reaches a server but replies never get back, and the firewall log shows drops of traffic it says it never saw start. Why?
answer: Asymmetric routing. Traffic leaves by one path and returns by another, so a stateful firewall sees only half the conversation and drops the half with no matching session.
detail:
Stateful inspection assumes it sees both directions. Break that assumption and it correctly drops traffic that looks unsolicited.
How it works
  • How the asymmetry arises: Redundant paths with different metrics, two internet circuits, a mismatched pair of firewalls, or a route change on one direction only.
  • Why the firewall is right to drop it: A reply arriving with no recorded outbound session is indistinguishable from an unsolicited inbound packet. Dropping it is the correct default.
  • How to confirm it: Traceroute in both directions, and compare. Capture on both firewalls and see whether one holds the outbound flow and the other the return.
  • The fixes: Make routing symmetric with route policy or metric adjustment, use a firewall cluster that shares state, or place the firewall where both directions must pass through it.
Where you see it
  • A dual-ISP edge where some sessions fail unpredictably
  • An HA firewall pair after a partial failover
exam: Expect this as an advanced routing or firewall scenario. The concept to hold is that stateful inspection requires symmetric paths, and asymmetric routing is what breaks it.

front: A VoIP call connects and rings, but one party hears nothing. Where is the fault?
answer: In the media path (RTP), not the signaling path. SIP set the call up successfully; the audio streams on separate dynamic UDP ports are being blocked or mistranslated.
detail:
SIP and RTP are separate. Understanding that split resolves most VoIP troubleshooting immediately.
How it works
  • Signaling succeeded, so SIP is fine: The phone rang and the call was answered. That proves SIP on 5060/5061 traversed the network correctly.
  • RTP uses a separate dynamic port range: Audio flows over UDP on high, negotiated ports — commonly 16384-32767. A firewall permitting only 5060 blocks every audio stream.
  • NAT rewrites addresses SIP put in its body: SIP messages carry IP addresses inside the payload. NAT changes the header but not the body, so the far end sends audio to an unroutable private address. A SIP ALG or a session border controller fixes this.
  • One-way means one direction is blocked: Audio flowing one way and not the other narrows it to the firewall or NAT on the silent side.
  • Not to be confused with quality problems: No audio is a path problem. Choppy audio is jitter and a QoS problem. They are different questions.
Where you see it
  • A new phone system where internal calls work and external calls are silent
  • Remote workers whose calls connect but have no audio
exam: The distinction the exam wants is signaling versus media. If a call sets up but has no audio, the answer involves RTP ports, NAT traversal or a SIP ALG — never the SIP port itself.

front: A user's Wi-Fi drops as they walk between areas. Is it coverage, roaming, or interference?
answer: Check RSSI and SNR at the failure point. Weak signal → coverage. Strong signal, poor throughput → interference or contention. Good signal on an old AP → a sticky client failing to roam.
detail:
Three different wireless problems produce the same complaint. The measurements separate them.
How it works
  • Coverage gap: RSSI falls below roughly -70 dBm and the client has nothing better to associate with. The fix is another AP or repositioning, not more power — more power extends downlink without helping the client's weaker uplink.
  • Sticky client: The client holds on to a distant AP at a very low rate because its roaming threshold is conservative. It technically has signal, so it will not leave. The fix is tuning the minimum data rate, reducing cell size, or enabling 802.11k/v to steer it.
  • Interference: Strong RSSI with low SNR means noise. A Wi-Fi analyzer shows competing APs and channel overlap; a spectrum analyzer shows non-Wi-Fi sources a Wi-Fi analyzer cannot see at all.
  • Contention: Good signal, low noise, poor throughput, many clients on one AP. Shared media means everyone waits. The fix is more APs with smaller cells.
  • DFS events: On 5 GHz DFS channels, detected radar forces the AP to change channel immediately, disconnecting clients. Recurring drops at a site near an airport or weather radar point here.
Where you see it
  • Warehouse or hospital staff whose sessions drop while walking
  • A conference room that performs badly only when full
exam: The two most-tested wireless troubleshooting ideas: strong signal with poor performance means interference or contention, not coverage, and lowering transmit power is often the correct fix because oversized cells create co-channel interference and sticky clients.

front: New devices on the guest network cannot get addresses, but existing devices work fine. Why?
answer: DHCP scope exhaustion. Every address in the pool is leased, so the server has nothing to offer new clients and they fall back to APIPA.
detail:
Existing clients keep working because they already hold valid leases. Only new arrivals fail — that asymmetry is the diagnostic clue.
How it works
  • Guest and wireless networks exhaust fastest: High device turnover plus a default lease of eight days or more means addresses stay reserved long after the device has left the building.
  • Shorten the lease first: A guest network with a two-hour lease recycles addresses continuously. This is usually a faster fix than renumbering the subnet.
  • Widen the scope if the subnet allows: If the scope covers only part of the subnet, extend it. If the subnet itself is too small, you need a larger prefix — a /24 supporting 254 hosts will not serve 400 devices.
  • Look for phantom leases: Devices that changed MAC through randomization, or a misconfigured relay causing duplicate requests, can consume far more leases than there are devices.
  • Confirm on the server: The scope statistics show addresses in use versus available. That single number confirms or eliminates the theory in seconds.
Where you see it
  • A conference or event day when the guest network stops admitting people
  • A growing office that outgrew its original addressing plan
exam: The tell is new clients fail while existing clients are fine. Distinguish this from a DHCP server outage, where existing clients also fail as their leases expire. The first-line fix on the exam is shorten the lease time.

front: Users get a certificate warning on an internal site that worked yesterday. What are the causes?
answer: In likelihood order: the certificate expired; the system clock is wrong; the name does not match the URL; the issuing CA is not trusted (self-signed or a missing intermediate); or the certificate was revoked.
detail:
TLS validation checks several things at once, and any one failure produces the same generic browser warning.
How it works
  • Expiry is the most common: Certificates are dated. 'Worked yesterday' plus a warning today usually means it expired overnight. Renewal reminders exist because this happens constantly.
  • Clock skew produces the same error: If the client's date is wrong, a perfectly valid certificate appears not-yet-valid or expired. This is another reason NTP matters, and it explains warnings on a single machine rather than everyone.
  • Name mismatch: The certificate is issued for one name and the user typed another — an IP address instead of the hostname, or a name missing from the Subject Alternative Names.
  • Missing intermediate certificate: The server presents its own certificate but not the intermediate that links it to the trusted root. Browsers with a cached intermediate work; a fresh client does not — which produces the maddening 'works for some people' pattern.
  • Self-signed certificates are never trusted: Fine internally if the root is distributed to clients, but a self-signed certificate on its own always warns.
Where you see it
  • An internal application that suddenly warns for every user
  • A site that warns on new devices but not on established ones
exam: Two useful discriminators. Everyone affected at once → expiry or revocation. One machine affected → its clock or its trust store. The missing-intermediate case is the classic explanation for inconsistent behaviour between clients.

front: The network is slow every weekday between 02:00 and 04:00, and again at 13:00. How do you approach it?
answer: A predictable schedule means a scheduled job. Use flow data (NetFlow/sFlow) and interface utilization graphs to identify the top talkers during those windows.
detail:
Time-correlated problems have time-correlated causes. This is the one performance scenario you can solve without touching a single device configuration.
How it works
  • Look at what runs on a schedule: Backups, replication, antivirus definition pushes, OS patch deployment, imaging, database maintenance and cloud sync jobs. The 13:00 spike is often a lunchtime pattern instead — streaming, personal devices.
  • Flow data names the culprit: NetFlow records who talked to whom, on what port and how much. Filtered to the window, the top talker is usually obvious in one query.
  • Baselines make it visible: Without a baseline you cannot tell whether current utilization is abnormal. With one, the deviation is the whole answer.
  • The fixes are policy, not hardware: Reschedule the job outside business hours, rate-limit it, apply QoS so it yields to interactive traffic, or move the replication to a dedicated link.
  • Rule out the boring explanation: A single misconfigured backup client re-running a full backup every night instead of an incremental explains a great many of these.
Where you see it
  • Recurring complaints that mysteriously resolve by mid-morning
  • Capacity planning ahead of a circuit renewal
exam: The exam-relevant tools here are NetFlow/sFlow for who is using bandwidth and a performance baseline for knowing what normal looks like. If a question asks how to identify the source of high utilization, flow data is the answer, not a protocol analyzer.

front: Half the office loses connectivity at once; the other half is unaffected. What is your first move?
answer: Find what the failed half has in common and the working half does not — one switch, one uplink, one VLAN, one DHCP scope, one wireless controller, or one power circuit.
detail:
The split itself is the most valuable evidence you have. Do not start at a workstation.
How it works
  • Map the failure, do not sample it: Ask which specific people or rooms are affected. A physical or logical boundary will emerge — one floor, one wing, one department, one VLAN.
  • A shared switch or uplink is most likely: Everyone on one access switch, or everyone behind one uplink to the core, fails together. Check that switch's status and its uplink counters.
  • A shared logical resource is next: One VLAN, one DHCP scope that exhausted, one SVI that went down, or one DNS server that half the clients use.
  • Check what changed: A change made last night to one switch stack, one ACL, or one routing statement explains most sudden partial outages.
  • Resist the individual troubleshooting instinct: Rebuilding a user's network settings when twenty people share the symptom wastes the outage. The commonality is the fault.
Where you see it
  • A partial outage after an overnight maintenance window
  • Sudden failure affecting one floor of a building
exam: This tests the identify the problem step — specifically 'identify symptoms' and 'determine scope'. The correct exam answer is almost always the one that gathers information about what the affected devices share, not the one that starts changing a single client.

front: A workstation negotiates 100 Mbps on a gigabit switch port. Everything works, just slowly. Why?
answer: Almost always a cable fault — one or more of the four pairs is broken or badly terminated. Gigabit requires all four pairs; 100 Mbps needs only two, so the link falls back rather than failing.
detail:
This is a satisfying diagnosis because the symptom directly implies the cause.
How it works
  • Gigabit needs all four pairs: 1000BASE-T transmits on all four pairs simultaneously in both directions. 100BASE-TX uses two. Lose a pair and the link silently drops to the lower speed.
  • The usual physical causes: A damaged patch cable, a punch-down where two conductors were seated poorly, a split pair, or a run stretched past 100 m.
  • A cable tester proves it in seconds: It reports which pairs are open, shorted or miswired. This is exactly what the tool exists for.
  • Rule out the software explanations too: A manually configured 100 Mbps setting on either end, or an old NIC or driver, produces the same result. Check the interface configuration before replacing cable.
  • Do not confuse it with duplex mismatch: A duplex mismatch shows terrible throughput with errors and late collisions. A pair fault shows a clean 100 Mbps link with no errors.
Where you see it
  • A single desk that transfers files far slower than its neighbours
  • A run that worked before the office was recabled
exam: This is an objective 5.2 favourite. The chain to remember: gigabit needs four pairs → a link at 100 Mbps means a pair is bad → confirm with a cable tester.

front: Users report the internet is slow. How do you establish whether the fault is yours or the carrier's?
answer: Test on both sides of the demarcation point and use traceroute to find where latency or loss begins. If degradation starts at the first provider hop and internal tests are clean, the fault is theirs.
detail:
Collecting this evidence before opening a ticket is the difference between a carrier fixing the problem and a carrier closing it as no-fault-found.
How it works
  • The demarc is the responsibility boundary: It is the physical point where the provider's network ends and yours begins. Testing at it removes your firewall, switching and Wi-Fi from the measurement.
  • Test internally first: Run iperf between two internal hosts. Good internal throughput proves the LAN is not the bottleneck and narrows the problem to the edge or beyond.
  • Traceroute locates the entry point: Latency that rises at a hop and stays elevated for every hop after it is real degradation. Latency at one hop that returns to normal afterwards is just that router deprioritizing ICMP replies.
  • Capture evidence over time: One bad traceroute proves nothing. Repeated tests with timestamps, from a wired host, at the demarc, are what a carrier will act on.
  • Check your own edge honestly: A saturated WAN link, an undersized firewall doing deep inspection, or a duplex mismatch on the handoff are all yours, and all look like carrier problems from a desk.
Where you see it
  • Escalating a circuit performance complaint to an ISP
  • Defending an SLA claim with measurements
exam: The concept CompTIA wants is the demarcation point as the boundary of responsibility, and traceroute plus throughput testing as the evidence. Expect a scenario asking what a technician should do before contacting the provider.

front: A server answers ping but the application will not connect. What is the next test?
answer: Move to Layer 4. Confirm the service is listening on the server (netstat -an), then test the port from the client (telnet host port, Test-NetConnection, or a port scan).
detail:
Ping already proved Layers 1 through 3. Repeating connectivity tests wastes the time you have.
How it works
  • Listening is not the same as reachable: The service may be bound only to 127.0.0.1 rather than all interfaces — it works locally and refuses everything remote.
  • Test the specific port from the client: A successful TCP connection to the port proves the whole path including firewalls. A refusal means something answered and said no; a timeout means something silently dropped it.
  • Refused versus timed out is diagnostic: Connection refused means the host received it and nothing was listening — the network is fine. Timeout means a firewall or ACL dropped it silently.
  • Then check the host firewall: Windows Firewall and iptables block far more application traffic than network firewalls do, and they are easy to forget after a server rebuild.
  • Then check the application itself: Wrong port configured, service stopped, expired certificate, exhausted license, or a full disk. At that point it is no longer a network problem.
Where you see it
  • A new application server that pings fine and serves nothing
  • Proving to an application team that the network path is open
exam: This tests whether you follow the OSI model upward instead of re-testing what you proved. The refused versus timed out distinction is worth memorizing — it separates 'nothing is listening' from 'a firewall is dropping it'.

front: A firewall rule was added to permit a new application, but the traffic is still blocked. The rule looks correct. Why?
answer: Rule order. ACLs are evaluated top-down, first match wins. An earlier, broader deny is matching the traffic before your new permit is ever reached.
detail:
An ACL is not a set of conditions that are all considered. It is a list read in order, and evaluation stops at the first match.
How it works
  • First match wins, then evaluation stops: If rule 10 denies the subnet and rule 90 permits the host, the host is denied. Nothing below the matching line is consulted.
  • Specific rules go above general ones: Order from most specific to least. A host permit must sit above the subnet deny, not below it.
  • There is always an implicit deny at the end: Anything not explicitly permitted is dropped. An ACL that contains only permits still blocks everything else, which surprises people who think an empty ACL is permissive.
  • Adding a rule usually appends it: On many platforms a new line lands at the bottom by default, which is exactly where it will never be reached. Insert it at the right sequence number.
  • Check the hit counters: Most platforms count matches per rule. A new rule with zero hits while traffic is failing proves something above it is matching first.
Where you see it
  • A new application permitted on paper but still failing in practice
  • Auditing why traffic that should be denied is getting through
exam: This is one of the most reliably tested firewall concepts. Two things to hold: top-down, first match wins, and the implicit deny any at the end of every ACL. If a scenario says the rule exists but traffic is blocked, the answer is almost always rule order.

front: A new subnet can reach the server, but the server cannot reply. Pings from the server to the new subnet fail. What is missing?
answer: A return route. The router or the server itself has no path back to the new subnet, so replies are dropped or sent to the wrong gateway.
detail:
Reachability is not symmetric by default. Every conversation needs a route in both directions and it is easy to configure only one.
How it works
  • Traffic reached the server, so the outbound path exists: The request arrived. That eliminates the client-side routing, the switching and the firewall in that direction.
  • Check the server's own routing table: A multi-homed server with a default gateway on the wrong interface sends replies out the wrong NIC. route print or ip route shows it.
  • Check the router between them: A new subnet added on one router but never advertised or statically defined on the other means the return traffic has nowhere to go.
  • Static routing scales badly for exactly this reason: Every new subnet needs a matching entry on every device that must reach it. Missing one is the normal failure mode, and why dynamic routing exists.
  • Traceroute from both ends: Running it in each direction shows which direction dies and at which hop, which is far faster than reading configurations.
Where you see it
  • A newly created VLAN whose hosts cannot be reached from the data centre
  • A multi-homed server that answers on one interface and not the other
exam: Expect this after a scenario describes adding a subnet or a site. The idea to hold is that routing must exist in both directions, and a one-way failure points at the return path, not the request path.

front: A busy office intermittently cannot open new connections to the internet, though existing sessions keep working. What is running out?
answer: PAT port exhaustion. The edge device translates many private hosts to one public IP by tracking unique source ports, and it has run out of available port numbers or NAT table entries.
detail:
PAT gives roughly 64,000 concurrent translations per public address in theory, far fewer in practice once timeouts and reserved ranges are accounted for.
How it works
  • Modern applications open many connections each: A single browser session can hold dozens of simultaneous connections. A few hundred users can consume tens of thousands of translations.
  • The symptom is specifically new connections: Established sessions have entries already. Only new ones fail, which produces intermittent, user-specific complaints rather than a clean outage.
  • Long timeouts make it worse: Translation entries linger after the session ends. Aggressive idle timeouts free them sooner.
  • Check the translation table size: The device reports active translations and its maximum. That number confirms or eliminates the theory immediately.
  • The fixes: Add public addresses to the NAT pool, shorten translation timeouts, or move heavy talkers behind their own address.
Where you see it
  • An office that grew without the NAT pool growing with it
  • A guest network sharing one public IP with hundreds of devices
exam: The pattern to recognize is existing connections fine, new connections failing, intermittently, for many users. Distinguish it from DHCP scope exhaustion, where clients cannot get addresses at all rather than failing only outbound.

front: After merging with another office over a new VPN, some hosts at each site cannot reach the other site at all. What is the likely cause?
answer: Overlapping IP address space. Both sites used the same RFC1918 range, so each host believes the remote address is local and never sends it to the tunnel.
detail:
Two organizations independently choosing 192.168.1.0/24 is close to a certainty, and it breaks site-to-site connectivity in a way that looks like a VPN fault.
How it works
  • The host never routes the traffic: If the destination matches the host's own subnet after masking, the host ARPs for it locally instead of sending it to the gateway. The VPN is never consulted.
  • The tunnel itself looks healthy: The VPN is up, the peers are established, and the logs are clean. That misleads people into troubleshooting the tunnel for hours.
  • Only overlapping ranges fail: Non-overlapping subnets at each site work perfectly, which produces the confusing partial pattern.
  • The fixes: Renumber one side, which is correct but disruptive. Or apply NAT on the tunnel so each side sees the other through a translated range.
  • Prevent it with planning: This is the practical argument for allocating from 10.0.0.0/8 with a documented scheme rather than defaulting to 192.168.1.0/24.
Where you see it
  • Any merger, acquisition or new partner connection
  • Connecting a home office whose router uses the same default range as the corporate LAN
exam: Expect this in a site-to-site VPN scenario where the tunnel is confirmed up but traffic does not pass. The answer is overlapping address space, and the remedies are renumbering or NAT.

front: A remote user's VPN connects successfully but they cannot reach any internal resources. Where do you look?
answer: Authentication succeeded, so look past it: routes pushed to the client, split-tunnel policy, the firewall rules for the VPN pool, and whether internal routing knows how to return traffic to that pool.
detail:
A connected tunnel proves authentication and the transport. Everything after that is routing and policy.
How it works
  • Check what routes the client received: route print or ip route on the client. If no internal subnets were pushed, the client sends everything to its local gateway instead of the tunnel.
  • Split tunnel may be excluding the target: A split-tunnel policy lists which subnets go through the VPN. A subnet missing from that list is simply not tunneled.
  • Firewall rules for the VPN pool: Remote clients get addresses from a separate pool that often needs its own explicit rules. A new pool with no rules connects fine and reaches nothing.
  • Return routing for the pool: Internal routers must know that the VPN pool is reachable via the concentrator. Without it, replies are dropped.
  • DNS for internal names: If the client kept its home DNS server, internal hostnames will not resolve even when the routing is perfect. That looks like no access but is name resolution.
Where you see it
  • A newly deployed remote-access VPN
  • An existing VPN after a new internal subnet was added
exam: The exam framing is 'the VPN connects but the user cannot access resources'. Reject any answer about credentials or the tunnel itself — connection succeeded eliminates those. The answer lies in routing, split-tunnel scope, or firewall policy.

front: Users report a destination is unreachable, and traceroute shows the same two routers repeating over and over. What is happening?
answer: A routing loop. Two routers each believe the other is the next hop for the destination, so packets bounce between them until the TTL reaches zero.
detail:
Unlike a Layer 2 loop, a routing loop does not melt the network — TTL kills each packet — but the destination is unreachable and the link between the two routers carries wasted traffic.
How it works
  • TTL is what limits the damage: Each router decrements it. At zero the packet is discarded and an ICMP Time Exceeded is returned, which is exactly what traceroute displays as the repeating pattern.
  • Usual causes: A static route pointing back toward the source, bad redistribution between two routing protocols, or a summary route that attracts traffic for networks that do not exist.
  • Distance-vector protocols have specific defences: Split horizon prevents advertising a route back out the interface it was learned on. Route poisoning and hold-down timers stop a withdrawn route from being relearned from a stale neighbour.
  • Check the routing table on both routers: show ip route for the destination on each. If each points at the other, you have found it.
  • Summarization can cause it: A router advertising a summary that includes networks it cannot actually reach attracts that traffic and may send it back toward its source.
Where you see it
  • A destination that became unreachable after a redistribution change
  • An unreachable network following a summarization change
exam: The traceroute output showing alternating repeated hops is the giveaway. Also expect a question naming the mechanisms that prevent loops: split horizon, route poisoning, hold-down timers, and TTL as the backstop.

front: Two switches are trunked. Traffic from VLAN 1 appears in VLAN 99 and the logs show native VLAN mismatch errors. What went wrong?
answer: The two ends of the trunk disagree about which VLAN is sent untagged. Frames untagged by one switch are placed into the other switch's native VLAN, merging two VLANs.
detail:
The native VLAN is the one exception to tagging on an 802.1Q trunk, and that exception is exactly where the security and connectivity problems live.
How it works
  • Untagged frames land in whatever the receiver calls native: Switch A sends VLAN 1 untagged. Switch B, whose native is 99, receives an untagged frame and assumes it belongs to VLAN 99. Two separate VLANs are now bridged.
  • CDP and LLDP detect it: Both protocols exchange native VLAN information and log a mismatch. That log entry is often the only obvious symptom.
  • It enables double-tagging VLAN hopping: An attacker on the native VLAN can craft a frame with two tags. The first switch strips the outer tag and forwards the frame with the inner tag into another VLAN.
  • The fixes: Match the native VLAN on both ends, change it away from the default VLAN 1, and do not use the native VLAN for user traffic.
Where you see it
  • A trunk built by two different engineers on different days
  • Unexplained traffic leaking between two VLANs
exam: Two exam angles. Connectivity — mismatched native VLANs merge traffic between VLANs. Security — the native VLAN is the enabler of double-tagging, and the mitigation is changing it off VLAN 1 and not carrying user traffic on it.

front: A new link aggregation bundle will not come up, and the member ports show as suspended. What must match?
answer: Every member port on both switches must agree on speed, duplex, allowed VLAN list, native VLAN, and channel mode. Any difference suspends the port rather than bundling it.
detail:
Suspension is a protection, not a failure. The switch refuses to bundle mismatched links because doing so would create a loop or black-hole traffic.
How it works
  • LACP negotiates and verifies: 802.3ad exchanges LACP frames so both ends confirm they agree before forwarding. A static bundle skips this, which is why a misconfigured static bundle can create a loop.
  • Mode compatibility matters: LACP active pairs with active or passive. Passive with passive never forms a bundle, because nobody initiates.
  • VLAN configuration must be identical: Different allowed VLAN lists on two members means frames for some VLANs would traverse only some links. The switch refuses.
  • Check both sides: The mismatch is frequently on the far end where you did not configure anything. show etherchannel summary reports the reason code.
  • Physical must match too: One member at 1 Gbps and another at 100 Mbps cannot be bundled.
Where you see it
  • Adding a second uplink between two switches for bandwidth and redundancy
  • A bundle that worked until someone changed a VLAN on one member
exam: Expect either 'what must be identical across EtherChannel members' or a suspended-port scenario. Also know the static versus LACP risk: static bundles have no negotiation, so a half-configured static bundle can form a loop.

front: A switch suddenly floods all traffic out every port and performance collapses across the segment. Sniffing shows traffic destined for other hosts. What is happening?
answer: The CAM (MAC address) table is full. With no room to learn real addresses, the switch floods unknown unicast frames out every port — behaving like a hub.
detail:
This is either a MAC flooding attack or, less dramatically, a Layer 2 loop generating enormous numbers of source addresses.
How it works
  • How the attack works: A tool sends frames with thousands of forged source MAC addresses. The switch dutifully learns each one until the table is exhausted.
  • Flooding is the failure mode: A switch that cannot look up a destination has only one safe behaviour: send it everywhere. That gives the attacker visibility into traffic that was never meant for them.
  • A loop produces similar symptoms: MAC flapping and constant relearning can also exhaust the table, so check spanning tree before assuming an attack.
  • The mitigation is port security: Limiting the number of MAC addresses learned per port makes the attack impossible from a user port. Violations can shut the port down or restrict it.
  • Confirm with the table size: show mac address-table count shows entries used against the maximum.
Where you see it
  • A security incident where an attacker is capturing traffic on a switched network
  • Segment-wide slowness with no obvious link fault
exam: The exam pairs MAC flooding with port security as the mitigation, and expects you to know that the switch fails open by flooding rather than failing closed. Contrast with ARP poisoning, which is mitigated by Dynamic ARP Inspection.

front: A user swaps their laptop for a new one and the port goes dead. Nothing else changed. Why?
answer: Port security recorded the old laptop's MAC address as the only permitted device. The new MAC is a violation, and the default action shut the port down.
detail:
Port security is doing exactly what it was configured to do. The problem is operational, not technical.
How it works
  • Sticky MAC learning is the usual culprit: The switch learned the first MAC it saw and wrote it into the running configuration. Any other device is now a violation.
  • Three violation modes: Protect silently drops the offending traffic. Restrict drops and logs and increments a counter. Shutdown err-disables the port, which is the default and the most disruptive.
  • Clearing requires more than a bounce: The stale sticky entry must be removed, or the port will shut down again the moment the new laptop transmits.
  • Check the log for the offending MAC: The violation message names the MAC that triggered it, which confirms the diagnosis immediately.
  • Not the same as 802.1X: Port security filters by hardware address. 802.1X authenticates a user or device identity against a RADIUS server, and is not defeated by MAC spoofing.
Where you see it
  • Hardware refresh cycles in an environment with sticky MAC learning
  • A user plugging a personal device into an office jack
