exam: Recognize the pattern: a port that dies after a device change. Also know the three violation modes by name and behaviour, and the contrast that MAC filtering and port security are both trivially defeated by MAC spoofing, which is the argument for 802.1X.

front: Clients can see the corporate SSID and try to connect, but authentication fails for everyone. WPA3-Enterprise is in use. Where do you look?
answer: The RADIUS path: is the server reachable from the WLC or AP, is the shared secret correct, has the RADIUS server certificate expired, and does the client trust the CA that issued it?
detail:
Enterprise wireless has more moving parts than PSK. Association working while authentication fails narrows the problem to the 802.1X exchange.
How it works
  • Association succeeded, so the radio is fine: The client found the SSID and negotiated the radio parameters. Signal, channel and band are not the issue.
  • Reachability between authenticator and server: The AP or controller is the authenticator and must reach RADIUS on UDP 1812. A firewall change or a routing change breaks every client at once.
  • The shared secret: A mismatched RADIUS shared secret fails silently from the client's perspective and produces a specific rejection in the server log.
  • Certificate expiry is the classic total outage: The RADIUS server presents a certificate during EAP. When it expires, every client that validates it refuses at once — a whole-site failure with no configuration change.
  • Client-side trust: With EAP-TLS or PEAP, the client must trust the issuing CA. A new device that never received the internal root certificate fails while existing devices work.
Where you see it
  • A site-wide wireless outage with no recent configuration change
  • New devices failing to join while existing ones stay connected
exam: The high-value discriminator is everyone fails at once versus only new devices fail. Everyone → server reachability, shared secret, or an expired server certificate. Only new devices → missing client trust or missing credentials.

front: A new IoT sensor cannot see the wireless network, though laptops and phones connect fine in the same room. What is the likely cause?
answer: The device is 2.4 GHz only and the SSID is being broadcast on 5 GHz, or 2.4 GHz has been disabled or is using a channel width or security mode the device does not support.
detail:
Low-cost IoT hardware is frequently 2.4 GHz only and often supports only older security standards, which conflicts with modern wireless hardening.
How it works
  • Band support is the first check: Many sensors, thermostats, cameras and printers have no 5 GHz radio at all. If the SSID exists only on 5 GHz, they will never see it.
  • WPA3-only breaks older clients: A device that supports only WPA2 cannot join a WPA3-only SSID. Transition mode allows both, at some security cost.
  • Channel width can matter: Some legacy devices fail on 40 MHz channels in 2.4 GHz. Setting 20 MHz is good practice anyway and often fixes them.
  • Band steering can work against you: Steering assumes dual-band clients. It generally ignores single-band devices, but aggressive configurations can interfere with them.
  • The right answer architecturally: Put IoT on its own SSID, its own VLAN and its own security profile, so the main network is not weakened to accommodate them.
Where you see it
  • Deploying sensors, cameras or smart devices onto a modern corporate WLAN
  • A printer that will not join after a wireless upgrade
exam: The exam angle is usually segmentation: the correct answer is a separate SSID and VLAN for IoT rather than downgrading security network-wide. Know that 2.4 GHz-only clients and WPA2-only clients are the two common compatibility limits.

front: Guests connect to the wireless network but the login page never appears. What breaks a captive portal?
answer: The portal works by intercepting an unencrypted HTTP request and redirecting it. Modern clients try HTTPS or DNS-over-HTTPS first, which cannot be transparently redirected.
detail:
Captive portals depend on a behaviour — plain HTTP on first request — that browsers and operating systems have been actively removing.
How it works
  • HTTPS cannot be silently redirected: Intercepting a TLS connection produces a certificate warning rather than a login page, because that interception is exactly what TLS is designed to prevent.
  • DNS must resolve before redirect: The portal typically answers DNS itself to force the redirect. If the client uses DoH or a hardcoded resolver, the interception never happens.
  • Devices probe a known URL: Phones and laptops request a specific plain-HTTP detection URL at join time. If that probe is blocked, the device never learns a portal exists.
  • Walled garden gaps: The portal must permit its own authentication, certificate validation and any identity provider before login. A missing entry leaves the page half-loaded.
  • Manual workaround: Browsing to a known plain-HTTP address forces the redirect and is a useful diagnostic as well as a user workaround.
Where you see it
  • Guest and conference wireless
  • Hotel and public networks that never present a login screen
exam: This is a modern scenario. The concept CompTIA wants is that a captive portal intercepts and redirects HTTP, and that the guest network should be segmented from internal resources regardless of who authenticates to it.

front: One conference room has strong signal but unusable Wi-Fi whenever it is full. Everywhere else is fine. What is it?
answer: Contention, not coverage. Wireless is shared media — one AP serving forty devices means every device waits its turn on a single channel.
detail:
Strong signal rules out coverage. Full room plus poor performance points at client density.
How it works
  • Airtime is the scarce resource: Only one device transmits at a time in a given channel. Adding clients divides the same airtime further, regardless of signal strength.
  • Slow clients penalize everyone: A distant client transmitting at a low data rate occupies airtime far longer than a fast one. Setting a minimum data rate forces such clients to roam or connect elsewhere.
  • OFDMA helps exactly this case: Wi-Fi 6 divides a channel into resource units so several clients share one transmission. It was designed for density, which is why it helps here and not on a single-client speed test.
  • The fixes are architectural: More APs with smaller cells and lower transmit power, band steering to move capable clients to 5 or 6 GHz, and a channel plan that avoids co-channel overlap between them.
  • More power is the wrong answer: It enlarges the cell, attracts more distant clients at low rates, and increases co-channel interference with neighbouring APs.
Where you see it
  • All-hands meetings and training rooms
  • Lecture halls and auditoriums
exam: The trap answer is 'increase transmit power'. The correct direction is more APs, smaller cells, lower power. Recognize strong signal plus poor throughput plus many clients as contention.

front: A server was moved to a new IP yesterday. Most users reached it immediately; a few still hit the old address. Why, and what should have been done first?
answer: Those clients or their resolvers are still serving the record from cache until its TTL expires. The record's TTL should have been lowered well before the migration.
detail:
DNS caching is a feature, and it becomes a migration problem only when nobody plans for it.
How it works
  • TTL controls cache lifetime: A record with a 24-hour TTL can be served from a cache for a full day after you change it. Nothing you do on the authoritative server shortens that.
  • Lower the TTL before the change: Drop it to a few minutes at least one full old-TTL period before the cutover, so caches expire quickly during the migration. Raise it again afterwards to reduce query load.
  • Caches exist at several layers: The client OS, the browser, the corporate resolver and the ISP resolver each cache independently. Flushing the client fixes one machine, not the population.
  • Confirm what is cached: dig shows the remaining TTL on a cached answer. Querying the authoritative server directly shows the true current record.
  • Keep the old address alive during transition: Leaving a redirect or the old service running until caches drain avoids the partial-outage window entirely.
Where you see it
  • Any planned server or site migration
  • Failing over to a disaster recovery site by DNS
exam: Expect the migration-planning version of this question: what should be done before changing a DNS record. The answer is lowering the TTL in advance. Also recognize 'some users reach the old server' as a caching symptom, not a configuration error.

front: Clients get valid IP addresses and can reach each other, but nobody can resolve names. DHCP is working. What was misconfigured?
answer: A DHCP option — most likely option 6, the DNS server list, pointing at a decommissioned or wrong resolver.
detail:
DHCP delivers more than an address. When the address is right and something else is wrong, the options are where to look.
How it works
  • Confirm what was actually issued: ipconfig /all shows the DNS servers the client received and which server issued the lease. Compare against what the scope is supposed to hand out.
  • The options that matter: 3 default gateway, 6 DNS servers, 15 domain name, 42 NTP servers, 66/67 TFTP server and boot filename for PXE and phones.
  • Symptoms map to options: Wrong option 3 breaks off-subnet access. Wrong option 6 breaks name resolution while IPs still work. Missing 66/67 breaks PXE boot and phone provisioning.
  • Scope options versus server options: A server-level option applies everywhere; a scope-level option overrides it for that scope. A change made at the wrong level produces inconsistent results between subnets.
  • A rogue server hands out its own options: If the issuing server in ipconfig /all is not yours, you have a rogue DHCP server, and DHCP snooping is the fix.
Where you see it
  • After decommissioning a domain controller or DNS server
  • A new subnet whose scope was copied from an old one
exam: The reliable signal is addressing works but one specific capability does not. Learn the option numbers 3, 6, 15, 66 and 67 — CompTIA lists them and asks which option delivers which value.

front: Internal users reach an application by name, but remote VPN users get the public address and fail. Why?
answer: Split-horizon DNS is answering differently by source. The VPN clients are being served the external view, or they are still using their home resolver rather than the internal one.
detail:
One name, two correct answers depending on where you are. That design is useful and is also a common source of confusion.
How it works
  • Two zones, same name: The internal view returns the private address; the external view returns the public one. Which you get depends on which resolver answers.
  • VPN clients must use internal DNS: If the tunnel does not push internal resolvers, or split tunneling leaves DNS going out locally, the client gets the public answer.
  • The public answer may not be reachable over the tunnel: Hairpinning back out to a public address from inside the tunnel frequently fails at the firewall, which is why the internal view exists.
  • Confirm which resolver answered: nslookup reports the server that responded. If it is the user's home router, the diagnosis is complete.
  • Keep the two views consistent: A record added to one view and forgotten in the other produces the same class of failure and is easy to miss.
Where you see it
  • Remote workers reaching internal applications by name
  • An application that works in the office and fails at home
exam: This tests whether you understand that DNS answers can legitimately differ by source. In a VPN scenario where names resolve to the wrong address, the answer involves the DNS servers pushed to the client, not the application.

front: Some clients on a subnet get correct addressing and others get addresses from an unfamiliar range with a different gateway. What is happening?
answer: Two DHCP servers are answering — either a rogue server or a second legitimate server with an overlapping scope. Whichever replies first wins each request.
detail:
The randomness is the diagnostic clue. A configuration error is consistent; a race between two servers is not.
How it works
  • The client accepts the first offer: DHCP has no authentication and no arbitration. Whichever server answers the broadcast first gets the client, which is why the split appears random.
  • Identify the issuing server: ipconfig /all names it. An unfamiliar address there is your answer, and it is usually a consumer router someone plugged in backwards.
  • Overlapping legitimate scopes are just as bad: Two properly configured servers whose scopes overlap will eventually issue the same address twice, producing duplicate-IP symptoms.
  • The mitigation is DHCP snooping: The switch trusts DHCP replies only from designated ports. Offers from any other port are dropped, which eliminates rogue servers entirely.
  • It also enables DAI: DHCP snooping builds the binding table that Dynamic ARP Inspection uses, so enabling it protects against ARP poisoning as well.
Where you see it
  • A consumer router plugged into a wall jack by a well-meaning user
  • Two data centre DHCP servers configured with overlapping scopes
exam: Recognize inconsistent addressing across clients on one subnet as competing DHCP servers. The mitigation the exam wants is DHCP snooping with trusted ports.

front: A link between two switches drops for a few seconds several times a day. The cable was replaced and the problem persists. What next?
answer: Suspect the transceiver (SFP) or the interface itself. Check optical power levels, error counters over time, and swap the optic before replacing anything larger.
detail:
Intermittent faults are the hardest class because they pass every test you run while you are watching.
How it works
  • Optics degrade rather than fail cleanly: A dying laser produces falling transmit power and rising errors long before the link goes fully down. show interface transceiver reports the levels on many platforms.
  • Correlate with counters over time: A one-off reading proves nothing. Graph input errors and CRCs and compare against the drop times from the logs.
  • Swap one variable at a time: Move the optic to a known-good port, or put a known-good optic in the same port. That distinguishes the transceiver from the interface.
  • Check for environmental correlation: Drops that cluster at the same times of day can be thermal, or can track a scheduled job saturating the link. Rule out congestion before condemning hardware.
  • Do not overlook the far end: Both ends have an optic. Replacing only yours is a coin flip.
Where you see it
  • A flapping uplink that has already survived a cable replacement
  • Links in a hot or poorly ventilated closet
exam: Objective 5.2 lists transceiver mismatch and signal strength as hardware issues. For intermittent optical faults the expected answer involves checking light levels and swapping the transceiver rather than re-pulling fiber.

front: A cable run passes a continuity test but shows high error rates under load. It runs alongside conduit carrying fluorescent lighting. What is happening and how do you prove it?
answer: EMI from the adjacent power and lighting, and possibly crosstalk from poor termination. A continuity tester cannot see either — you need a cable certifier.
detail:
Continuity proves the wires connect. It says nothing about whether the signal survives at speed.
How it works
  • A tester and a certifier answer different questions: A tester checks that eight conductors reach the right pins. A certifier measures attenuation, NEXT, return loss and delay skew against the TIA standard and issues a pass or fail.
  • EMI corrupts frames without breaking the link: The link stays up and the counters climb. Errors trigger retransmissions, which is why throughput collapses under load but a ping still succeeds.
  • Crosstalk usually comes from termination: Untwisting more than about half an inch of pair at the jack destroys the noise cancellation the twist provides. It is the most common installation defect.
  • The physical fixes: Reroute away from power and lighting, maintain separation, use shielded cable (properly bonded at one end) in noisy environments, and re-terminate with minimal untwist.
  • Distance counts too: Beyond 100 m the signal degrades regardless of noise. Measure the actual run, including the slack in the ceiling.
Where you see it
  • Cabling installed alongside electrical conduit
  • Runs near motors, lifts, welders or industrial equipment
exam: The tool distinction is the point: a cable tester validates wiring, a certifier validates performance. If a scenario says the cable tests good but performs badly, a basic tester was used and the answer involves certification, EMI or crosstalk.

front: A user reports their whole floor went down right after they tidied their desk. What did they most likely do?
answer: Plugged both ends of a patch cable into two wall jacks, creating a Layer 2 loop back through the switch.
detail:
This is the most common accidental outage in an office, and it is why BPDU Guard exists.
How it works
  • Two jacks on the same VLAN form a loop: Both jacks land on the same switch. A cable between them gives broadcast frames a circular path with no TTL to stop them.
  • It escalates in seconds: Each pass through the switch duplicates the broadcast. CPU saturates, the MAC table thrashes, and the segment stops forwarding useful traffic.
  • Find it by MAC flapping: The log shows the same MAC address bouncing between two ports. Those two ports are the ends of the loop.
  • BPDU Guard prevents the whole class of problem: On access ports, receiving a BPDU shuts the port down immediately. It also stops users adding unmanaged switches.
  • Loopback detection is the backstop: Some platforms send a special frame and disable the port if it comes back — useful where BPDU Guard alone does not catch a loop through a device that does not forward BPDUs.
Where you see it
  • Office moves and desk reorganizations
  • Any environment with live wall jacks and available patch cables
exam: The scenario wording usually involves a user, a patch cable and a sudden outage. The preventive answer is BPDU Guard on access ports; the immediate answer is to find and physically break the loop.

front: A wiring closet's equipment reboots during brief power events, and one switch has now failed permanently. What was missing?
answer: A properly sized and maintained UPS. Brief sags and surges reach the equipment directly, and repeated hard power cycles kill hardware.
detail:
Power is a Layer 1 problem that gets ignored until it destroys something expensive.
How it works
  • A UPS does more than provide runtime: It conditions power — absorbing sags, surges and brief outages that would otherwise reach the equipment. That protection matters more than the battery minutes.
  • Batteries have a service life: Typically three to five years. An untested UPS is an assumption, not a control. Test under load on a schedule.
  • Size it for the load and the goal: Enough capacity to ride through brief events, or enough to shut things down gracefully. Adding equipment to a closet without recalculating the load is how a UPS silently becomes undersized.
  • A managed PDU adds visibility and control: Per-outlet metering shows actual draw, and remote power cycling lets you reboot a hung device without driving to the site.
  • Environment kills equipment too: Heat is the other closet killer. Monitor temperature and humidity alongside power.
Where you see it
  • Branch offices and closets on unreliable power
  • Any closet where equipment has been added over the years
exam: Objective 3.3 covers power and environmental controls. Expect a question about what a UPS provides beyond battery runtime — the answer includes power conditioning — and about monitoring temperature and humidity in equipment spaces.

front: A file transfer over a high-bandwidth, high-latency WAN link runs far slower than the link should allow, with no packet loss. Why?
answer: The TCP window is too small for the bandwidth-delay product. The sender fills the window, then stops and waits for acknowledgements that take a full round trip to arrive.
detail:
This is the classic 'long fat network' problem, and it is why a fast link between distant sites can feel slow with no fault present.
How it works
  • Bandwidth-delay product is the pipe's capacity: Bandwidth multiplied by round-trip time gives how much data can be in flight. A 100 Mbps link with 100 ms RTT holds over a megabyte — far more than a default window.
  • Without window scaling the ceiling is low: The original TCP window field caps at 64 KB. Window scaling (RFC 1323) multiplies it, and both ends must support and negotiate it.
  • The signature is no loss and low throughput: Errors and discards are clean, latency is high but stable, and a single transfer plateaus well below the link rate. Multiple parallel transfers fill the link, which confirms it.
  • Parallel streams are the workaround: Transfer tools that open several connections sidestep the per-connection window limit. That is why some applications saturate the link and others do not.
  • WAN optimization exists for this: Accelerators terminate TCP locally and use a tuned session across the WAN, which is the productized version of the same fix.
Where you see it
  • Replication or backup between distant data centres
  • A new international circuit that benchmarks badly on a single transfer
exam: The tell is high bandwidth, high latency, no loss, one slow transfer, but parallel transfers fill the link. Know the term bandwidth-delay product and that TCP window scaling is the mechanism that addresses it.

front: During busy periods one application becomes unusable while everything else is fine. There is no packet loss on the interface overall. What explains it?
answer: QoS is doing its job — that application's traffic is in a lower-priority class and is being dropped or delayed first when the link congests.
detail:
Selective degradation of one application during congestion is a policy outcome, not a fault.
How it works
  • QoS decides who suffers: When a link saturates, something must be dropped. Classification and queuing determine what. An unclassified application falls into the default class and is dropped first.
  • Check the class counters, not just the interface: Per-class drop counters show which queue is discarding. The interface total may look healthy while one class is being decimated.
  • Marking may be wrong or stripped: DSCP markings set at the edge can be reset by a device that does not trust them, or never applied because the traffic was not matched by the classifier.
  • Shaping versus policing changes the symptom: Shaping buffers excess traffic, producing delay and jitter. Policing drops or remarks it, producing loss. The symptom tells you which is in play.
  • The fix is classification, not bandwidth: Adding bandwidth helps until the next growth. Correctly classifying the application into an appropriate class fixes it properly.
Where you see it
  • A new business application deployed without a QoS classification
  • VoIP or video that degrades only when the link is busy
exam: This tests whether you understand QoS as managed unfairness. If a scenario describes one application degrading while others are fine during congestion, look at classification and marking rather than the link.

front: After enabling jumbo frames on a storage server, its throughput collapses and some transfers fail entirely. What went wrong?
answer: Jumbo frames were not enabled consistently end to end. Switches in the path still enforce a 1500-byte MTU, so the oversized frames are dropped as giants.
detail:
Jumbo frames are all-or-nothing along a path. A single device at the default MTU breaks the whole benefit.
How it works
  • Every device in the path must agree: Server NIC, every switch port and every intermediate interface. One default-MTU switch discards the oversized frames silently.
  • The symptom is size-dependent: Small operations succeed and large transfers fail. That is the same signature as an MTU mismatch, because it is one.
  • Look for giants in the counters: Frames exceeding the interface MTU are counted as giants and dropped. Rising giants immediately after an MTU change is conclusive.
  • Verify with a sized ping: Send a 9000-byte payload with Don't Fragment set. If it fails while a 1500-byte payload succeeds, the path does not support jumbo frames.
  • Only turn it on where it pays: Jumbo frames help bulk transfer on storage and backup networks. On general-purpose LANs the gain is small and the misconfiguration risk is real.
Where you see it
  • iSCSI or NFS storage networks
  • Backup and replication VLANs
exam: This is the practical version of the MTU question. Hold two facts: jumbo frames must be configured consistently end to end, and oversized frames appear as giants in the interface counters.

front: Users report downloads are fine but uploads crawl. The circuit is advertised at 300 Mbps. Is this a fault?
answer: Probably not. Most consumer and many business broadband services are asymmetric — the advertised figure is the download rate, and upload is a fraction of it.
detail:
Knowing the circuit type before troubleshooting saves a great deal of wasted effort.
How it works
  • Cable and DSL are asymmetric by design: DOCSIS and DSL allocate far more capacity downstream. A 300/20 service is normal and not a fault.
  • Fibre and dedicated circuits are usually symmetric: A dedicated internet access circuit or fibre service typically provides equal rates in both directions. If a symmetric circuit is asymmetric in practice, that is a real fault.
  • Check the service order, not just the marketing: The contracted rate in both directions is the number that matters when raising a ticket.
  • Uploads expose the return path: Cloud backup, video calls and file sharing are upload-heavy and are usually the first workloads to reveal an undersized uplink.
  • Confirm with a directional test: A speed test at the demarc reporting both directions distinguishes an asymmetric service from a degraded one.
Where you see it
  • Cloud backup that never finishes overnight
  • Video conferencing where the remote party sees poor quality but you see them clearly
exam: The exam point is that asymmetric service is a design characteristic of some circuit types, not a defect. Recognize the difference between an asymmetric service performing to spec and a symmetric circuit that has degraded.

front: A link between a server and a switch shows terrible throughput under load, with late collisions on one side and CRC errors on the other. What is the cause?
answer: A duplex mismatch — one side hardcoded to full duplex, the other left on autonegotiation and therefore defaulting to half.
detail:
This is the classic mismatch, and the error pattern is diagnostic on its own.
How it works
  • Autonegotiation needs both ends: If one side is hardcoded, the other cannot negotiate and falls back to half duplex. Speed is usually detected correctly, so the link comes up and looks fine.
  • The error signature is split: The half-duplex side reports late collisions and runts because it detects the other side transmitting while it is. The full-duplex side reports CRC and FCS errors from the truncated frames.
  • It only hurts under load: At low traffic the two sides rarely transmit simultaneously. The problem appears exactly when the link is being used, which is why it survives casual testing.
  • The fix is to match, not to guess: Set both ends the same. Either both auto or both hardcoded to identical values. Hardcoding one end only is what created the problem.
  • Full duplex should never show collisions: Any collision counter on a link you believe is full duplex is evidence the far end disagrees.
Where you see it
  • A server whose backup window keeps overrunning
  • A link that was hardcoded years ago and forgotten
exam: CompTIA tests this through the counters. Late collisions and runts on one side plus CRCs on the other means duplex mismatch, and the answer is to match the settings on both ends.

front: An older switch will not link to another switch with a standard patch cable, though the same cable works fine to a PC. What is needed?
answer: A crossover cable, because the older device lacks Auto-MDI-X. Modern equipment detects and corrects the pinout automatically, so this only appears with legacy hardware.
detail:
Straight-through connects unlike devices; crossover connects like devices. Auto-MDI-X made the distinction mostly historical.
How it works
  • Transmit must meet receive: Two switches both transmit on the same pins. Without a crossover, both send into each other's transmit pair and nothing is received.
  • Auto-MDI-X removed the problem: Gigabit Ethernet requires it, so any modern device negotiates the correct pinout regardless of cable. That is why the same cable works to a PC and not to the old switch.
  • Crossover is A on one end, B on the other: T568A and T568B differ only in the orange and green pairs. Using one standard at each end swaps transmit and receive.
  • Do not confuse it with a rollover cable: A rollover reverses all eight conductors and is used for console access with a serial adapter, not for Ethernet. It is a common distractor.
  • Uplink ports were the old workaround: Some legacy switches had a dedicated uplink port that was internally crossed, often sharing a physical port with a switch or button.
Where you see it
  • Connecting to legacy switches, hubs or industrial equipment
  • Bench testing two devices directly without a switch
exam: Know all three cable types and their uses: straight-through for unlike devices, crossover for like devices, rollover for console access. The rollover option is the trap in this question.

front: A remote switch is unreachable over the network after a configuration change. What access method still works and why?
answer: Out-of-band management — a console connection through a terminal server, or a dedicated management port on a separate network. In-band access depends on the network you just broke.
detail:
The entire value of out-of-band management is that it survives the failure you are trying to fix.
How it works
  • In-band management fails with the network: SSH to a switch's management IP travels over the production network. Break routing, VLANs or an ACL and you lose the only way to undo it.
  • Console is the true last resort: A serial console works regardless of network state, which is why the port exists. A console server or terminal server aggregates them so you can reach them remotely.
  • A separate management network is the middle ground: A dedicated management VLAN or physical network reduces exposure and often survives production faults, though it is still a network.
  • Cellular out-of-band for remote sites: A modem attached to a console server gives access when the site's WAN is down entirely — the difference between a phone call and a drive.
  • Prevent the lockout in the first place: A reload timer that reverts the configuration unless you confirm within a set window turns a lockout into a short outage.
Where you see it
  • Recovering a device after an ACL or routing mistake
  • Managing a branch site whose circuit is down
exam: Objective 3.5 covers this directly. Expect a scenario where an in-band change caused the lockout and the correct answer is out-of-band management, and know a console connection as the method that does not depend on the network.

front: Users at one site suddenly cannot log in to domain resources. Nothing was changed. What should you check that is not authentication?
answer: The clock. Kerberos rejects tickets when client and server clocks differ by more than the allowed skew, typically five minutes. An NTP failure produces a site-wide authentication outage.
detail:
This is the most commonly missed root cause on the exam because the symptom points at authentication and the fault is in time.
How it works
  • Kerberos timestamps every ticket: Timestamps prevent replay attacks. A ticket outside the tolerance is treated as invalid regardless of correct credentials.
  • Five minutes is the usual default: Small drift is tolerated. Once a local clock crosses the threshold, every ticket from that machine is refused at once.
  • An NTP source failure explains a whole site: If the site's time source dies or becomes unreachable, every device there drifts together and fails together — which looks exactly like a domain problem.
  • Certificates fail the same way: TLS validates a certificate against the current time. A machine with a badly wrong clock reports valid certificates as expired or not yet valid.
  • Check the time before rebuilding anything: Comparing the clock on a failing machine against a known-good source takes seconds and rules out or confirms the whole theory.
Where you see it
  • A branch site whose time source or WAN link failed
  • A virtual machine restored from a snapshot with a stale clock
exam: Expect the indirect framing: authentication or certificate failures with no configuration change. The answer is NTP and clock skew. This is why NTP appears in the operations objectives as a dependency for security.

front: One external website is unreachable for everyone in the office. Everything else on the internet works. Is this your problem?
answer: Almost certainly not. When one destination fails and all others work, the fault is at that destination, its DNS, or somewhere in the path beyond your control — but prove it before saying so.
detail:
Scope is the fastest diagnostic tool available. One destination failing is a very different problem from one client failing.
How it works
  • Test from outside your network: A phone on cellular, or a public looking-glass service, shows whether the site is down for everyone or only for you. That single test usually ends the investigation.
  • Separate DNS from reachability: Resolve the name against a public resolver. If the name does not resolve anywhere, it is their DNS. If it resolves and does not respond, it is their hosting or the path.
  • Traceroute to find where it stops: If the path dies inside your network or at your firewall, it is yours. If it dies several hops into a transit provider, it is not.
  • Consider your own filtering: Content filtering, a URL category block, a threat-intelligence feed or a stale firewall rule can block exactly one site. Check the proxy and firewall logs before concluding it is external.
  • Document and move on: If it is external, record the evidence and set expectations rather than continuing to troubleshoot something you cannot fix.
Where you see it
  • Users insisting the network is broken because one site is down
  • A site blocked by a content filter category nobody remembers enabling
exam: This tests establishing scope during the identify-the-problem step. The reasoning is that a fault affecting one destination and no others is unlikely to be your network — but the exam still expects you to verify with an external test and check your own filtering.

front: Laptops work in the office but cannot browse from home, though the VPN connects and internal applications work. What is a likely cause?
answer: A proxy configuration — a hardcoded proxy or a PAC file that is only reachable inside the office. The browser tries to reach a proxy that does not exist on the home network.
detail:
Proxy settings are silent when they work and baffling when they do not, because everything except web browsing behaves normally.
How it works
  • A hardcoded proxy fails off-network: The browser sends every request to an internal address that is unreachable from home, so browsing fails while non-proxied applications work.
  • A PAC file must be retrievable: Automatic configuration fetches a script from a URL. If that URL is internal and unreachable, the browser may fall back to direct or may fail entirely depending on configuration.
  • WPAD discovery has the same weakness: Automatic discovery relies on DNS or DHCP pointing at an internal server. Off-network it either fails or, worse, can be hijacked by an attacker.
  • The symptom is browsing-only: Ping, VPN and internal applications all work. Only HTTP and HTTPS through the browser fail, which localizes the fault immediately.
  • The fix: Use a PAC file that handles both locations, publish it somewhere reachable, or rely on the VPN's full tunnel so the proxy is always in reach.
Where you see it
  • Laptops that move between office and home
  • A new remote-work rollout where browsing breaks for everyone off-site
exam: The discriminator is browsing fails while everything else works. That pattern points at proxy configuration or DNS, not at connectivity — and the VPN connecting successfully rules out the tunnel.

front: A network printer works for a while, then becomes unreachable, then works again after someone restarts it. What is the likely cause?
answer: A DHCP address change. The printer's lease expired and it received a different address, while workstations and the print server still point at the old one.
detail:
Anything referenced by IP address rather than by name needs a stable address, and DHCP does not provide one by default.
How it works
  • Print queues often store an IP, not a name: A port configured with a raw IP address breaks the moment that address changes. The printer is fine; the pointer is stale.
  • Restarting it appears to fix it: The reboot triggers a fresh DHCP request. Sometimes it gets the old address back, which makes the problem look intermittent and random.
  • The correct fix is a reservation: A DHCP reservation ties the address to the printer's MAC. The device still uses DHCP, so options and settings stay centrally managed, but the address never changes.
  • Static addressing has a trap: Assigning a static address inside the DHCP scope without an exclusion eventually produces a duplicate IP when the server leases the same address to something else.
  • Name-based queues avoid the class of problem: Pointing the queue at a DNS name with dynamic DNS updates removes the dependency on the address entirely.
Where you see it
  • Printers, cameras, scanners and appliances on DHCP
  • Any device referenced by IP address in an application configuration
exam: The exam answer for a device that must keep the same address is a DHCP reservation, not a static assignment — and if static is used, an exclusion is required. Recognize the recurring, self-resolving pattern as a lease change.

front: New workstations fail to boot from the network in a newly created VLAN, though they get IP addresses fine. What is missing?
answer: The DHCP options that point at the boot server — option 66 (TFTP server name) and option 67 (boot filename) — or an IP helper for the PXE traffic.
detail:
PXE is DHCP plus TFTP. Getting an address is only the first half.
How it works
  • Addressing succeeded, so DHCP works: That eliminates the scope, the relay for DHCP itself and the Layer 2 path. The failure is specifically in the boot-server handoff.
  • Options 66 and 67 carry the pointer: 66 names the server holding the boot image; 67 names the file to request. Without them the client has an address and nowhere to boot from.
  • TFTP must be reachable across the subnet: The boot file transfers over UDP 69. A firewall or ACL between the new VLAN and the deployment server blocks it silently.
  • Some environments use a proxy DHCP service: Deployment products sometimes answer PXE requests separately from the main DHCP server, which needs its own reachability and sometimes its own relay entry.
  • Architecture matters: UEFI and legacy BIOS boot need different boot files. A scope serving the wrong one fails only for one class of machine.
Where you see it
  • Imaging new hardware in a newly built VLAN
  • A deployment server moved to a new address
exam: Objective 3.4 lists the DHCP options explicitly. Memorize 66 = TFTP server, 67 = boot filename, and recognize that PXE failures with working addressing point at those options or at TFTP reachability.

front: A segment is saturated with traffic, but spanning tree is stable and there is no loop. Captures show large volumes of multicast. What is happening?
answer: Multicast flooding. Without IGMP snooping, a switch treats multicast like broadcast and floods it out every port in the VLAN.
detail:
Not every storm is a loop. Multicast without snooping saturates a segment while spanning tree remains perfectly healthy.
How it works
  • Switches flood multicast by default: A multicast MAC address is not learned like a unicast address, so the switch has no port to send it to and floods it everywhere.
  • IGMP snooping fixes it: The switch listens to IGMP join and leave messages and forwards each multicast group only to ports that asked for it. That is the entire solution.
  • Common heavy sources: IP television and video distribution, market data feeds, imaging and deployment tools, and some storage and clustering protocols.
  • A querier is required: IGMP snooping needs an IGMP querier on the segment to keep group memberships current. Snooping enabled without a querier can drop multicast entirely after the memberships time out — the opposite failure.
  • Distinguish it from a loop: A loop shows MAC flapping and duplicated frames. Multicast flooding shows high volume of legitimate, non-duplicated multicast to a group address.
Where you see it
  • Video distribution or IPTV deployed onto a general-purpose VLAN
  • Imaging tools that use multicast to deploy many machines at once
exam: The exam contrast is broadcast storm (loop, fixed by STP) versus multicast flooding (fixed by IGMP snooping). If a scenario has high traffic with a healthy spanning tree and multicast in the capture, snooping is the answer.

front: A user reports an application is slow. How do you determine whether the problem is the network at all?
answer: Change one variable and re-test. Move the user to a wired port, try a different machine on the same port, and try the same machine on a different segment. Each swap eliminates a layer.
detail:
A large share of 'network' tickets are not network problems. Establishing that quickly is a skill, and doing it without blame is a bigger one.
How it works
  • Wired versus wireless: If the problem disappears on a wired port, it is wireless — signal, contention or roaming. If it persists, the radio is exonerated and you have halved the search.
  • Different user, same machine: Isolates a profile or credential problem from a machine problem.
  • Same user, different machine: Isolates the machine from the user and from their location.
  • Different segment or site: If it follows the user everywhere, the fault is likely the application or the server, not the local network.
  • Test the server side directly: Running the application from a machine adjacent to the server removes the network entirely. If it is still slow there, the answer is not yours.
Where you see it
  • Any vague slowness complaint with no measurable network fault
  • Disputes between network and application teams about ownership
exam: This is the practical expression of duplicate the problem and establish a theory. The exam rewards answers that isolate variables systematically over answers that begin changing configuration.

front: When is escalation the correct answer rather than a failure to solve the problem?
answer: When the fault is outside your authority or expertise, when the fix requires a change window or approval you do not hold, or when the problem is the vendor's or carrier's. Escalation is legitimate at step 3 (a theory you cannot test) and step 5 (a solution you cannot implement).
detail:
The methodology names escalation explicitly. Treating it as defeat leads to unauthorized changes and prolonged outages.
How it works
  • Step 3: cannot test the theory: You believe the carrier circuit is degraded but you cannot test their equipment. Escalating with evidence is the correct next action.
  • Step 5: cannot implement the fix: The fix requires a firewall change owned by security, or a reboot of a production database. Escalation routes it to whoever can authorize it.
  • Escalate with evidence, not with a symptom: 'The internet is slow' gets closed as no-fault-found. Traceroutes, throughput tests at the demarc and timestamps get worked.
  • Know the boundaries in advance: Which systems you own, which the vendor owns, where the demarcation point is, and what the SLA promises. That knowledge is what makes escalation fast rather than apologetic.
  • Escalating too early is also a failure: Handing over a problem without gathering basic information wastes the next person's time and is why some escalation paths are slow.
Where you see it
  • Carrier circuit faults
  • Changes that require a maintenance window or another team's approval
exam: Expect a scenario asking for the next step where the correct answer is to escalate. The exam treats escalation as a legitimate outcome of steps 3 and 5, never as an alternative to the first two steps.

front: The outage is fixed and users are working again. What is left to do, and what happens if you skip it?
answer: Verify full system functionality, implement preventive measures, and document findings, actions and outcomes. Skipping this is why the same outage recurs and why nobody knows what was changed.
detail:
The last two steps produce no visible benefit today and all of the benefit later, which is exactly why they get skipped.
How it works
  • Verification is broader than the symptom: The user can print again — but did the change break routing for another VLAN? Verification means testing the system, not the complaint.
  • Preventive measures belong to this step: If a user-added switch caused the outage, enabling BPDU Guard is part of closing the ticket, not a separate project.
  • Documentation is the organization's memory: The next person to see these symptoms should find the answer in minutes. Without a record, every recurrence is solved from scratch.
  • Update the diagrams and configuration baseline: A change made during an outage that never reaches the documentation becomes undocumented drift, and the baseline stops being trustworthy.
  • Lessons learned close the loop: Recording what the real cause was — including when the first theory was wrong — is what improves the next investigation.
Where you see it
  • Closing any incident ticket
  • Post-incident review after a significant outage
exam: The exam asks this as a next-step question after a fix is described. Documentation is always the final step, and verification always precedes it. Any answer that ends the process at 'implement the solution' is wrong.

front: A manager asks whether current network utilization is a problem. What do you need in order to answer, and what if you do not have it?
answer: A performance baseline — recorded normal utilization, latency, error rates and traffic mix. Without one, you cannot distinguish 'busy' from 'abnormal', and every performance question becomes an opinion.
detail:
A baseline converts performance troubleshooting from argument into measurement.
How it works
  • Normal is a measured value, not a feeling: Sixty percent utilization on an uplink may be entirely routine for a Tuesday afternoon or may be double last month. Only a baseline distinguishes them.
  • It must cover a representative period: A day tells you nothing about month-end. Capture across enough time to include the recurring peaks.
  • Baselines drive capacity planning: The trend line, not the current number, is what tells you when a circuit needs upgrading — before users complain rather than after.
  • Re-baseline after significant change: New applications, more staff or a topology change make the old baseline misleading. Documentation and baselines age.
  • It also detects security anomalies: Traffic that does not fit the established pattern — new destinations, odd ports, unusual volumes at night — is visible only against a known normal.
Where you see it
  • Answering 'is the network the problem' with evidence
  • Justifying a circuit upgrade in a budget conversation
exam: Objective 3.1 covers baselines and objective 5.4 covers performance. The concept the exam wants is that a baseline defines normal so deviation is measurable, and that it is prerequisite to meaningful monitoring and alerting.

front: An outage began at 09:00. Where do you look first, and why is this more reliable than starting with the symptoms?
answer: The change log. Most incidents are caused by a change, so correlating the outage start time against recent changes finds the cause faster than working the symptoms.
detail:
Hardware fails occasionally. Configurations get changed constantly. Play the odds.
How it works
  • Correlate by time: A change deployed at 08:55 and an outage at 09:00 is not a coincidence. Even a change that looks unrelated deserves examination before you start bisecting the network.
  • Changes include more than configuration: Patches, firmware upgrades, certificate renewals, expired licences, scheduled jobs, and a scheduled task that ran for the first time all count.
  • A missing change record is itself information: If the change log is empty and something clearly changed, someone made an undocumented change. That is worth knowing for reasons beyond this outage.
  • Rollback is a valid first response: If a recent change is the likely cause, reverting it restores service and gives you time to work out why. That is what the rollback plan is for.
  • This is step 1, not a shortcut: 'Determine if anything has changed' is part of identifying the problem. It is not skipping the methodology, it is executing it.
Where you see it
  • Any outage beginning shortly after a maintenance window
  • Recurring problems that started on a specific date nobody noted
exam: The exam builds many scenarios around a recent change and rewards the answer that investigates it. Determine if anything has changed is a named part of step 1, and it is the highest-yield question in troubleshooting.
